# Introduction

This second edition of Real World Physics is written to match the Leaving Certificate Physics specification introduced in September 2025. It covers all topics to the depth required and is designed to fully support both teachers and students throughout the course.
Each chapter includes:

- Clear teaching objectives, keywords, and references to the relevant strand(s) of the course
- Numbered sections with matching exercises to reinforce learning
- Worked examples to guide students through important concepts and calculations
- All student experiments required by the learning outcomes
- Definition boxes for key terms to support understanding
- Formula boxes to highlight essential equations
- Practice questions in the style and format of the published SEC exam papers
- Model answers to exam questions
- Chapter summaries and learning outcome checklists to encourage student reflection

Higher Level content is clearly shown in the margins next to the relevant text.

The textbook also explores the role of science in society.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-009.jpg?height=960&width=1234&top_left_y=758&top_left_x=1614)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-009.jpg?height=679&width=939&top_left_y=1671&top_left_x=1548)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-009.jpg?height=642&width=850&top_left_y=2376&top_left_x=1836)

Real-world applications of physics are highlighted across the chapters, along with contributions made by key scientists and the lasting impact of their work. All experiments have been carefully structured and are supported by step-by-step online videos.
Chapter 1, 'The Nature of Science', introduces students to the scientific method - how knowledge is developed through observation, forming and testing hypotheses, experimentation and analysis. It also covers core concepts such as measurement, types of error, SI units, scientific notation, and the importance of accuracy, precision and clear communication in science.
We sincerely hope this book supports both students and teachers in engaging with and appreciating the study of physics.
Finally, we would like to express our thanks to our families for their unwavering support and encouragement throughout the writing of this book. We wish to thank Seán Finn, Declan Kennedy, Ryan Gallagher, Stephen Murphy and David O'Connell for all their help during the filming of the experiment videos. We are also deeply grateful to the team at Folens - Dirk Folens, Conor Walker, Priscilla O'Connor, Rebecca Dobson and Michael Plunkett - and the outstanding teams at Orso Publishing, EMC Design and Dog Day Media for their expertise and dedication.

# 1 The Nature of Science

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand what scientific knowledge is
- To give students an understanding of how scientists work
- To give students an appreciation of the role of science in society
- To give students an appreciation of what a model in physics is
- To ensure students can identify sources of random and systematic error when taking measurements
- To enable students to evaluate data in terms of accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility
- To ensure students can express any derived unit in terms of base (fundamental) units
- To ensure students understand the concepts of significant figures and order of magnitude


## Keywords

- Scientific knowledge
- Peer review
- Repeatability
- Reproducibility
- Models in physics
- Physical quantity
- Magnitude
- Error in measurements
- Systematic error
- Random error
- Accuracy
- Precision
- Scientific notation
- Significant figures
- Base unit, fundamental unit
- Derived unit
- Dimensions of a physical quantity


### 1.1 The nature of scientific knowledge

As long as humans have lived on Earth, they have had to have some form of understanding of their surroundings. To survive they needed a mental picture of what was going on around them. They had to deal with and try to understand the dangers that they and their loved ones regularly faced. They had to have shelter and a supply of food. They had to know how to interact with other people - human beings are social animals. The better their picture of the real world around them, and the more truly it reflected it, the more control they had over their lives and their ability to survive. Knowing how to survive is and always has been of utmost importance to humankind.
Describing various aspects of the world around us, explaining them, trying to predict what would happen if we did such a thing, is something we all do all the time.
There are, however, many different ways of acquiring 'knowledge' that enable one to negotiate one's way in the world. Some are much more reliable and useful than others.
The kind of knowledge that we want to look at here is called scientific knowledge.

## How do we get scientific knowledge?

The following series of steps broadly outlines the way that scientific knowledge is acquired. It is also known as the scientific method. It is a step-by-step approach that helps us test ideas, answer questions and discover new scientific knowledge.

1. Ask a question. You choose an area or topic to be investigated. You identify a research question or questions that you want answers for.
2. Observation. You make observations of the phenomenon you are studying. You see it take place. You may record your observations. As you carry out this background research, you may make some definitions, make some measurements, carry out some exploratory experiments.
3. Form a hypothesis and make predictions. Here you try to come up with a theoretical explanation for your observations and measurements. You use your intuition, hunches, best guess as to what an explanation might look like. You may create a model of the phenomenon. This is an idealised representation of the system, that could involve words, diagrams, numbers, graphs and equations.

## Models in physics

- Models are simplified representations of the phenomena being studied, and they are based on certain assumptions.
- Models can be modified or improved as more information and data becomes available from experiment.
- Models can predict the behaviour of the system or phenomenon being studied.

You then make predictions that follow from your hypothesis or model.
4. Do experiments and collect data to see if your predictions are correct. In doing so, you are testing your hypothesis.
5. Analyse the data and draw conclusions. Here you carefully analyse and interpret the data. You draw conclusions from the data.
6. Communicate your results. Your conclusions here may support your initial hypothesis, in which case you might decide to share them with other scientists. You may also decide that your hypothesis needs modification and further questions need to be asked. You might find limits to your model's applicability. This could bring you back to stage one for a further iteration of the six steps.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-014.jpg?height=2230&width=2438&top_left_y=1598&top_left_x=191)
Figure 1.1 The main steps of the scientific method

## Important requirements for practising scientists

Clear communication. Scientists must be able to explain their ideas and discoveries clearly so that other scientists around the world can understand and make use of these ideas and discoveries.
International conventions. Scientists around the world adopt the same regulations (conventions) and systems when writing up reports of their work. For example, physicists agree to use the SI system of units when they make and record measurements. This makes it easy to compare measurements made in one country with those made in other countries.
Peer review. When scientists carry out research, their findings are usually published in scientific journals or books. However, before the research reports are published, the work is reviewed by other scientists who work in that field. These scientists are called peers since they work in similar areas to the authors of the research articles. The editor of the journal or book will ensure that these other scientists check if the research work has been carried out correctly and if the conclusions are valid. This ensures that articles with mistakes or false claims are not published.
Repeatability. If a scientist carries out an experiment and obtains a particular result, then if the method is reliable, the experiment should be repeatable. Repeatability means that an experiment can be done again by the same person using the same method and get the same results. Repeatability ensures that the results did not just happen by chance. If the experiment does not have repeatability, then the results cannot be considered reliable.
Reproducibility. If a scientist carries out an experiment and obtains a particular result, then if the method is reliable, the experiment should be reproducible. Reproducibility means that different scientists, in different laboratories, can get the same results by following the same procedure.

## Why is scientific knowledge important to us?

One of the main reasons that scientific knowledge is important to us is the phenomenal variety of invaluable uses it can be put to.
Scientific knowledge can be used to make our lives much safer, longer and less painful than the lives of many people 200 years ago. Think carefully about some of the major successes of modern medicine. Consider how different your life and the life of your loved ones might be if:

- Nobody had invented microscopes, and the germ theory of disease had never been discovered.
- Neither antibiotics nor anaesthetics existed.
- Medical imaging (such as X-rays, MRIs, CAT scans and ultrasound scans) did not exist.
- Radiation therapy had never been invented.

Scientific knowledge is at the heart of all modern power supplies, transport and communication systems. However, there are ethical and sustainability issues surrounding many applications of scientific knowledge. As a student of science and physics, you need to be aware of many of these important and sometimes controversial issues. You will meet such issues throughout the course and will need to be able to evaluate the impact science and technology has on society.
Most of the scientific ideas you will meet in this course are accepted because there is very good evidence for them. In many places you will evaluate this evidence and do experiments to verify the correctness of it. As a student of Leaving Certificate Physics, you need to learn how to obtain and evaluate data that you collect yourself in the lab.

### 1.2 Measurement and units

## Physical quantities

Physics is the branch of science that studies matter, energy and the relationship between them. Experiments in physics nearly always involve making measurements. Many of the investigations that you will do in the laboratory will involve measurement. This brings us to the idea of a physical quantity. It is defined as follows:

Any property of matter that can be measured is called a physical quantity (or simply a quantity).

Examples of quantities (that you will meet):

| time | acceleration | energy | potential difference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| length (distance) | mass | power | electric current |
| area | density | gravitational field strength | resistance |
| volume | momentum | temperature | resistivity |
| displacement | force | frequency | magnetic flux |
| speed | pressure | electric charge | magnetic flux density |
| velocity | work | electric field strength | activity of a radioactive source |

## What is measuring?

When you measure a quantity, you usually compare it with a standard amount of the same quantity. This standard amount is called a unit.

For example:
a) A measurement finds that the length of a piece of wire is 12 metres. This means that this piece of wire is 12 times longer than the metre. The metre is the unit of length.
b) A measurement finds that the size of an electric current in a wire is 2 amperes. This means that the current in this wire is twice as large as the ampere. The ampere is the unit of electric current.
The result of a measurement is usually a number multiplied by a unit. This (the number and unit) is called the magnitude (or size) of the quantity being measured.

## SI units

In 1960 scientists agreed to use a particular system of units which they called the International System of Units. Any unit of this system is called an SI unit. SI units will be used throughout your physics course. Some examples of quantities and their SI units are shown in Table 1.1. Later in this chapter, SI units will be discussed further.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-016.jpg?height=1059&width=1157&top_left_y=2168&top_left_x=1464)
Figure 1.4

| Quantity | time | displacement | speed | force | resistance | frequency |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Sl unit | second | metre | metre per second | newton | ohm | hertz |

### 1.3 Error in measurements

Any time you make a numerical measurement in physics, the result you get will almost always differ from the correct value. Said another way, 'Every measurement has some error in it.'
Errors can occur for a number of reasons. For example there may be limitations in:
a) The measuring instruments used
b) The person using them
c) The overall design of the experiment

Errors that occur can broadly be put into two categories. These are called systematic errors and random errors.

## Systematic error

A systematic error is an error that causes a measured value to be always greater than the true value or always less than the true value. The amount by which the measured value differs from the true value may always be the same or may vary.

## 1. Systematic errors due to instrumentation

Systematic error can occur when the measuring equipment being used always makes an error in the same way. For example:
a) A weighing scale may not be correctly calibrated, say reading 0.05 g with nothing on it. It will then always add 0.05 g to every measurement made with it (Figure 1.5).
b) An analogue ammeter may point to slightly below zero when there is no current. If it is then used to read a value of an electric current, it will consistently give a lower value than the true value.

## 2. Systematic errors caused by a person not using the correct procedure

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-017.jpg?height=857&width=1202&top_left_y=1347&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 1.5 An incorrectly calibrated balance

For example, parallax error when using a metre stick would be a systematic error if, instead of viewing the metre stick perpendicularly, someone consistently reads it from the same incorrect angle. This means that the measured length will always be different from the true length by the same amount (Figure 1.6).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-017.jpg?height=730&width=2426&top_left_y=2669&top_left_x=322)
Figure 1.6 Observer A reads the correct value ( 1.5 cm ), but Observer B reads 1.8 cm due to viewing at an incorrect angle. Using the metre stick on edge, when possible, considerably reduces the possibility of parallax error.

## 3. Systematic errors due to limitations in the design of an experiment

For example, when measuring specific heat capacity of a liquid using a heating coil, some heat energy may escape to the surroundings. The rise in temperature of the liquid will consequently not be as large as it should be, always giving a value of the specific heat capacity that is too big. Here the size of the systematic error will vary with repeated measurements (see page 7).

## Summary: systematic errors

- Systematic errors shift all measurements consistently in one direction. In other words, systematic errors cause all measurements to be consistently too high or too low compared to the true value.
- Systematic errors cannot be reduced or eliminated by repeated trials - they can only be corrected by undertaking measures such as fixing calibration of instruments or correcting poor techniques.
- Systematic errors reduce accuracy, as all values are shifted in one direction away from the correct value (see page 7).
- Systematic errors do not necessarily affect precision, as all the incorrect results could still be clustered close together (see page 7).

Systematic errors can be minimised by:

- Ensuring instruments are calibrated correctly before use
- Following the correct procedure when using a particular measuring instrument
- Being aware of limitations in the design of an experiment, and taking measures to counteract or allow for them


## Random error

If you repeat the same measurement a number of times, you will very often get slightly different answers. Some values will be greater than the true value and some will be less. The errors occurring here are called random errors. Random errors can occur for a number of different reasons.

## 1. Random errors due to instrumentation

Some measuring instruments have slight random variations in their outputs each time they are used (sometimes due to slight changes in environmental conditions between readings). For example:
a) Air currents affecting the reading of an electronic balance can give rise to random errors each time the balance is used during the experiment.
b) Fluctuations in room temperature could affect how an instrument behaves.

## 2. Random errors caused by a person making the measurement

For example:
a) The experimenter uses or reads the instrument slightly differently each time.
b) Human reaction time could cause variations in starting and stopping stopwatches when measuring times.

Note: Parallax error when using a metre stick could be considered as a random error if, instead of viewing the metre stick perpendicularly, the experimenter reads it at a different incorrect angle each time.

## Summary: random errors

- Random errors are unpredictable variations in the value of a repeated measurement that vary in both directions around the true value. Some measurements will be too high and others too low compared to the true value.
- Random errors are unpredictable and inconsistent.
- Random errors can be reduced by repeating measurements and averaging results.
- Random errors may not necessarily affect accuracy due to repeated measurements being taken and averaging of results (see page 7).
- Random errors affect precision because random errors give rise to results that are scattered from each other rather than being clustered close together (see page 7).

Random errors can be minimised in the following ways:

- Taking several measurements and getting an average causes the errors to cancel each other. When doing this, any extreme values may be omitted, as they could have an undue influence on the average.
- Depending on what is being measured, a graph can also be used to reduce random error. You will see this on page 38.
- Following the correct procedure when using a particular measuring instrument can reduce random error.
In the experiments and investigations that involve taking measurements that you will carry out, you need to be able to identify potential sources of random and systematic error, and where possible, you must adjust your procedure to minimise each of them.


## Worked Example 1

A student measured the focal length of a convex lens four times. The values obtained were $16.1 \mathrm{~cm}, 15.9 \mathrm{~cm}, 15.9 \mathrm{~cm}$ and 16.1 cm . The actual value of the focal length is 16.0 cm .
a) Is there evidence of systematic error in these readings? Justify your answer.
b) Is there evidence of random error in these readings? Justify your answer.

## Solution

a) No, some of the values obtained were greater than the actual value and some were less.
b) There is some random error, since the values vary around the true value. However, the amount of random error is small.

## Accuracy and precision

Accuracy indicates how close a measurement is to the correct value. The nearer it is, the more accurate the measurement. The correct value is often referred to as the 'true' or 'actual' value.
For example, if the true length of an object is 57.84 cm and you measure it to be 57.85 cm , then your measurement is very accurate.
Precision indicates how close a set of repeated measurements are to each other.
For example, suppose you measure the mass of an object three times on a balance and get the results 66.23 g .66 .22 g and 66.24 g . These results are very close

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-019.jpg?height=583&width=1193&top_left_y=1875&top_left_x=1549)
Figure 1.7 A GPS satellite has to be able to measure time accurately to within an accuracy of at least 40 nanoseconds or less to function properly. $40 \mathrm{~ns}=0.000000040 \mathrm{~s}$.

to each other, so the balance gives precise readings.

- If the balance has been calibrated correctly and used correctly, these readings are also accurate.
- If the balance was not calibrated correctly, and the actual mass of the object was 65.00 g , then the readings are not accurate. They are, however, still precise.
Scientists always try to obtain results that are both accurate and precise. In any investigation or experiment that you do, you must be able to identify any potential sources of random and systematic error.


## Accuracy and precision

- Precision refers to how close repeated measurements are to each other.
- Precise measurements are clustered closely together.
- Accuracy refers to how close a measured value is to the true value of the quantity being measured.
- Accurate measurements are clustered around the correct value.


## Worked Example 2

The correct volume of a solution is $23.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. A student measured the volume of this solution three times and recorded the volumes as $23.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}, 23.6 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ and $23.7 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Are these results accurate, precise or both?

## Solution

The results are not accurate, as they are significantly different from the correct volume.
The results are precise, as they are close to each other.

## Percentage error

Suppose we have an object whose length has been measured with sophisticated equipment and is known to be 95.25 cm . Let's call 95.25 cm the true value of the length.

Suppose you measure the length of the object with a metre stick and estimate it to be 95.22 cm .
What is the error in your measurement?

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { The error } & =\text { the true value - the estimate } \\
& =95.25-95.22 \\
& =0.03 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

What is the percentage error in a measurement? By definition: Percentage error $=\frac{\text { error }}{\text { true value }}(100)$

Error = true value - estimate

$$
\text { Percentage error }=\frac{\text { error }}{\text { true value }}(100)
$$

So, the percentage error in your measurement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Percentage error } & =\frac{0.03}{95.25}(100) \\
& =0.03 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

The percentage error gives us a good indication of the accuracy of our measurement. This is a small percentage error, so the measurement is accurate.

## Calculating percentage error when you don't know the true value of the quantity being measured

Suppose you measure the length of an object with a metre stick and your answer is 16.7 cm .
What is the likely error in your measurement?
Generally speaking, we take the estimated error with an instrument like this to be one half the smallest division of the scale on the stick, which is 0.5 mm .
This means that the length was measured to the nearest tenth of a cm and usually that the exact value of the length lies between 16.65 and 16.75 cm , i.e. $16.7 \pm 0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$.

We can make an estimate of the likely percentage error using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Percentage error } & =\frac{\text { estimated error }}{\text { measured value }}(100) \\
& =\frac{0.5}{16.7}(100) \\
& =3 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

When you don't know the true value: Percentage error $=\frac{\text { estimated error }}{\text { measured value }}(100)$

## Worked Example 3

The diameter of a wire is being measured. A student reads the value of 0.4 mm when using a vernier calipers, with 0.1 mm graduations.
a) What is the likely error in the measurement?
b) Calculate the percentage error in the measurement.

## Solution

a) The likely error with an instrument like this is taken to be one half the smallest division of its scale, which is 0.05 mm .
b) Since we don't know the true value of the length, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Percentage error } & =\frac{\text { estimated error }}{\text { measured value }}(100) \\
& =\frac{0.50}{0.4}(100) \\
& =12.5 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

### 1.4 Basic units and derived units

## Basic (base or fundamental) units

An independent unit could have been chosen for the measurement of each quantity. Different units would then not be related to each other in an easy way. To simplify matters, seven quantities, called base quantities, have been chosen and the unit given to each is called a base unit, a basic unit or a fundamental unit. These seven base units are precisely defined. We need not worry about the exact definitions. Table 1.2 shows the name and symbol of the five basic quantities and basic units on our course.

| Basic quantity | Symbol | Name of base SI unit | Symbol |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| length | $l$ | metre | m |
| time | $t$ | second | s |
| mass | $m$ | kilogram | kg |
| electric current | I | ampere | A |
| temperature | $T$ | kelvin | K |

Table 1.2

## Derived units

The unit of every other quantity is called a derived unit because it can be expressed as the product or quotient of one or more of the basic units. Table 1.3 shows some examples of quantities and their derived units.

The unit of any quantity can be written as a product or quotient of one or more base units.

| Physical quantity | Symbol | Name of Sl unit | Symbol |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| area | A | square metre | $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ |
| volume | V | cubic metre | $\mathrm{m}^{3}$ |
| speed | $v$ or $u$ | metre per second | $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ or $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ |
| density | $\rho$ | kilogram per cubic metre | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ or $\mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ |

Table 1.3

Recall from your maths that $\frac{1}{x}$ is written as $x^{-1}$. So, $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{m}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{~s}}\right)=\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$

## Finding the derived unit of a quantity

## Worked Example 4

Find the SI unit of volume.

## Solution

Since: volume $=$ length × breadth × height
SI unit of volume
= (unit of length)(unit of breadth)(unit of height)
$=(\mathrm{m})(\mathrm{m})(\mathrm{m})$
$=\mathrm{m}^{3}=$ the cubic metre

## Worked Example 5

Find the SI unit of speed.
Solution
speed $=\frac{\text { distance }}{\text { time }}$
So, the SI unit of speed $=\frac{\text { unit of distance }}{\text { unit of time }}$
$=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$
$=\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$
It is called the metre per second.

## Worked Example 6

Find the SI unit of density.

## Solution

density = $\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { volume }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { So, the SI unit of density } & =\frac{\text { unit of mass }}{\text { unit of volume }} \\
& =\frac{\text { kilogram }}{\text { cubic metre }} \\
& =\text { kilogram per cubic metre } \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{~m}^{3}} \\
& =\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes a unit is given the name of a scientist who made some important discovery in the area of science where that unit often occurs. When this happens, the unit symbol is written with a capital letter, but the name of the unit is not. Table 1.4 shows some units of this kind that you will meet.

| Quantity | Sl unit | Symbol | Unit in terms of base units |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| force $(F)$ | newton | N | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-2}$ |
| pressure ( $p$ ) | pascal | Pa | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ |
| work ( $W$ ) | joule | J | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ |
| energy ( $E$ ) | joule | J | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ |
| power ( $P$ ) | watt | W | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-3}$ |
| frequency ( $f$ ) | hertz | Hz | $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ |
| magnetic flux density ( $B$ ) | tesla | T | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{s}^{-2} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}$ |
| magnetic flux $(\Phi)$ | weber | Wb | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}$ |
| activity of a radioactive source $(A)$ | becquerel | Bq | $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ |

Table 1.4

## Using SI units

- When solving numerical problems in physics, you should use only SI units. In any problem you do, make sure that the value of each quantity is expressed in the correct SI unit before you start.
- When doing calculations, it is not necessary to write down units at each step of the argument. However, when a result is arrived at, it must be written with the correct unit (or unit symbol) after it. Marks will definitely be lost in an exam if you do not!
- When writing down the magnitude of a quantity with the appropriate unit symbol, a space is left between the number and the unit symbol. For example, a length of 5 metres is written as 5 m , not 5 m .
- When writing a unit in terms of basic units, a space is left between the symbol of each basic unit. For example, the unit of density is abbreviated $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, not $\mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$, and the unit of speed is abbreviated $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$, not $\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-023.jpg?height=1190&width=1202&top_left_y=2571&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 1.10

## Multiples and fractions of the standard units

Sometimes the standard SI units are too large or too small to be used easily. We therefore use the multiples or submultiples of SI units shown in Table 1.5. Note that:

- The name of a unit has the prefix written before it, e.g. 10 kilometres, 5 millinewtons.
- There is no space between the prefix and the symbol for the unit, e.g. 60 millimetres is written as 60 mm ; 20 kilowatts is written as 20 kW .
- Mainly multiples of 10 to the power of 3 are used.
- A more comprehensive table similar to Table 1.5 can be found in the Formulae and Tables (F\&T), page 45.

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $10^{12}$ | tera | T |
| $10^{9}$ | giga | G |
| $10^{6}$ | mega | M |
| $10^{3}$ | kilo | k |

### 1.5 Scientific notation

You probably studied scientific notation in Junior Cycle mathematics. Here is a very brief review. If a number is written in the form $a \times 10^{n}$, where $a$ is a number between 1 and $10(1 \leqslant a<10)$ and $n$ is an integer $(n \in Z)$, that number is said to be written in scientific notation.
For example:
a) The mass of the Sun is 1989000000000000000000000000000 kg . This is much more conveniently written in scientific notation as $1.989 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{~kg}$
b) The diameter of a proton is about 0.000000000000001 m , which is more conveniently written in scientific notation as $1 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}$, or using prefixes discussed earlier: 1 femtometre $=1 \mathrm{fm}$

## Worked Example 8

Write the following numbers in scientific notation:
a) 3000
b) 43
c) 5984.4
d) 1000000
e) 0.1
f) 0.00001
g) 0.0000001234
h) 0.0000000000000000001602

## Solution

a) $3 \times 10^{3}$
b) $4.3 \times 10^{1}$
c) $5.9844 \times 10^{3}$
d) $1 \times 10^{6}$
e) $1 \times 10^{-1}$
f) $1 \times 10^{-5}$
g) $1.234 \times 10^{-7}$
h) $1.602 \times 10^{-19}$

If a number is written in scientific notation, the power of 10 is called its order of magnitude. The order of magnitude can be any integer.
For example: $\quad 2.3 \times 10^{5}$ has an order of magnitude of 5
$9.23 \times 10^{-7}$ has an order of magnitude of -7

## Making order of magnitude estimates

## Worked Example 9

Make an order of magnitude estimate of the value of $4132 \times 234600$.

## Solution

Write each number in scientific notation:
$4132=4.132 \times 10^{3}$ and $234600=2.346 \times 10^{5}$
The order of magnitude of 4132 is 3 and the order of magnitude of 234600 is 5
Therefore, the order of magnitude of the product is $3+5=8$
The order of magnitude estimate of the value is $10^{8}$

A more accurate estimate can be made by using more information.

## Worked Example 10

Estimate the value of $4132 \times 234600$.

## Solution

Step 1: Write each number in scientific notation:
$4132=4.132 \times 10^{3}$ and $234600=2.346 \times 10^{5}$
Step 2: Round the non-power of 10 part in each to a whole number:
$4 \times 10^{3}$ and $2 \times 10^{5}$
Step 3: Do the multiplication in your head, giving $8 \times 10^{8}$
Step 4: Compare with the correct value (use your calculator): $9.69 \times 10^{8}$

## Significant figures

You are probably familiar with rounding a number correct to a specified number of decimal places. Here we learn how to round a number to a specified number of significant figures.
In the number 39 478.445, the digit 3 is the most significant figure. It is the digit that contributes most to the value of the number. The digit 9 is the next most significant figure, and so on. In any number, the first non-zero digit (coming from the left) is the first significant figure. Leading zeros are not significant, but zeros in between two other significant figures are significant.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-026.jpg?height=682&width=1587&top_left_y=2747&top_left_x=266)

Leading zeros are not significant

| Number | Number rounded to <br> $\mathbf{1}$ significant figure | Number rounded to <br> $\mathbf{2}$ significant figures | Number rounded to <br> $\mathbf{3}$ significant figures |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 9548 | 10000 | 9500 | 9550 |
| 0.01946 | 0.02 | 0.019 | 0.0195 |

## Worked Example 11

Write the following numbers correct to four significant figures:
a) 39478.445
b) 0.00965734

## Solution

a) The fifth significant figure in 39478.445 is 8
$8 \geqslant 5$, therefore the seven must be increased by 1
The answer is therefore 39480.
b) The fifth significant figure in 0.00965734 is 3
$3 \leqslant 5$, therefore the fourth significant figure remains at 7
The answer is therefore 0.009657

## Numbers that are the result of measurements

- Suppose that the length of an object is measured and is found to be 16.7 cm .
- This means that the length was measured to the nearest tenth of a cm and usually that the exact value of the length lies between 16.65 and 16.75 cm .
- When we take measurements in the laboratory, the last figure is really an estimated figure, and we treat it as a significant figure.
- This measurement 16.7 cm therefore has three significant figures, namely 1,6 and 7
- Suppose the same length was measured with a more accurate instrument and the result was 16.72 cm . This means that the length was measured to the nearest hundredth of a cm and that the exact value of the length lies between 16.715 and 16.725 cm .
- This measurement has four significant figures, namely 1, 6, 7 and 2
- Suppose the measured mass of an object is 17 grams. This is the same as a mass of 0.017 kg . Has the number of significant figures in the measurement increased? No. As we saw above, any zeros occurring to the left of the first non-zero digit in a number are not significant figures.
- Suppose the measured mass of an object is 23 kg . This is the same as a mass of 23000 grams. Are the zeroes to the right significant? As it stands, they are not.
- However, suppose the measured mass of an object is 23.0 kg . The zero here is significant because it was measured.
- This is the same as a mass of 23000 grams. Are the zeroes to the right in this number significant? The first is, but the other two are not.
We can show these clearly by using scientific notation. The part of the number that is not the $10^{n}$ shows the number of significant figures in the measurement.
For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
23 \mathrm{~kg} & =23000 \text { grams }=2.3 \times 10^{4} \text { grams } \\
23.0 \mathrm{~kg} & =23000 \text { grams }=2.30 \times 10^{4} \text { grams }
\end{aligned}
$$

If the numbers you need to do calculations with are measurements, the following rules hold.
Rule 1: When adding or subtracting numbers (measurements) with different numbers of significant figures, the least significant figure in the answer must have the same position relative to the decimal point as the least significant figure in the number whose least significant figure was furthest to the left. This sounds difficult, but it is easy. Study Worked Examples 12 and 13 (page 16).

## Worked Example 12

Suppose the measured lengths of two straight metal bars are 16.4 m and 2.25 m . What is their combined length?

## Solution

$16.4+2.25=18.65$

- 4 is the least significant figure in 16.4 , and 5 is the least significant figure in 2.25
- 4 is the least significant figure that is farthest to the left (relative to the decimal point). Therefore, the final answer must be rounded to this position. So 18.65 is rounded to 18.7
Answer = 18.7 m


## Worked Example 13

Suppose the measured volumes of two spheres are $608 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ and $0.97 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$. What is their combined volume?

## Solution

$608+0.97=608.77$

- 8 is the least significant figure in 608 , and 7 is the least significant figure in 0.97
- 8 is the least significant figure that is farthest to the left (relative to the decimal point). Therefore, the final answer must be rounded to this position. So 608.77 becomes 609
Answer $=609 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$

Rule 2: When multiplying or dividing numbers (which are measurements) with different numbers of significant figures, the answer must be rounded off to the number of significant figures equal to that of the number with the least number of significant figures.
For example:
a) $\begin{aligned} 5.62 \times 0.40 & =2.248 \\ & =2.2\end{aligned}$
b) $1.57 \times 0.2=0.314$
$=0.3$
c) $67.6 \times 4.9=331.24$
$=330$

### 1.6 Unit analysis

You saw on page 10 that the five fundamental or base quantities (used in this course) are length, time, mass, electric current and temperature, and that the corresponding base quantities are the metre, the second, the kilogram, the ampere and the kelvin. You also saw that the unit of any quantity can be expressed in terms of the basic quantities in a unique way. You will need to be able to express the unit of any quantity you meet, as you proceed through the course, in base units. Study the following examples.

## Worked Example 14

When a force $F$ acts on a body of mass $m$ and causes that body to get an acceleration $a$, you will see in Chapter 8 that: Force $=$ mass × acceleration, i.e. $F=m a$. If the unit of acceleration is the $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-2}$, find the SI unit of force in terms of basic units.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F=m a \Rightarrow \text { unit of force } & =(\text { unit of mass)(unit of acceleration) } \\
& =\left(\mathrm{kg}^{\circ}\right)\left(\mathrm{m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right) \\
& =\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

This unit is usually called the newton $(\mathrm{N})$ in honour of the great scientist and mathematician Isaac Newton.

## Worked Example 15

You will see on page 181 that when a force $F$ moves through a distance $s$ in the same direction as the force, the work $W$ done is given by the formula:
Work = force × distance, i.e. $W=F s$. Find:
a) The SI unit of work in terms of the newton
b) The SI unit of work in terms of basic units

## Solution

a) Work $=$ force × distance $\Rightarrow$ SI unit of work $=$ (unit of force)(unit of distance)
= newton metre
This unit is usually called the joule $(J)$ in honour of the scientist James Joule.
Thus, $1 \mathrm{~J}=1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}$
b) From Worked Example 14: $1 \mathrm{~N}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \text { Unit of work } & =\mathrm{N} \mathrm{~m} \\
& =\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right)(\mathrm{m}) \\
& =\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the unit of work, the joule, in base units, is $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$.

It is true, and should seem reasonable to you, that you can only add (or subtract) quantities that have the same units.
For example, you would never add 5 kilometres to 2 seconds or subtract 3 days from $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
However, quantities with different units, as you know, can be multiplied and divided.
For example, you may already know that: speed $=\frac{\text { distance travelled }}{\text { time taken }}$

$$
\text { or voltage }=\text { current } \text { × } \text { resistance }
$$

It follows from this that in any equation in physics, where the variables represent quantities, all terms must have the same units.

Note: In a mathematical equation, a 'term' is numbers or variables multiplied or divided, for example:

$$
\frac{3 x^{2} y}{4 t} \text { or } 4 k \text { or } \frac{1}{x}
$$

In a mathematical expression, terms are separated by + or - .

## Worked Example 16

In the equation $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}, s$ is distance, $u$ is velocity, $t$ is time and $a$ is acceleration.
Show that the units of each term in the equation are the same, and hence that the units of both sides of the equation are the same.

## Solution

Unit of distance $s$ is the metre, $m$
Units of velocity × time, $u t$, are $\left(\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\right)(\mathrm{s})=\mathrm{m}$
Units of $\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ are $\left(\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-2}\right)\left(\mathrm{s}^{2}\right)=\mathrm{m}$
Units of LHS $=m$ and units of RHS $=m$

## Worked Example 17

A student claims that if an object is projected upwards from the surface of a planet with a velocity $v$, it will escape from the planet's gravity (and the planet) if its velocity is greater than the value given by the formula:

$$
v=\frac{M}{r}
$$

where $M$ is the mass of the planet and $r$ is its radius. Could this formula be correct?

## Solution

To see if this formula is plausible, we do a unit analysis on the formula. In other words, we check if the units of each side of the formula are the same, by expressing them in base units.

LHS: units of $v=\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$

$$
\text { RHS: units of } \frac{M}{r}=\frac{\text { unit of mass }}{\text { unit of distance }}=\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{~m}}=\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}
$$

The units on both sides are in base units and cannot be simplified any further. The units are not the same. It follows that this formula could not possibly be correct.
Note that even if the units were the same on both sides, it does not mean the formula is correct. All we can say for sure is that if the formula is correct the units on both sides must be the same.

Note: A few quantities that you will meet in this course have no SI unit. We say that they are dimensionless. This happens in some cases if the defining equation of a quantity is the ratio of two quantities with the same unit. Some examples are: refractive index (Chapter 3), atomic number (Chapter 29) and number of turns (Chapter 27). pH in chemistry is another example.

## Summary What I should know

- A physical quantity is any property of matter that can be measured.
- A systematic error is an error that causes a measured value to be always greater than the true value or always less than the true value.
- Random errors are unpredictable variations in the value of a repeated measurement that vary in both directions around the true value. Some measurements will be too high and others too low compared to the true value.
- Accuracy indicates how close a measurement is to the correct value. Accurate measurements are clustered around the correct value.
- Precision indicates how close a set of repeated measurements are to each other. Precise measurements are clustered closely together.
- The SI unit of any quantity can be written as a product or quotient of one or more base units.
- The order of magnitude of a number is the power of 10 , when the number is written in scientific notation. The order of magnitude can be any integer.
- Error = the true value - the estimate
- Percentage error $=\frac{\text { error }}{\text { true value }}(100)$
- Percentage error $=\frac{\text { estimated error }}{\text { measured value }}(100)$

## Keywords

### 2.1 Understanding the nature of light

## Light is a form of energy

You have studied the principle of conservation of energy at Junior Cycle. There, you learned that energy in one form, such as electrical energy, can be converted into other forms, such as kinetic energy; in the same way, other forms of energy (including kinetic energy) can be converted into electrical energy. This is also the case for light, because light is a form of energy.
Examples in which light is converted to and from other forms of energy include:

- Electrical energy is converted to light energy in an LED bulb, or in the screen of a phone (Figure 2.1), television or laptop.
- Chemical energy is converted to light energy in a fire.
- Light hitting a photocell is converted to electrical energy. Solar panels are made from an array of photocells, allowing them to convert large amounts of light energy to electrical energy.
- When light from the Sun or from a lamp shines on a device called a Crookes radiometer (Figure 2.2), the vanes (sails) rotate. It therefore converts light energy to kinetic energy.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-032.jpg?height=961&width=737&top_left_y=2207&top_left_x=1884)
Figure 2.2 A Crookes radiometer converts light energy into kinetic energy.

Figure 2.1 The screen of your smartphone converts electrical energy into light energy.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-032.jpg?height=877&width=440&top_left_y=2259&top_left_x=1276)

## The speed of light

The speed of light is about $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (or $300000 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ). This value is on page 47 of the Formulae and Tables book.
Light is a form of energy that travels away from the source producing it at a speed of about $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

The Italian scientist Galileo Galilei attempted to measure the speed of light around 1638 AD. He was unsuccessful and concluded that either it was extremely large or light travelled from one place to another instantaneously. You can read more about Galileo in Chapter 8.
In 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer estimated it to be $2.3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. In other words, the speed of light was not infinite but it was indeed very large.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

The Sun is $1.5 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~m}$ from the Earth. How long does it take light to travel from the Sun to the Earth?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { time taken } & =\frac{\text { distance }}{\text { speed }} \\
& =\frac{1.5 \times 10^{11}}{3 \times 10^{8}} \\
& =500 \mathrm{~s} \\
& =8.33 \text { minutes }
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, light reaching the Earth now left the Sun 8.33 minutes ago.

## Ole Romer

Ole Christensen
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-033.jpg?height=480&width=385&top_left_y=481&top_left_x=2360)
Rømer (1644-1710) was a Danish astronomer. He was the first to show that light travels at a finite speed, which he estimated to be $2.3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. He was also the first to use the melting point of ice and the boiling point of water as two fixed points used to make a temperature scale on a thermometer.

## Light usually travels in straight lines

Light usually travels in straight lines. You can see this clearly with lasers, or when a car headlamp or a flashlight shines through mist so that the beams become visible (Figure 2.3).

## Demonstration Experiment 2.1

To show that light travels in straight lines

## Equipment

Lightbulb with holder, power supply, three sheets of cardboard, some thread.

## Method

1. Set up a bulb and three sheets of cardboard as shown in Figure 2.4. Position the cards so they are not perfectly aligned.
2. Try to look through all three holes at once and see the lightbulb if you can.
3. Pass a piece of thread through the holes and then pull it taut, so the sheets of cardboard align.
4. You should find that you can now see the lightbulb. This shows that light travels in straight lines.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-033.jpg?height=554&width=1247&top_left_y=3291&top_left_x=371)

Figure 2.3 Dust and moisture in the air reveal the path of the light.

## Light rays and light beams

A light ray is a straight line showing the direction in which light is travelling.
You will use a narrow beam of light produced with a ray box or with a laser to represent a light ray in many of your investigations with light.

### 2.2 Vision and light

## Light is necessary for vision

If all the lights and electronic devices were switched off and all the doors and windows blocked, nobody would be able to read this text.
For an object to be seen, light from that object must enter somebody's eye.
An object that gives out its own light is called a luminous object. The Sun, stars, a fire and an operating LED bulb are examples of luminous objects.
Most objects do not give out their own light. Such objects are said to be non-luminous. Nonluminous objects can only be seen when light from some other source bounces off the object and goes into somebody's eye. The Moon, the planets and most everyday objects are non-luminous. Since light is necessary for sight, it is sometimes called visible light. Light itself, however, cannot be seen - only the object or source from which the light comes can be seen.

## How the brain uses light to perceive the position and size of objects

Figure 2.6 shows some of the light leaving a point $A$ at the top and a point $B$ at the bottom of a luminous object. A small diverging beam of light from $A$ enters the eye of the observer. The brain interprets light entering the eye as having travelled in straight line paths from each point on the object. The brain of the observer therefore sees $A$ at the point from which the light from $A$ diverges, and $B$ at the point from which the light from $B$ diverges. So the observer sees $A$ and $B$ in different positions, and the brain uses the angle between light from the top of the object and from the bottom of the object to determine the size the object appears.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-034.jpg?height=503&width=775&top_left_y=3235&top_left_x=1875)
Figure 2.6 Some of the light leaving a point $A$ at the top and a point $B$ at the bottom of a luminous object. A small diverging beam of light from $A$ enters the eye of the observer.

### 2.3 Types of reflection

When light strikes an object, some of the light is absorbed into the object and some always bounces back from the object. The bouncing of light from an object is called reflection.

Reflection of light is the bouncing of light from an object.
The way in which light bounces off an object depends on:

1. The material that the object is made from
2. The surface of the object (how rough or smooth it is)

## Diffuse reflection

For many objects, reflected light is scattered in all directions from the surface (Figure 2.7). Reflection like this is called diffuse reflection.
Every point on a diffusely reflecting object has light scattered from it in all directions. Most of the objects in the room you are in now are reflecting light diffusely. This is why they can be seen from all directions.
Diffuse reflection occurs when light strikes a rough or matte surface. It can also occur for certain polished surfaces. For example, you can polish marble or a painted car door extremely smooth, but it will still diffusely reflect light to a significant extent.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-035.jpg?height=577&width=945&top_left_y=996&top_left_x=1797)
Figure 2.7 Diffuse reflection: each person can see the object.

Diffuse reflection occurs when the reflected light from an object is scattered in all directions from the surface of the object.

## Regular reflection

Suppose you shine a ray of light onto a flat, highly polished metal surface. A surface like this is called a plane mirror. The word 'plane' just means the mirror is flat rather than curved. The ray is reflected from the mirror as shown in Figure 2.8. The reflected ray makes the same angle with the mirror as the original ray that hit it. Reflection like this is called regular reflection.
If, instead of a plane mirror, you shine a ray of light onto a smooth glass block, most of the light enters and continues through the block. However, a small amount of the light undergoes regular reflection at the smooth surface of the block (Figure 2.9).
Some highly polished, glossy surfaces can show regular and diffuse reflection at the same time. For example, when light strikes a shiny car (Figure 2.10), light is diffusely reflected from it and the car can be seen from all positions facing it. However, mirror-like reflections can also be seen in the car. You will see in Section 2.4 that these mirror-like reflections are caused by regular reflection.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-035.jpg?height=936&width=789&top_left_y=2838&top_left_x=328)
Figure 2.8 Regular reflection of light from a plane mirror

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-035.jpg?height=890&width=786&top_left_y=2832&top_left_x=1145)
Figure 2.9 Weak regular reflection when light strikes a glass block

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-035.jpg?height=831&width=789&top_left_y=2838&top_left_x=1956)
Figure 2.10 Diffuse reflection and weak regular reflection when light reflects from a smooth painted surface

### 2.4 The laws of reflection of light

## Terms used to describe regular reflection

There are several terms that you should understand when describing regular reflection. Figure 2.11 is a ray diagram. It shows the behaviour of light when it undergoes regular reflection.

- The ray that strikes the mirror is the incident ray.
- The line drawn at right angles to the mirror where the incident ray strikes the mirror is called the normal at the point of incidence.
- The ray of light that bounces from the mirror is called the reflected ray.
- The angle between the incident ray and the normal is the angle of incidence. Its symbol is $i$.
- The angle between the reflected ray and the normal is the angle of reflection. Its symbol is $r$.
When light is reflected from a plane mirror, experiments

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-036.jpg?height=607&width=1091&top_left_y=673&top_left_x=1530)
Figure 2.11

show that the following laws always hold.

## Laws of reflection of light

Law 1: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.

Law 2: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection $(\angle i=\angle r)$.

Figure 2.12 illustrates the laws of reflection with a ray diagram. Law 1 simply says that the reflected ray lies in the plane formed by the incident ray and the normal. In other words, the reflected ray is not deflected to the right or to the left.

Regular reflection occurs when light is reflected obeying the laws of reflection.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-036.jpg?height=812&width=912&top_left_y=1399&top_left_x=1709)
Figure 2.12 Law 1: The incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in the same plane. Law 2: $\angle i=\angle r$

## Demonstration Experiment 2.2

## To demonstrate the laws of reflection

## Equipment

Power supply, ray box (or laser), sheet of paper, finely pared pencil.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-036.jpg?height=584&width=1153&top_left_y=2890&top_left_x=247)
Figure 2.13(A)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-036.jpg?height=584&width=1157&top_left_y=2890&top_left_x=1432)
Figure 2.13(B)

## Method

1. Set up the equipment as in Figure 2.13(A).
2. Adjust the ray box to produce a very narrow beam (a ray).
3. With a pencil, mark two dots on the incident ray. Similarly, mark two dots on the reflected ray (Figure 2.13(B)).
4. Draw a straight line along the reflecting edge of the mirror.
5. Remove the mirror and draw in the incident ray and the reflected ray. Use the dots you drew to guide you.
6. Using a protractor, draw in the normal at the point of incidence.
7. With the protractor, measure the angle of incidence $(i)$ and the angle of reflection $(r)$. Record these values.
8. Repeat the experiment for different values of the angle of incidence ( $i$ ), moving the ray box to achieve a different angle each time.

## Observations

In each case you should find that:
a) The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, demonstrating law 2.
b) The incident and reflected rays will both be travelling parallel to the paper, that is, they are in the same plane, demonstrating law 1.

Note: If, in Figure 2.13, you use the ray box to send a ray of light towards the mirror along the line of the original reflected ray, it will always be reflected from the mirror along the line of the original incident ray. This follows from the laws of reflection. We describe this by saying that a light ray can always retrace its path in the opposite direction.

### 2.5 The image produced in a plane mirror

## The image of a point object in a plane mirror

Figure 2.14 illustrates how an image of a point object is formed in a plane mirror. A point object is one with negligible dimensions. When a point object diffusely reflects light, light rays are emitted from it in all directions.

- Light spreads out diffusely (in all directions) from the point object $P$. Three of these light rays are shown spreading out from the object and striking a plane mirror.
- Each ray is reflected from the mirror, obeying the laws of reflection - the angle of reflection being equal to the angle of incidence for each ray.
- If the reflected rays are traced back behind the mirror, as shown by the dashed lines, they meet at the point $Q$.
- Since the brain interprets light striking the eye as

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-037.jpg?height=896&width=1215&top_left_y=1823&top_left_x=1530)
Figure 2.14 How an image is formed in a plane mirror.

having travelled in a straight line path, an observer looking at the mirror will see what appears to be $P$ behind the mirror at the point $Q$.

- This apparent object $Q$ is called an image of $P$. The rays entering the eye appear to the eye to be coming from $Q$, even though no light rays actually pass through $Q$.
- We say the image at $Q$ is formed by the apparent intersection of rays (i.e. the rays appear to intersect at $Q$ ).
- This type of image is called a virtual image.

A virtual image is an image formed by the apparent intersection of rays.
A virtual image of a point object in a plane mirror is:

- On the perpendicular from the object to the mirror
- The same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of the mirror

a) What is the new angle of incidence?
b) What is the new angle of reflection?
c) Through what angle did the reflected ray rotate?

### 2.6 Uses of mirrors in technological and medical contexts

In this chapter, you have looked at reflection and at plane mirrors, and you have seen some of their practical uses. In reality, however, many of the technological and medical applications of mirrors involve curved mirrors. The details of curved mirrors are not required in this course, but using what you know about plane mirrors lets you reach some interesting new conclusions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-039.jpg?height=737&width=607&top_left_y=2734&top_left_x=1425)
Figure 2.22(A)

Figure 2.22(A) shows five small plane mirrors with a

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-039.jpg?height=740&width=685&top_left_y=2734&top_left_x=2060)
Figure 2.22(B)

parallel beam of light shining on them. The rays are reflected back along their own paths.
Figure 2.22 (B) shows the same five mirrors, with four of them rotated by the right amount so that the light falling on all five mirrors is brought together at the one place. Crudely speaking, the set-up has converted a parallel beam into a converging beam.

If instead of five plane mirrors, you positioned a hundred smaller mirrors correctly, you would effectively have a curved mirror that brings a parallel beam of light to a focus at one point $(F)$. This type of structure is used in a solar furnace, which concentrates rays from the Sun onto a single spot in order to 'harvest' the energy and heat up the target (Figure 2.23).
Since light can always retrace its path, it follows that if you put a point source of light at the focus $F$, the light from that source will emerge from the mirror as a parallel beam (Figure 2.24). This type of mirror is used in headlights, searchlights and floodlights to produce a focused parallel beam of light rays.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-040.jpg?height=629&width=1183&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 2.23 A solar furnace being used to cook food.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-040.jpg?height=897&width=1127&top_left_y=1080&top_left_x=1494)
Figure 2.24

Figure 2.25

Figure 2.26 is similar to Figure 2.22, but this time the mirrors are arranged so that the rays all appear to be coming from the same point behind the mirror. Increasing the number of mirrors, as above, results in a curved mirror that converts a parallel beam into a diverging beam.
Since light can always retrace its path, it follows that light from a very wide field of view will emerge from the mirror as a parallel beam. This phenomenon is used where it is useful to see objects from a wide range of angles, such as in car wing mirrors (Figure 2.27), mirrors at a concealed road entrance and mirrors in shop security systems (Figure 2.28). Just as in a plane mirror, a virtual image can be formed by this type of mirror. However,

Figure 2.26

the image is much smaller than a similar image in a plane mirror.

## Summary What I should know

- A luminous object gives out its own light. A non-luminous object does not give out its own light.
- Light is a form of energy.
- Light travels at a very high speed ( $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in a vacuum).
- Light usually travels in straight lines.
- A diverging beam of light is one that gets wider.
- A converging beam of light is one that gets narrower.
- A parallel beam of light remains the same width.
- A light ray is a straight line showing the direction in which light is travelling.
- Reflection is the bouncing of light from an object.
- Diffuse reflection is the scattering of reflected light in all directions from the surface of an object.
- The laws of reflection of light state:

Law 1: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
Law 2: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection ( $i=r$ ).

- Regular reflection is when light is reflected obeying the laws of reflection.
- A virtual image is an image formed by the apparent intersection of rays.
- An image formed in a plane mirror is a virtual image.
- Some everyday applications of plane mirrors (e.g. bathroom mirrors and periscopes).

# 3 Refraction of Light

## Objectives

- To give students an understanding of the refraction of light
- To make students aware of the conditions under which refraction of light will occur
- To ensure students understand the laws of refraction of light
- To ensure students know what is meant by the refractive index of a medium
- To ensure students know what is meant by the refractive index between two media
- To make students aware that refraction will only occur when light enters a medium with a different refractive index
- To give students an understanding of critical angle and total internal reflection
- To ensure students know the function and uses of optical fibres
- To allow students to appreciate some real-world uses of the refraction of light


### 3.1 What is refraction of light?

## Light rays changing direction

## Keywords

- Transparent medium
- Refraction
- Incident ray
- Normal at the point of incidence
- Refracted ray
- Angle of incidence ( $i$ )
- Angle of refraction ( $r$ )
- Optical density
- Virtual image
- Snell's law
- Refractive index of a medium
- Refractive index between two media
- Critical angle
- Total internal reflection
- Optical fibre

In Chapter 2, you learned that light travels in straight lines. In this chapter, you will see what happens when light goes from one transparent medium into another. A transparent medium is a clear substance through which light can easily travel. This means it is a substance that you can see through clearly (e.g. glass, air, water, diamond).

- In Figure 3.1(A), a ray of light travels from one medium (air) into another (glass), and out again.
- You can see that the ray changes direction (it bends) when it goes into the second medium.
- This bending of light is called the refraction of light. You can see that refraction also occurs when the ray leaves the glass block, that is, when the ray travels from glass into air.
- Notice that the ray does not bend (no refraction occurs) if it strikes the second medium at a right angle (Figure 3.1(B)).

A transparent medium is a substance through which light can travel and through which you can see clearly.

Refraction is the bending of a ray of light when it goes from one medium to another.

Figure 3.1(A) A ray of light travels from one medium (air) into another (glass) and out again.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-042.jpg?height=662&width=1183&top_left_y=3128&top_left_x=1432)
Figure 3.1(B) No refraction occurs when the ray strikes the glass at a right angle.

## Terms used to describe refraction

When a ray of light falls on a glass block (Figure 3.2) or on another transparent medium, the following terms are used:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-043.jpg?height=864&width=1046&top_left_y=530&top_left_x=325)
Figure 3.2

| Incident ray | The ray of light falling on the glass block |
| :--- | :--- |
| The normal | The line drawn at right angles to the glass block where the ray strikes the block |
| Refracted ray | The ray of light inside the glass block |
| Angle of incidence ( $i$ ) | The angle between the incident ray and the normal |
| Angle of refraction ( $r$ ) | The angle between the refracted ray and the normal |

## Demonstration Experiment 3.1

## To demonstrate refraction

## Equipment

Power supply, ray box or laser, sheet of paper, finely pared pencil.

## Method

1. Use the equipment shown in Figure 3.3(A). Adjust the ray box to produce a very narrow beam, i.e. a ray.
2. Shine the ray, at an angle, onto one side of the glass block. Observe how the ray bends on entering the glass, and also that some light is reflected from the block (Figure 3.3(B)).
3. Observe that the ray bends again on leaving the block and that the ray coming out of the glass (the emergent ray) is parallel to the ray striking the block.
4. Shine the ray onto the glass block so that it strikes the block at a right angle. Observe that the ray does not bend on entering the glass, but simply passes straight through.
5. Repeat the experiment for different angles of incidence. You will see that the angle of refraction increases as the angle of incidence increases (Figure 3.4).
6. However, if you measured the size of the angles, you would see that they do not increase proportionally.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-043.jpg?height=997&width=1150&top_left_y=2786&top_left_x=371)
Figure 3.3(A)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-043.jpg?height=1003&width=1150&top_left_y=2780&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 3.3(B)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-044.jpg?height=581&width=2329&top_left_y=315&top_left_x=247)
Figure 3.4 As the angle of incidence increases, so does the angle of refraction, but they do not increase proportionally.

In Demonstration Experiment 3.1, you saw that:

- When a ray of light goes from air into glass, it is refracted (it bends) towards the normal.
- When a ray goes from glass into air, it is refracted away from the normal.

We say glass is optically denser than air. We also say that air is optically rarer than glass.

## Note: In general:

- When light travels from an optically rarer to an optically denser medium, it is refracted towards the normal (Figure 3.5).
- When light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, it is refracted away from the normal (Figure 3.6).
Note also that an optically denser medium is not always physically denser, but often it is.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-044.jpg?height=997&width=1154&top_left_y=1904&top_left_x=224)
Figure 3.5

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-044.jpg?height=1004&width=1151&top_left_y=1904&top_left_x=1399)
Figure 3.6

## Examples of refraction

There are many real-world examples of the effects of refraction of light. For example:

- Water in a swimming pool appears to be less deep than it actually is.
- Writing seen through a thick glass block appears to be nearer to the top of the block than it really is (Figure 3.7).
- If you partially submerge an object in water, it appears to bend at the water surface (Figure 3.8).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-044.jpg?height=584&width=1196&top_left_y=3138&top_left_x=1419)
Figure 3.7

In all cases, the effect is greater if you view the surface at a sharper angle. This can be explained by the refraction of light as follows:

- Figure $3.9(\mathrm{~A})$ shows a small object in shallow water, at point $P$.
- Light rays from the object undergo refraction as they hit the water's surface. To an observer looking from an angle, these rays appear to be diverging from the point $Q$.
- The observer therefore sees a virtual image of $P$ at $Q$, nearer to the surface than the object really is.
- The distance $S P$ is the real depth of the object, and $S Q$ is the apparent depth of the object in the water.
In Figure 3.9(B), you can see that the apparent depth decreases even further as you view the object more from the side, and that the apparent depth is greatest when viewing vertically from above.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-045.jpg?height=763&width=988&top_left_y=276&top_left_x=1757)
Figure 3.8

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-045.jpg?height=642&width=1196&top_left_y=1204&top_left_x=325)
Figure 3.9(A)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-045.jpg?height=639&width=1196&top_left_y=1204&top_left_x=1549)
Figure 3.9(B)

### 3.2 The laws of refraction of light and refractive index

## The laws of refraction of light

When light undergoes refraction, and the angle of incidence is changed, the angle of refraction does not change proportionally. Instead, the ratio $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ remains the same no matter what the angle of incidence is. This can be shown experimentally, and you will verify this yourself in Student Experiment 3.1 (page 37). How light behaves when it undergoes refraction is summarised in the laws of refraction.

## The first law of refraction of light

1st law: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the refracted ray all lie in the same plane (Figure 3.10).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-045.jpg?height=789&width=997&top_left_y=2047&top_left_x=1748)
Figure 3.10 The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the refracted ray all lie in the same plane.

## Snell's law

2nd law: The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant. In other words, $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=n$, where $n$ is a constant.

The value of $n$ depends on the two media in question, and it is called the refractive index between the two media. This is discussed in more detail later in this chapter.
The second law of refraction is sometimes called Snell's law after the Dutch mathematician Willebrord Snellius.

## Willebrord Snellius

Willebrord Snellius (1580-1626),
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-045.jpg?height=271&width=317&top_left_y=3275&top_left_x=2428)
also known as Snell, was a Dutch astronomer and mathematician. His best-known achievement was the discovery in 1621 of what is now known as Snell's law. Snell died at the relatively young age of 46 , and his discovery wasn't published in his lifetime.

## Refractive index of a medium

The refractive index of a medium ( $\boldsymbol{n}$ ) is the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction when light travels from a vacuum into that medium.

The difference between the amount of refraction that occurs when light travels from air or from a vacuum into a medium is very small. For our purposes, this can be ignored. So the refractive index of a medium is also equal to the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction when light travels from air into that medium.

The refractive index of a medium $n=\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ when light travels from air or a vacuum into that medium.
(F\&T, page 60)

Table 3.1 gives the refractive index of some common media (substances).

| Substance | Refractive index |
| :---: | :---: |
| Vacuum | 1 |
| Air | $1.0003 \approx 1$ |
| Water | 1.33 |
| Glass (crown) | 1.5 |
| Glass (flint) | 1.6 |
| Diamond | 2.42 |

## Table 3.1

## Note:

- The bigger the refractive index of a medium, the greater the amount by which that medium bends the light for a given angle of incidence.
- $n$ (the refractive index of a medium) is always 1 or greater. This is because when light goes from a vacuum into another medium, it always bends towards the normal.

$$
\begin{array}{cc}
\Rightarrow & r<i \\
\Rightarrow & \sin r<\sin i \\
\Rightarrow & n=\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}>1
\end{array}
$$

## Worked Example 1

## Question

A ray of light enters glass from air. The angle of incidence is $30^{\circ}$ and the angle of refraction is $19^{\circ}$. What is the refractive index of the glass?

## Solution

For light travelling from air to glass:
Refractive index of glass, $n=\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{\sin 30^{\circ}}{\sin 19^{\circ}} \\
& =1.54
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A ray of light enters water from air (Figure 3.11). If the angle of incidence is $40^{\circ}$, find the angle of refraction. The refractive index of water is 1.33 .

## Solution

Refractive index of water, $n=\frac{\sin 40^{\circ}}{\sin r}=1.33$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \sin r & =\frac{\sin 40^{\circ}}{1.33}=0.4833 \\
\Rightarrow \text { Angle of refraction } r & =\sin ^{-1}(0.4833) \\
& =28.9^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-047.jpg?height=596&width=597&top_left_y=410&top_left_x=2109)
Figure 3.11 The angle of refraction $r$

## The refractive index between two media

The refractive index between two media is the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction when light travels from one of those media into the other.

The order in which the light passes through the media is important. For example, when light travels from glass into water, the refractive index is 0.91 . When it travels from water into glass, the refractive index is 1.1 .
You write this as:

$$
{ }_{\mathrm{g}} n_{\mathrm{w}}=0.91 \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{w}_{\mathrm{g}}=1.1
$$

The relationship between these two numbers can be expressed as follows:

$$
0.91=\frac{1}{1.1} \quad \text { or } \quad 1.1=\frac{1}{0.9}
$$

This result is true for any two media. For example:

$$
\text { if }{ }_{\mathrm{a}} n_{\mathrm{g}}=\frac{3}{2} \quad \text { then } \quad{ }_{\mathrm{g}} n_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}=\frac{2}{3}
$$

The reason for this can be seen if you look at Figure 3.12.
Say you shine a ray of light from glass into air along $Z Y$. Experiment always shows that the ray in air will be travelling along $Y X$.
So from the diagram:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-047.jpg?height=736&width=737&top_left_y=1774&top_left_x=2008)
Figure 3.12

$$
\begin{aligned}
{ }_{\mathrm{a}} n_{\mathrm{g}} & =\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} \quad \text { and } \quad{ }_{\mathrm{g}} n_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\sin r}{\sin i} \\
\text { But: } \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} & =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{\sin r}{\sin i}\right)} \\
\text { Thus: }{ }_{\mathrm{a}} n_{\mathrm{g}} & =\frac{1}{{ }_{\mathrm{g}} n_{\mathrm{a}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

For any two media $x$ and $y$ : ${ }_{x} n_{y}=\frac{1}{y^{n}{ }_{x}}$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

The refractive index between flint glass and water is 0.85 . What is the refractive index between water and flint glass?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
w_{g} & =\frac{1}{g_{g} w} \\
& =\frac{1}{0.85} \\
& =1.18
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

w $n_{g}=\frac{9}{8}$, where w and g represent water and glass, respectively.
Light enters water from glass. If the angle of incidence is $40^{\circ}$, find the angle of refraction.

## Solution

Draw a diagram to be clear on exactly what is being asked (Figure 3.13).

$$
\begin{aligned}
{ }_{\mathrm{w}} n_{\mathrm{g}} & =\frac{9}{8} \\
\Rightarrow{ }_{\mathrm{g}} n_{\mathrm{w}} & =\frac{8}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$

In going from glass to water:

$$
\begin{aligned}
{ }_{8} n_{w} & =\frac{\sin 40^{\circ}}{\sin r} \\
& =\frac{8}{9} \\
\Rightarrow \sin r & =\frac{\left(9 \sin 40^{\circ}\right)}{8} \\
\Rightarrow \text { Angle of refraction } r & =\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{9 \times 0.6428}{8}\right) \\
& =46.3^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-048.jpg?height=701&width=668&top_left_y=677&top_left_x=1504)
