## Student Experiment 3.1

a) To verify that the value of $\frac{\boldsymbol{\operatorname { s i n }} i}{\boldsymbol{\operatorname { s i n }} r}$ remains constant as the value of $i$ is changed when light undergoes refraction at a glass block.
b) To confirm that the value of the ratio $\frac{\boldsymbol{\operatorname { s i n }} i}{\boldsymbol{\operatorname { s i n }} r}$ is the given refractive index of the block.

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will use a ray box and a glass block (Figure 3.15) to investigate the relationship between the angle of incidence $i$ and angle of reflection $r$.
By taking measurements and graphing results, you will verify that $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is a constant, and hence verify that the constant value of $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is the known refractive index of the glass.

- You will use a ray box to produce a ray of light which strikes a glass block (Figure 3.15).
- The angle of incidence $i$ of the ray on the block and the angle of refraction $r$ within the block can then be measured.
- You will repeat this for different values of $i$, and verify that the ratio $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is a constant.
- You will confirm that the constant value of $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is the given

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-049.jpg?height=935&width=916&top_left_y=781&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 3.15

refractive index of the glass.

- You will also plot a graph of $\sin i$ against $\sin r$. A straight line through the origin will result, again verifying that the ratio $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is a constant. The slope of the graph is the refractive index $n$.


## Equipment

Power supply, ray box (or laser), rectangular glass block of known refractive index, sheet of paper, pencil, a ruler and a protractor.

## Method

1. Place the glass block on top of a sheet of paper, resting on a flat workbench.
2. Trace the outline of the glass block with a finely pared pencil. During Step 3 and Step 4, make sure to keep the block on the marked position.
3. Using the ray box as in Figure 3.15, shine a ray of light onto the block.
4. With a pencil, mark the incident ray with two dots and mark the ray emerging from the other side of the block with two more dots. Make sure the dots on each ray are reasonably far apart.
5. Remove the ray box and the block from the paper.
6. Use the dots to draw the incident ray and the emergent ray.
7. With your pencil, join the point where the incident ray meets the glass block with the point where the emergent ray meets the glass block with a straight line. This is the refracted ray within the block.
8. Draw in the normal at the point of incidence using a protractor (Figure 3.16). The angle of incidence and the corresponding angle of refraction are now drawn on the paper.
9. With a protractor, measure and record the values of these angles.
10. By placing the block on different parts of the paper or by using different sheets of paper, repeat Steps 2 to 9 for at least five different angles of incidence, to get a series of angles of incidence $i$ and corresponding angles of refraction $r$.

| $i$ | $r$ | $\sin i$ | $\sin r$ | $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  |  |  |  |

Average value of $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=$

Refractive index of material in block =

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-050.jpg?height=1003&width=1154&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1422)

## Handling the data

## Method 1

1. Complete the table using your calculator to find the values of $\sin i, \sin r$ and $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$. The values in the last column of the table should all be approximately the same.
2. Calculate the average value of $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ (the last column in the table). This will be found to be the refractive index $n$ of the glass block.

## Method 2

1. On graph paper, plot a graph of $\sin i$ (on the $y$-axis) against $\sin r$ (on the $x$-axis).
2. All the points should lie on, or be very close to, a straight line passing through the origin (Figure 3.17).
3. The fact that the graph is a straight line through the origin verifies that $\sin i \propto \sin r$ and that the ratio $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is a constant.
4. Measure the slope of the graph. This will be the refractive index $n$ of the glass block.

## Sources of error

- If the block moves from its marked position before marking the four dots you will introduce systematic error in the values of $i$ and $r$.
- Ensure the two dots marking the incident ray are spaced well apart. This reduces random error in drawing the position of the incident ray. The same applies for the emergent ray.
- Take care to avoid parallax error when using the protractor.
- Use a finely pared pencil for all drawing.
- Do not use a value of $i$ that is very small. If you do, the measured values of both $i$ and $r$ will have a large percentage error.


### 3.3 Refractive index in terms of relative speeds

When light travels from one medium to another, its speed usually changes (it is fastest in a vacuum at $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ). This speed change causes it to change direction on entering the second medium. This is explained more fully on page 272.

In fact, if the speed of light in medium 1 is $c_{1}$ and the speed in medium 2 is $c_{2}$, then:

$$
\text { i.e. } \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}
$$

(F\&T, page 59)
(Figure 3.18)

HL If medium 1 is air, then for any medium $x$, this equation becomes:
From this, it follows that if the speed of light in both media is the same, then no refraction will occur when light travels from one medium to the other.

If medium 1 is air, then for any medium $x$, this equation becomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{air} n_{x} & =\frac{c_{\text {air }}}{c_{x}} \\
\text { Refractive index of a medium } & =\frac{\text { speed of light in air }}{\text { speed of light in medium }}
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging this equation gives:

$$
\text { Speed of light in medium }=\frac{\text { speed of light in air }}{\text { refractive index of a medium }}
$$

It follows from this that:

- The greater the refractive index of a medium, the more light slows as

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-051.jpg?height=692&width=853&top_left_y=1044&top_left_x=1895)
Figure 3.18 The ratio of the speed of light in medium 1 to medium 2 is the same as the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction.

- If two different media have the same refractive index, the speed of light in each is the same and hence light will not undergo refraction in going from one of those media to the other

Note: When light travels from one medium to another, refraction will not occur if:

- The light enters the second medium parallel to the normal or
- Light travels at the same speed in each medium or
- The refractive indices of both media are the same.

The second and third bullet points amount to the same thing. In other words, if one is true then the other must also be true.

## Worked Example 5

## Question

What is the refractive index of a medium in which light travels at a speed of $2 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ? Speed of light in air $=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{x} & =\frac{c_{\text {air }}}{c_{x}} \\
& =\frac{\text { speed in air }}{\text { speed in medium }} \\
& =\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2 \times 10^{8}} \\
& =1.5
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 6

## Question

The refractive index of water = 1.33 and the speed of light in air = $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
Calculate the speed of light in water.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{\mathrm{w}} & =\frac{c_{\text {air }}}{c_{\text {water }}} \\
& =\frac{\text { speed in air }}{\text { speed in water }} \\
& =1.33
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \text { Speed in water } & =\frac{\text { speed in air }}{1.33} \\
& =\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.33} \\
& =2.26 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 3.4 Critical angle and total internal reflection

You saw on page 32 that when a light ray travels from an optically denser medium to an optically rarer medium, it is refracted away from the normal (i.e. $r>i$ ).
You also saw that when refraction occurs, if the angle of incidence is increased, so is the angle of refraction (Figure 3.4). So when a light ray moves from an optically denser medium to an optically rarer medium, and the angle of incidence increases, there comes a point at which the angle of refraction becomes $90^{\circ}$ (as shown in Figure 3.19(A)). The angle of incidence at which this happens is called the critical angle for those two media, and it is usually represented by the symbol $C$.

When light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, the angle of incidence whose corresponding angle of refraction is $90^{\circ}$ is called the critical angle ( $C$ ) for those two media.

If the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, the light ray does not enter the second medium at all. Instead, it is completely reflected back into the first medium, following the laws of reflection. This phenomenon is called total internal reflection (Figure 3.19(B)). The word 'total' means exactly what it says here - all the light is reflected, none is absorbed. In the best ordinary mirror available, about $4 \%$ of the light incident on the mirror is absorbed, while the rest is reflected.

When light going from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium strikes the second medium with an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle, it does not enter the second, rarer, medium. It is all reflected back into the denser medium. This is called total internal reflection.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-052.jpg?height=603&width=1040&top_left_y=1894&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 3.19(A) The angle of incidence increases until it reaches $C$, the critical angle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-052.jpg?height=681&width=1040&top_left_y=2728&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 3.19(B) When the angle of incidence is larger than $C$, light is always totally internally reflected.

## Demonstration Experiment 3.2

To demonstrate total internal reflection

## Equipment

Ray box（or a laser），semicircular block．

## Method

1．Set up a ray box and a semicircular slab of glass，as in Figure 3．20（A）．
2．Start with a small angle of incidence，then slowly increase this angle．
3．Soon the critical angle will be reached and the refracted ray will skim along the flat face of the glass．
4．If the angle of incidence is then increased further，the refracted ray jumps from that shown in Figure 3．20（B） to that in Figure 3．20（C），a totally internally reflected ray．

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-053.jpg?height=708&width=2337&top_left_y=1136&top_left_x=366)
Figure 3.20

## 3．5 Relationship between refractive index and critical angle

Figure 3.21 shows a ray of light going from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium and striking the rarer medium at the critical angle．Applying Snell＇s law：

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{y} & =\frac{\sin C}{\sin 90^{\circ}} \\
& =\frac{\sin C}{1} \\
& =\sin C
\end{aligned}
$$

If the second medium（the rarer one）is air，or a vacuum，this equation becomes：

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-053.jpg?height=447&width=623&top_left_y=2324&top_left_x=2122)
Figure 3.21

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{\mathrm{air}} & =\sin C \\
\Rightarrow \mathrm{air}_{x} & =\frac{1}{\sin C}
\end{aligned}
$$

Refractive index of medium $n=\frac{1}{\sin C}$ ，where $C$ is the critical angle．

## Worked Example 7

## Question

The critical angle for a certain medium at a boundary with air is $50^{\circ}$ ．
Find its refractive index．

## Solution

Refractive index $n=\frac{1}{\sin C}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{1}{\sin 50^{\circ}} \\
& =1.3
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 8

## Question

The refractive index of glass is 1.5 . What is the critical angle for this glass surrounded by air?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
{ }_{\mathrm{a}} n_{\mathrm{g}} & =\frac{1}{\sin C} \\
\Rightarrow \sin C & =\frac{1}{{ }_{\mathrm{a}} n_{\mathrm{g}}} \\
& =\frac{1}{1.5} \\
& =0.6667
\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\quad \sin C=0.6667$

$$
\Rightarrow C=\sin ^{-1} 0.6667
$$

⇒ Critical angle $C=41.8^{\circ}$

## Student Experiment 3.2

a) To measure the critical angle ( $C$ ) for a transparent material, e.g. glass
b) To confirm that the value of $\frac{1}{\sin C}$ is the given refractive index, $n$, of the material, i.e. to verify that: $n=\frac{1}{\sin C}$

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will use a ray box and a semicircular glass block to find and measure the critical angle, $C$, for light going from glass into air. You will then verify that $\frac{1}{\sin C}=n$, where $n$ is the refractive index of the material of the glass block.

## Equipment

Ray box, semicircular glass block, sheet of paper, pencil, protractor.

## Method

1. Place a semicircular glass block on a sheet of paper and draw its outline with a finely pared pencil.
2. Mark the centre of the straight edge of the block on the paper.
3. Shine a ray of light towards the centre, as shown in Figure 3.22(A), starting with a small angle of incidence.
4. Slowly increase this angle.
5. Soon, the critical angle is reached and the refracted ray skims along the flat face of the glass (Figure 3.22(B)). When this happens, mark the point where the ray from the ray box enters the glass block.
6. Remove the ray box and the block from the paper.
7. With a ruler, draw the position of the ray that was inside the block (the incident ray).
8. Using a protractor, draw in the normal. Measure the value of the critical angle $C$. Record this value.
9. Redo the experiment three or four times.
10. Calculate the average value of $C$.
11. Calculate the value of $\frac{1}{\sin C}$. This gives the refractive index, $n$, of the glass.

## Sources of error

1. Make sure you do not accidentally move the glass block once you have drawn in its outline and marked its centre.
2. Draw all lines with a ruler and a finely pared pencil.
3. Ensure that the protractor is read from directly above, to avoid parallax error.

## Using a $\mathbf{4 5}^{\circ}-\mathbf{9 0 ^ { \circ }}-\mathbf{4 5 ^ { \circ }}$ prism to turn a ray of light through $\mathbf{9 0}^{\boldsymbol{\circ}}$ or $180^{\boldsymbol{\circ}}$

- If a ray of light enters a glass prism as shown in Figure 3.23(A), it strikes the right-hand side of the prism at an angle of incidence of $45^{\circ}$.
- This angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, therefore total internal reflection occurs at $O$ and the ray is reflected as shown.
- Since the angle of reflection is also $45^{\circ}$, the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is $90^{\circ}$; thus the prism turns the ray through $90^{\circ}$.
- Similarly, the same prism can turn a ray through $180^{\circ}$ (Figure 3.23 (B)).


## Worked Example 9

## Question

If a prism is to turn a ray of light through $90^{\circ}$ as in Figure 3.23(A), what is the smallest possible value of the refractive index of the material in the prism?

## Solution

For any medium: refractive index $n=\frac{1}{\sin C}$. Therefore, the larger $C$, the smaller $n$.

For total internal reflection to occur, the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle $C$.
The angle of incidence is $45^{\circ}$. Therefore, $45^{\circ}>C$
$\Rightarrow C$ must be less than $45^{\circ}$.
If $C$ were $45^{\circ}$, then $n=\frac{1}{\sin C}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{1}{\sin 45^{\circ}} \\
& =1.414
\end{aligned}
$$

But $C$ must be less than $45^{\circ}$, therefore the refractive index $n$ must be greater than 1.414.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-055.jpg?height=720&width=737&top_left_y=1800&top_left_x=2008)

Figure 3.23(B)

## Worked Example 10

## Question

A point source of light $P$ is 2 m below the surface of the water in a still pond. Find the radius of the circle at the surface through which light can pass into air, given that the refractive index of water $n=\frac{4}{3}$.

## Solution

Figure 3.24 shows the situation. Light from the source will not leave the water if it strikes the water at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
Refractive index of water $n=\frac{4}{3}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \sin C & =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)}=\frac{3}{4} \\
\Rightarrow \text { Critical angle } C & =\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) \\
& =48.59^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram (using SOHCAHTOA):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan C & =\frac{r}{2} \\
\Rightarrow r & =2 \tan C \\
\Rightarrow r & =2 \tan 48.59^{\circ} \\
& =2.27 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-056.jpg?height=708&width=785&top_left_y=800&top_left_x=1380)
Figure 3.24

Since a light ray travelling in the opposite direction will trace the same path, it follows from Worked Example 10 that only light from above the water surface that strikes the surface within the radius $r$ (Figure 3.24) will reach $P$ (see Figure 3.25(A)). Therefore, if you are underwater and looking upwards, the surroundings above the water will look as though they are compressed within this circle. Divers refer to this circle as Snell's Window (Figure 3.25(B)).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-056.jpg?height=860&width=1202&top_left_y=2223&top_left_x=198)

### 3.6 Applications of total internal reflection

## Cat's-eye reflectors

Total internal reflection occurs in the cat's-eye reflectors commonly used on our roads (Figure 3.27). Light enters the glass part and is reflected from its back surface by total internal reflection.

## Corner cube reflectors

Corner cube reflectors are another practical example of total internal reflection. Imagine three plane mirrors positioned at right angles to each other, as shown in Figure 3.28. When a ray of light strikes one mirror, it

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-057.jpg?height=587&width=1205&top_left_y=2024&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 3.27 Cat's-eye reflector on a road

reflects off the other two in turn, eventually emerging parallel to its original direction. A corner made of glass or plastic can be used to give the same result. Light entering the material undergoes total internal reflection three times within the corner of the cube, sending it back in the direction it came from. This principle is utilised in safety reflectors on bicycles or cars (Figure 3.29), where the material is shaped into many small right-angled prisms to achieve this effect.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-057.jpg?height=734&width=1202&top_left_y=3053&top_left_x=325)
Figure 3.28

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-057.jpg?height=737&width=1203&top_left_y=3053&top_left_x=1545)
Figure 3.29

## Optical fibres

A very thin transparent rod (usually of glass), through which light can travel by total internal reflection, is called an optical fibre.

Optical fibres are solid, but because the fibres are very thin, they can bend easily and can carry light around corners and into places with limited access (Figure 3.30). They therefore have many applications in technology and medicine.
Optical fibres work as follows:

- Light enters the fibre and strikes the inside of the fibre at an angle greater than the critical angle. Total internal reflection occurs.
- The ray is reflected to the opposite side and total internal reflection occurs again (Figure 3.31).
- This process continues and the light travels through the fibre.
Light can escape from optical fibres in two ways:
- If an optical fibre is bent through too large an angle, the ray travelling inside it may strike it at an angle less than the critical angle. If this happens, the light will not be totally internally reflected and will

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-058.jpg?height=1388&width=1163&top_left_y=263&top_left_x=1458)
Figure 3.30 An optical fibre passing through the eye of a needle

leave the fibre (Figure 3.32).

- If an optical fibre comes into contact with another fibre (or another part of itself), a ray of light inside it will meet a glass-glass boundary rather than glass-air. The light ray will therefore simply travel from one fibre into the other (Figure 3.33). One method to prevent this is to coat the optical fibre with a layer of glass with lower refractive index. Even if two fibres then come in contact, total internal reflection should still occur (Figure 3.34).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-058.jpg?height=880&width=1202&top_left_y=2213&top_left_x=198)
Figure 3.31 Light passes through an optical fibre by total internal reflection.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-058.jpg?height=720&width=1202&top_left_y=2207&top_left_x=1419)
Figure 3.32 Light escaping from an overly curved optical fibre. The angle of incidence $i$, is greater than the critical angle, so total internal reflection occurs. The angle of incidence $i_{2}$ is less than the critical angle, so the ray undergoes refraction and leaves the fibre.

## Summary What I should know

- Refraction of light is the bending of light when it travels from one medium to another in which its speed is different.
- Refraction will not occur if:
i) The light enters the second medium parallel to the normal, or
ii) If the refractive index of the second medium and the first medium are the same, or
iii) If light travels at the same speed in each medium
- When light travels from an optically rarer to an optically denser medium, it is refracted towards the normal.
- When light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, it is refracted away from the normal.
- The laws of refraction of light:

1st law: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the refracted ray all lie in the same plane.
2nd law (Snell's law): The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant. i.e. $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=n$, where $n$ is a constant.

- The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction when light travels from a vacuum (or air) into that medium.
- The refractive index between two media is the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction when light travels from one of those media into the other.
- When light travels from medium 1 , where its speed is $c_{1}$, to medium 2 , where its speed is $c_{2}$, then:

$$
n_{2}=\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}} \quad \text { i.e. } \quad \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}
$$

- When light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, the angle of incidence whose corresponding angle of refraction is $90^{\circ}$ is called the critical angle $(C)$ for those two media.
- When light going from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium strikes the second medium with an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle, it does not enter the second medium. It is all reflected back into the denser medium. This is called total internal reflection.
- The refractive index of a medium $n=\frac{1}{\sin C}$ where $C$ is the critical angle.
- An optical fibre is a very thin, flexible, transparent rod (usually of glass) through which light can travel by total internal reflection.

# 4 Lenses

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand what a converging and a diverging lens is
- To make students aware of the focusing properties of a converging lens and a diverging lens
- To ensure students can use ray diagrams to establish the position and nature of an image formed in a converging or a diverging lens, no matter what the position of the object
- To allow students to appreciate some real-world uses of converging and diverging lenses in technological and medical contexts
- To help students appreciate what a model is, in the context of physics
- To enable students to see that in Chapters 2 and 3 they have been studying the geometrical optics model of light (also called the ray model of light)


## Keywords

- Converging lens, convex lens
- Diverging lens, concave lens
- Optic centre
- Principal axis, axis
- Focal point, focus
- Focal length
- Real image
- Virtual image
- Magnifying glass
- Ray model of light
- Geometrical optics model of light


### 4.1 Converging and diverging lenses

In this chapter, you will look at refraction of light by lenses. You will study two types of lens a convex lens and a concave lens (Figure 4.1). Convex lenses are thicker at the centre than at the sides, and concave lenses are thicker at the sides than at the centre.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-063.jpg?height=860&width=854&top_left_y=2298&top_left_x=341)
Figure 4.1

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-063.jpg?height=864&width=1189&top_left_y=2298&top_left_x=1214)
Figure 4.2

Lenses are found in many everyday objects, such as eye glasses, contact lenses, the peephole in doors, cameras, projectors, telescopes, binoculars and microscopes.

- The centre of a lens is called the optic centre (Figure 4.2).
- The straight line passing through the optic centre, at right angles to the face of the lens, is called the principal axis or simply the axis of the lens (Figure 4.2).


## Focusing property of lenses

A parallel beam of light falling on a convex lens is refracted and brought together at a specific point beyond the lens (Figure 4.3). Since a convex lens changes a parallel beam into a converging beam, it is also called a converging lens.
A parallel beam of light falling on a concave lens is refracted such that the light spreads out as if it were coming from a particular point behind the lens (Figure 4.4). Since a concave lens changes a parallel beam into a diverging beam, it is also called a diverging lens.
If the parallel beam is parallel to the axis of the lens, the point to which it converges (for the convex lens) and the point from which it diverges (for the concave lens) is called the principal focus of the lens. This is also known as the focal point or simply the focus of the lens.
The distance from the optic centre to the focus is called the focal length of the lens.
Note that:

- There is a focus at each side of both types of lens.
- Each focus in a given lens is the same distance from the optic centre.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-064.jpg?height=508&width=1597&top_left_y=1276&top_left_x=197)
Figure 4.3 A parallel beam of light falling on a converging lens

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-064.jpg?height=630&width=818&top_left_y=1093&top_left_x=1803)
Figure 4.4 A parallel beam of light falling on a diverging lens

A converging lens of short focal length has a greater converging effect on a parallel beam of light than a lens of long focal length (Figure 4.5). The same is true for diverging lenses. The shorter the focal length, the greater the diverging effect.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-064.jpg?height=525&width=2436&top_left_y=2145&top_left_x=188)
Figure 4.5 Effect of different focal lengths in (A) converging and (B) diverging lenses

Figure 4.6 shows the path of three particular light rays that pass through a converging lens. These results can be verified in a lab using a ray box and a converging lens, and they are important to this topic. You should make sure you learn and memorise them.

| 1. A ray that strikes the optic centre passes straight through the lens. | 2. A ray that strikes the lens travelling parallel to the axis passes through the focus at the other side of the lens. | 3. A ray that passes through the focus and then strikes the lens emerges parallel to the principal axis. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-064.jpg?height=319&width=719&top_left_y=3407&top_left_x=231) | ![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-064.jpg?height=293&width=706&top_left_y=3410&top_left_x=1048) | ![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-064.jpg?height=289&width=716&top_left_y=3414&top_left_x=1835) |

Figure 4.6 Refraction of three light rays by a converging lens

### 4.2 How an image is formed in a converging lens

Figure 4.7 shows an object in front of a converging lens. Every point on the object is giving out light in all directions. Three light rays from a point $P$ at the top of the object are shown striking the lens and being refracted.
After refraction at the lens, each of the rays passes through the same point $X$. It can also be shown that any other ray from $P$ would also pass through $X$ after refraction. It follows that an eye (i.e. an observer) as shown in Figure 4.7 will see an image of the object, with

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-065.jpg?height=431&width=1218&top_left_y=449&top_left_x=1535)
Figure 4.7 How a real image is produced in a converging lens

the top of the image at $X$, since rays that were originally diverging from $P$ are now diverging from $X$,
By repeating this process for other points on the object, you would find that an image of the whole object is formed as shown in Figure 4.7.
This image is caused by the actual intersection of rays. Such an image is called a real image.
Note also that, unlike an image in a plane mirror, the image is a different size to the object.

## Properties of a real image

A real image exists in space, unlike a virtual image. A real image can be seen on a screen: for example, the image on a traditional cinema screen is a real image. You can easily project a real image onto a screen with the equipment shown in Figure 4.8.
The cross-threads are illuminated by the ray box and behave as a bright object. If the distance from the screen to the lens is varied, a position will be found for which there is a clear image of the cross-threads formed on the screen. If such an image cannot be found, the lens is too near the ray box and should be moved further away from it.
Other examples of real images produced by converging

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-065.jpg?height=698&width=1199&top_left_y=1588&top_left_x=1554)
Figure 4.8

lenses are the image that forms on the retina of an eye, or the image on the sensor (or film) of a camera.
We will also see how a given real image can itself be magnified. If the observer in Figure 4.7 wanted to examine the real image more closely, a magnifying glass could be used (pages 54-55, 63-64).

A real image is an image formed by the actual intersection of light rays. Such an image can be located on a screen.

## How the image changes as the position of the object changes

You can use a ray diagram to show how and where the image is formed when the object is at different distances from a converging lens. There are five relevant distances in this scenario, and those are when the object distance from the lens is:
a) Greater than two focal lengths from the lens (>2f)
b) Equal to two focal lengths from the lens (at $2 f$ )
c) Between one and two focal lengths from the lens (between $f$ and $2 f$ )
d) At the focal point (f)
e) Inside the focus (<f)

To find where the image is located, you need to draw any two of the rays shown in Figure 4.6.
Try to draw the relevant ray diagrams yourself before looking at Figure 4.9.

## Real image in a converging lens

Figure 4.9 shows how the image is formed when the object is outside the focus. In each case, the image formed is real and inverted (upside down).

- A: When the object is outside $2 f$, the real image is diminished.
- B: When the object is at $2 f$, the real image is the same size as the object and at $2 f$ on the other side of the lens.
- C: When the object is between $2 f$ and $f$, the real image is magnified. The nearer to $f$ the object is placed, the larger the image.


## For a converging lens:

If the object is outside the focus, the image is real and located at the opposite side of the lens to the object. The image is inverted (i.e. upside down).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-066.jpg?height=1290&width=1196&top_left_y=348&top_left_x=1409)
Figure 4.9 A real image in a converging lens

## Virtual image in a converging lens

Figure 4.10 shows how the image is formed when the object is at the focus or closer. In each case, the image is virtual and the right way up.

- A: The nearer the object is to $f$, the farther the virtual image is from the lens.
- B: With the object at $f$, the image is at infinity.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-066.jpg?height=555&width=2432&top_left_y=2203&top_left_x=192)
Figure 4.10 Effect of different focal lengths in (A) converging and (B) diverging lenses

## For a converging lens:

If the object is inside or at the focus, the image is virtual and it is located at the same side of the lens as the object. The image is upright (i.e. the right way up) and it is magnified.

## A real image:

- Is formed by the actual intersection of rays
- Can be formed on a screen
- Is inverted


## A virtual image:

- Is formed by the apparent intersection of rays
- Cannot be formed on a screen
- Is upright


## The magnifying glass

Figure 4.11 shows again the virtual image produced when the object is inside the focus of a converging lens. The image is upright and magnified. This is a converging lens being used as a magnifying glass, which can be used to make small objects appear bigger (Figure 4.12).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-067.jpg?height=600&width=1183&top_left_y=279&top_left_x=325)
Figure 4.11 A virtual image produced in a converging lens

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-067.jpg?height=607&width=785&top_left_y=276&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 4.12 A magnifying glass makes the text in this nutritional label appear larger

## Image of a distant object in a converging lens

In Figure 4.9 you saw that, as the object moves further away from a converging lens, the image gets nearer to the focus.
It turns out that if an object is a large distance (we say at infinity) from a converging lens, the image formed is real and it is formed at the focus (or more precisely, on the focal plane).
This is because light from any point on a distant object arrives at the lens as a beam of parallel light.
Suppose $P$ is a point on an object that is a large distance from a converging lens (Figure 4.13). $P$ gives out light in all directions. What will the rays striking the lens look like?
The rays are diverging when they leave $P$, but because $P$ is so far away, when they arrive at the lens, the amount by which they diverge is tiny and therefore hard to detect

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-067.jpg?height=796&width=1189&top_left_y=1233&top_left_x=1556)
Figure 4.13 Image of a distant object in a converging lens

or measure. So for all practical purposes, light from $P$ arrives at the lens as a parallel beam. You would see that the lens converges the beam to a point on the focal plane at the other side of the lens.
Rays from another point $Q$ on the distant object will also arrive as a parallel beam. This beam will have a slightly different angle of incidence on the lens, and so it will converge at a different point on the focal plane.
A real image is therefore formed on the focal plane. This image is inverted and much smaller than the object (Figure 4.14).

Note: If an object is a large distance (we say at infinity) from a converging lens, the image formed is real and at the focus (or more precisely, on the focal plane).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-067.jpg?height=574&width=831&top_left_y=2304&top_left_x=1914)
Figure 4.14 A converging lens produces a real image of a distant window on a screen.

### 4.3 Formula for a converging lens

A simple formula applies to a converging lens when the image formed is real. This formula is given to you on page 60 of the Formulae and Tables, and you will do an experiment to verify that the formula is correct (Student Experiment 4.1).
If the image is virtual, a slightly different version of the formula is used.
Let $u$ be the distance from the object to the optic centre of the lens, let $v$ be the distance from the image to the optic centre of the lens, and let $f$ be the focal length.

## For a converging lens:

If the image is real: $\quad \frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}$
(F\&T, page 60)
If the image is virtual: $\quad \frac{1}{u}-\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}$

## Worked Example 1

## Question

An object is placed 40 cm from a converging lens of focal length 30 cm .
Find the position and nature of the image.

## Solution

Here $u=40, f=30$ and $v$ is to be found.
Since the object is outside the focus, the image is real and the formula to be used is:

$$
\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}
$$

Note that even if you are not sure whether the image is real or virtual, you can still use this formula. If $v$ then turns out to be positive, the image is real; if $v$ turns out to be negative, the image is virtual.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{f} \\
\frac{1}{40}+\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{30} \\
\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{30}-\frac{1}{40} \\
\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{4-3}{120} \\
& =\frac{1}{120} \\
v & =120
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the image is real and 120 cm at the other side of the lens to the object.

## Worked Example 2

## Question

An object is placed 10 cm in front of a converging lens of focal length 20 cm .
Find the position and nature of the image.

## Solution

The object is inside the focus, therefore the image is virtual and the formula to use is: $\frac{1}{u}-\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}$. However, let's assume we don't know whether the image is real or virtual and use the formula $\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{f} \\
\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{20} \\
\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{20}-\frac{1}{10} \\
\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1-2}{20} \\
\frac{1}{v} & =-\frac{1}{20} \\
v & =-20
\end{aligned}
$$

A negative value for $v$ tells us the image is virtual. It is 20 cm from the lens at the same side of the lens as the object.

## Summary

For a converging lens: $\quad \frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}$
(F\&T, page 60)
where $u$ is always positive:
> $v$ is positive for a real image
> $v$ is negative for a virtual image

## Student Experiment 4.1

To verify the mathematical model $\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}$ for a converging lens

## Summary of method

In this experiment，you will place an illuminated cross－threads as an object in front of a converging lens，and locate the image on a screen．You will measure the distance $u$ from the cross－threads to the centre of the lens and the distance $v$ from the image on the screen to the centre of the lens．
For each pair of data values，you will calculate the value of $\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}$ and，from that，a value of $f$ ．You will calculate the average value of $f$ and confirm that it is the same as the known focal length of the lens，thus verifying the model．

## Equipment

A converging lens of known focal length，a stand for the lens，a ray box，a sheet of white cardboard，a retort stand and clamp，a metre stick and an illuminated object．
The illuminated object can be made by cutting a small hole（about 1 cm in diameter）in a sheet of cardboard and sticking two pieces of thread across it（forming cross－threads）．The ray box can then be shone through the hole．

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-070.jpg?height=754&width=1444&top_left_y=2675&top_left_x=686)
Figure 4.17

## Method

1. Find an approximate value for the focal length by focusing an image of a distant object (such as a window several metres away) on the screen. The distance from the image to the lens is approximately its focal length. Measure and record this distance.
2. Set up the equipment as shown in Figure 4.17. The illuminated object should be a distance from the lens greater than the rough focal length found in Step 1.
3. Adjust the position of the cardboard screen until the image of the cross-threads is in sharpest focus and most clearly visible on it.
4. With a metre stick, measure the distance $u$ from the cross-threads to the centre of the lens and then measure the distance $v$ from the real image on the cardboard screen to the centre of the lens. Read these values to three significant figures where possible. Record these values.
5. Change the value of $u$ and repeat Steps 3 and 4. Do this at least four more times. Some values of $u$ should be chosen to give a diminished image and some to give a magnified one.

## Experimental data and results

Approximate focal length found by focusing image of distant object on screen =

| $u(\mathrm{~cm})$ | $v(\mathrm{~cm})$ | $\frac{1}{u}$ | $\frac{1}{v}$ | $\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}$ | $f(\mathrm{~cm})$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |

## Handling the data

## Method 1

1. Complete the table and observe that the values of $\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}$ are all approximately the same. When calculating the values of $\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}$, retain at least three significant figures in your calculations.
2. Calculate the average value of $f$. You will see that it is the same as the known focal length of the lens (or of the approximate value found in Step 1, if the true value is unknown), thus verifying the model.

## Method 2

1. For each pair $u$ and $v$, calculate the value of $\frac{1}{u}$ and of $\frac{1}{v}$.
2. On graph paper, plot a graph of values of $\frac{1}{u}$ against corresponding values of $\frac{1}{v}$. Draw the straight line that best fits the points and produce it to meet both axes.
3. Read from the graph the value of $\frac{1}{u}$ where the graph cuts the $\frac{1}{u}$ axis.
4. Read the value of $\frac{1}{v}$ where it cuts the $\frac{1}{v}$ axis.
5. Get the average of these two values $\left(=\frac{1}{f}\right)$. This is the focal length of the lens. It should agree closely with the known focal length of the lens, thus verifying the model.

## Sources of error

Errors arise when:
a) Judging when the image is in sharpest focus on the screen. This will cause random error in measuring $v$.
b) Measuring the distance from the optic centre of the lens. This can cause random error in measuring both $u$ and $v$. However, if you only measure to the surface of the lens, you will introduce systematic error also,
c) Using the metre stick. Ensure you avoid parallax error. This error would be systematic if you always read the scale from the same incorrect angle. It would be random if you viewed it from a different angle each time.

## For a diverging lens:

1. The image is always virtual and upright (i.e. the right way up) and located on the same side of the lens as the object.
2. The image is always diminished. The nearer the object is to the lens, the bigger the image is.

### 4.5 Formula for a diverging lens

A simple formula applies to a diverging lens. You need not prove the formula. Just simply remember it.
Let $u$ be the distance from the object to the optic centre of the lens, let $v$ be the distance from the image to the optic centre of the lens, and let $f$ be the focal length.

## For a diverging lens:

$$
\frac{1}{u}-\frac{1}{v}=-\frac{1}{f}
$$

The following formula summarises both the converging and the diverging lens:

$$
\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}
$$

(F\&T, page 60)
where: $u$ is always positive
$v$ is positive for a real image
$f$ is positive for a converging lens
$v$ is negative for a virtual image
$f$ is negative for a diverging lens

## Worked Example 3

## Question

An object is placed 40 cm from a diverging lens of focal length 50 cm . Find the position and nature of the image.

## Solution

Here $u=40 \mathrm{~cm}, f=50 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $v$ is unknown.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{u}-\frac{1}{v} & =-\frac{1}{f} \\
\frac{1}{40}-\frac{1}{v} & =-\frac{1}{50} \\
-\frac{1}{v} & =-\frac{1}{50}-\frac{1}{40} \\
\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{50}+\frac{1}{40} \\
\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{(4+5)}{200}=0.045 \\
v & =22.2 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

The image is virtual and 22.2 cm from the lens.

### 4.6 Uses of lenses in technological and medical contexts

## Correcting defects of vision

Figure 4.22 shows a simple diagram of the eye.

- The retina is a light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye. If light strikes the retina, electrical signals are sent to the brain through the optic nerve. The result is sight.
- The cornea and the lens together form a converging system. Light from an object is focused by this system, producing a real image on the retina.
- When a real image is brought into focus on the retina, that object is seen clearly. If the image is brought to focus in front of or behind the retina, the object is seen blurred.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-074.jpg?height=698&width=844&top_left_y=2988&top_left_x=1777)
Figure 4.22

| Short-sighted | Long-sighted |
| :--- | :--- |
| A short-sighted person can see nearby objects clearly, but cannot bring distant objects into focus. <br> Short sight can be corrected with a diverging lens, as shown in Figure 4.23. This person needs distance glasses. | A long-sighted person can see distant objects clearly, but cannot bring nearby objects into focus. <br> Long sight can be corrected with a converging lens, as shown in Figure 4.24. This person needs reading glasses. |
| A <br> Distant object | A <br> B |

Figure 4.23 Short-sighted eye viewing a distant object (A) without and (B) with distance glasses

Figure 4.24 Long-sighted eye viewing a nearby object (A) without and (B) with reading glasses

## The camera

Film cameras, digital cameras and phone cameras all have a converging lens. This produces a real image on film or on a digital sensor, which records the image (Figure 4.25).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-075.jpg?height=581&width=1228&top_left_y=2011&top_left_x=1517)

Figure 4.27 How images are formed and magnified in a compound microscope. (A) The object is placed outside but near the focus of the objective lens. (B) The real image is then placed inside the focus of the eyepiece lens.

## The astronomical telescope

In an astronomical telescope, a converging lens (the objective lens) produces a real image of a distant object on its focal plane (just like that in Figure 4.13). As in the compound microscope, this image is then placed inside the focus of the eyepiece lens, which behaves as a magnifying glass and magnifies the image (Figure 4.28).

### 4.7 Models in physics

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-076.jpg?height=675&width=1196&top_left_y=1171&top_left_x=1425)
Figure 4.28 An astronomical telescope

In the last three chapters, you have looked at the behaviour of light in different circumstances. Using some basic experimental results, you should have gained knowledge that allows you to explain many optical phenomena, and to predict how light will behave in certain situations. In this process, you will have created what scientists call a model.
The model in this case is called the geometrical optics model of light, or the ray model of light.
Your underlying assumptions were:

- Light travels in straight-line paths called rays.
- Light obeys the laws of reflection.
- Light obeys the laws of refraction.

You should have also done experiments in the lab, to verify that these results hold.
At Junior Cycle, you used the ray model of light to explain shadows, the seasons, the phases of the moon and eclipses.
In the last three chapters, you used the ray model to predict and explain the following:

- Image formation in a plane mirror, and hence how a periscope works
- How curved mirrors can be used in searchlights, solar furnaces, car mirrors, etc.
- Why water looks less deep than it actually is
- Total internal reflection, and why Snell's Window occurs
- Optical fibres, endoscopes and laparoscopes
- Image formation by converging and diverging lenses
- How to correct the eye for short and long sight, using lenses
- The basic operation of a microscope, telescope and camera

Geometrical optics is a very powerful model. However, it is only a model. Its assumptions are approximations and can become invalid in certain circumstances. For example:

- The shadows produced by point sources of light are not truly sharp if examined closely.
- Light will only travel in a straight line if we keep it away from very small objects or very small gaps ( $<10^{-2} \mathrm{~mm}$ ).
- To explain phenomena at this small level, you need to look at a more sophisticated model of light, known as the wave model.


# 5 Speed, Displacement and Velocity

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand speed, average speed, constant speed and instantaneous speed
- To ensure students understand displacement, velocity, average velocity, constant velocity and instantaneous velocity
- To help students appreciate that if average speed is measured over a very short time interval or over a very small distance, its value is the instantaneous speed to a very high degree of accuracy
- To ensure students can draw a displacement-time graph, given appropriate data
- To ensure students can interpret and describe the motion that a particular displacement-time graph represents


### 5.1 Time

- The SI unit of time is the second (s).
- Time is a scalar quantity, which means it has no direction in space. This is explained more fully in Chapter 7.
- The symbol for time is $t$.
- Small amounts of time are measured in milliseconds (ms), microseconds ( $\mu \mathrm{s}$ ) or nanoseconds (ns).
- Larger time intervals are usually measured in hours, days or years.
- When calculating numerical problems in physics, time should always be expressed in seconds.
- In the laboratory, you measure time with a stopwatch, a stop-clock or an electronic timer (Figure 5.1).

The SI unit of time is the second (s).

Note: 1 millisecond $(\mathrm{ms})=10^{-3} \mathrm{~s}$
1 microsecond $(\mu \mathrm{s})=10^{-6} \mathrm{~s}$
1 nanosecond (ns) $=10^{-9} \mathrm{~s}$
(F\&T, page 45)

## Worked Example 1

## Question

How many seconds are there in one year?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \text { year } & =365 \text { days } \\
& =(365)(24) \text { hours } \\
& =(365)(24)(60) \text { minutes } \\
& =(365)(24)(60)(60) \text { seconds } \\
& =31536000 \text { seconds } \\
& =3.1536 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Keywords

- Time
- Second (s)
- Scalar
- Distance
- Metre (m)
- Speed
- Metre per second ( $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ )
- Average speed
- Constant speed
- Instantaneous speed
- Displacement
- Vector
- Velocity
- Average velocity
- Constant velocity
- Instantaneous velocity
- Displacement-time graph
- Tangent

### 5.2 Distance

- The Sl unit of distance is the metre (m).
- Distance is a scalar quantity.
- The symbol for distance is $s$ or $d$.
- Small distances can be measured in centimetres (cm), millimetres (mm), micrometres $(\mu \mathrm{m})$ or nanometres $(\mathrm{nm})$.
- Longer distances can be measured in kilometres.
- When calculating numerical problems in physics, distances should always be expressed in metres.

The SI unit of distance is the metre (m).
In the laboratory, you can use a measuring tape or a metre stick, or a data logger and motion sensor to measure distances.
For smaller distances, you can use analogue or digital vernier calipers (Figure 5.2).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-079.jpg?height=724&width=518&top_left_y=712&top_left_x=1380)

(B) Digital vernier calipers. Vernier calipers can measure distance to an accuracy of 0.01 cm .

### 5.3 Speed

- Speed is the rate of change of distance with respect to time. The symbol for speed is $v$ or $u$.
- Speed is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is metre per second (m s-1).

Speed is the rate of change of distance with respect to time.
The SI unit of speed is the metre per second ( $\mathbf{m ~ s}^{-1}$ or m/s).

## Average speed

If an object travels a distance $s$ in a time $t$, its average speed during that time is, by definition, equal to $\frac{s}{t}$. In words, this is the total distance travelled divided by the time taken.
Sometimes, instead of $s$ and $t$, the symbol $\Delta s$ (the change in $s$ ) is used to represent a distance travelled and $\Delta t$ (the change in $t$ ) is used to represent the time taken. Using this notation:

Average speed during the time interval $=\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$
The unit for speed is metre per second, since:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Average speed }=\frac{\text { distance }}{\text { time }} \\
& \text { Unit of speed }=\frac{\text { unit of distance }}{\text { unit of time }} \\
& \begin{aligned}
\text { Unit of speed } & =\frac{\text { metre }}{\text { second }} \\
& =\text { metre per second } \\
& =\mathrm{ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

Average speed $=\frac{\text { distance }}{\text { time }}$ or, using symbols:

$$
v=\frac{s}{t}
$$

Or:

$$
v=\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A sprinter runs 200 metres in 22 seconds. Calculate her average speed over the 200 m.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { average speed } & =\frac{\text { distance }}{\text { time }} \\
& =\frac{200}{22} \\
& =9.09 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

A man walks with an average speed of $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. How long will it take him to walk 1 km ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { time taken } & =\frac{\text { distance travelled }}{\text { average speed }} \\
& =\frac{1000}{2} \\
& =500 \text { seconds }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Constant speed

An object has a constant speed if it neither speeds up nor slows down. Or more precisely, an object moves with constant speed if its average speed is always the same, regardless of which part of the journey it is measured over. The words 'steady' or 'uniform' are sometimes used instead of 'constant'.

## Varying speed

Most moving objects have varying speed. Sometimes they are speeding up and at other times they are slowing down. For example, if you drop something, it moves downwards with increasing speed.

## Speed at an instant (instantaneous speed)

Suppose you are travelling in a car and, at a certain instant, the reading on the speedometer is $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
This does not necessarily mean that the car travelled 10 m in the last second. Nor does it necessarily mean that the car will travel 10 m in the next second.
It does, however, mean that the car would travel 10 m in the next second if the car's speed stopped changing at that instant and remained constant from then on.
$10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ is called the car's instantaneous speed (Figure 5.4).

## Measuring instantaneous speed

In practice, to measure instantaneous speed, the average speed is measured over a very short time interval or a very small distance. The calculated value is the instantaneous speed to a high degree of accuracy at any instant during that short time interval. If more accuracy is required, the time interval or distance is made smaller.

Note: If average speed is measured over a very short time interval or a very small distance, its value is the instantaneous speed to very high degree of accuracy at any instant during that short time interval.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-081.jpg?height=538&width=1199&top_left_y=1914&top_left_x=325)
Figure 5.4 The speedometer on a car shows the car's speed at any instant.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-081.jpg?height=792&width=1199&top_left_y=1497&top_left_x=1546)
Figure 5.5 The fastest land-speed record over one mile is $1227.985 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}(763.035 \mathrm{mph})$. This was achieved by Andy Green in Thrust SSC in October 1997, and the record still stands today. Thrust is the first car to have travelled faster than sound.

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A dog runs along a road at a constant speed of $3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
a) How far will it travel in 10 s ?
b) How far will it travel in $\frac{1}{4}$ hour?

## Solution

a) distance $=$ speed × time

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(3)(10) \\
& =30 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) First convert hours to seconds:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.25 \text { hours } & =15 \text { minutes } \\
& =(15)(60) \text { seconds } \\
& =900 \mathrm{~s} \\
\text { distance } & =\text { speed × time } \\
& =(3)(900) \\
& =2700 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A car has a steady speed of $63 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$.
a) How far does it travel in 12 seconds?
b) How long does it take it to travel 400 m ?

## Solution

a) Convert $\mathrm{km} \mathrm{h}^{-1}$ to $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
63 \text { kilometres per hour } & =63000 \text { metres per hour } \\
& =\frac{63000}{(60)(60)} \mathrm{ms}^{-1} \\
& =17.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \\
\text { distance } & =\text { speed × time } \\
& =(17.5)(12) \\
& =210 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) time $=$ distance × speed

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{400}{17.5} \\
& =22.9 \text { seconds }
\end{aligned}
$$

### 5.4 Displacement

Suppose a man walks from $A$ to $B$ by the path shown in Figure 5.6. When he is at $B$, he is 40 metres north-east of $A$. His displacement from $A$ is now 40 metres north-east. You can also say that he underwent a displacement of 40 metres north-east in going from $A$ to $B$.

Note: The displacement undergone by the man in Figure 5.6 is different from the distance he travelled, since the distance is the length of the curved path he took.

Displacement is distance in a given direction.

- The symbol for displacement is $s$.
- The unit of displacement is the metre (m).
- Displacement is a vector quantity, since it has a direction (this is explained further in Chapter 7).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-082.jpg?height=922&width=987&top_left_y=2793&top_left_x=1634)
Figure 5.6 The displacement of $B$ from $A$ is 40 m north-east (or $40 \mathrm{~m} 45^{\circ}$ north of east).

### 5.5 Velocity

Velocity is a quantity very like speed; velocity is simply speed in a given direction. For example, if a car is moving northwards at a speed of $20 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, it has a velocity of $20 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ north.

Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time.

- The usual symbol for velocity is $v$ or $u$.
- The unit of velocity is the metre per second ( $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ or $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ ).
- Velocity is a vector quantity.

The unit of velocity is metre per second (m s-1 or m/s).

## Average velocity

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average velocity } & =\frac{\text { distance travelled in a given direc }}{\text { time taken }} \\
\text { or } \quad \text { Average velocity } & =\frac{\text { displacement undergone }}{\text { time taken }}
\end{aligned}
$$

These definitions are equivalent, since distance travelled in a given direction is the definition of displacement.

## Worked Example 6

## Question

In 12 seconds, a man travels from $A$ to $B$ by the path shown in Figure 5.6. The total distance travelled is 68 m . The overall displacement he undergoes is 40 m north-east. Calculate:
a) His average speed
b) His average velocity

## Solution

a) average speed $=\frac{\text { distance travelled }}{\text { time taken }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{68}{12} \\
& =5.67 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) average velocity $=\frac{\text { displacement undergone }}{\text { time taken }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{40 \text { metres north-east }}{12 \text { seconds }} \\
& =3.33 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \text { north-east }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Constant velocity

A body has constant velocity if all the following are true:

- It does not speed up
- It does not slow down
- It does not change direction.

Its average velocity is the same, no matter the time interval (during the motion) over which it is measured.
If an object moves in a straight line and does not speed up or slow down, it has a constant velocity.

## Varying velocity

If a moving object does not have constant velocity, it is said to have varying velocity. Figure 5.8 shows a freely falling object near the Earth's surface. It moves in a straight line downwards, with increasing speed. Therefore, its velocity is varying. Figure 5.9 shows a stone moving in a circular path with a constant speed. Its speed does not change, but its velocity is changing because the direction in which it moves is always changing.

Note: Just as average speed is equal to instantaneous speed if measured over a very short time interval or small distance, average velocity = instantaneous velocity (to a high degree of accuracy), provided the average velocity is measured over a very short time interval or over a very small distance.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-084.jpg?height=1001&width=795&top_left_y=1106&top_left_x=1110)
Figure 5.8 As the bone falls, its speed increases. Therefore, its velocity is varying even though it moves in a straight line.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-084.jpg?height=825&width=688&top_left_y=1106&top_left_x=1933)
Figure 5.9 The stone is moving around in a circle at a steady speed. The direction in which it moves is continually changing. Therefore, it has a varying velocity.

### 5.6 Measuring velocity in the laboratory

To find the velocity of an object moving in a straight line, physicists measure the time taken for the object to move a given distance. Dividing the distance by the time will give its average speed and including the direction will give its average velocity. There are many different sets of laboratory equipment that will allow you to measure velocity.

## Measuring velocity with a ticker timer and ticker tape

Ticker tape is a thin strip of paper on which a black dot appears when it is struck by a pointed object. The tape can be attached to a moving object (such as a trolley) with a thumbtack, so that when the trolley moves, it pulls the tape through the ticker timer (Figure 5.13).
The ticker timer operates on a 50 Hz AC source, so that a striker in it hits the ticker tape 50 times per second. This means it produces a dot on the tape every $\frac{1}{50}$ th of a second. From the tape, the distance travelled and the time taken to travel that

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-085.jpg?height=566&width=1316&top_left_y=2993&top_left_x=1430)
Figure 5.13

distance can be found. And, from this the (average) speed of the trolley can also be calculated, as shown in Worked Example 7.

## Worked Example 7

## Question

Find the velocity of the trolley that produced the ticker tape shown in Figure 5.14. The trolley moved in a straight line and the distance between dots $A$ and $B$ is 15 cm .

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-086.jpg?height=235&width=1203&top_left_y=641&top_left_x=240)
Figure 5.14 A piece of ticker tape from an object moving with constant velocity.

## Solution

On the tape, the dots are evenly spaced. This means the velocity is constant.

$$
15 \mathrm{~cm}=0.15 \mathrm{~m}
$$

Number of spaces between $A$ and $B=10$. Each space represents $\frac{1}{50}$ th of a second.
Therefore, time taken to travel from $A$ to $B=10 \times \frac{1}{50} \mathrm{~s}=0.2 \mathrm{~s}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { velocity } & =\frac{\text { distance }}{\text { time }} \\
& =\frac{0.15}{0.2} \\
& =0.75 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now answer the questions in the following table. They refer to the trolley in Figure 5.13. Try to answer each question before looking at the corresponding answer in the right-hand column or moving on to the next question.

| Question | Answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| If you put a trolley on a horizontal runway and give it a push, will it move at constant velocity? | No, it slows down (and comes to a stop if the runway is long enough). |
| Why does it slow down? | The force of friction between the trolley and the runway slows it down (see page 76). |
| How could you prevent the trolley from slowing down? | Raise the starting end of the runway by the right amount. |
| What happens if you raise the runway too much? | The trolley will speed up. |
| Other than by looking at it, how could you check that the trolley is moving at a constant velocity? | Using a ticker timer and ticker tape, the dots produced would be evenly spaced. |
| If the trolley was slowing down or speeding up, what would the ticker tape look like? | The dots would be getting closer if it is slowing down. <br> The dots would be getting further apart if it was speeding up |

## Student Experiment 5.1 （Method A）

To investigate the constant linear motion of a trolley using a ticker timer and ticker tape

## Summary of method

In this experiment，you will cause a trolley to move along a runway at a constant velocity．From the evenly spaced dots on the ticker tape attached to it，you will calculate the trolley＇s velocity．You will also confirm that it was，in fact，moving at a constant velocity．

## Equipment

A trolley，a runway，a ticker timer and ticker tape，a suitable power supply，a metre stick and a thumbtack．

## Method

1．Dust the runway and trolley wheels to remove any grit or dirt，which could cause the velocity to vary．
2．Compensate the runway for friction．To do this，raise one end of the runway by resting it on wooden blocks or books（Figure 5．15）．Adjust the height until the trolley，if given a gentle push，moves down the runway at constant velocity．
3．Place the timer and the trolley on the raised end of the runway．Pass a suitable length of tape through the timer and attach it to the trolley with a thumbtack．Ensure that the tape can run freely through the timer．
4．Switch on the timer and give the trolley a gentle push．It should move away with constant velocity．
5．Stop the trolley at the end of the runway，switch off the timer and remove the ticker tape．It should have a series of equally spaced dots on it，like the tape shown in Figure 5．14．
6．Ignoring the unevenly spaced dots at the start of the tape（which were produced when you were pushing the trolley），measure and record the distance（ $s$ ）between two dots（ $A$ and $B$ ）with a metre stick．Be careful to avoid parallax error when using the metre stick．
7．Count the number of spaces $(n)$ between $A$ and $B$ ．This is the number $(n)$ of fiftieths of a second that it took the trolley to move through distance $s$ ．Record this number．
8．Complete the table below，calculating the time $t$ and the average velocity between $A$ and $B$ ．
9．From the tape，also calculate the average velocity over the first 5 spaces from $A$ and the average velocity over the last 5 spaces ending at $B$ ．Within the tolerance of experimental error，these should be the same and equal to the value from $A$ to $B$ ．This will allow you to verify that the trolley was moving at a constant velocity．
10．Repeat the experiment with the trolley travelling at different constant velocities．

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-087.jpg?height=593&width=1364&top_left_y=2132&top_left_x=1339)
Figure 5．15 A ticker timer and ticker tape can be used to measure the constant velocity of a trolley．

## Table of results

| Distance，$s$（m） | No．of spaces，$n$ | Time taken，$t(\mathrm{~s})$ $n \times \frac{1}{50}$ | Velocity，$v\left(\mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right)$ $v=\frac{s}{t}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |

Note：You could measure the distance between two consecutive dots on the tape and divide it by $\frac{1}{50}$ th of a second to calculate the velocity．However，this result would tend to be inaccurate since errors in measuring a small length will be a significant percentage of this length．

## Sources of error

- Dirt or grit on the runway or surface of the wheels can cause the velocity to vary. Make sure these are clean.
- If the trolley wheels cannot rotate freely, the velocity can vary. Lubricate or oil the wheel bearings.
- Make sure to use the metre stick correctly when measuring the distance, avoiding parallax error.


## Questions

1. Why is the runway raised at one end?
2. How do you know when it is raised to the correct height?
3. If the dots on the tape are not evenly spaced, what does this tell you about the velocity of the trolley? What should you do to remedy this?

## The linear air track

- A linear air track is a long rigid tube with a series of holes along both of its upper faces (Figure 5.16).
- Air from a blower comes out of the holes and lifts a V-shaped metal rider up just above the track, so that the rider appears to float on a cushion of air. There is no friction between the rider and the track.
- If you then give the rider a gentle push, it moves off readily. If the track is level, it should keep going with constant velocity until it reaches the end of the track. The track can be made level using levelling screws on the legs.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-088.jpg?height=896&width=1905&top_left_y=1849&top_left_x=195)
Figure 5.16 A linear air track, a light gate and a scaler timer

## Measuring velocity with a light gate and a scaler timer

A light gate and a scaler timer can also be used with a linear air track to measure velocity. In the light gate, a beam of light shines onto a photo diode (Figure 5.16). When the beam of light is blocked by something passing through the light gate, the timer starts. When the interruption stops, the timer stops, giving a total time during which the object is passing through the gate. If a piece of card of known length (say 4 cm) is mounted on the rider, this distance can be used with the recorded time to find the velocity of the rider as it passes through the light gate. Since the time interval over which the velocity is measured is small, the measured velocity will be very near to the instantaneous velocity of the rider at any point during which it passes through the light gate.

## Student Experiment 5.1 (Method B)

To investigate the constant linear motion of a rider on a linear air track using a light gate and a scaler timer

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will cause a metal rider to move along a linear air track at a constant velocity. By directly measuring the time taken for the rider to travel a known distance, you will calculate its velocity. By measuring its velocity at two different places, you will confirm that its velocity was constant.

## Equipment

A linear air track, an air blower and a rider, a scaler timer, a light gate and a metre stick, a retort stand and clamp, and a spirit level.

## Method

1. Place the air track on the bench and adjust the levelling screws until the track looks level. Check this with a spirit level.
2. Turn on the air blower and place the rider on the track.
3. Further adjust the levelling screws until the rider stays still, without sliding in either direction at any place on the track. The track is now level. If the rider is given a gentle push, it should move along the track at constant velocity. Turn off the blower.
4. Mount the light gate on a retort stand and connect it to the scaler timer (Figure 5.16). Place the timing gate about halfway down the track at such a height that the card on the rider will interrupt the light beam without hitting the gate.
5. Turn on the timer and check that the light gate and timer are operating properly. The numbers on the clock of the timer should be changing when the light beam is broken.
6. Reset the timer to zero.
7. Connect the piece of card onto the rider and make sure it is parallel to the direction in which the rider will move. Turn on the blower and give the rider a push. It will move along the track at a constant velocity.
8. Record the value on the timer (the transit time, $t$ ) in a results table like the one shown below.
9. With a metre stick, measure the length $l$ of the card. Record this. Make sure to avoid parallax error when using the metre stick.
10. Complete the results table by calculating the value of the velocity.
11. If a second timing gate is available, find the velocity of the rider at another point on the track. See if the rider is moving at constant velocity.
12. Repeat the experiment several times with the rider travelling at a different velocity each time.

## Table of results

| Length of card, $l(\mathrm{~m})$ | Transit time, $t(\mathrm{~s})$ | Velocity, $v\left(\mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right)$ <br> $v=\frac{l}{t}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
|  |  |  |
|  |  |  |

## Sources of error

- Parallax error using the metre stick to measure the length of the card.
- The card on the rider may not be parallel to the direction in which the rider is moving.
- The light beam may not be perpendicular to both the card and the direction in which the rider is moving.


## Questions

1. Why should the track be level?
2. How could you be sure that the track was level?
3. Other than by watching it move, how would you know if the rider was not moving at constant velocity?

### 5.7 Displacement-time graphs

In Junior Cycle science, you studied distance-time graphs. Now you will look at these in more detail and consider displacement-time graphs.
In Figure 5.17, a car moves along a straight road travelling east. The distance of the front of the car from a point $P$ on the road is measured every second. For example, after four seconds, its distance is 12 m east of $P$. The data is recorded in Table 5.1.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-090.jpg?height=701&width=1423&top_left_y=423&top_left_x=1198)
Figure 5.17 A car moves along a straight road travelling east

| Time (s) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | ---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Distance east of <br> $P(\mathrm{~m})$ | 0 | 3 | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 18 | 21 |

## Table 5.1

The data in Table 5.1 can be plotted on a graph (Figure 5.18). This type of graph is called a distance-time graph or, if the direction of motion is factored in, a displacement-time graph.
From the graph you can see that:

- Since the graph passes through the origin, the car was at $P$ when $t=0$.
- As time increases, the distance and the displacement of the car from $P$ also increase.
- Since the graph is a straight line, the speed of the car is constant (if you find the average speed from the graph over any time interval, it will always be the same).
- Since its speed is constant and the car is moving in the same direction, its velocity is also constant.


## The slope of a displacement-time graph is the velocity

You saw at Junior Cycle that the slope of a distance-time graph is the speed. Likewise, the slope of a displacement-time graph is the velocity.
Figure 5.19 is a displacement-time graph of an object moving in a straight line at constant velocity. If the displacement at time $t_{1}$ is $s_{1}$, and at time $t_{2}$ it is $s_{2}$, then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Slope of graph } & =\frac{\text { rise }}{\text { run }} \\
& =\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}} \\
& =\frac{s_{2}-s_{1}}{t_{2}-t_{1}} \\
& =\frac{\text { displacement undergone in time } t_{2}-t_{1}}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\text { velocity }
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-090.jpg?height=1124&width=896&top_left_y=1608&top_left_x=1725)
Figure 5.18

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-090.jpg?height=675&width=896&top_left_y=2858&top_left_x=1725)
Figure 5.19

Note: A displacement-time graph for an object moving with constant velocity is a straight line. The slope of the graph is the velocity of the object.

In Figure 5.20, an object is moving in a straight line. The displacement, in metres, of the object from a fixed point $O$ on the line is measured continuously. Displacements to the right of $O$ are given a positive sign and those to the left of $O$ have a negative sign.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-091.jpg?height=310&width=1645&top_left_y=332&top_left_x=1048)
Figure 5.20

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average velocity } & =\frac{\text { displacement undergone in time }}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{s_{2}-s_{1}}{t_{2}-t_{1}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if an object is moving to the right, its velocity will be positive (since $s_{2}-s_{1}$ will be positive).
If an object is moving to the left, its velocity will be negative (since $s_{2}-s_{1}$ will be negative). Suppose you draw a displacement-time graph of its motion. Since the velocity is the slope of the graph, the following must be true:

- If the slope is zero (a horizontal line), the object is stopped.
- If the slope is positive, the object is moving to the right.
- If the slope is negative, the object is moving to the left.
- If the slope changes, the object's velocity changes.
- If the slope increases (the graph gets steeper), the object is speeding up.
- If the slope decreases (gets less steep), the object is slowing down.

## Equipment

A runway, a trolley, a motion sensor, and a data logger and computer.
