## Worked Example 8

## Question

An object moves along the $x$-axis (Figure 5.20, page 79). Its displacement, in metres, from the origin $O$ is measured. Displacements to the right of $O$ are given a positive sign and those to the left of $O$ a negative sign.
Figure 5.22 is a displacement-time graph of the object for the first 25 seconds after the clock was started. Describe the motion in detail.

## Solution

For the first 5 seconds, the object is stopped at a point 3 m to the right of the origin (region $A$ to $B$ ).

For the next 4 seconds it moves to the right at a speed of $0.75 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (slope of $B$ to $C$ ) until it is at a point 6 m to the right of $O$.

It then stops and remains stopped for the next 3 seconds (region $C$ to $D$ ).

For the next 5 seconds, it reverses its direction of motion. It moves to the left, passing the origin after 3 seconds and arriving at a point 4 m to the left of the origin when the 5 seconds are up. Its velocity here is $-2.0 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (slope of $D$ to $F$ ).

It immediately reverses direction again and heads back to the origin at a speed of $+0.67 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (slope of $F$ to $G$ ), arriving there 6 seconds later.
It remains stopped at the origin for the next 2 seconds.
There is no further information available after that.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-092.jpg?height=975&width=1044&top_left_y=458&top_left_x=1519)
Figure 5.22 Displacement-time graph of the object for first 25 seconds

## Worked Example 9

## Question

Figure 5.23 shows the displacement-time graph of an object moving in a straight line. Describe the motion.

## Solution

The slope of the graph is always positive. Therefore, the object is always moving in the same direction.

At the end of each second, the slope increases. This means the speed and, therefore, the velocity of the object increases after every second.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-092.jpg?height=1131&width=773&top_left_y=2584&top_left_x=1803)
Figure 5.23

## How to find the slope of a curved displacement-time graph

If the speed of an object is changing continuously, the corresponding displacement-time graph will be a smooth curve. Its slope will also change continuously. The slope at any point on a curved line is the slope of the tangent at that point. This slope is the velocity at that point.
Figure 5.24 shows the displacement-time graph for an object dropped from rest during the first 3 seconds of its motion (for example, the dog's bone in Figure 5.8). The slope of the tangent at the point $(2,19.6)$ is the instantaneous speed of the object after 2 seconds of falling, that is at $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-093.jpg?height=1124&width=997&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=1751)

## Worked Example 10

## Question

a) Figure $5.25(\mathrm{~A})$ is a graph of displacement $s$ against time $t$, over the time interval $t=0 \mathrm{~s}$ to $t=5 \mathrm{~s}$, of an object moving in a straight line.
Is the velocity of the object constant? Justify your answer.
b) Figure 5.25(B) shows the displacement $s$ against time $t$, over the time interval
$t=2.90 \mathrm{~s}$ to $t=3.10 \mathrm{~s}$ for the same object and motion.
Explain why this graph appears to represent a different type of motion to that represented in

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-093.jpg?height=854&width=1492&top_left_y=1617&top_left_x=1214)
Figure 5.25(A)

Figure 5.25(B)

Figure 5.25(A).
c) Use the graph in Figure 5.25(B) to calculate the average velocity of the object over the time interval $t=2.90 \mathrm{~s}$ to $t=3.10 \mathrm{~s}$.
d) Estimate the instantaneous velocity of the car at $t=3.00 \mathrm{~s}$.

## Solution

a) No, velocity is not constant. The slope of the graph increases as time increases. Therefore, the velocity is increasing.
b) Even though the velocity is changing, during the very short time interval in Figure 5.25(B) the change in the velocity is so small that the change in the slope of the graph cannot be detected with the equipment used. The graph is, therefore, approximately a straight line of constant slope. This reflects what you have already learned in this chapter: that if average velocity is measured over a very short time interval, its value is the instantaneous velocity, to a very high degree of accuracy, at any instant during that small time interval.
c) average velocity $=\frac{\text { displacement undergone }}{\text { time taken }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{9.6-8.3}{3.10-2.90} \\
& =6.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

d) The instantaneous velocity, to a very high degree of accuracy, at any instant during that small time interval is the average velocity. Therefore, instantaneous velocity at $t=3 \mathrm{~s}$ is also $6.5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

## Summary What I should know

- The SI unit of time is the second (s).
- The SI unit of distance is the metre (m).
- Speed is the rate of change of distance with respect to time.
- Average speed $=\frac{\text { distance travelled }}{\text { time taken }}$, or $v=\frac{s}{t}$, or $v=\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$
- The SI unit of speed is the metre per second ( $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ or $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ ).
- Displacement is distance in a given direction.
- The SI unit of displacement is the metre (m).
- Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time.
- The SI unit of velocity is the metre per second ( $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ or $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ ).
- Average velocity $=\frac{\text { displacement undergone }}{\text { time taken }}$
- average velocity = instantaneous velocity (to a high degree of accuracy) provided the average velocity is measured over a very short time interval or a very small distance.
- An object has constant velocity if it is not speeding up, not slowing down and not changing direction.
- The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed.
- The slope of a displacement-time graph is the velocity.

Alternatively, if a body moves in a straight line and its velocity changes by an amount $\Delta v$ during a time interval $\Delta t$, its average acceleration is given by:

$$
a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average acceleration }=\frac{\text { change in velocity }}{\text { time taken }} & =\frac{\text { final velocity }- \text { initial velocity }}{\text { time taken }} \\
a & =\frac{v-u}{t} \\
a & =\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}
\end{aligned}
$$

## SI unit of acceleration

Since:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average acceleration } & =\frac{\text { change in velocity }}{\text { time taken }} \\
\text { Unit of acceleration } & =\frac{\text { unit of velocity }}{\text { unit of time }} \\
& =\frac{\text { metre per second }}{\text { second }} \\
& =\text { metre per second squared } \\
& =\mathrm{ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The SI unit of acceleration is the metre per second squared ( $\mathbf{m ~ s}^{\mathbf{- 2}}$ ).

## Worked Example 1

## Question

The velocity of a car changes from $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ east to $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ east in 5 seconds. Calculate its average acceleration.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average acceleration } & =\frac{\text { final velocity }- \text { initial velocity }}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{40-10}{5} \\
& =6 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2} \text { east }
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, this car is gaining speed at the rate of $6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ every second. Or, in other words, its eastward speed is increasing by 6 metres per second every second.

## Worked Example 2

## Question

The speed of a bicycle moving in a straight line decreases from $15 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ to $3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in 6 seconds. Find its average acceleration.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average acceleration } & =\frac{\text { final velocity }- \text { initial velocity }}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{3-15}{6} \\
& =-2 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Here the speed of the bike is decreasing. The acceleration has a negative sign indicating this.
A slowing down or a negative acceleration is sometimes called a deceleration. While the bicycle is slowing down, its speed decreases by an average of $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ every second. It is losing speed at the rate of $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ per second.

### 6.2 Constant (uniform) acceleration

If an object is picking up velocity or losing velocity at the same steady rate, its acceleration is constant (or uniform). In other words, if the average acceleration between any two points in a journey is always the same, that body has constant acceleration.
This chapter will only consider constant acceleration.

## Equations of motion for an object moving in a straight line with constant acceleration

When an object (with initial velocity $u$ ) moves in a straight line with constant acceleration $a$, its displacement $s$ from its starting point and its velocity $v$ change with time $t$. The following equations describe how these quantities are related.

$$
v=u+a t \quad s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \quad v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s
$$

(F\&T, page 50)
These equations are used in Worked Examples 3-6 below. They are also referred to as the 'kinematics equations under constant acceleration'. They are derived on page 90.

Note: Follow this sequence when solving problems with these equations.

- List the quantities you know and the ones you need to calculate.
- Write down the three equations.
- Decide which of the three equations has only one unknown in it.
- Substitute in the known values in this equation and solve for the unknown.


## Worked Example 3

## Question

a) A car starting from rest has an acceleration of $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$. Find:
i) Its velocity after 8 seconds
ii) The distance it travels in 8 seconds
b) After how many seconds is its velocity $100 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ?

## Solution

a) Here $u=0$ (the car starts from rest), $\quad a=4, \quad t=8, \quad v=? \quad$ and $\quad s=$ ?
i) To find $v$ :

Use,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& v=u+a t \\
& v=0+(4)(8) \\
& v=32 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

ii) To find $s$ :

$$
\text { Use, } \begin{aligned}
s & =u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\
s & =(0)(8)+\frac{1}{2}(4)(8)^{2} \\
s & =0+(2)(64) \\
s & =128 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) You have $u=0, a=4, v=100$ and $t$ is unknown. To find $t$ :

$$
\text { Use, } \begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \\
100 & =0+4 t \\
t & =\frac{100}{4}=25 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A car with constant acceleration travels a distance of 100 m while its velocity changes from $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ to $25 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Calculate its acceleration.

## Solution

Here $\quad u=10, \quad v=25, \quad s=100 \quad$ and $\quad a=$ ?
To find $a$ :
Use,

$$
\begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s \\
25^{2} & =10^{2}+2 a(100) \\
625-100 & =200 a \\
a & =2.625 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A car travelling with a speed of $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ passes a pole on the roadside at a certain instant. It immediately accelerates with an acceleration of $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$. How far is it from the pole when its speed is $30 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ?

## Solution

Here $\quad u=10, \quad a=2, \quad v=30 \quad$ and $\quad s=$ ?
To find $s$ :
Use,

$$
\begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s \\
30^{2} & =10^{2}+(2)(2) s \\
900 & =100+4 s \\
800 & =4 s \\
s & =\frac{800}{4} \\
& =200 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 6

## Question

A train, which has a constant acceleration, travels a distance of 2 km in 50 s . If its initial velocity is $20 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, find its acceleration during this time.

## Solution

Here $\quad u=20, \quad s=2000, \quad t=50 \quad$ and $\quad a=$ ?
To find $a$ :
Use, $\quad s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2000 & =(20)(50)+\frac{1}{2} a(50)^{2} \\
2000 & =1000+1250 a \\
1250 a & =1000 \\
a & =\frac{1000}{1250} \\
& =0.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Deriving the equations of motion

To derive $v=u+a t$
From the definition of acceleration, you have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a & =\frac{v-u}{t} \\
a t & =v-u \\
v & =u+a t
\end{aligned}
$$

To derive $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$
It can be proved (and you may assume it to be true) that when the acceleration is constant:

$$
\text { Average velocity }=\frac{\text { initial velocity }- \text { final velocity }}{2}
$$

So,

$$
\text { average velocity }=\frac{u+v}{2}
$$

On page 86 you saw that, average acceleration $=\frac{\text { displacement }}{\text { time }}$
And that,

$$
\text { displacement }=\text { average velocity × time }
$$

So,

$$
s=\frac{u+v}{2} t
$$

Substituting $u+a t$ for $v$ in this equation gives:
which simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& s=\frac{(u+u+a t) t}{2} \\
& s=\frac{(2 u+a t) t}{2} \\
& s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## To derive $\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathbf{2}} \boldsymbol{=} \boldsymbol{u}^{\mathbf{2}} \boldsymbol{+} \mathbf{2 a s}$

Squaring both sides of

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \quad \text { gives } v^{2}=(u+a t)^{2} \\
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 u a t+(a t)^{2} \\
& =u^{2}+2 u a t+a^{2} t^{2} \\
& =u^{2}+2 a\left(u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

But,

$$
u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}=s
$$

So,

$$
v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s
$$

### 6.3 Velocity-time graphs

A graph showing the speed of an object plotted against time is called a speed-time graph.
If the direction of the motion is also specified, it is a velocity-time graph.

## The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration

You saw at Junior Cycle that the slope of a speed-time graph is equal to the acceleration. Likewise, the slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
In Figure 6.3:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Slope of graph } & =\frac{v_{2}-v_{1}}{t_{2}-t_{1}}=\frac{\text { change in velocity in time } t_{2}-t_{1}}{\text { time taken }} \quad\left(\text { slope }=\frac{\text { rise }}{\text { run }}=\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}\right) \\
& =\text { acceleration }
\end{aligned}
$$

In Figure 6.4, the slope of the graph is 2 . This is also the acceleration of the body.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-103.jpg?height=707&width=818&top_left_y=1823&top_left_x=1113)
Figure 6.3

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-103.jpg?height=805&width=809&top_left_y=1823&top_left_x=1946)
Figure 6.4

## Worked Example 7

## Question

Figure 6.5 shows the velocity-time graph of a body moving in a straight line in the same direction. Describe its motion throughout the journey.

## Solution

- For the first 5 seconds, the body's velocity is increasing at a steady rate (region $O$ to $A$ ). Its acceleration is $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ (slope of $O$ to $A$ ).
- For the next 6 seconds, its velocity is constant at $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (region $A$ to $B$ ). Its acceleration is zero (slope of $A$ to $B$ ).
- Its velocity then decreases at a steady rate for the next two

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-103.jpg?height=642&width=913&top_left_y=2858&top_left_x=1793)
Figure 6.5

- Its velocity then remains constant at $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ for the next 6 seconds (region $C$ to $D$ ).

In the final second, it slows down with an acceleration of $-4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ (slope of $D$ to $E$ ) and stops.

## The area under a velocity-time graph is the distance travelled

No matter how complicated the motion, the area under a velocity-time graph is the distance travelled. It's easier to see why this is true when dealing with motion in a straight line. Figure 6.6 shows the graph of a body with initial velocity $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and an acceleration of $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$,
To calculate the area under the graph from $t=0$ to $t=6$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Area under graph } & =\text { area of □ }+ \text { area of } \\
& =(4)(6)+\frac{1}{2}(6)(16-4) \\
& =24+36 \\
& =60
\end{aligned}
$$

Distance travelled in 6 seconds:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-104.jpg?height=623&width=883&top_left_y=390&top_left_x=1738)
Figure 6.6

$$
\begin{aligned}
s & =u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\
& =(4)(6)+\frac{1}{2}(2)(6)^{2} \\
& =24+36 \\
& =60 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

This result is always true, and you can assume it to be so without proof.
A velocity-time graph of a body moving with constant acceleration is a straight line.
The slope is the acceleration.
The area under the graph is the distance travelled.

## Worked Example 8

## Question

An object moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. A velocity-time graph is plotted for the motion. If the object is moving to the right, its velocity is positive. If it is moving to the left, its velocity is negative. Describe the motion represented by each graph in Figure 6.7.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-104.jpg?height=1443&width=1522&top_left_y=2298&top_left_x=289)
Figure 6.7

## Solution

a) The object moves to the right at a steady speed.
b) It moves to the left at a steady speed.
c) It moves to the right, with its speed increasing at a steady rate.
d) It moves to the left, with its speed increasing at a steady rate.
e) It moves to the right with its speed decreasing at a steady rate until it stops and then immediately starts moving to the left with its speed increasing at the same rate.
f) It moves to the left with decreasing speed until it stops and then immediately starts moving to the right with its speed increasing at the same rate.
g) Starting from rest, it moves to the left with its speed increasing at a steady rate.
h) Starting from rest, it moves to the right with its speed increasing at a steady rate. It then slows down at the same rate until it stops and then immediately starts moving to the left with increasing speed. It then slows down at the same rate until it stops.
i) Starting from rest, it moves to the left with its speed increasing at a steady rate. It then slows down at the same rate until it stops.

## Demonstration Experiment 6.1

To demonstrate how a data logger can be used to measure the acceleration of an object

## Equipment

A runway, a trolley, a motion sensor, and a data logger and computer.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-107.jpg?height=473&width=1339&top_left_y=755&top_left_x=371)
Figure 6.11

## Method

1. Place the trolley on the runway and raise one end of the runway until the trolley, if released without pushing, accelerates down the runway (Figure 6.11).
2. Connect the motion sensor to a computer that runs the data-logging software.
3. Set the data-logging software to plot a graph of velocity against time.
4. Place the trolley in front of the motion sensor.
5. Release the trolley down the runway and immediately start the sensor.
6. The data-logging software will produce a velocity-time graph of the motion.
7. You can use the slope tool to measure the acceleration of the trolley at any time from the graph.

### 6.4 Measuring constant acceleration

## Measuring constant acceleration using a ticker timer and ticker tape

A piece of ticker tape is passed through a ticker timer and attached to a trolley. If the trolley then moves with constant acceleration, the dots produced on the tape will become progressively further apart (Figure 6.12). This is because the trolley moves further during each time interval as its speed increases.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-107.jpg?height=493&width=1834&top_left_y=2799&top_left_x=322)
Figure 6.12 Ticker tape from an accelerating object

- Measure the average velocity over three dots (two spaces) near the start of the tape to find $u$ (Figure 6.12).
- Measure the average velocity over three dots near the end of the tape to find $v$.
- With negligible error, $t$ is the time taken to go from $A$ to $B$ in Figure 6.12. This can be read from the tape.
- The acceleration $a$ can be calculated using:

$$
a=\frac{v-u}{t}
$$

## Worked Example 9

## Question

Find the acceleration of the ticker tape in Figure 6.12.

## Solution

$s_{1}=1.2 \mathrm{~cm}=0.012 \mathrm{~m} ; \quad s_{2}=3.6 \mathrm{~cm}=0.036 \mathrm{~m}$.
Each distance is travelled in $\frac{2}{50} \mathrm{~s}=0.04 \mathrm{~s}$.
Time $(t)$ for speed to change from $u$ to $v=$ time taken to go from $A$ to $B=8\left(\frac{1}{50}\right)=0.16 \mathrm{~s}$.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
u=\frac{s_{1}}{0.04}=\frac{0.012}{0.04}=0.3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} & a=\frac{v-u}{t}=\frac{0.9-0.3}{0.16} \\
v=\frac{s_{2}}{0.04}=\frac{0.036}{0.04}=0.9 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} & \Rightarrow \text { Acceleration, } a=3.75 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{array}
$$

## Measuring constant acceleration using two timing gates and a scaler timer

With the equipment in Figure 6.13:

- The acceleration $a$ can be calculated using the formula:

$$
a=\frac{v^{2}-u^{2}}{2 s} \quad\left(\text { from }, v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s\right)
$$

- $u$ is measured with the first timing gate.
- $v$ is measured with the second timing gate.
- $s$ is the distance between the two light beams and can be measured with a metre stick.

## Student Experiment 6.1 (Method A)

To investigate the varying linear motion of a trolley using a ticker timer and ticker tape

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will accelerate a trolley along a runway by raising one end of the runway. From the unevenly spaced dots produced on the ticker tape attached to it, you will calculate its acceleration.

## Equipment

A trolley, a runway, a ticker timer and ticker tape, a suitable AC power supply, a metre stick and a thumbtack or sticky tape.

## Method

1. Dust the runway and trolley wheels to remove any grit or dirt, as this can cause the acceleration to vary.
2. Raise one end of the runway and rest it on blocks or books. Adjust the height of the runway so that the trolley accelerates down the runway if released.
3. Set up the ticker timer and trolley at the high end of the runway. Pass the tape through the timer and attach it to the trolley.
4. Switch on the timer and release the trolley down the runway.
5. Stop the trolley at the end of the runway, switch off the timer and remove the tape. The tape should look something like Figure 6.14.
6. Ignoring the first few blurred dots on the tape in (as seen in Figure 6.14), measure the length of two adjacent spaces near the start of the tape ( $s_{1}$ ) and measure the length of two adjacent spaces near the end of the tape ( $s_{2}$ ). Record these values.
7. Count the number of spaces $(n)$ between the middle dot of $s_{1}$ and the middle dot of $s_{2}$ (that is between $A$ and $B$ in Figure 6.14). Record this in a table of results like the one shown below.
8. Complete the table, calculating the acceleration $a$.
9. Repeat the experiment with the runway at different slopes, giving different values for the acceleration.

| $s_{1}$ (cm) | $\boldsymbol{s}_{\mathbf{2}} \boldsymbol{(} \mathbf{c m} \boldsymbol{)}$ | $n$ | Initial velocity $u\left(\mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right)$ | Final velocity $v\left(\mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right)$ | Time $t$ (s) | Acceleration $\boldsymbol{a}\left(\mathrm{cm} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\right)$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  |  | $u=\frac{s_{1}}{\left(\frac{2}{50}\right)}$ | $v=\frac{s_{2}}{\left(\frac{2}{50}\right)}$ | $t=n \frac{1}{50}$ | $a=\frac{v-u}{t}$ |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

## Sources of error

- Dirt or grit on the runway or surface of the wheels can cause the velocity to vary. Make sure they are clean.
- If the trolley wheels cannot rotate freely, the velocity can vary. Lubricate or oil the wheel bearings.
- Make sure to use the metre stick correctly when measuring the distance, avoiding parallax error.

1. Other than by looking at it, how would you know that the trolley was accelerating?
2. If you used the formula $s=\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ to find the acceleration, why must $s$ be measured from the first dot produced on the tape? What is the disadvantage of using this method?
3. List two precautions you would take in this experiment to ensure an accurate result.

## Student Experiment 6.1 (Method B)

To investigate the varying linear motion of a rider on an air track using two timing gates and a scaler timer

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will accelerate the rider along the air track by exerting a constant force on it. The force is caused by weights hanging on a scale pan at the end of the track (Figure 6.13).
You will calculate the acceleration from the formula:

$$
a=\frac{v^{2}-u^{2}}{2 s}
$$

## Equipment

A linear air track, an air blower and a rider, a scaler timer, 2 timing gates, 2 retort stands (depending on timing gates used), a metre stick, a scale pan, a pulley, thread and some weights.

## Method

1. Set up the air track on the bench and adjust the levelling screws until it looks to be reasonably level. Connect the air blower and place the rider on the track. Further adjust the levelling screws until the rider remains at rest at any position on the track.
2. Mount each timing gate on a retort stand and connect them to the scaler timer (check with the manual or with your teacher if necessary). Turn on the timer and check that each light gate is operating properly - the numbers on the timer should change when the light beam is broken and remain the same when the beam is complete. Place one timing gate near each end of the track. Adjust the heights of the gates so that the card on the rider will interrupt the light beam.
3. Connect the rider to the scale pan with the thread and place some small weights on the scale pan. Place the rider at the opposite end of the track to the pulley. Place the thread over the pulley and hold the pan in place with your hand.
4. Connect the piece of card to the rider and turn on the blower. Release the pan. The trolley should accelerate along the track, interrupting each beam as it does so.
5. Catch the rider at the end of the track. Switch off the air blower.
6. Record the readings on the scaler timer ( $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ ). Switch off the timer and measure (with a metre stick) the distance ( $s$ ) between the two light beams. Record this value also. If the length ( $l$ ) of the card on the rider is not known, measure and record its value too.
7. Complete a table of results like the one shown below and calculate the acceleration of the rider.
8. If time permits, repeat the experiment with different weights on the pan, giving different values for the acceleration.

| Transit time 1, $t_{1}(\mathrm{~s})$ | Transit time 2, $t_{2}(\mathrm{~s})$ | Distance between gates, $s$ (cm) | Length of card, $l$ (cm) | Initial velocity, $u$ ( $\mathrm{cm} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ ) | Final velocity, v ( $\mathrm{cm} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ ) | Acceleration, $a\left(\mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right)$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  |  |  | $u=\frac{l}{t_{1}}$ | $v=\frac{l}{t_{2}}$ | $a=\frac{v^{2}-u^{2}}{2 s}$ |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

## Sources of error

- Parallax error using the metre stick to measure the length of the card.
- The card on the rider may not be parallel to the direction in which the rider is moving.
- The light beam may not be perpendicular to both the card and the direction in which the rider is moving.


### 6.5 Acceleration due to gravity, $g$

If you drop an object, the force of gravity causes it to accelerate downwards. This force is called the weight of the object.
If you drop a coin and a feather from the same height, the coin reaches the ground first. The feather takes much longer to fall because air resistance (or air friction) stops it picking up as much speed as the coin. However, if the coin and the feather are placed in a container and the air is removed from the container to form a vacuum (Figure 6.15), the coin and feather fall together and reach the bottom at the same time. Lack of air resistance in a vacuum means the feather falls with the same acceleration as the coin.

Experiments show that in the absence of air resistance all objects near the Earth's surface, if released, fall downwards with the same acceleration. This acceleration is called acceleration due to gravity. Its symbol is $g$.

The exact value of $g$ varies slightly from place to place on the Earth's surface (Table 6.1). However, correct to one decimal place, $g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ anywhere near the surface of the Earth.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-111.jpg?height=1352&width=1167&top_left_y=319&top_left_x=1565)
Figure 6.15 When the air is removed from the tube, the coin and the feather fall with the same acceleration.

| Location | Equator <br> (sea level) | North Pole | Dublin | Top of Mount Everest |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Acceleration due to <br> gravity $g\left(\right.$ in $\left.\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-2}\right)$ | 9.78 | 9.83 | 9.81 | 9.77 |

## Table 6.1

- The value of $g$ decreases as you move away from the surface of the Earth. The decrease is only very small unless the distance is very large (for example, 33 km above the surface the value of $g$ is about $0.1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ less than its value on the surface).
- On other planets and celestial bodies, the value of acceleration due to gravity is different. For example, on the Moon it is about $1.6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, whereas on Jupiter it is about $25 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$. You will see on page 173 that the value depends on the mass and radius of the planet.
- Since acceleration due to gravity is constant, the three equations of motion for an object moving with constant acceleration apply to a falling object, or to an object thrown vertically upwards near the Earth's surface.


## Isaac Newton

Isaac Newton (1643-1727) invented
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-111.jpg?height=274&width=320&top_left_y=2373&top_left_x=2428)
the area of mathematics called differential calculus, which is still the central mathematical tool in physics today.
He proposed a theory of light and colour and discovered that sunlight is composed of all the colours of the rainbow, which could be separated by a prism.
Newton also invented the reflecting telescope.
He devised the laws of mechanics and his famous three laws of motion which, even today, govern the motion of all large-scale objects travelling at speeds not close to the speed of light.
He proposed the law of universal gravitation, which governs the orbits of the planets and satellites and also accounts for objects falling near the surface of the Earth.

## Worked Example 10

## Question

An object is dropped from the top of a building that is 30 m high.
a) With what speed does the object hit the ground?
b) How long does it take to reach the ground?

## Solution

For the downward motion of the object $u=0$ (it is dropped from rest), $s=30 \mathrm{~m}, a=9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}, v=$ ? and $t=$ ?

## a) To find $v$ :

$$
\text { Use, } \quad \begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s \\
v^{2} & =0^{2}+2(9.8)(30) \\
v^{2} & =588 \\
v & =\sqrt{588}=24.2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) To find $r$ :

$$
\text { Use, } \begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \\
24.2 & =0+9.8 t \\
t & =\frac{24.2}{9.8}=2.47 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 11

## Question

An object falls from the top of a building and strikes the ground 5 seconds later. Find the height of the building.

## Solution

$u=0, t=5, a=9.8$.
Let $s=$ height of building
Use,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\
& s=(0)(5)+\frac{1}{2}(9.8)(5)^{2} \\
& s=0+122.5 \\
& s=122.5 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 12

## Question

A stone is thrown vertically upwards with an initial velocity of $20 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Find the greatest height reached by the stone.

## Solution

Since the stone is thrown upwards and acceleration due to gravity acts downwards, the acceleration must be given a negative sign. At the highest point, the stone stops for an instant before falling back down.
For the upward journey, $\quad u=20, \quad a=-9.8, \quad v=0, \quad s=$ ?
Use,

$$
\begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s \\
0^{2} & =20^{2}-2(9.8) s \\
s & =\frac{20^{2}}{(2)(9.8)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$s$, the greatest height $=20.41 \mathrm{~m}$

## Measuring acceleration due to gravity (g) using a free-fall apparatus and a scaler timer

- Suppose you drop a small steel ball from rest. It accelerates downwards with acceleration due to gravity, symbolised by $g$.
- Suppose you measure the time, $t$, it takes to fall through a known distance $s$.
- Since it is dropped from rest, $u=0$. So, the formula $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ becomes $\quad s=\frac{1}{2} g t^{2}$
- Solving this for $g$ gives:

$$
g=\frac{2 s}{t^{2}}
$$

- Since $s$ and $t$ are known, acceleration due to gravity ( $g$ ) can be calculated.

Figure 6.17 shows one type of equipment especially made for this purpose. When the switch is at $A$, the electromagnet is energised and it holds the steel ball in place. When the switch is quickly turned to position $B$, the solenoid ceases to be an electromagnet and the ball immediately drops. At the same instant, the timer is switched on. When the ball strikes the trapdoor, the timer is switched off. Thus, the time taken to fall the distance $s$ is known. The distance $s$ is measured with a metre stick.
The procedure is repeated four or five times, each time for a different value of $s$. The average value of $g$ is then calculated.

## Handling the data graphically

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-114.jpg?height=887&width=1404&top_left_y=1946&top_left_x=1217)
Figure 6.17

If a graph of $s$ against $t^{2}$ is drawn, it is a straight line through the origin (Figure 6.18).
Acceleration due to gravity is equal to the slope of the graph multiplied by 2 .
This is so because the equation of any line through the origin of slope $m$ is $y=m x$. Comparing this with $s=\frac{1}{2} g t^{2}$, you can see that the slope of the graph of $s$ against $t^{2}$ is equal to $\frac{1}{2} g$.
Therefore, $g=2 \times$ slope of graph.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-114.jpg?height=738&width=680&top_left_y=3099&top_left_x=1942)
Figure 6.18

## Summary of method

Using a $g$ free－fall apparatus and a scaler timer，you will allow a steel ball to fall through a known distance $s$ ．You will measure the time taken $t$ for the fall．Using the formula $s=\frac{1}{2} g t^{2}$ ， you can calculate acceleration due to gravity．

## Summary What I should know

- Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time.
- Average acceleration $=\frac{\text { change in velocity }}{\text { time taken }}$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text { or } & a=\frac{v-u}{t} \\
\text { or } & a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}
\end{array}
$$

- The SI unit of acceleration is the metre per second squared ( $\mathbf{m ~ \mathbf { s } ^ { - \mathbf { 2 } }}$ or $\mathbf{m} / \mathbf{s}^{\mathbf{2}}$ ).
- An object has constant acceleration if its average acceleration is always the same, no matter the time interval over which it is calculated.
- The kinematic equations are used to solve problems for objects moving with constant acceleration:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \\
s & =u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s
\end{aligned}
$$

- How to derive the kinematic equations
- The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
- The area under a velocity-time graph is the distance travelled (or the displacement).
- The kinematic equations $v=u+a t, \quad s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \quad$ and $\quad v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s \quad$ can be used to solve problems involving vertical motion under gravity near the surface of the Earth.

# 7 Vectors and Scalars

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity
- To ensure students can identify whether a given quantity is a vector or a scalar
- To enable students to use the parallelogram law or the triangle law to calculate the resultant of two vectors
- To ensure students understand the significance of resolving a given vector into two perpendicular components
- To enable students to calculate the components of a vector in two given perpendicular directions


## Keywords

- Quantity
- Magnitude
- Direction
- Scalar quantity
- Vector quantity
- Vector
- Resultant (of two vectors)
- Net force
- Parallelogram law
- Triangle law
- Perpendicular components (of a vector)
- Resolving (a vector into perpendicular components)


### 7.1 Physical quantities

You learned in Chapter 1 that:

- A quantity is any physical property that can be measured
- The result of any measurement is a number and a unit
- The number and unit is called the magnitude (or size) of the quantity being measured

In physics, quantities can be divided into two classes: scalar quantities and vector quantities.
For every quantity in this course, you need to be able to say whether it is a scalar or a vector quantity.

## Scalar quantities

A scalar quantity is one that has magnitude only. It has no direction in space associated with it.

## Examples of scalar quantities

| length | frequency | energy | electric charge |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| area | mass | work | electric current |
| volume | density | power | resistance |
| time | pressure | temperature | potential difference |

Any scalar quantity is fully represented by a number and a unit. The result of combining two amounts of the same scalar quantity (the resultant) is found by normal addition.
For example: $1000 \mathrm{~kg}+500 \mathrm{~kg}=1500 \mathrm{~kg}$
A scalar quantity is a quantity that has magnitude only and has no direction in space.

## Vector quantities

A quantity that has both magnitude and a direction in space is called a vector quantity.

- To fully represent a vector quantity, you need to give both its magnitude and its direction.
- The only vector quantities in this course are listed on page 107. All the other quantities that you meet are scalar quantities.

A vector quantity is a quantity that has both magnitude and a direction in space.

## Some vector quantities

| displacement | force |
| :---: | :---: |
| velocity | electric field strength |
| acceleration | magnetic flux density |
| momentum | gravitational field strength |

## Representing vector quantities

- A vector quantity is represented on a diagram by an arrow.
- The length of the arrow represents its magnitude.
- The direction of the arrow shows its direction. For example, a force of 10 newtons acting in a south-easterly direction is represented as in Figure 7.1(A). A velocity of $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ to the right is represented as in Figure 7.1(B).
The arrows used to represent vector quantities are usually just called vectors, so that is how this book will do it from here on.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-119.jpg?height=580&width=600&top_left_y=778&top_left_x=1533)
Figure 7.1(A) A force of 10 N acting in a southeasterly direction

## Finding the resultant (combined effect) of two vectors

The resultant of two vectors is the single vector that, acting alone, has the same effect as the two other vectors acting together.
For example, two forces pushing on an object can be replaced by a single force that has exactly the same effect as the combination of the two. This single force is called the resultant. It can also be called the net force acting on the object.

The resultant of two vectors is the single vector that, acting alone, has the same effect as the two other vectors acting together.

## When the vectors point in the same direction

To find the resultant of two vectors pointing in the same direction, you just need to add the magnitudes together. The direction of the resultant is their common direction.

- The combined effect of a 5 m displacement east followed by a 10 m displacement east is a displacement of $10+5=15 \mathrm{~m}$ east (Figure 7.2(A)).
- The combined effect of a force of 2 N and a force of 4 N , both acting in the same direction on an object, is a force of $4+2=6 \mathrm{~N}$ in that direction (Figure 7.2(B)).


## When the vectors point in opposite directions

When vectors point in opposite directions, the resultant is still found by adding the magnitudes, but you also need to keep in mind that if one direction is positive then the opposite direction is negative.

- If a train moves forwards at $5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and a girl walks from the front to the back of the train at $3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, the velocity of the girl over the ground is $5+(-3)=2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (Figure 7.3(A)).
- The resultant of a 10 N force and a 6 N force acting in the opposite direction is a force of $10+(-6)=4 \mathrm{~N}$ in the direction of the 10 N force (Figure 7.3(B)). Note that in Figure 7.3(B), the 10 N force acts to the left, but if you had taken right to be the positive direction, then the resultant would have a negative value, that is, -4 N .

Note: Putting it simply, if two vectors point in opposite directions:

- The magnitude of the resultant is found by subtracting the smaller magnitude from the bigger one
- The direction of the resultant is the direction of the bigger one

### 7.2 Vectors in two dimensions

You've seen so far in this chapter that the arrows used to represent amounts of a vector quantity are called vectors. The resultant of two vectors is a single vector that, acting alone, has the same effect as the two original vectors acting together.
The resultant of two vectors that do not act in the same or opposite directions can be found from the parallelogram law or the triangle law.

## The parallelogram law for finding the resultant of two vectors

If two vectors, drawn tail to tail, are the adjacent sides $A B$ and $A D$ of the parallelogram $A B C D$ (Figure 7.7), the diagonal from $A$ to $C$ of this parallelogram is their resultant.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-120.jpg?height=460&width=925&top_left_y=3401&top_left_x=1696)
Figure 7.7

## The triangle law for finding the resultant of two vectors

If two vectors are drawn head to tail (Figure 7.8), the vector from the tail of the first to the head of the second is their resultant.
It makes no difference whether you use the parallelogram law or the triangle law to find the resultant of two vectors. From Figure 7.7 and Figure 7.8, you should be able to see that each law gives the same vector as the resultant.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-121.jpg?height=453&width=927&top_left_y=285&top_left_x=1820)
Figure 7.8

The parallelogram and triangle laws are also each known as the law of addition of vectors. They can be used for any type of vector: displacements, velocities, forces, and so on.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

A walking horse undergoes a displacement of 3.0 km east followed by a displacement of 5.0 km north. What is its overall displacement from its starting point?

## Solution

The overall displacement from the starting point is equivalent to the resultant of the two displacements.
Figure 7.9 shows the 3 km displacement represented by the vector arrow $A B$ and the 5 km displacement vector $A D$. By the parallelogram law, the vector $A C$ represents the resultant displacement.
The magnitude of the resultant can be found using the theorem of Pythagoras on the triangle $A B C$.

Magnitude of resultant = length of arrow $A C=\sqrt{3^{2}+5^{2}}=5.8 \mathrm{~km}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-121.jpg?height=838&width=655&top_left_y=1158&top_left_x=2044)
Figure 7.9

The direction of the resultant is found using trigonometry in the triangle $A B C$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan \theta & =\frac{5}{3} \\
\Rightarrow \theta & =\tan ^{-1} \frac{5}{3} \\
& =59.0^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

∴ Resultant displacement is 5.8 km at an angle of $59.0^{\circ}$ north from the easterly direction.

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A ship moves parallel to a straight riverbank at $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (Figure 7.10). A man runs across the ship at right angles to the direction of forward motion of the ship at a speed of $3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Find the overall velocity of the man in magnitude and direction.

## Solution

The overall velocity of the man is the resultant of the two given velocities. Figure 7.10 shows these represented by vectors, and the diagonal of the parallelogram represents the resultant.
Magnitude of resultant = length of arrow $A C=\sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}}=5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-121.jpg?height=588&width=927&top_left_y=2731&top_left_x=1768)
Figure 7.10

(Theorem of Pythagoras)
Direction of resultant $=\theta^{\circ}$ to forward direction of motion of ship where $\quad \tan \theta=\frac{3}{4}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \theta & =\tan ^{-1} \frac{3}{4} \\
\theta & =37^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

Resultant velocity of man $=5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at $37^{\circ}$ to the forward direction of motion of the ship.

## Worked Example 3

## Question

A plane is flying horizontally northwards at a speed of $100 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. It suddenly encounters a wind of $60 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ blowing to the east, and the wind's velocity combines with the plane's initial velocity. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the plane's new velocity.

## Solution

The new velocity of the plane is the resultant of a velocity $100 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ north and a velocity of $60 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ east (Figure 7.11)
Magnitude of resultant = length of diagonal

$$
=\sqrt{100+60^{2}}=117 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \quad \text { (Theorem of Pythagoras) }
$$

Direction of resultant $=\theta^{\circ}$ north of east
Where $\tan \theta=\frac{100}{60}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-122.jpg?height=867&width=591&top_left_y=403&top_left_x=1985)
Figure 7.11

$$
\Rightarrow \theta=\tan ^{-1} \frac{100}{60}=59^{\circ}
$$

New velocity of plane $=117 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ at an angle of $59^{\circ}$ north from the easterly direction.

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A force of 2 N and a force of 4 N acting in the same direction are applied to an object. Show how the triangle law (or the parallelogram law) gives their resultant as 6 N in the same direction.

## Solution

Figure 7.12 shows a force of 2 N and 4 N at $20^{\circ}, 5^{\circ}$ and $0^{\circ}$ to each other. In each case, the resultant of the two forces, as given by the triangle law, is shown in red (the vector from the tail of the first to the head of the second). As the angle decreases from $20^{\circ}$ to $0^{\circ}$, the resultant, as given by the triangle law, becomes nearer and nearer to 6 N in magnitude. When they are in the same straight line, the resultant is 6 N in their common direction. However, the triangle has collapsed.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-122.jpg?height=773&width=714&top_left_y=1777&top_left_x=1865)
Figure 7.12

Note: The triangle (or parallelogram) law also gives the resultant if two vectors are in the same straight line. See questions 6 and 7 in Exercise 7.2 below.

## Finding the resultant experimentally

You have already seen that:

- Force is a vector quantity
- The unit of force is the newton (N)
- The resultant of two forces is a single force that, acting alone, has the same effect as the two forces acting together.
How can you find the resultant of two forces in the laboratory?
Consider the following:
- Suppose three forces $X, Y$ and $Z$ act on a small object and keep it at rest (Figure 7.17), such that the overall resultant force on the object is zero.
- Suppose the resultant of $X$ and $Y$ is a force $R$.
- $R$ must therefore be the same size as $Z$ but in the opposite direction, since if it was not, the object would not remain at rest.
So, if three forces are keeping a small object at rest, the resultant of any two of them is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the third force. This

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-124.jpg?height=486&width=675&top_left_y=735&top_left_x=1946)
Figure 7.17

principle is investigated in Student Experiment 7.1.

Note: If three forces are keeping a particle at rest, the resultant of any two of them must be equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the third force.

## Worked Example 5

## Question

Suppose the trolley in Figure 7.18 is stationary under the action of the three horizontal forces shown. What can you deduce about the resultant of any two of the forces from this?

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-124.jpg?height=209&width=958&top_left_y=1839&top_left_x=1175)
Figure 7.18

## Solution

If you have three forces keeping an object at rest, you know that the resultant of any two of them is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the third force.
Therefore, the resultant of 10 N to the left and 6 N to the right is equal but opposite to 4 N to the right.
∴ The resultant of 10 to the left and 6 N to the right is equal to 4 N to the left.
or The resultant of 10 to the left and 4 N to the right is equal but opposite to 6 N to the right.
∴ The resultant of 10 to the left and 4 N to the right is equal to 6 N to the left.
or The resultant of 4 N to the right and 6 N to the right is equal but opposite to 10 N to the left.
∴ The resultant of 4 N to the right and 6 N to the right is equal to 10 N to the right.

## Student Experiment 7.1(A)

To verify the law of addition of vectors in two dimensions for forces

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will keep a small object (a knot in thread) in equilibrium underthe action of three known forces. You will use the parallelogram law (or the triangle law) to calculate the resultant of two of them. It will turn out to be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the third force, verifying the parallelogram law (or the triangle law).

## Equipment

A board that can be mounted vertically, two smooth pulleys, three sets of slotted weights, a sheet of paper, some thread, adhesive tape.

## Method

1. Place the sheet of paper on the board and secure it with the tape and the pulleys. Ensure the pulleys can turn freely.
2. Mount the board vertically and set up the thread and weights as in Figure 7.19(A). Adjust the weights as necessary until the system comes to equilibrium.
3. Disturb the system and ensure the weights come back to equilibrium in the same positions. If they don't, check the pulleys for friction.
4. Record the value of each set of slotted weights.
5. Mark the position of each thread on the paper with two dots, drawn with pencil.
6. Remove the weights, the thread and the sheet of paper.
7. On the paper, draw in a straight line along the direction of each thread (Figure 7.19(B)).
8. With a ruler, draw a vector arrow along one of the lines proportional to the force acting in that direction (e.g. 2.0 cm per newton).
9. Using the same scale, do the same for the other two forces.
10. Complete the parallelogram with two of these forces as adjacent sides, and draw the diagonal from the point marking the knot.
11. Calculate the number of force units that this diagonal represents.

## Result

a) The diagonal will be in the opposite direction to the third force.
b) The number of force units it represents will be the same as the third force.

You know the third force is equal but opposite to the resultant of the other two forces. So, the diagonal represents the resultant of the two forces in magnitude and direction. This verifies the law of addition of vectors for forces.
Repeat the experiment with different weights and the pulleys in different positions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-125.jpg?height=789&width=1052&top_left_y=2796&top_left_x=374)
Figure 7.19(A)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-125.jpg?height=691&width=782&top_left_y=2842&top_left_x=1523)
Figure 7.19(B)

## Sources of error

- The pulleys may not turn freely. Clean and lubricate their bearings until they turn smoothly and freely.
- Make sure to record the weights correctly. If in doubt, check the total weight of each set on a weighing scale.
- Take great care marking the positions of the threads. Use a finely pared pencil. Mark a point on the paper that is on the perpendicular from the thread to the paper. On each thread, mark two points that are far apart from each other.
- Avoid parallax error when using the ruler.


## Student Experiment 7.1(B)

To verify the law of addition of vectors in one dimension for forces

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will use two spring balances to keep a trolley in

SCAN ME equilibrium under the action of two forces acting in opposite directions.
You will observe that the reading on each balance is the same.
You will repeat the experiment with two forces acting in one direction and one force in the other. You will observe that the reading on the single balance is the same as the sum of the readings on the two balances acting in the opposite direction.
These results are predicted by the parallelogram (or triangle) law, hence they verify the law.

## Equipment

A trolley, a runway, three spring balances.

## Method: Part 1

1. Place a trolley on a smooth horizontal runway or bench.
2. Connect two spring balances to the trolley, as

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-126.jpg?height=284&width=1242&top_left_y=2005&top_left_x=891)
Figure 7.20

shown in Figure 7.20.
3. Adjust the tension in each balance so that the trolley remains at rest.
4. Ensure the balances are in the same straight line and that this line is perpendicular to the direction in which the trolley is free to roll. You may need two people to do this.
6. Read and record the value shown on each balance.
7. Repeat several times for different values of the force.

## Observations

The reading on each balance will be the same, showing that two forces of equal magnitude acting in opposite directions have a zero resultant. This is exactly what the parallelogram or triangle law predicts.

## Method: Part 2

1. Place a trolley on a smooth horizontal runway or bench.
2. Connect three spring balances to the trolley, two acting in the same direction and the third acting in the opposite direction.
3. Adjust the tension in each balance so that the trolley remains at rest. You may need two people to do this.
4. Read and record the value shown on each balance.
5. Repeat several times for different values of the forces.

## Observations

You will find that the sum of the readings on the two balances acting in the same direction is equal to the reading on the balance acting in the opposite direction. This is exactly what the parallelogram or triangle law predicts.
The result also verifies that the resultant of two different collinear forces (forces in one line) acting in opposite directions is the difference in their magnitudes acting in the direction of the larger force. Again, this is exactly what the parallelogram or triangle law predicts. This verifies the laws of addition of vectors for forces in one dimension.

## Sources of error:

- Make sure the surfaces of the wheels, the runway and the bench are clean, smooth and low friction. Any friction will cause errors in the readings on the balances.
- Similarly, the trolley wheels must be able to rotate freely. Lubricate or oil the wheel bearings if necessary.


### 7.3 Resolving a vector into perpendicular components

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-127.jpg?height=571&width=928&top_left_y=1562&top_left_x=319)
Figure 7.21(A)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-127.jpg?height=568&width=916&top_left_y=1565&top_left_x=1269)
Figure 7.21(B)

Figure 7.21(A) shows a trolley on a horizontal surface. A vertical force of 50.0 N and a horizontal force of 86.6 N act on the trolley. Using the parallelogram law, the resultant force on the trolley is:

$$
\sqrt{50.0^{2}+86.6^{2}}=100 \mathrm{~N} \quad \text { at angle }=\tan ^{-1} \frac{50.0}{85.6}=30^{\circ} \text { to the horizontal }
$$

This shows that a vertical force of 50 N and a horizontal force of 86.6 N acting on an object is the same as a single force of 100 N at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal acting on the same object (Figure 7.21(B)).
In this next section, you will look at the reverse process. That is, if you are given a force of 100 N at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, how do you find the vertical force and the horizontal force that are equivalent to it?
In other words, given a vector, you want to express it in terms of two other vectors at right angles to each other, so that it is the resultant of these two. These two vectors are called perpendicular components of the given vector.

Resolving a vector into perpendicular components means expressing the vector in terms of two other perpendicular vectors, such that the original vector is the resultant of these two vectors. These two vectors are called perpendicular components of the given vector.

In Figure 7.22 the same vector $x$ is drawn three times. If you choose any direction other than the direction of vector $x$, you can always draw two perpendicular components of $x$, one which is parallel to your chosen direction and the other perpendicular to it. You can choose the pair of perpendicular directions to make it easy for you to solve the physics problem you are working on. Three such possible pairs of perpendicular components of vector $x$ are illustrated in Figure 7.22.

In Figure 7.23, a 100 N force acts on the cart in the direction shown, and the force is resolved into a horizontal component $x$ and a vertical component $y$. Each component represents the complete effect of the given vector in that direction. The cart behaves exactly as if a 50.0 N force was trying to lift it vertically upwards and a force of 86.6 N was trying to pull it along the ground. If the weight of the cart is less than 50.0 N , it will be lifted off the ground. And to prevent the cart from moving horizontally along the ground, a force of 86.6 N acting to the left is required.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-128.jpg?height=522&width=1482&top_left_y=706&top_left_x=198)
Figure 7.22 Three different possible pairs of perpendicular components of the same vector $x$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-128.jpg?height=588&width=904&top_left_y=706&top_left_x=1700)
Figure 7.23

## Calculating the magnitude of the perpendicular components

If a vector of magnitude $v$ has two perpendicular components $x$ and $y$, and $v$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the component $x$, then the magnitudes of the components are:

$$
x=v \cos \theta \quad y=v \sin \theta
$$

(See Figure 7.24)

Proof: In the shaded triangle in
Figure 7.24:

$$
\begin{array}{rlrl} 
& & \cos \theta & =\frac{\text { adjacent }}{\text { hypotenuse }} \\
\Rightarrow & \quad \cos \theta & =\frac{x}{v} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \quad x & =v \cos \theta \\
& \text { Also } \sin \theta & =\frac{\text { opposite }}{\text { hypotenuse }} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \quad \sin \theta & =\frac{y}{v} \\
\Rightarrow \quad y & =v \sin \theta
\end{array}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-128.jpg?height=515&width=655&top_left_y=1878&top_left_x=1113)
Figure 7.24(A)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-128.jpg?height=521&width=835&top_left_y=1874&top_left_x=1788)
Figure 7.24(B)

## Worked Example 6

## Question

Find the vertical and horizontal components of a vector of magnitude 20 N acting at $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal.

## Solution

Figure 7.25 shows the components.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Horizontal component } & =x=20 \cos 60^{\circ}=10 \mathrm{~N} \\
\text { Vertical component } & =y=20 \sin 60^{\circ}=17 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-128.jpg?height=734&width=610&top_left_y=2815&top_left_x=1549)
Figure 7.25

## Worked Example 7

## Question

A woman pulls a crate along a horizontal surface with a force of 300 N . The force makes an angle of $20^{\circ}$ with the horizontal.
a) Find the effective vertical force the woman exerts on the crate.
b) Find the effective horizontal force the woman

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-129.jpg?height=373&width=826&top_left_y=403&top_left_x=1467)
Figure 7.26

c) If a horizontal frictional force of 112 N between the crate and the ground opposes motion, what is the net horizontal force on the crate?

## Solution

Figure 7.26 shows the situation. The required forces are the vertical component of the 300 N force and the horizontal component of the force.
a) Effective vertical force $=300 \sin 20^{\circ}=300 \times 0.342=103 \mathrm{~N}$
b) Effective horizontal force $=300 \cos 20^{\circ}=282 \mathrm{~N}$
c) Net horizontal force $=282-112=170 \mathrm{~N}$

Note: A downward vertical force of at least 103 N is needed to keep the crate on the ground. A horizontal force of 282 N is needed to prevent the crate from moving along the ground.

When resolving a vector into two perpendicular components, proceed as follows:

- At the tail of the vector arrow, draw the two required perpendicular directions.
- Complete the rectangle with the given vector as the diagonal.
- The component vectors are the adjacent sides of this rectangle.
- Use information given in the question to work out the angle between one of the components and the given vector.
- Calculate the magnitude of the components using: $x=v \cos \theta \quad y=v \sin \theta$

## Question

An object is projected with an initial velocity of $210 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $27^{\circ}$ above a horizontal surface. Resolve this velocity into horizontal and vertical components.

## Solution

Figure 7.27 shows the velocity vector and its two components.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-129.jpg?height=355&width=590&top_left_y=2702&top_left_x=1699)

Horizontal component $=x=210 \cos 27^{\circ}=187 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
Vertical component = y = $210 \sin 27^{\circ}=95.3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

## Question

At a certain instant, a pendulum is in the position shown in Figure 7.29, inclined at $50^{\circ}$ to the vertical. The weight of the pendulum bob is 200 N . Resolve this weight into components parallel and perpendicular to the pendulum.

Again, taking care to draw in the components correctly:

11. A swimmer wants to cross a river that is 80 m wide. The banks of the river are parallel and the river is flowing with a velocity of $5.0 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ parallel to the banks (Figure 7.36). The swimmer sets out to swim across the river with a speed of $2.2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ perpendicular to the banks.
a) What is the resultant velocity of the swimmer?

## Summary What I should know

- A scalar quantity is a quantity that has magnitude only and no direction in space.
- A vector quantity is a quantity that has both a magnitude and a direction in space.
- A vector quantity is represented on a diagram by an arrow. The length of the arrow represents its magnitude. The direction of the arrow shows its direction.
- The resultant of two vectors is the single vector that, acting alone, has the same effect as the two other vectors acting together.
- The parallelogram law or the triangle law can be used to find the resultant of two vectors.
- The law of addition of vectors is another name for the parallelogram law or triangle law.
- If three forces keep a particle at rest, the resultant of any two of them is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the third force.
- Resolving a vector into perpendicular components is expressing it in terms of two other perpendicular vectors, such that it is the resultant of these two. These two are called perpendicular components of the given vector.
- If you resolve a vector into two perpendicular components, each component represents the complete effect of the given vector in the direction that the component points.
- If a vector of magnitude $v$ has two perpendicular components $x$ and $y$, and $v$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the component $x$, then the magnitudes of the components are:

$$
x=v \cos \theta \quad \text { and } \quad y=v \sin \theta
$$

## Learning outcomes

Now I am able to:
Identify any given quantity as a scalar or a vector

Calculate the resultant of two vectors that act in the same or opposite direction
Calculate the resultant of two vectors in magnitude and direction, using the parallelogram law or triangle law

Using primary data, carry out an experiment to verify the law of addition of vectors in one and two dimensions

Using secondary data, verify the law of addition of vectors in one and two dimensions
Resolve a vector into components in two given perpendicular directions

# 8 Force, Mass and Momentum

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand force, mass, weight and momentum
- To ensure students appreciate how the acceleration of an object depends on its mass and the force acting on it
- To ensure students understand Newton's three laws of motion
- To ensure students can apply Newton's three laws of motion to model real-world situations
- To ensure students appreciate different types of forces, such as gravitational forces, normal reaction forces, tension forces, friction forces and air resistance
- To ensure students understand the principle of conservation of momentum and appreciate its significance
- To ensure students can model the motion of projectiles
- To ensure students can model collisions in one dimension and two dimensions


## \subsection*{8.1 Force <br> <br> 8.1 Force}

In Chapters 5 and 6, you learned how to model the way objects move. That area of physics is called kinematics. In this chapter, you will learn why objects move in the way they do. This area of physics is called dynamics, and it brings you to the quantity called force.
Figure 8.1 shows a block on a bench. If the block is given a push and let go, it moves along the bench. This shows that a force can cause an object to start moving.
However, the moving block soon comes to a stop. This is because the bench exerts a force on the block that opposes its motion along the bench. This force is called friction. This observation shows that a force can cause a moving object to slow down and stop.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-134.jpg?height=405&width=2417&top_left_y=2636&top_left_x=201)
Figure 8.1

If you want to keep the block moving at a steady speed along the bench, you must keep pushing (or pulling) it with a force large enough to overcome the force of friction (Figure 8.2).

Friction is a force that opposes motion. It tends to slow or stop one surface sliding across another.

Now consider what would happen if you polished the bench and the block, and applied a lubricant such as a layer of oil. The block would move much further before stopping. This is because the force of friction opposing its motion would be reduced.

## Keywords

- Force
- Friction
- The newton (N)
- Mass
- The kilogram (kg)
- Centre of mass
- Weight
- Centre of gravity
- Momentum
- The kilogram metre per second ( $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ )
- Gravitational force
- Normal reaction force
- Tension
- Air resistance

Figure 8.2 A forward force large enough to overcome friction must be maintained to keep the block moving.

In the $16^{\text {th }}$ century, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei realised that if you could remove all the forces of friction acting on a body like the block above, and then give that body a push, it would continue moving at a steady speed in a straight line forever.

## He concluded that:

A force acting on a body causes its velocity to change, or in other words, force causes acceleration.
A linear air track (page 76) shows clearly the way an object behaves when the forces of friction are almost zero.

A force causes the velocity of an object to change (causes the object to speed up, slow down or change direction).

## Galileo Galilei

Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) was an Italian astronomer,
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-135.jpg?height=271&width=303&top_left_y=1054&top_left_x=1621)
physicist and engineer. He is sometimes known as the father of modern science. Galileo made fundamental contributions to our knowledge of motion, astronomy, strength of materials and the scientific method.

He was one of the first to:

- Separate science from philosophy and religion by using experiments and observation to discover the facts of nature
- State that the laws of nature are written in mathematics

He showed that:

- A freely falling body has constant acceleration independent of the weight of the body.
- The distance it falls is directly proportional to time squared ( $s \propto t^{2}$ ).
- The horizontal and vertical motion of a body (a projectile) can be treated separately. The vertical acceleration due to gravity does not affect its horizontal velocity.
He made better telescopes than those that were available at the time, and showed that:
- The planet Venus has phases, just like the phases of the Moon.
- The planet Jupiter has four moons orbiting it.

This provided good evidence for the Copernican view that the planets orbit the Sun.
He also discovered:

- The craters on the Moon
- The rings of Saturn
- Sunspots on the Sun
- That the Milky Way is made up of stars


## Force as a vector quantity

- Since a force has a direction in which it acts, it is a vector quantity.
- The symbol for force is $F$.
- The SI unit of force is the newton (N) (Section 8.3).

The SI unit of force is the newton (N).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-135.jpg?height=1124&width=613&top_left_y=2324&top_left_x=2011)
Figure 8.3 One newton is about the weight of a 100 gram object.

## External forces

If a force is to cause an object to accelerate, that force must be coming from outside the object. In Figure 8.4 the force lifting the person comes from the cable. That is, the force the cable exerts on the person comes from outside the person. It is called an external force.

Note: Only an external force acting on an object can change its velocity.

## Force and the acceleration it causes

Suppose an object rests on a frictionless horizontal bench and you apply a horizontal force to it. The bigger the force you exert on the object, the more speed it picks up in a given time. Or in other words, the bigger the force, the bigger the acceleration.
Accurate experiments show that the acceleration $a$ of a body is directly proportional to the force $F$ causing it. This is written as $a \propto F$ (see page 132).
This means that two times the force causes two times the acceleration, three times the force causes three times the acceleration, and so on (Figure 8.5).

The acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the force causing it. That is, for a given body: $\quad a \propto F$

In Experiment 8.1, you will verify this in the laboratory.

### 8.2 Mass

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-136.jpg?height=1446&width=1394&top_left_y=270&top_left_x=1227)
Figure 8.4

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-136.jpg?height=801&width=929&top_left_y=1722&top_left_x=1692)
Figure 8.5

In Junior Cycle, you saw that the mass of a body is a measure of the amount of matter in that body. In Experiment 8.1 you will also see that the greater the amount of matter in an object, the less acceleration it will get from a given force.
More precisely, you will see that the acceleration produced by a given force is inversely proportional to the mass of the body being accelerated.
It follows that if a force gives a body an acceleration $a$, then the same force will give two of those bodies together half that acceleration, and the same force will give three of those bodies together one third that acceleration (Figure 8.6).

- The mass of a body is a measure of the amount of matter in that body.
- The mass of a body is also a measure of how difficult it is to accelerate that body.
- Mass is a scalar quantity.
- The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).
- The mass of an object is a fixed value. It does not change. If something has a mass of 20 kg here on Earth, it will have a mass of 20 kg on the Moon, on Jupiter and everywhere else.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-136.jpg?height=1105&width=668&top_left_y=2659&top_left_x=1953)
Figure 8.6

The acceleration of a body $\propto \frac{1}{\text { mass }}$
so, for a given force: $\quad a \propto \frac{1}{m}$
In Experiment 8.1, you verify this in the laboratory.
The mass ( $m$ ) of a body is a measure of the amount of matter in that body, or a measure of how difficult it is to accelerate that body.

The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). The kilogram is one of the seven SI base (or fundamental) units.

Since $a \propto F$ and $a \propto \frac{1}{m}$, it follows that:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a \propto F \times \frac{1}{m} \\
& a \propto \frac{F}{m} \quad \Rightarrow F \propto m a \\
& \quad \Rightarrow F=k m a \text { where } k \text { is a constant. }
\end{aligned}
$$

### 8.3 The newton

The SI unit of force is the newton.
1 newton (N) is the force that gives a mass of 1 kilogram an acceleration of $1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$.
1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of $1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$
Substituting these values into $F=k m a$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 & =k \times 1 \times 1 \\
\Rightarrow k & =1
\end{aligned}
$$

This leads to an important equation:

$$
F=m a
$$

If a force, $F$ acts on an object of mass, $m$ and it produces an acceleration, $a$ then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =m a \\
\text { Force } & =\text { mass } \text { × } \text { acceleration }
\end{aligned}
$$

(F\&T, page 50)

## Note: Unit analysis

The newton in terms of base units:
From $F=m a$, it follows that:
The SI unit of force $=\mathrm{SI}$ unit of mass × SI unit of acceleration
i.e. $\quad 1 \mathrm{~N}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$

## Worked Example 1

## Question

What force gives a 10 kg mass an acceleration of $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =m a \\
& =10 \times 4 \\
& =40 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A car of mass 1200 kg strikes a tree and comes to a stop with a deceleration of $60 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$. Calculate the decelerating force acting on the car during the collision.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
a=60 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} \quad & m=1200 \mathrm{~kg} \quad F=? \\
F & =m a \\
& =1200 \times 60 \\
& =72000 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

Find the acceleration of a car of mass 1000 kg and its two occupants of masses 60 kg and 110 kg under the action of a force of magnitude 2000 N .

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =m a \\
a & =\frac{F}{m} \\
& =\frac{2000}{1000+60+110} \\
& =1.71 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 5 kg , which is initially at rest.
a) Find the acceleration of the body.
b) What is the velocity of the body after 8 seconds?

## Solution

a) $F=20 \mathrm{~N} \quad m=5 \mathrm{~kg} \quad a=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =m a \\
a & =\frac{F}{m} \\
& =\frac{20}{5} \\
& =4 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) $u=0 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \quad t=8 \mathrm{~s} \quad a=4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} \quad v=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \\
& =0+(4 \times 8) \\
& =32 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A body of mass 105 kg has a velocity of $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. What force is required to stop it in 0.5 s ?

## Solution

$u=10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \quad v=0 \quad t=0.5 \mathrm{~s} \quad a=? \quad F=$ ?
Find $a$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \\
a & =v-\frac{u}{t} \\
& =0-\frac{10}{0.5} \\
& =-20 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Find $F$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =m a \\
& =105 \times 20 \\
& =2100 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

If two (or more) forces act on an object of mass $m$, and you want to find the acceleration $a$ produced, the value of $F$ that is used in $F=m a$ is the resultant or net force acting on the object. That is why the equation is sometimes written as $F_{\text {net }}=m a$. You saw in Chapter 7 how to find the resultant or net force acting on an object.

Note: In the equation

$$
\text { Force }=\text { mass } \text { × } \text { acceleration }
$$

the force is the resultant or net force acting on the object.

$$
F_{\text {net }}=m a
$$

Figure 8.7

Use $F=m a$
$F$ is the net or resultant force on the mass. $a$ is the acceleration produced.

## Worked Example 7

## Question

A force of 7.2 kN is applied to a golf ball at rest by the head of a golf club. The ball has a mass of 46.2 g and the club and the ball are in contact for a time of 0.49 ms . Calculate the velocity of the ball immediately after contact.

## Solution

Let $v$ be the velocity of the ball immediately after contact.

$$
\text { acceleration of ball, } \begin{aligned}
a & =\frac{v-u}{t} \\
& =\frac{v-0}{0.49 \times 10^{-3}}=\frac{v}{4.9 \times 10^{-4}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying $F=m a$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
7.2 \times 10^{3} & =\left(\frac{46.2}{10^{3}}\right)\left(\frac{v}{4.9 \times 10^{-4}}\right) \\
v & =\frac{\left(7.2 \times 10^{3}\right)\left(4.9 \times 10^{-4}\right)}{46.2 \times 10^{-3}}=76.4 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$
