### 8.4 Weight and mass

## Centre of mass

You have seen that when you apply a net force to a body, that body accelerates. As well as causing the body to accelerate, a force may also cause it to turn or rotate. Whether it causes rotation or not depends on whether the line along which the force acts passes through a point called the centre of mass of the body.
If the body has uniform composition and has a simple regular shape, the centre of mass is its geometrical centre. However, the centre of mass can be at any point within a body, and for some irregular shaped bodies, like a

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-141.jpg?height=467&width=746&top_left_y=481&top_left_x=2005)
Figure 8.9

horseshoe, it can even be outside of the material that makes up the body.
In Figure 8.9, suppose the body has a mass $m$ and the applied force is $F$. In Figure 8.9(A), the force that acts along a line passing through the centre of mass causes the body to accelerate without rotating.
In Figure 8.9(B), the force does not act along a line passing through the centre of mass and causes the body to rotate as well as accelerate.
In both cases the acceleration of the centre of mass is the same and is equal to $\frac{F}{m}$.
The centre of mass of a body is the point through which the line of action of a force must pass if the body is to accelerate without rotating.

If the resultant force (net force) acting on an object is $F_{\text {net }}$ and if the total mass of the object is $m$, then the acceleration of the centre of mass $a_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is given by:

$$
F_{\mathrm{net}}=m a_{\mathrm{cm}}
$$

## Weight

- In the absence of air resistance, all objects near the Earth's surface, if released, will fall downwards with the same constant acceleration.
- This acceleration is called the acceleration due to gravity. Its symbol is $g$ and its value is $9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$.
- The force causing this acceleration is the force of gravity and it is called the weight of the object.
- Since weight is a force, the SI unit of weight is the newton (N).
- Unlike mass, the weight of an object can change. It is dependent on the force of gravity.

The weight of an object is the force of the Earth's gravity acting on it.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-141.jpg?height=776&width=747&top_left_y=2008&top_left_x=1998)
Figure 8.10

Figure 8.10 shows an object of mass $m$ kilograms falling with an acceleration $g$.
The force acting on it is its weight $W$. Applying $F=m a$ gives $W=m g$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
W & =m g \\
\text { Weight } & =\text { mass × acceleration due to gravity }
\end{aligned}
$$

(F\&T, page 56)

The SI unit of weight is the newton (N).

## Worked Example 8

## Question

Find the weight of an object of mass 24 kg , near the Earth's surface.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
W & =m g \\
& =(24)(9.8) \\
& =235 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 9

## Question

What is the mass of a car of weight 15000 N near the Earth's surface?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
W & =m g \\
m & =\frac{W}{g} \\
& =\frac{15000}{9.8} \\
& =1531 \mathrm{~kg}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Centre of gravity

- If you carefully release an object, like a hammer, and let it fall, it accelerates downward without rotating.
- The downward force acting on the hammer is its weight.
- Since the weight doesn't cause it to rotate, the weight must be acting through the centre of mass of the object.
- The point through which the entire weight of an object acts is called its centre of gravity.
- Therefore the centre of gravity and the centre of mass of an object are the same point.

If the acceleration due to gravity was different at different points in the object, this result would not hold. You don't need to worry about cases like this in this course.

The centre of gravity of a body is the point through which the entire weight of the body acts.
For the purposes of this course, the centre of gravity is the same point as the centre of mass.

b) The distance travelled while the force acts

What other force acting on its own would then stop the stone in 0.1 seconds?

## Some types of force

A gravitational force: Figure 8.11(A) shows a block on a horizontal table. The force acting downwards on the block is the force of gravity. This gravitational force is the weight ( $W$ ) of the block.
A normal reaction force: The block is not accelerating downwards. There must therefore be an upward force acting on it to counter the effect of the weight downwards. The bench exerts this upward force. It acts perpendicular to the bench and is called the normal reaction force $(N)$ of the bench. The word 'normal' just means perpendicular.

A tension force: In Figure 8.11 (B), a rope tied to the block exerts a horizontal force $T$ on the block. This force acts along the direction of the rope and is called a tension force. The force $T$ tends to pull the block along the table.

A frictional force: If the force $T$ is small enough, the block does not move. As soon as the force $T$ is applied to move the block, a force opposing it appears. This force is called friction $\left(\boldsymbol{F}_{\mathbf{f}}\right)$. As $T$ increases so does $F_{\mathrm{f}}$ but only up to a certain value. After that, $T$ is greater than $F_{\mathrm{f}}$ and the object accelerates in the direction of $T$.

Air resistance: If you try to move an object through air, there is a frictional force trying to slow it down called air resistance.

- The higher the speed of the object, the greater the air resistance.
- The bigger the cross-sectional area of the object perpendicular to the air flow, the greater the air resistance.
- The size of the air resistance also depends on the shape of the object.

Similarly, an object moving through a liquid also experiences a resistant force.

## Student Experiment 8.1

To verify that $F_{\text {net }}=m a$
This experiment has two parts.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-143.jpg?height=597&width=1427&top_left_y=266&top_left_x=1331)

## 8．1（B）To show that the acceleration produced by a given force is inversely proportional to the mass of the object being accelerated，i．e．$a \propto \frac{1}{m}$

## Summary of method

Using the same equipment as in Experiment 8．1（A），you will keep the accelerating force $F$ constant by not changing the weights on the scale pan（Figure 8．12）．You will measure the acceleration，$a$ ， produced with a motion sensor and a data logger．By placing extra weights on the trolley，you will increase the mass being accelerated and again measure the acceleration．You will repeat this a number of times．By plotting a graph of $a$ against $\frac{1}{m}$ ，a straight line through the origin will result，verifying that：$a \propto \frac{1}{m}$ ．

## Equipment

A trolley，a runway，a motion sensor，a data logger，a computer or laptop（depending on the data logger）， a low－friction pulley，a scale pan，a set of masses（e．g． $0-800 \mathrm{~g}$ ）and some string．

## Method

1．Find the mass of the trolley．
2．Raise one end of the runway slightly，so that the trolley will move along the runway at constant speed when given a gentle push and released．
3．Connect the motion sensor to the data logger（or computer）．
4．Set the data logging software to measure acceleration．
5．Connect the scale pan to the trolley and place a mass on it（say 200 g ）．
6．Place the trolley in front of the motion sensor and hold the trolley in place．
7．Release the trolley and turn on the motion sensor．Allow it to accelerate down the runway．
8．Before the trolley reaches the end of the runway，switch off the motion sensor and stop the trolley．
9．Measure and record the total mass（ $m$ ）of the trolley and any weights on it．
10．Record the value of the acceleration．
11．Place more mass on the trolley and repeat steps 6－10．
12．Repeat step 11 a number of times with a larger mass on the trolley each time．
13．Complete the table below．
14．On graph paper，plot a graph of acceleration a on the $y$－axis against $\frac{1}{m}$ on the $x$－axis．

## Table

| Acceleration $a$ <br> $\left(\mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right)$ | Total mass of the trolley and weights on it，$m(\mathrm{~g})$ |
| :---: | :--- |
|  |  |

## Results

A graph similar to Figure 8.14 should result．A straight line through the origin verifies that：$a \propto \frac{1}{m}$ ．

## Sources of error

－Friction between the trolley and the runway．Do not forget to compensate the runway for friction．
－Accelerating force not constant．The mass on the scale pan must be kept constant throughout the experiment．

### 8.5 Momentum and Newton's laws of motion

- The momentum of a body is, by definition, equal to its mass multiplied by its velocity

$$
\text { momentum }=\text { mass } \text { × } \text { velocity; } p=m v
$$

- The symbol for momentum is $p$.
- Momentum is a vector quantity. Its direction is that of the velocity.
- The SI unit of momentum is the kilogram metre per second ( $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ )

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { since } p=m v \\
& \text { unit of momentum }=(\text { unit of mass }) \times(\text { unit of velocity }) \\
&=(\text { kilogram }) \times(\text { metre per second })=\text { kilogram metre per second }\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right) \\
& \text { Momentum }=\text { mass × velocity } \\
& p=m v \\
&(F \& T, \text { page } 51)
\end{aligned}
$$

The SI unit of momentum is the kilogram metre per second ( $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ ).

## Worked Example 10

## Question

A bus has a mass of 20000 kg . It is moving at $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ eastwards. Find its momentum.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
p & =m v \\
& =(20000)(4) \\
& =80000 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \text { east }
\end{aligned}
$$

| Mass | $m$ | kilogram | kg | kg |
| Momentum | $p$ | kilogram metre per second | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ | $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ |

## Newton's laws of motion

The way in which force affects the motion of a body was first stated completely by Isaac Newton in 1687 in his three laws of motion. These provide a general summary for much of the information covered in the chapter so far.

Newton's first law of motion states that every body will remain in a state of rest or travelling with a constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it.

Newton's second law of motion states that when a net force acts on a body, the rate of change of the body's momentum is directly proportional to the force and takes place in the direction of the force.

Newton's third law of motion states that if a body A exerts a force on a body B, then body B exerts an equal but opposite force on body $A$, i.e. action and reaction are equal and opposite.

## Newton's first law of motion

Newton's first law of motion states that every body will remain in a state of rest or will carry on travelling at a constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it. This law was known by Galileo before Newton was alive. It has already been discussed on page 123.
This law means that:

- If there is an overall (net or resultant) force acting on a body, that body will accelerate.
- If there is no resultant force acting on a body, it will have zero acceleration.

Therefore if a body is at rest, it will remain at rest, and if it is moving, it will remain moving with a constant speed in a fixed direction, i.e. with constant velocity.
Newton's first law can easily be demonstrated with a linear air track. If the track is level and a rider is placed on it with zero velocity, it remains at rest on the track. If the rider is given a push and let go, it moves along the track with a steady speed until it comes to the end of the track. If any horizontal force acts on the rider, its speed either increases or decreases, or it tries to turn off the track.
Suppose you are travelling along in a car at $30 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and the car stops suddenly, perhaps hitting an obstacle. You were moving at $30 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and by Newton's first law you will continue to do so (perhaps through the windscreen of the car) until some force causes your velocity to change (Figure 8.15). The purpose of a seatbelt and/or an airbag in a car is to provide this force in a fashion that will do you least harm.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-147.jpg?height=906&width=1769&top_left_y=2972&top_left_x=325)
Figure 8.15

## Newton's second law of motion

Newton's second law states: force $\propto$ rate of change of momentum.
If follows from this that: $F=m a$, and so $F=m a$ is a special case of Newton's second law.
Therefore, Student Experiments 8.1(A) and (B) on pages 131-133 show that $a \propto F$ and $a \propto \frac{1}{m}$ can be used to verify Newton's second law.

## Note: To show $F=m a$ is a special case of Newton's second law

Newton's second law states: force $\propto$ rate of change of momentum

$$
\begin{aligned}
& F \propto \frac{\text { change in momentum }}{\text { time taken for change }} \\
& F \propto \frac{\text { final momentum - initial momentum }}{\text { time taken }} \\
& F=\frac{m v-m u}{t} \\
& F=\frac{k m(v-u)}{t}
\end{aligned}
$$

But acceleration $a=\frac{v-u}{t} \quad \therefore F=k m a$ where $k$ is a constant
Since 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of $1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, these values can be substituted into this equation to find $k$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 & =k \times 1 \times 1 \\
\Rightarrow k & =1
\end{aligned}
$$

This gives:

$$
F=m a
$$

Since the constant $k=1$, the second law equation above becomes:

$$
F=\frac{m(v-u)}{t}
$$

Force is equal to the rate of change of momentum.

## Newton's third law of motion

This law states that forces always occur in pairs. If you see a body accelerating under the action of a force, there must be another body experiencing a force of the same size but that acts in the opposite direction to the first force. Note that the two forces act on different bodies. Some examples are as follows:

- When a car crashes into a wall, the wall exerts a force on the car that slows the car down abruptly and damages the car. The car exerts an equal but opposite force on the wall that pushes the wall forward, thus damaging the wall.
- When a rocket (or a jet) wants to accelerate forwards, it expels

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-148.jpg?height=955&width=1590&top_left_y=2402&top_left_x=1031)
Figure 8.16 Newton's third law can explain why the rocket accelerates forward.

a mass of hot gas at high speed backwards from it (Figure 8.16). The rocket exerts a force on the gas pushing the gas backwards and the gas exerts an equal but opposite force on the rocket, causing it to accelerate forwards.

## Terminal velocity

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-149.jpg?height=1173&width=737&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=325)
Figure 8.17 Accelerating to terminal velocity

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-149.jpg?height=1173&width=1671&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1074)
Figure 8.18 Falling at a steady speed

- Figure 8.17 shows a person falling from an aeroplane.
- Initially, the only force acting on him is his weight and he accelerates down.
- As he starts to move downwards, air resistance (air friction) begins to act. Air resistance opposes motion and therefore acts upwards.
- As the speed increases, the size of the air resistance increases.
- Eventually, a speed is reached where the air resistance is equal but opposite to the weight of the man.
- The resultant force on the man is now zero so he now no longer accelerates.
- Since he is moving, Newton's first law states that he continues to move with constant velocity (Figure 8.18). This velocity is called terminal velocity.


## Worked Example 11

## Question

A crane lifts a block of mass 20 kg from the ground to the top of a building by means of a cable.
a) What force does the cable exert on the block if the block is accelerating upwards at $1.5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ ?
b) What force does the cable exert on the block if it is moving upwards at constant speed?

## Solution

a) Figure 8.19 shows the forces acting on the block. They are its weight ( $W=20 \times g$ ) and the tension in the string ( $T$ ).
If the block accelerates upwards, $T$ must be bigger than $W$ and the net upwards force is $T-W$.
Applying $F=m a$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T-W & =m a \\
\Rightarrow T-(20)(9.8) & =(20)(1.5) \\
\Rightarrow T & =226 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) Constant velocity ⇒ acceleration $=0 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$. Applying $F=m a$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T-W & =m a \\
\Rightarrow T & =W=(20)(0) \\
\Rightarrow T & =W=196 \mathrm{~N} \text { (the weight of the block) }
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-149.jpg?height=760&width=398&top_left_y=3014&top_left_x=2116)
Figure 8.19

## Worked Example 12

## Question

A woman of mass 80 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift. If the displayed unit is newtons, find the reading on the scales when the lift:
a) Is at rest
b) Moves upwards with a steady speed of $3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
c) Moves downwards with a steady speed of $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
d) Accelerates upwards at $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$
e) Accelerates downwards at $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$
f) Accelerates downwards at $9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$

## Solution

Figure 8.20 shows the forces acting on the woman. The upward force on the woman due to the floor of the lift is called the normal reaction. This is the reading on the scales.
In each part of this worked example, apply $F=m a$ in the direction of the acceleration.
In each of $\mathbf{a}$ ), $\mathbf{b}$ ) and $\mathbf{c}$ ), the acceleration is zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
80 g-N & =(80)(0) \\
N & =80 g \\
& =\text { the weight of the woman }=784 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

d) $N-80 g=80 \times 2 \Rightarrow N=160+784=944 \mathrm{~N}$
e) $80 g-N=80 \times 2 \Rightarrow N=784-160=624 N$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-150.jpg?height=871&width=828&top_left_y=1080&top_left_x=1344)
Figure 8.20

f) $80 g-N=80 \times 9.8 \Rightarrow N=0$

In the final part, the reading on the scales is zero, and relative to the lift the woman is weightless. This is true in any object falling under gravity, and astronauts use this fact to train on Earth: by going up in a plane and then following a parabolic path that simulates free-fall, everyone inside experiences weightlessness (Figure 8.21).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-150.jpg?height=1153&width=1795&top_left_y=2409&top_left_x=240)

## Worked Example 13

## Question

A ball of mass 210 g is travelling at a speed of $5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. It rebounds from a wall and travels in the opposite direction at the same speed. The ball was in contact with the wall for 0.22 seconds. Use Newton's laws of motion to calculate the force the wall exerts on the ball.

## Solution

Figure 8.22 shows the ball before and after rebounding from the wall. Taking the direction towards the wall as the negative direction: Momentum of ball before $=$ mass × velocity

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{210}{1000} \times(-5) \\
& =-1.05 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Momentum of ball after

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\text { mass × velocity }=\frac{210}{1000} \times(+5) \\
& =1.05 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { force } & =\frac{\text { change in momentum }}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{(\text { final momentum }- \text { initial momentum })}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{(1.05-(-1.05))}{0.22} \\
& =9.55 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-151.jpg?height=658&width=769&top_left_y=882&top_left_x=1725)
Figure 8.22

### 8.6 Projectiles

If an object is thrown - projected - horizontally from the top of a cliff with a known speed, you can calculate its position and velocity at any moment after the projection. Galileo in the early 1600s was the first to explain how; he had actually discovered Newton's first law and used it to explain the motion of projectiles.
In Figure 8.23, an object is projected horizontally from the top of a cliff with a horizontal speed of $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Since there are no horizontal forces acting on the object, it has no horizontal acceleration. Therefore,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-152.jpg?height=587&width=1202&top_left_y=901&top_left_x=1419)
Figure 8.23

its horizontal velocity does not change. The object continues to move to the right at a steady speed of $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
However, at the same time there is a vertical force acting on the object (its weight). This gives it a constant downward acceleration. So its vertical velocity increases in exactly the same manner as an object dropped from rest.

## Worked Example 14

## Question

An object is projected horizontally from the top of a cliff with a velocity of $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. The top of the cliff is 200 m above horizontal ground (Figure 8.23). Ignoring air resistance, find:
a) The vertical velocity of the object after 2.0 seconds
b) The time it takes the stone to reach the ground
c) The distance from the foot of the cliff to the point where the object strikes the ground

## Solution

- The only force acting on the object is its weight, which acts vertically downwards.
- This causes the object to accelerate downwards, from rest, at $9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$.
- Its vertical velocity changes in exactly the same way as the velocity of an object dropped from rest.
- No horizontal force acts on the object, so its horizontal velocity remains constant at $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
a) For its vertical motion: $u=0 \quad a=-9.8 \quad t=2.0 \quad v=?$

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \\
& =0+(9.8)(2.0) \\
& =19.6 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) For its vertical motion: $u=0 \quad a=9.8 \quad s=200$

$$
\begin{aligned}
s & =u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\
200 & =(0)(t)+\frac{1}{2}(9.8)(t)^{2} \\
t & =\sqrt{\frac{(2)(200)}{9.8}} \\
& =6.4 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the time it takes the object to reach the ground.
c) Horizontal distance travelled in this time $=u t=40 \times 6.4=256 \mathrm{~m}$

## Worked Example 15

## Question

An object is projected with a velocity of $100 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal from a point on level ground.
a) Resolve its initial velocity into its vertical and horizontal components.
b) Explain why the horizontal velocity of the object does not change during its flight.
c) Explain how the vertical velocity of the object changes as the object moves.
d) Calculate the greatest height the object reaches above the ground.
e) Calculate the total time of flight, i.e. the time it takes the object to reach the ground again.
f) Find the horizontal distance from the point of projection to the point where the ball strikes the ground.

## Solution

a) From Figure 8.24:
horizontal component of initial velocity $=100 \cos 60^{\circ}=50 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ vertical component of initial velocity $=100 \sin 60^{\circ}=86.6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
b) No horizontal force acts on the object, so its horizontal velocity remains constant at $50 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ throughout its flight (Figure 8.25).
c) Due to gravity, the object always has a downward vertical acceleration of $9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$. Its vertical velocity therefore changes in exactly the same way as an object thrown vertically upwards with an initial speed of $86.6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Figure 8.25 also shows how its vertical velocity changes during the flight.
d) At its greatest height, its vertical velocity is instantaneously zero.

Figure 8.24

For the upward vertical motion: $u=86.6 \quad a=-9.8 \quad v=0 \quad s=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s \\
0^{2} & =+(2)(-9.8)(s) \\
s & =\frac{86.6^{2}}{19.6} \\
& =383 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, its greatest vertical height is 383 m
e) The time of flight is the time until the object lands, that is, its vertical displacement is again zero.
Vertically: $u=86.6$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a=-9.8 \quad s & =0 \\
s & =u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\
0 & =86.6 t+\frac{1}{2}(-9.8) t^{2} \\
0 & =86.6 t-4.9 t \\
t(86.6-4.9 t) & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t & =0 \text { (initial launch) } \\
86.6-4.9 t & =0 \\
t & =\frac{86.6}{4.9} \\
& =17.7 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 8 Force, Mass and Momentum

f) Horizontal distance from point of projection to where it again strikes the ground is the distance travelled in 17.7 s at a speed of $50 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(\text { horizontal speed)(time of flight) } \\
& =(50)(17.7) \\
& =885 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

Horizontal component $=30 \cos 40^{\circ}=22.98 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
Vertical component $=30 \sin 40^{\circ}=19.28 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
b) At its greatest height, its vertical velocity is instantaneously zero.

For the upward motion: $u=19.28, a=-9.8, v=0, s=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s \\
0^{2} & =19.28^{2}+(2)(-9.8) s \\
s & =\frac{19.28^{2}}{19.6} \\

\end{aligned}
$$

c) Horizontal component of velocity after 3.0 seconds is $22.98 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

To find the vertical component of the velocity after 3.0 seconds:
For the vertical motion: $u=19.28 \quad a=-9.8 \quad v=? \quad t=3.0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =u+a t \\
v & =19.28+(-9.8)(3.0) \\
& =-10.12 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \\
& =10.12 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \text { downwards }
\end{aligned}
$$

Resultant velocity after 3.0 seconds:

From Figure 8.27:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =22.98^{2}+10.12^{2} \\

& =25.1 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \\
\tan \theta & =\frac{10.12}{22.98} \\
\theta & =\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{10.12}{22.98}\right) \\
& =23.8^{\circ} \\
v & =25.1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \text { at } 23.8^{\circ} \text { below the horizontal. }
\end{aligned}
$$

### 8.7 The principle of conservation of momentum

Experimentally it is found that when bodies collide, the total momentum of the bodies before and after the collision is the same. This is an example of the principle of conservation of momentum.

The principle of conservation of momentum states that, in any interaction between two or more bodies, the total momentum of the bodies before the interaction is equal to the total momentum after the interaction, provided no external forces act on the system of bodies.

In Figure 8.28, two masses are shown just before and just after they collide. The principle of conservation of momentum states that:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-156.jpg?height=636&width=766&top_left_y=1315&top_left_x=1855)
Figure 8.28

$$
m_{1} u_{1}+m_{2} u_{2}=m_{1} v_{1}+m_{2} v_{2}
$$

## Worked Example 17

## Question

A body of mass 20 kg moving at a speed of $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ collides with a body of mass 14 kg , which is at rest. If the two bodies stick together on colliding, find the velocity with which the combined mass moves off (Figure 8.29).

## Solution

The mass of the combined body after the collision is 34 kg . Let its unknown velocity be $v$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-156.jpg?height=616&width=760&top_left_y=2246&top_left_x=1425)
Figure 8.29

Conservation of momentum: Consonn
momentum before collision = momentum after collision

$$
\begin{aligned}
(20)(4)+(14)(0) & =34 v \\
80+0 & =34 v \\
v & =\frac{80}{34} \\
& =2.35 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \text { in the direction that the } 20 \mathrm{~kg} \text { mass was originally moving }
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the total momentum of a number of bodies, you must take into account the fact that momentum is a vector quantity. For bodies moving in the same straight line, momentum in one direction is given a positive sign, and momentum in the opposite direction is given a negative sign. The total momentum is then found by algebraic addition.

## Worked Example 18

## Question

A 10 kg mass is moving at a speed of $5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. A mass of 4 kg is moving at a speed of $20 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in the opposite direction. Find their total momentum.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { total momentum before collision } & =(10)(5)+(4)(-20) \\
& =-30 \\
& =30 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \text { in the direction of the } 4 \mathrm{~kg} \text { mass }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 19

## Question

A body of mass 20 kg with a velocity of $3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ collides with another body of mass 15 kg , which is moving at $6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in the opposite direction.
The two bodies stick together on colliding. Find the velocity with which the combined mass moves off (Figure 8.30)

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { momentum before } & =\text { momentum after } \\
(20)(3)+(15)(-60) & =35 v \\
60-90 & =35 v \\
v & =\frac{-30}{35} \\
& =-0.86 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-157.jpg?height=627&width=813&top_left_y=1454&top_left_x=1503)
Figure 8.30

The combined mass moves off at $0.86 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in the direction of the motion of the 15 kg mass before the collision (to the left in the diagram, shown by the negative symbol here).

## Worked Example 20

## Question

Sphere A of mass 500 g is travelling horizontally with a speed of $5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ when it collides with sphere B of mass 200 g , travelling in the opposite direction at a speed of $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Sphere A comes to rest as a result of the collision. Calculate the new velocity of sphere B.

## Solution

Let $v$ be the speed of sphere B after the collision. momentum before = momentum after

$$
\begin{aligned}
(0.5)(5)+(0.2)(-10) & =(0.5)(0)+0.2 v \\
2.5-2.0 & =0.2 v \\
v & =\frac{0.5}{0.2} \\
& =2.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \text { in the direction of sphere A's original motion }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 21

## Question

A gun of mass 3 kg fires a bullet of mass 10 g with a velocity of $500 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (Figure 8.33). Calculate the recoil velocity of the gun.

## Solution

Before, the system had no momentum. After, both the gun and the bullet have momentum - but in the opposite directions to each other. The sum of these momentums must be zero.
Let $v$ metres per second be the recoil velocity of the gun. Then by the principle of conservation of momentum:
Momentum before = momentum after

$$
\begin{aligned}
(3)(0)+(0.01)(0) & =(0.01)(500)+3 v \\
0 & =5+3 v \\
v & =-\frac{5}{3} \\
& =-1.67 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. the gun recoils backwards at a speed of $1.67 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

## Student Experiment 8.2

To investigate the principle of conservation of momentum

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will measure the velocity of a trolley before and after it collides with, and sticks to, another trolley. You will measure the mass of each trolley. You will calculate the momentum of the trolley before the collision and the momentum of the combined trolleys after the collision, and see that they are the same.

## Equipment

A runway, two trolleys and some known masses (e.g. $250 \mathrm{~g}, 500 \mathrm{~g}$ and 1000 g ), a ticker timer, ticker tape and power supply, two magnets that can be mounted on the fronts of the trolleys (or some other means of making the trolleys stick when they collide), a box.

WARNING! Place a box containing a cushion or crumpled paper on the floor by the bench under the end of

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-159.jpg?height=529&width=1072&top_left_y=3219&top_left_x=1380)
Figure 8.34

the runway so that if the trolleys fall they cannot land on your feet.

## Method

1. Use the equipment as shown in Figure 8.34.
2. Raise one end of the runway so that trolley 1 with the ticker tape attached will move down the runway at constant speed if given a gentle push and released.
3. Place trolley 1 at the upper end of the runway and trolley 2 about half way down. Turn on the ticker timer. Give trolley 1 a gentle push, so that it moves down the runway and collides with and sticks to trolley 2.
4. Stop the trolleys at the end of the runway and remove the ticker tape. It should look like the tape shown in Figure 8.35.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-160.jpg?height=265&width=1945&top_left_y=927&top_left_x=240)
Figure 8.35

5. Repeat the experiment with different masses on each trolley and with the trolleys travelling at different speeds. All results can be recorded in a copy of the table shown.
6. Calculate the velocity of trolley 1 before $(u)$ and after $(v)$ the collision from the ticker tape. (Use the method shown on page 95)
7. Using a balance, find the mass of trolley $1\left(m_{1}\right)$ and trolley $2\left(m_{2}\right)$.
8. Find the momentum before the collision ( $m_{1} u$ ) and the momentum after (( $\left.m_{1}+m_{2}\right) v$ ).

| Before collision |  |  |  |  | After collision |  |  |  |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Velocity from ticker tape |  |  | Mass | Momentum | Velocity from ticker tape |  |  | Mass | Momentum |
| $S_{1}$ | number of spaces ( $n$ ) in length $S_{\mathrm{r}}$ | $u=\frac{S_{1}}{\left(\frac{n}{50}\right)}$ | $m_{1}$ | $m_{1} u$ | $S_{2}$ | number of spaces ( $n$ ) in length $S_{2}$ | $v=\frac{S_{2}}{\left(\frac{n}{50}\right)}$ | $m_{2}$ | $\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right) v$ |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

## Results

The momentum before the collision should be equal to the momentum after the collision, $m_{1} u=\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right) v$.

## Sources of error

To verify the principle of conservation of momentum, you must ensure no net external force acts on the bodies. Both friction and gravity can act on the trolleys here, which is why you need to raise one end of the runway so that the force of gravity cancels the force of friction and the net external force acting on the trolley is zero.
Ensure the wheels of the trolly can roll freely. Lubricate them if necessary.
When measuring distances on the ticker tape:

- Select as large a distance as possible over which the velocities are measured
- Avoid parallax errors when measuring the distances.

### 8.8 Collisions in two dimensions

For all collisions in two dimensions:

- Consider the question and pick two perpendicular directions. Call one the $x$ direction and the other the $y$ direction.
- Resolve the momentum of each body before the collision into its components in the $x$ and $y$ directions.
- Resolve the momentum of each body after the collision into its components in the $x$ and $y$ directions.
- Write down equations using the principle of conservation of momentum:
- Total momentum before the collision in the $x$ direction $=$ total momentum in the $x$ direction after the collision
- Total momentum before the collision in the $y$ direction $=$ total momentum in the $y$ direction after the collision.
- Solve these equations to solve the problem.


## Worked Example 22

## Question

A car and a lorry are travelling along roads that intersect at right angles (Figure 8.36). The car, of mass 1500 kg , is travelling at $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and crashes into the lorry, which has a mass of 5000 kg and is travelling at $30 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. If the vehicles coalesce (stick together) on impact, find the magnitude and direction of the velocity of the wreckage immediately after the collision.

## Solution

Figure 8.36 shows the situation before and after the collision.
Let $x$ and $y$ be the velocity components of the wreckage immediately after the collision.
Apply conservation of momentum parallel to the original direction of motion of the lorry:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { momentum before } & =\text { momentum after } \\
(5000)(30)+(1500)(0) & =6500 x \\
150000+0 & =6500 x \\
x & =\frac{150000}{6500} \\
& =23.1 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-162.jpg?height=811&width=972&top_left_y=1250&top_left_x=1617)
Figure 8.36

Apply conservation of momentum parallel to the original direction of motion of the car:
momentum before = momentum after

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1500)(40)+(5000)(0) & =6500 y \\
60000+0 & =6500 y \\
y & =\frac{60000}{6500} \\
& =9.23 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Magnitude of the velocity $v$ of the wreckage immediately after the collision:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{23.1^{2}+9.23^{2}} \\
& =24.9 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Direction of the velocity of the wreckage:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan \theta & =\frac{y}{x} \\
& =\frac{9.23}{23.1} \\
\theta & =\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{9.23}{23.1}\right) \\
& =21.8^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, $v=24.9 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at $21.8^{\circ}$ to the original direction of motion of the lorry.

## Worked Example 23

## Question

A ball of mass 0.4 kg , travelling at $6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, collides with another ball of the same size but mass 0.3 kg , which is at rest. After the collision, the 0.3 kg ball moves with a speed of $2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $40^{\circ}$ with the direction of the 0.4 kg ball's original velocity. Find the magnitude and direction of the 0.4 kg ball's velocity after the collision.

## Solution

Figure 8.37 shows the situation before and after the collision.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-163.jpg?height=884&width=1606&top_left_y=927&top_left_x=371)
Figure 8.37

Let $x$ and $y$ be the velocity components of the 0.4 kg ball after the collision.
$2 \cos 40^{\circ}$ and $2 \sin 40^{\circ}$ are the velocity components of the 0.3 kg ball after the collision.
Apply conservation of momentum parallel to the original direction of motion:
momentum before = momentum after

$$
\begin{aligned}
(0.4)(6)+(0.3)(0) & =(0.3)\left(2 \cos 40^{\circ}\right)+0.4 x \\
2.4+0 & =0.46+0.4 x \\
x & =\frac{1.94}{0.4} \\
& =4.85 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply conservation of momentum perpendicular to the original direction of motion:
momentum before $=$ momentum after

$$
\begin{aligned}
(0.4)(0)+(0.3)(0) & =(0.3)\left(2 \sin 40^{\circ}\right)+0.4 y \\
0 & =0.386+0.4 y \\
y & =\frac{-0.386}{0.4} \\
& =-0.965 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Magnitude of the 0.4 kg ball's velocity $v$ after the collision:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{4.85^{2}+0.965^{2}} \\
& =4.95 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Direction of the 0.4 kg ball's velocity after the collision:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tan \theta & =\frac{y}{x} \\
& =\frac{0.965}{4.85} \\
\theta & =\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{0.965}{4.85}\right) \\
& =11.3^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

$v=4.94 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at $11.3^{\circ}$ to the original direction of motion.

## Acceleration of spacecraft

Conservation of momentum can also be used to explain the acceleration of a rocket or jet, using the same mathematics as for collisions. The rocket fires hot gases backwards with a certain momentum. This gives the rocket the same momentum in the opposite direction, i.e, the change in the rocket's momentum is equal to the momentum given to the gases. The rocket therefore accelerates forwards. The same holds for a jet aircraft. Since the principle of conservation of momentum follows from Newton's three laws, this explanation of how a spacecraft accelerates and that on page 136 are equivalent.

## Worked Example 24

## Question

A spacecraft of mass 400 kg moving at $1000 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ejects a mass of 20 kg at a speed of $2000 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at right angles to the direction in which the craft is moving. Calculate the resultant velocity of the craft in magnitude and direction.

## Solution

Since no forces act in the original direction of motion, the velocity of the craft in this direction remains $1000 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Let $x$ be the recoil velocity acquired by the craft at right angles to the $1000 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ (Figure 8.38).
Apply conservation of momentum perpendicular to the original direction of motion:
momentum before = momentum after

$$
\begin{aligned}
(400)(0) & =(20)(-2000)+380 x \\
0 & =-40000+380 x \\
4 & =\frac{-40000}{380} \\
& =-105.26 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-164.jpg?height=857&width=900&top_left_y=1295&top_left_x=1676)
Figure 8.38

Resultant velocity, $v$, of spacecraft (Figure 8.39) is found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} \\
& =\sqrt{105.26^{2}+1000^{2}} \\
& =1005.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \\
\tan \theta & =\frac{y}{x} \\
& =\frac{105.26}{1000} \\
\theta & =\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{105.26}{1000}\right) \\
& =6^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

$v=1005.5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at $6^{\circ}$ to the original direction of motion.

Figure 8.39

## Collisions are governed by Newton's laws of motion

The principle of conservation of momentum can be shown to follow from Newton's laws. Therefore it is not surprising that Newton's laws also govern collisions and can be used to solve problems involving collisions.

## Worked Example 25

## Question

A body A, of mass 20 kg and moving at a speed of $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, collides with a body B, of mass 14 kg , which is at rest. The two bodies stick together on colliding and move away with a common velocity $v$ (Figure 8.40).
Use Newton's laws to verify that $v=2.35 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

## Solution

The velocity of $A$ only changes when it is acted on by a force from $B$.
The velocity of B only changes when it is acted on by a force from A .
So, Newton's first law applies - neither body changes velocity unless a force acts.

Suppose it takes $t$ seconds after the collision starts for the combined mass to reach a velocity $v$.
For body A: $u_{\mathrm{A}}=4 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \quad v_{\mathrm{A}}=v \quad a_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{4-v}{t}$
By Newton's second law, the force on A is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{A} & =m_{A} a_{A} \\
& =(20)\left(\frac{4-v}{t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

For body B: $u_{\mathrm{B}}=0 \quad v_{\mathrm{B}}=v \quad a_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{v-0}{t}=\frac{v}{t}$
By Newton's second law, the force on $B$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{\mathrm{B}} & =m_{\mathrm{B}} a_{\mathrm{B}} \\
& =(14)\left(\frac{v}{t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's third law, the forces are equal and opposite, $F_{\mathrm{A}}=F_{\mathrm{B}}$, so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(20)\left(\frac{4-v}{t}\right) & =(14)\left(\frac{v}{t}\right) \\
(20)(4-v) & =14 v \\
80-20 v & =14 v \\
v & =\frac{80}{34} \\
& =2.35 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Summary What I should know

- A force is anything that causes the velocity of an object to change (to speed up, slow down or change direction). In other words, force causes acceleration.
- The SI unit of force is the newton (N).
- The mass of a body is a measure of the amount of matter in that body.
- The mass of a body is also a measure of how difficult it is to accelerate that body.
- The SI unit of mass is the kilogram, kg.
- The kilogram is a base (or fundamental) SI unit.
- The acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the force causing it, that is, for a given body: $a \propto F$
- The acceleration produced by a given force is inversely proportional to the mass of the body being accelerated, that is, for a given force: $a \propto \frac{1}{\text { mass }}$
- 1 newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kilogram an acceleration of $1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\left(1 \mathrm{~N}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right)$
- If a force $F$ acts on an object of mass $m$ and it produces an acceleration $a$, then:

$$
F=m a, \quad \text { that is, } \quad \text { force }=\text { mass } \text { × } \text { acceleration }
$$

- The weight of an object (on Earth) is the force of the Earth's gravity acting on it.
- $W=m g$; that is, weight $=$ mass × acceleration due to gravity
- The SI unit of weight is the newton (N).
- The momentum of a body is equal to its mass multiplied by its velocity; that is,

$$
\text { momentum }=\text { mass × velocity } \quad p=m v
$$

- The $\mathbf{S I}$ unit of momentum is the kilogram metre per second $\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\right)$.
- Newton's first law of motion states that every body will remain in a state of rest or travelling with a constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it.
- Newton's second law of motion states that when a net force acts on a body, the rate of change of the body's momentum is directly proportional to the force and takes place in the direction of the force.
- Newton's third law of motion states that if a body A exerts a force on a body B, then body B exerts an equal but opposite force on body $A$, that is, action and reaction are equal and opposite.
- The principle of conservation of momentum states that, in any interaction between two or more bodies, the total momentum of the bodies before the interaction is equal to the total momentum after the interaction, provided no external forces act on the system of bodies.

## 9.1 Density

Which is heavier: steel, water or polystyrene? As it stands, this question is meaningless. It clearly depends on the volume of each substance that you have. To compare the masses of the same volumes of different substances, you can use the quantity density. By definition, the density of a substance is its mass per unit volume. Put another way, the density of a substance is given by the mass of $1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ of that substance (Figure 9.1).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-168.jpg?height=603&width=2417&top_left_y=2454&top_left_x=198)
Figure $9.11 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ of steel, $1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ of water and $1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ of polystyrene have significantly different masses.

- The density of a substance is its mass per unit volume.
- The symbol for density is $\rho$ (the Greek letter rho).
- For any substance: density $=\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { volume }} ; \rho=\frac{m}{V}$
- Density is a scalar quantity.
- The SI unit of density is the kilogram per cubic metre ( $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ ).

[^1]$$
\text { density }=\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { volume }} ; \rho=\frac{m}{V}
$$
(F\&T, page 57)
Since: $\quad \rho=\frac{m}{V^{\prime}}$,
SI unit of density $=\frac{\text { unit of mass }}{\text { unit of volume }}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{~m}^{3}} \\
& =\text { kilograms per cubic metre }\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The SI unit of density is the kilogram per cubic metre ( $\mathbf{k g ~ m}^{\mathbf{- 3}}$ ).
Note:

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
1 \mathrm{~kg} & =10^{3} \mathrm{~g} \quad \Longrightarrow 1 \mathrm{~g} \quad=10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg} \quad \text { and } \\
1 \mathrm{~m}^{3} & =10^{6} \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \Longrightarrow 1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \quad=10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{3} \\
1 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} & =10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg} / 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{3}=10^{3} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \quad \text { i.e. } \quad 1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}=1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}
\end{array}
$$

## Worked Example 1

## Question

A piece of wood has a volume of $0.02 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ and a mass of 10 kg . Find its density.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\rho & =\frac{m}{V} \\
& =\frac{10}{0.02} \\
& =500 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A piece of copper of mass 420 g has a volume of $47.19 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. What is its density?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
420 \mathrm{~g} & =420 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg}=0.42 \mathrm{~kg} \\
47.19 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} & =47.19 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{3} \\
\rho & =\frac{m}{v} \\
& =\frac{0.42}{47.19 \times 10^{-6}} \\
& =8.9 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

The density of aluminium is $2.7 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$. What is the volume of 120 grams of aluminium?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
120 \mathrm{~g} & =120 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg} \\
\rho & =\frac{m}{V} \\
V & =\frac{m}{\rho} \\
& =\frac{120 \times 10^{-3}}{2.7 \times 10^{3}} \\
& =4.44 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Measuring density

To measure the density of something, all you need to do is find its mass and find its volume. Then divide the mass by the volume. You would have done this in the laboratory at Junior Cycle for both solids and liquids.

## Flotation and density

Both liquids and gases can flow, and are known as fluids.
A fluid is a substance that can flow. In physics, a fluid is a liquid or a gas.

Note: You saw at Junior Cycle that if something floats in a liquid or a gas, it must be less dense than the liquid or the gas, whereas if it sinks, it is denser. For example, hydrogen or helium are both less dense than air whereas carbon dioxide is more dense. That is why a balloon of hydrogen or helium will float in air whereas one of carbon dioxide will sink.

- If something floats in a fluid, it is less dense than the fluid.
- If something sinks in a fluid, it is more dense than the fluid.


### 9.2 Pressure

If you walk on soft snow, your weight will cause you to sink into it. If, however, you wear snowshoes that spread your weight over a much larger area of snow, you will not sink as much.

Similarly, you cannot push your thumb into a wooden table, but using the same force on a sharp thumbtack will cause the point of the thumbtack to go into the wood.

In situations like these, it is the pressure that determines how easily you can sink something into a given substance.

- Pressure is defined as force per unit area.
- So, if a force $F$ acts evenly over an area $A$, the pressure $P$ at any point on that area is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Pressure } & =\frac{\text { force }}{\text { area }} \\
P & =\frac{F}{A}
\end{aligned}
$$

(F\&T, page 57)

- The symbol for pressure is $P$ or $p$.
- Pressure is a scalar quantity
- $P=\frac{F}{A^{\prime}}$, so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { unit of pressure } & =\frac{\text { unit of force }}{\text { unit of area }} \\
& =\frac{\text { newton }}{\text { square metre }} \\
& =\text { newton per square metre }\left(\mathrm{N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

## Blaise Pascal

Blaise Pascal (1623-1622)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-171.jpg?height=274&width=317&top_left_y=1517&top_left_x=2428)
was a French philosopher, mathematician, physicist and inventor. He worked on probability theory and the scientific method, and invented a mechanical calculator. He clarified the ideas of pressure and a vacuum. He also was the first to establish a public transport system.

- The newton per square metre is also called the pascal (Pa).

Pressure is force per unit area.

The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa).

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 1 \text { pascal = } 1 \text { newton per square metre } \\
& \text { i.e. } 1 \mathrm{~Pa}=1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Note: Unit Analysis

The pascal can be expressed in base units as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \mathrm{~Pa} & =1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2} \\
& =1\left(\mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right) \mathrm{m}^{-2}\left(1 \mathrm{~N}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right) \\
\Longrightarrow 1 \mathrm{~Pa} & =1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A force of 600 N acts evenly on a surface of area $5 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$. What pressure does it exert?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =\frac{F}{A} \\
& =\frac{600}{5} \\
& =120 \mathrm{~Pa}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A force of 40 N acts on an area of $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$. What pressure does it exert?

## Solution

$1 \mathrm{~m}^{2}=10000 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \Longrightarrow 1 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}=\frac{1}{10000} \mathrm{~m}^{2}=1 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Longrightarrow 25 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} & =25 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \\
P & =\frac{F}{A} \\
& =\frac{40}{25 \times 10^{-4}} \\
& =16000 \mathrm{~Pa}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Question

Figure 9.3 shows a rectangular block of mass 5 kg resting on a horizontal table. Find the value of the pressure on the table if:
a) Side $A$ is on the table
b) Side $B$ is on the table

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { force acting on table } & =\text { weight of block } \\
& =m g \\
& =(5)(9.8) \\
& =49 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

a) Side A :

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =\frac{F}{A} \\
& =\frac{49}{(0.04)(0.12)} \\
& =1.02 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~Pa}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) Side B:

\end{aligned}
$$

### 9.3 Pressure due to a liquid

In Figure 9.5, the weight of the liquid is acting on the base of the beaker and thus exerts pressure on the base.

## Worked Example 7

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-173.jpg?height=668&width=883&top_left_y=1230&top_left_x=1865)
Figure 9.5 The weight of the liquid causes pressure in the liquid.

## Question

Suppose a bucket contains 8 kg of water. If the area of the base of the bucket is $0.4 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$, calculate the pressure at the base of the bucket due to the water.

## Solution

Weight of liquid acting down on base
$=m g=(8)(9.8)=78.4 \mathrm{~N}$
Pressure at base due to the liquid
$=\frac{F}{A}=\frac{78.4}{0.42}=196 \mathrm{~Pa}$
In reality, the total pressure (or the absolute pressure) at the base of the bucket is larger than 196 Pa. The Earth's atmosphere also exerts pressure down on the top of the liquid. This must be added to the 196 Pa to get the total or absolute pressure at the base of the bucket (see page 166)
It can be shown that:
At depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$ where acceleration due to gravity is $g$, the pressure $P$ due to the liquid is given by:

$$
P=h \rho g
$$

Or said another way:

## Suppose:

1. A liquid has a density $\rho$
2. The difference in depth between two points in the liquid is $h$
3. The difference in pressure between two points in the

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-173.jpg?height=629&width=1033&top_left_y=3115&top_left_x=1666)
Figure 9.6

liquid is $P$
Then: $\quad P=h \rho g \quad$ (See Figure 9.6) (F\&T, page 57)

If an object is placed in a liquid, the liquid exerts a pressure on that object. It also exerts a pressure on the walls of the container.
Pressure in a liquid obeys the following laws:

- Pressure increases linearly with depth.

This follows from the above since $P=h \rho g$. It can be demonstrated as in Figure 9.7, where the water from the deepest hole squirts out the farthest.

- Pressure acts perpendicular (at right angles) to any surface put in the liquid.

This can be demonstrated as shown in Figure 9.8 The water emerges from each hole perpendicular to the surface.

- At a given depth, the value of the pressure is the same in all directions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-175.jpg?height=903&width=747&top_left_y=966&top_left_x=325)
Figure 9.7 Pressure increases with depth.

### 9.4 The buoyancy force on an object immersed in a liquid

Figure 9.10 shows an object immersed in a liquid. The pressure of the liquid acts inwards on the object as shown. Because pressure increases with depth, the pressure underneath is greater than the pressure on top. The liquid therefore exerts an overall upwards force on the body. Worked Example 11 shows an example of this. This upwards force due to the liquid is called the buoyancy force or the upthrust.

Buoyancy force (also called upthrust) is the overall upward force that is exerted on an object immersed in a fluid. This force is caused by the greater pressure on the parts of the object that are deeper in the fluid.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-176.jpg?height=740&width=584&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=1627)
Figure 9.10 The buoyancy force is the upward force exerted on an object immersed in a fluid.

## Worked Example 11

## Question

A rectangular wooden block has dimensions 14 cm by 12 cm by 20 cm . It is placed with its upper surface at a depth of 30 cm in a basin of water, as in Figure 9.11.
a) Find:
i) The pressure at the upper surface of the block due to the water
ii) The pressure at the lower surface of the block due to the water
iii) The force on the upper surface due to the water
iv) The force on the lower surface due to the water.
b) If the weight of the block is 26 N , determine whether the block will float or sink. (density of water $=1000 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$ )

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-176.jpg?height=1192&width=848&top_left_y=1572&top_left_x=1337)
Figure 9.11

## Solution

a) i) pressure at top $=h \rho g=(0.3)(1000)(9.8)=2940 \mathrm{~Pa}$
ii) pressure at bottom $=h \rho g=(0.5)(1000)(9.8)=4900 \mathrm{~Pa}$
iii) $F=P A \Longrightarrow$ downward force on top $=(2940)(0.12 \times 0.14)=49.4 \mathrm{~N}$
iv) upward force on bottom $=P A=(4900)(0.12 \times 0.14)=82.3 \mathrm{~N}$
b) total downward force on block $=49.4 \mathrm{~N}+$ weight of block $=49.4+26=75.4 \mathrm{~N}$
total upward force $=82.3 \mathrm{~N}$
resultant force on block is upwards and of magnitude $=82.3-(49.4+26.0)=6.9 \mathrm{~N}$
Therefore, if the block is released it will float.

When an object is floating on a liquid (Figure 9.12), there is still a buoyancy force acting on the submerged part of the object. Since the object is not accelerating vertically, this buoyancy force must be equal in magnitude to the weight of the object.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-177.jpg?height=919&width=1795&top_left_y=478&top_left_x=325)

### 9.5 Pressure in gases and atmospheric pressure

## Pressure in a gas

Just like liquids, gases can also exert pressure.
The formula $P=h \rho g$ also holds for gases, provided the density of the gas remains fixed.
Just like for liquids, pressure in a gas:

- Increases with depth
- Acts perpendicular to any surface in the gas
- Is the same value in all directions at any point

However, the density of a gas is usually very small, so the difference in pressure between two points is usually negligible unless the vertical distance between the points is very large. In a tank containing a gas, you can assume the pressure is almost the same everywhere.

## Atmospheric pressure

The Earth is covered with a layer of air called the atmosphere. As you move farther from the surface of the Earth, the air becomes less dense. Although there is no actual upper limit to the atmosphere, most of it lies below 200 km . The gases of the Earth's atmosphere have weight, and due to this weight, there is pressure called atmospheric pressure acting on any object.

- The average value of atmospheric pressure at sea level is taken to be $1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$.
- Its actual value varies depending on the type of weather system present.
- Its value decreases as you move away from the surface of the Earth. For example, at the top of Mt Everest ( 8848 m above sea level), atmospheric pressure is about $\frac{1}{3}$ the value at sea level.
- The value of atmospheric pressure can be read on a barometer.


## Worked Example 12

## Question

A school laboratory has a floor area of $88 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ and a ceiling height of 3 m .
a) Ignoring the volume taken up by furniture etc., estimate the volume of air in the laboratory.
b) If the density of air is $1.2 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$, calculate the mass and the weight of the air in the laboratory.

## Solution

a) volume of air = volume of laboratory

$$
=(\text { floor area })(\text { height })=(88)(3)=264 \mathrm{~m}^{3}
$$

b) $\quad \rho=\frac{m}{V}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
m & =\rho V \\
& =(1.2)(264) \\
& =316.8 \mathrm{~kg}
\end{aligned}
$$

mass of air in the lab $=316.8 \mathrm{~kg}$ and its weight $=(316.8)(9.8)=3105 \mathrm{~N}$

## Worked Example 13

## Question

The pressure on the cover of a book due to the Earth's atmosphere is $1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$.
If the area of the top of the front cover of the book is $621 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$, calculate the force on the cover of the book due to the atmosphere.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =\frac{F}{A} \\
F & =P A \\
& =\left(1 \times 10^{5}\right)\left(621 \times 10^{-4}\right) \\
& =6210 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this is a very large force, equivalent to the weight of 663 kg on Earth. However, a similar force acts on the other side of the front cover so that there is no net force on the cover.

Since a gas exerts a pressure on a surface in the same way as a liquid, atmospheric pressure acts on the top of the liquid in the container in Figure 9.15. So, the total pressure (or the absolute pressure) at the bottom of the liquid

$$
\begin{array}{lccc}
= & \text { atmospheric pressure } & + & \text { pressure due to the liquid } \\
= & P_{\mathrm{atm}} & + & h \rho g
\end{array}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-178.jpg?height=616&width=636&top_left_y=3008&top_left_x=1940)

## Student Experiment 9.1

a) To determine acceleration due to gravity $g$, using the formula: $g=\frac{h}{P \rho}$ (from $P=h \rho g$ )
b) To verify that the equation $g=\frac{h}{P \rho}$ gives an accurate value for $g$ and thus that the equation accurately models pressure in a liquid near the Earth's surface.

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will measure the pressure $P$ at several measured depths $h$ in a liquid of known density $\rho$. You will then calculate a value for acceleration due to gravity $g$, using the above formula.

## Equipment

An absolute pressure sensor and plastic tubing that connects to it, some method to connect the pressure sensor to the metre stick, a graduated cylinder that can hold liquid to at least a depth of 40 cm , a metre stick, a data logger and a computer.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-180.jpg?height=1395&width=896&top_left_y=1718&top_left_x=1263)
Figure 9.17 Experiment to determine acceleration due to gravity

## Method

1. Connect the pressure sensor and tube to the metre stick (Figure 9.17).
2. Measure and record the pressure when the bottom of the tube is not immersed in the water, i.e. measure $P_{\text {abs }}$ when $h=0$. This is atmospheric pressure $P_{\text {atm }}$.
3. Place the bottom of the tubing at a fixed depth (e.g. 5 cm ) in a graduated cylinder filled with a liquid of known density $\rho$ (e.g. water).
4. Measure the depth, $h$, of the bottom of the tubing below the surface of the liquid.
5. Record the value of the pressure $P_{\text {abs }}$ given by the data logger.
6. Repeat this procedure for a series of increasing depths (e.g. 5 cm each time), recording all values in the table.

## Handling the data

## Method 1

For each pair of values, calculate a value for $g$ using: $g=\frac{\left(P_{\mathrm{abs}}-P_{\mathrm{atm}}\right)}{h \rho}$ Ignoring any clear outliers, calculate the average value of $g$.
It will be close to $9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, verifying that the equation $g=\frac{P}{h \rho}$ models accurately the pressure in a liquid of constant density.

| Depth $h$ (m) | 0 |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $P_{\text {abs }}(\mathrm{Pa})$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| $g\left(\mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right) =\frac{\boldsymbol{P}_{\text {abs }}-\boldsymbol{P}_{\text {atm }}}{h \rho}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

## Method 2

Plot a graph of $P_{\text {abs }}$ against $h$ (or get the software to do it).
Draw the line of best fit and measure its slope. Calculate $g$ from: $g=\frac{\text { slope }}{\rho}$
It will be close to $9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, verifying that the equation $g=\frac{P}{h \rho}$ models accurately the pressure in a liquid of constant density.

## Explanation of the graph:

Comparing: $y=m x+c$ with $P_{\text {abs }}=\rho g h+P_{\text {atm }}$ you can see that the slope of the graph of $P_{\text {abs }}$ against $h$ is $\rho g$ i.e. slope $=\rho g \Longrightarrow g=\frac{\text { slope }}{\rho}$

## Sources of error

1. Make sure the open entrance at the bottom of the tube is horizontal when in the water.
2. Read the bottom of the meniscus of the water in the graduated cylinder when reading the depth.
3. If some water enters the end of the plastic tube, $h$ is the distance from the top of this piece of water to the meniscus in the graduated cylinder.
4. Avoid the error of parallax when reading the metre stick.

### 9.6 Gravity - the cement of the universe

## Universal gravitation

In 1666, Sir Isaac Newton first stated his theory of gravitation. He realised that the force causing objects to fall downwards (towards the Earth) was the same kind of force that keeps the planets of the Solar System orbiting the Sun. He called it the Force of Gravity. In his theory, he described the following law, which is now called Newton's law of universal gravitation:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-182.jpg?height=297&width=812&top_left_y=1627&top_left_x=1399)
Figure 9.18 Two point masses at a certain distance apart, each exerting a force on the other

Newton's law of universal gravitation states that any two point masses in the universe attract each other with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

Suppose the two point masses are $m_{1}$ and $m_{2} \mathrm{~kg}$, and they are a distance $d \mathrm{~m}$ apart (Figure 9.18).

- Then the law states that: $m_{1}$ exerts a force $F$ on $m_{2}$ attracting it towards $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ exerts a force $F$ on $m_{1}$ attracting it towards $m_{2}$
So, gravitational forces are always attractive.
- The size of the force on each mass is the same, even if one mass is much larger than the other.
- The law states that: $F \propto m_{1} m_{2}$ so you see that $F \propto m_{1}$ and $F \propto m_{2}$
- The law also states that the size of the force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the two bodies; that is, $F \propto \frac{1}{d^{2}}$
This means that:
- If the distance between the bodies is doubled, the force becomes four times smaller. If the distance between them is tripled, the force becomes nine times smaller, etc.
- If the distance between the bodies is halved, the force becomes four times bigger. If the distance between the bodies is made 4 times smaller, the force becomes 16 times bigger, etc.
So, Newton's law of universal gravitation is an example of an inverse square law.
- Since $F \propto m_{1} m_{2}$ and $F \propto \frac{1}{d^{2}}$, then $F \propto \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}}$

$$
\Rightarrow F=G \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}}
$$

where $G$ is a constant.

$$
F=G \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}} \text { where } G \text { is a constant. }
$$

$G$ is called the universal gravitation constant
(F\&T, page 56)
The value of $G$ is $6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$. This is an extremely small number.
A more exact value is given in F\&T page 46.
Note: Newton was able to show that the gravitational force between two spherical bodies is the same as if each had all its mass at its centre and the distance between the bodies is the distance between their centres.
In the Worked Examples below, assume that the Earth, Moon and planets are perfect spheres.

## Worked Example 14

## Question

Find the gravitational force of attraction between two steel spheres, each of mass 80 kg , if the distance between their centres is 0.5 m . ( $G=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$ )

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =G \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}} \\
& =\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right) \frac{(80)(80)}{0.5^{2}} \\
& =1.72 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~N} \\
& =0,0000017 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this is a very small force.
Since $G$ is such a small number $\left(0.000000000067 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}\right)$, the gravitational force between two bodies is negligible unless at least one of them has a very large mass. For everyday objects on Earth, the gravitational forces between them are so small that they are negligible compared to the much larger everyday forces that objects are subject to.

## Worked Example 15

## Question

Find the gravitational attraction between a man of mass 90 kg and the Earth when the man is standing on the surface of the Earth.
(Mass of Earth $=6 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$; radius of Earth $=6.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m} ; G=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$ )

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =G \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}} \\
& =\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right) \frac{\left(6 \times 10^{24}\right)(90)}{\left(6.4 \times 10^{6}\right)^{2}} \\
& =883.3 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

This force is equal to the weight of the man: $W=m g=(90)(9.81)=883 \mathrm{~N}$

The value of the universal gravitation constant $G$ is the same anywhere in the universe. Its value can be found by experiment. This was first done by Henry Cavendish in 1731, in Cambridge.

From $F=G \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}} \quad G$ is given by $\quad G=\frac{F d^{2}}{m_{1} m_{2}}$
So, the unit of $G$ is the $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{kg}^{2}=\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$
In words, this is the newton metre squared per kilogram squared.

## Gravity and the Solar System

The force of gravity is the force that keeps the planets of the Solar System orbiting the Sun (Figure 9.19). It also keeps moons orbiting planets. The gravitational forces involved are large, since the masses of the bodies are large. It is also the force that keeps artificial satellites orbiting the Earth (Page 207).
The force of gravity keeps the Earth's atmosphere attached to the Earth. On some planets and moons, the gravity is too weak to hold the atmosphere, and any gas escapes into space. This is why our Moon has no atmosphere (Figure 9.20).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-184.jpg?height=863&width=1482&top_left_y=270&top_left_x=1139)
Figure 9.19 The force of gravity keeps the planets orbiting the Sun.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-184.jpg?height=718&width=2010&top_left_y=1337&top_left_x=201)
Figure 9.20 The Moon's gravity is too weak to maintain an atmosphere. Any gas molecules placed there would eventually escape into space.

### 9.7 Gravity and weight

Recall that weight is a force (measured in newtons) and that the weight $W$ of an object of mass $m$ on the surface of the Earth is given by:

$$
W=m g
$$

where $g$ is acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth.
Figure 9.21 shows an object of mass $m$ on the surface of the Earth. Its weight is also the force of gravitational attraction between it and the Earth, which from Newton's law of gravitation is given by:

$$
W=\frac{G M m}{R^{2}}
$$

where $M$ is the mass of the Earth and $R$ its radius.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-185.jpg?height=662&width=776&top_left_y=429&top_left_x=1966)
Figure 9.21

$$
\begin{aligned}
W=m g \text { and } W & =\frac{G M m}{R^{2}}, \text { so: } \\
m g & =\frac{G M m}{R^{2}} \\
g & =\frac{G M}{R^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

acceleration due to gravity, $g=\frac{G M}{R^{2}}$

From this equation, you can see that the value of acceleration due to gravity, and hence the weight of any object, depends on the mass of the Earth and its distance from the centre of the Earth, which at sea level is roughly equivalent to the Earth's radius.
The Earth is not a perfect sphere, as its polar radius is less than the radius at its equator. Thus, acceleration due to gravity and the weight of any object is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator (page 99). Correct to one decimal place, however, $g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ anywhere near the surface of the Earth.
This formula applies on other planets too, using the correct values for $M$ and $R$ on the given planet.
A formula almost identical to the above applies to any object above the surface of the Earth (Figure 9.22). If $d$ is the distance from the centre of the Earth to the object, and $g_{d}$ is acceleration due to gravity at that point, then the formula is:

Acceleration due to gravity at a distance $d$ from the centre of the Earth

$$
g_{d}=\frac{G M}{d^{2}}
$$

(F\&T, page 56)

It follows that the value of acceleration due to gravity, and hence weight, decreases as you move away from the Earth ( $d$ increases).
In the following worked examples, take: $G=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$,
$g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, radius of the Earth $=6.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$, mass of Earth $=6 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$.

## Worked Example 16

## Question

a) Find the value of acceleration due to gravity on the surface of Mars, given that the radius of Mars is $3.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$ and the mass of Mars is $6.6 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{~kg}$.
b) Hence find the weight of a 90 kg man on Mars.

## Solution

a) $g=\frac{G M}{R^{2}}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-185.jpg?height=759&width=763&top_left_y=2656&top_left_x=1979)
Figure 9.22 The value of acceleration due to gravity, and hence weight, decreases as you move away from the Earth

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6.6 \times 10^{23}\right)}{\left(3.4 \times 10^{6}\right)^{2}} \\
& =3.8 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) Weight of man $=W=m g=(90)(3.8)=342 \mathrm{~N}$

## Worked Example 17

## Question

a) Find acceleration due to gravity 1000 km above the Earth's surface.
b) What is the weight of a woman of mass 60 kg at this height?

## Solution

a) $g_{d}=\frac{G M}{d^{2}}$

From Figure 9.22:

$$
\begin{aligned}
d & =R+1000 \times 10^{3}=6.4 \times 10^{6}+1 \times 10^{6} \\
g_{d} & =\frac{\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{24}\right)}{\left(6.4 \times 10^{6}+1 \times 10^{6}\right)^{2}} \\
& =7.3 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) $W=m g=(60)(7.3)=438 \mathrm{~N}$

## Worked Example 18

## Question

Given that the value of $g$ on the surface of the Earth is $9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, at what height above the Earth's surface is acceleration due to gravity equal to half its value on the surface of the Earth?

## Solution

Let $d$ be the distance from the centre of the Earth to the point where acceleration is half the value at the surface.
$g_{d}=\frac{G M}{d^{2}}$
Half the value of acceleration on the surface $=\frac{9.8}{2}=4.9 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$
So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4.9 & =\frac{\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6.6 \times 10^{24}\right)}{d^{2}} \\
d & =\sqrt{\frac{\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{24}\right)}{4.9}} \\
& =9.1 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

∴ Height above surface $=9.1 \times 10^{6}-6.4 \times 10^{6}=2.7 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$ above the surface.

### 9.8 Gravitational fields

Another way to look at gravity is to use the idea of a gravitational field. Suppose there is a large planet in empty space. Due to the planet, the space around it is now different to what the space was if the planet was not there. This planet, in some way, has modified the space in its vicinity. You could say the mass of the planet has created a gravitational field in the space around it.
If another mass is brought into this field, the field then exerts a gravitational force on that mass. In this example, the force on the mass is towards the large planet.
The gravitational field is strong near the planet and it gets weaker as you move away from the planet.
The strength of the field is represented using a vector quantity called gravitational field strength.
The gravitational field strength at any point in a gravitational field is defined as the force per unit mass at that point, i.e. the gravitational field strength is the force per kilogram.

So, if a mass of 1 kg experiences a force of 400 N at a point in a gravitational field, you can say that the gravitational field strength there is 400 newtons per kilogram, i.e. $400 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1}$. Its direction is the direction of the force (towards the centre of the body creating the field).
Suppose a mass of 12 kg experiences a force of 576 N at a point in a gravitational field.
The gravitational field strength there is $\frac{576}{12}=48 \mathrm{Nkg}^{-1}$
If a mass $m$ experiences a force $F$ when placed in a gravitational field, the gravitational field strength at that point is, by definition, $\frac{F}{m}$
The symbol for gravitational field strength is $g$, thus: Gravitational field strength $g=\frac{F}{m}$
Gravitational field strength

$$
g=\frac{F}{m}
$$

(F\&T, page 56)

The SI unit of gravitational field strength is the newton per kilogram ( $\mathbf{N ~ k g}^{-\mathbf{1}}$ ).
If a mass $m$ experiences a force $F$ in a gravitational field, then the gravitational field strength at that point is $g=\frac{F}{m}$
If a mass $m$ experiences a force $F$ in a gravitational field, then its acceleration at that point is $a=\frac{F}{m}$ So the value of gravitational field strength at a point is always the same as the acceleration due to gravity at that point. That is why the symbol $g$ is used for gravitational field strength.

Note: The value of gravitational field strength at a point is always the same as the acceleration due to gravity at that point.

A gravitational field can be represented on a diagram by lines called gravitational field lines. These lines have arrowheads that show the direction of the gravitational field strength vector. Figure 9.23 shows the shape of the gravitational field near the Earth. Note that where the gravitational field is strong, the field lines are close together. And where the field is weaker, the lines

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-187.jpg?height=1257&width=1323&top_left_y=2194&top_left_x=1425)
Figure 9.23 Gravitational field near the Earth

are farther apart.

## Worked Example 19

## Question

Find the value of gravitational field strength at a distance $d$ from the centre of a planet of mass $M$.

## Solution

Force on an object of mass $m$ at this point is: $F=\frac{G M m}{d^{2}}$
Gravitational field strength: $g=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{\left(\frac{G M m}{d^{2}}\right)}{m}$
Gravitational field strength: $g=\frac{G M}{d^{2}}$ towards the centre of the planet,
which is the same formula for acceleration due to gravity at that point.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
