### 9.9 Escape velocity

If an object is projected vertically upwards from the ground at a very high speed, and if acceleration due to gravity remains constant with height, the object would always reach a greatest height and then fall back to the ground.

However, acceleration due to gravity does not remain constant. It decreases with distance from the centre of the Earth $d$ according to the formula: $g_{d}=\frac{G M}{d^{2}}$. The value of $g$ decreases inversely with the distance squared.

Because of this rapid decrease in $g$ with distance, it is possible for an object to escape completely from the Earth's gravitational field if it is given a large enough initial velocity. This value is called the escape velocity. Assuming air resistance can be neglected, the escape velocity from Earth's surface is about $11200 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
It can be shown that the escape velocity $v_{\mathrm{e}}$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth is given by:
$v_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}}$
where $M$ is the mass of the Earth and $G$ the universal gravitation constant.

## HL

## Worked Example 21

## Question

Calculate the escape velocity of an object from the surface of the Earth.
Take: $G=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$, radius of Earth $=6.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$, mass of Earth $=6 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{\mathrm{e}} & =\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{(2)\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{24}\right)}{6.4 \times 10^{6}}} \\
& =11200 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

The same formula can be applied to other celestial bodies (planets, moons, stars, and so on), replacing the values of $M$ and $r$ as appropriate.

The escape velocity $v_{e}$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of any celestial body is given by:

$$
v_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}}
$$

where $M$ is the mass of the celestial body and $G$ the universal gravitation constant

## SEC examination question (HL)

The gravitational field strength $g$ at the surface of the Earth is $g_{\text {surface }}=9.81 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1}$. This is partly due to the radius of the Earth, which is approximately 6378 km .
a) Calculate the value of the gravitational field strength at a height of 900 km above the surface of the Earth.
b) Calculate the escape velocity at this height.
c) The mass of a rocket can be over $7 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~kg}$.
i) Predict how the mass of a rocket affects its escape velocity.
ii) Justify your answer.
d) Rockets are launched at the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida, which is roughly at sea level. Suggest a reason why Kennedy Space Centre was not built at a height of 900 km above the surface of the Earth.

## Solution

a) The gravitational field strength $g$, at a distance $d$ from the centre of a planet is given by:

$$
g_{d}=\frac{G M}{d^{2}}
$$

where $G$ is the universal gravitational constant and $M$ is the mass of the Earth At the surface of the Earth:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{\text {surface }} & =\frac{G M}{\left(6378 \times 10^{3}\right)^{2}} \\
& =9.81 \\
\Rightarrow G M & =(9.81)\left(6378 \times 10^{3}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

At a height $h$ of 900 km above the surface of the Earth, gravitational field strength $g^{\mathrm{h}}$ is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{h} & =\frac{G M}{\left(6378 \times 10^{3}+900 \times 10^{3}\right)^{2}} \\
& =\frac{(9.81)\left(6378 \times 10^{3}\right)^{2}}{\left(6378 \times 10^{3}+900 \times 10^{3}\right)^{2}} \\
& =7.53 \mathrm{Nkg}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Its direction is towards the centre of the Earth.
b) The escape velocity $v_{e}$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of a celestial body of mass $M$ is given by:

$$
v_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}}
$$

Therefore, using the value of $G M$ from a) above, the escape velocity from 900 km above the Earth:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{\mathrm{e}} & =\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{(2)\left((9.81)\left(6378 \times 10^{3}\right)^{2}\right)}{\left.6378 \times 10^{3}+900 \times 10^{3}\right)}} \\
& =10472 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

c) i) The mass of a rocket does not affect its escape velocity.
ii) From the formula $v_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}}$ you can see that the escape velocity $v_{\mathrm{e}}$ only depends on the mass $M$ of the body it is escaping from, its distance $r$ from the centre of that body and the universal gravitational constant $G$.
d) The huge expense and difficulty in bringing the space centre from Earth to a height of 900 km .

## Summary What I should know

- Density is mass per unit volume; that is, density = $\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { volume }}, \quad \rho=\frac{m}{V}$
- The SI unit of density is the kilogram per cubic metre ( $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ ).
- Pressure is force per unit area; that is, pressure = force , $\quad P=\frac{F}{A}$
- The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa).
- 1 pascal = 1 newton per square metre; that is, $1 \mathrm{~Pa}=1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}$
- At depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$, where acceleration due to gravity is $g$, the pressure $P$ due to the liquid is given by: $\quad P=h \rho g$
- In a liquid of density $\rho$, the difference in pressure $P$, between two points whose depth difference in the liquid is $h$, is given by: $P=h \rho g$
- In a fluid, pressure:
i) Increases with depth
ii) Acts perpendicular to any surface in the fluid
iii) At a given depth is the same in all directions
- In a liquid whose surface is exposed to atmospheric pressure: total (or absolute) pressure at depth $h=$ atmospheric pressure + pressure due to the liquid

$$
P_{\text {abs }}=P_{\text {attm }}+h \rho g
$$

- Buoyancy force (also called upthrust) is the overall upward force that is exerted on an object immersed in a fluid. This force is caused by the greater pressure on the parts of the object that are deeper in the fluid.
- When an object is floating on a liquid, there is a buoyancy force acting on the submerged part of the object. This buoyancy force is equal in magnitude to the weight of the object.
- Newton's law of universal gravitation states that any two point masses in the universe attract each other with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them; that is,

$$
F=\frac{G m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}}
$$

- Newton's law of universal gravitation is an example of an inverse square law.
- Acceleration due to gravity on the Earth's surface can be modelled by the equation

$$
g=\frac{G M}{R^{2}}
$$

- The gravitational field strength $g$, at a point in a gravitational field, is the force per unit mass at that point; that is,

$$
g=\frac{F}{m}
$$

- The SI unit of gravitational field strength is the newton per kilogram ( $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ ).


# 10 Work, Energy and Power

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand work, energy, power and efficiency
- To ensure students appreciate the significance of kinetic, potential and electromagnetic energy
- To ensure students appreciate the different forms of energy
- To ensure students understand, appreciate and are able to apply the principle of conservation of energy to real-world situations
- To ensure students can model real-world situations involving gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, work done and power


### 10.1 Work

A person pushing a car along a level road is said to be doing work. The amount of work done depends on the force the person exerts and the distance through which the force acts. This concept of work is very important in physics.

## Keywords

- Work (or work done)
- Energy
- The joule (J)
- Kinetic energy
- Potential energy
- Electromagnetic energy
- Internal energy (heat)
- Sound energy
- Chemical energy
- Electrical energy
- Nuclear energy
- Principle of conservation of energy
- Elastic potential energy
- Gravitational potential energy
- Renewable energy, non-renewable energy
- Power, average power
- The watt (W)
- Percentage efficiency
- If a force $F$ moves a body through a displacement $s$ in the direction of the force, the work done, $W$, is by definition equal to the force multiplied by the displacement; that is, $W=F s$
- Work is a scalar quantity. Its usual symbol is $W$.
- The SI unit of work is the joule (J).


## Sl unit of work

Since $W=F s$, the SI unit of work $=($ unit of $F) \times($ unit of $s)=$ newton × metre $(\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m})$

This unit is called the joule in honour of James Joule (1818-89) who carried out early research into the concept of work, and the related quantity energy.

When a force $F$ moves a body through a displacement $s$ in the direction of the force, the work done $W$ is equal to the force multiplied by the displacement.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Work } & =\text { force × displacement } \\
W & =F s
\end{aligned}
$$

(F\&T page 55)

Note: Note that:
1 millijoule $(\mathrm{mJ})=10^{-3} \mathrm{~J}$
1 kilojoule $(\mathrm{kJ})=10^{3}$ ]
1 megajoule $(\mathrm{MJ})=10^{6} \mathrm{~J}$

## James Prescott Joule

James Prescott Joule (1818-1889) was
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-193.jpg?height=271&width=317&top_left_y=2845&top_left_x=2428)
an English physicist who established that different forms of energy are the same thing and can be converted into each other. He established that heat and work are also equivalent. He therefore discovered the idea of the principle of conservation of energy. He discovered that the heat produced by an electric current in a conductor is directly proportional to the resistance of the conductor and to the square of the current. In 1852, with William Thompson (Lord Kelvin), he discovered the theoretical principle of operation of the heat pump, and was the first to state that energy could be used to cause heat to flow from a cooler region to a hotter one.

## Worked Example 4

## Question

Find the work done in bringing a 1000 kg car from rest to $30 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in 10 seconds.

## Solution

Consider the quantities you know and those you need to find:
$u=0, \quad v=30 \quad t=10, \quad s=? \quad a=$ ?
Now calculate the acceleration and then the distance travelled.
To find $a$, use:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =u+2 a t \\
30 & =0+10 a \\
a & =\frac{30}{10} \\
& =3 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

To find $s$, use:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v^{2} & =u^{2}+2 a s \\
30^{2} & =0^{2}+(2)(3) s \\
s & =\frac{30^{2}}{6} \\
& =150 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

force exerted on car, $F=m a$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(1000)(3) \\
& =3000 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

work done $=$ force × distance

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(3000)(150) \\
& =450000 \\
& =450 \mathrm{~kJ}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 10.2 Energy

- Energy is the ability to do work. Anything that can do work has energy, i.e. anything that can exert a force through a distance has energy.
- Energy is a scalar quantity.
- Since the energy of a body is the amount of work it can do, the SI unit of energy is the same as the unit of work, i.e. the joule.

Energy ( $\boldsymbol{E}$ ) is the ability to do work. The amount of energy something has is the amount of work it can do.

The SI unit of energy is the joule (J).

## Different forms of energy

Since a body can do work for different reasons, it can have energy for different reasons. It is useful to classify energy according to the reasons that a body has it.

## Kinetic energy

All moving objects have energy due to their motion. The energy a body has due to its motion is called kinetic energy (see page 186).

## Potential energy

Potential energy is the energy a body has due to its position in a force field (see page 188).

## Electromagnetic energy (also called radiant energy)

Electromagnetic energy is the energy transmitted from one place to another in the form of electromagnetic waves, which travel at the speed of light (see page 264). Figure 10.2 shows the spectrum of electromagnetic waves.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-196.jpg?height=603&width=2426&top_left_y=2145&top_left_x=195)
Figure 10.2

## Internal energy (heat energy)

Internal energy (heat) comes from the motion of particles. The molecules of every substance, whether solid, liquid or gas, are always moving. If heat is supplied to a substance, the motion (the vibration) of its molecules increases as its temperature rises. The kinetic energy of the molecules, and therefore the internal energy of the substance, therefore increases.

## Sound energy

All sound is caused by some object that is vibrating. As sound travels through a substance, the vibration from the source is passed on from molecule to molecule in that substance. Each molecule therefore acquires energy in the form of kinetic and potential energy, as the sound wave passes (page 289), and this is sound energy.

## Chemical energy

The energy given out (or sometimes taken in), in the form of heat, light or kinetic energy during a chemical reaction, is called chemical energy. For example, when something is burned, some of the chemical energy stored in it is changed into heat and light energy (Figure 10.3).
As these people warm themselves by the fire, chemical energy is being converted to heat and light energy.

## Electrical energy

When an electric current flows in a metal wire, subatomic particles called electrons move in the wire. As they move, they lose potential energy called electrical energy. This potential energy appears as heat and other forms of energy in the wire.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-197.jpg?height=935&width=1196&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=1549)
Figure 10.3

## Nuclear energy

The energy given out from the nuclei of certain atoms during nuclear reactions (fission or fusion, for example) is called nuclear energy. This is the source of energy in nuclear reactors (Chapter 30).

### 10.3 Principle of conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one body to another, or changed from one form to another. This fact is one of the most important principles in physics. In every chemical or physical reaction, there is no net gain or loss of energy, but rather any loss must be accompanied by an equal gain. This is called the principle of conservation of energy.

The principle of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, but can only be converted from one form to another.

## Examples of energy conversions

Energy can be changed from one form to another. Sometimes these changes occur by themselves, but sometimes special equipment or conditions are needed to bring about a particular conversion. Figure 10.4 shows some examples.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-197.jpg?height=1268&width=1743&top_left_y=2633&top_left_x=328)
Figure 10.4

### 10.4 Kinetic energy

The kinetic energy, $E_{\mathrm{k}}$ of a body is the energy that body has due to its motion.
The kinetic energy, $E_{\mathrm{k}}$ of a body of mass $m$ moving with a speed $\boldsymbol{v}$ is given by:

$$
E_{\mathrm{k}}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}
$$

You do not need to be able to prove this formula.

Kinetic energy:

$$
E_{\mathrm{k}}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}
$$

(F\&T page 55)

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A body of mass 1000 kg is moving with a velocity of $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Calculate its kinetic energy.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{\mathrm{k}} & =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \\
& =\frac{1}{2}(1000)(40)^{2} \\
& =800000 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 6

## Question

A mass of 30 kg has a kinetic energy of 1000 J . Find its speed.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{\mathrm{k}} & =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \\
1000 & =\frac{1}{2}(30) v^{2} \\
v & =\sqrt{\frac{(2)(1000)}{30}} \\
& =8.16 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Work as the transfer of energy

When a body does work, it loses energy. For example, if you carry a block upstairs, you do work and the chemical energy in your muscles decreases. If work is done on a body, it gains energy. For example, the block being carried gains energy as it moves up. Any time work is done, energy is transferred.

## Worked Example 7

## Question

Find the work done in bringing a 1000 kg car from rest to a speed of $30 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in 10 seconds.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { work done } & =\text { change in kinetic energy } \\
& =\frac{1}{2}(1000)(30)^{2}-0 \\
& =450000 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note: Worked Example 7 illustrates well how using the concepts of work and energy to solve a problem in dynamics often provides a much simpler solution than using Newton's laws. Compare this with Worked Example 4 above.

## Worked Example 8

## Question

A bullet of mass 2 g travelling with a speed of $150 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ penetrates 0.6 m into a block of wood before coming to rest. Find the force that the wood exerts on the bullet.

## Solution

kinetic energy of bullet, $E_{\mathrm{k}}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right)(150)^{2} \\
& =22.5 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

This kinetic energy is 'lost' by the bullet and must equal the work done by the bullet in coming to rest. If $F$ is the force that the bullet exerts on the wood, then the wood exerts an equal but opposite force on the bullet.

$$
\text { work done, } \begin{aligned}
W & =F d \\
F & =\frac{W}{d} \\
& =\frac{22.5}{0.6} \\
& =37.5 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 10.5 Potential energy

The potential energy ( $E_{p}$ ) of a body is the energy it has due to its position in a force field.
The force field may be gravitational or electric or elastic, and therefore there are different forms of potential energy corresponding to each of these.

The potential energy, $E_{p^{\prime}}$ of a body is the energy it has due to its position in a force field.

## Elastic potential energy

If a force is applied to an elastic body, it may change shape. In other words, it may become compressed or stretched. Some of the work done by the force in stretching or compressing it becomes stored in the body as elastic potential energy. If the force is removed, the stretched or compressed body does work in coming back to its original shape. Figures 10.5 and 10.6 show two examples.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-200.jpg?height=584&width=838&top_left_y=644&top_left_x=1783)
Figure 10.5

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-200.jpg?height=584&width=838&top_left_y=1380&top_left_x=1783)
Figure 10.6

The stretched bow and string have potential energy stored in them. If they are allowed to come back to their original shape, this energy appears as kinetic energy of the arrow.
When a ball hits a tennis racket, kinetic energy is briefly transferred to elastic potential energy in the ball and strings. This is then rapidly transferred back to kinetic energy as the ball rebounds off the racket.

## Electric potential energy (electrical energy)

This will be discussed more fully in Chapter 19.

## Gravitational potential energy

Gravitational potential energy is the energy a body has because of its position in a gravitational field. For example, a concrete block held 3 m above the ground has more energy than an identical block on the ground. This is due to the fact that if the first block is released, it will fall with its weight doing work. But the lower block cannot do this, and so it has lower potential energy.
More generally, if two bodies are a vertical distance $h$ apart, the higher one has more potential energy than the lower one. The larger $h$ is, the greater the potential energy difference.

## Formula for gravitational potential energy

The difference in potential energy $E_{\mathrm{p}}$ between two points that are a vertical distance $h$ apart in a uniform gravitational field is given by:

Gravitational potential energy difference:

$$
E_{\mathrm{p}}=m g h
$$

(F\&T page 55)
If the small mass in Figure 10.7 is released, it falls under the action of its weight. Suppose it falls through a distance $h$, then:
work done by weight $=$ force × distance $=m g h$ joules.
This must be the potential energy 'lost' by the mass.
If an extended object falls, the loss in potential energy of the object is still given by $E_{\mathrm{p}}=m g h$ except that now the value of $h$ used must be the distance fallen by the centre of gravity (centre of mass) of the object.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-200.jpg?height=1000&width=1456&top_left_y=2627&top_left_x=1165)
Figure 10.7 Potential energy 'lost' by a falling object $=m g h$, where the value of $h$ is the vertical distance fallen by the centre of gravity (centre of mass) of the object. The gain in potential energy for an object projected upwards is given by the same formula.

## Worked Example 9

## Question

A particle of mass 35 kg is projected upwards through a vertical height of 1200 metres. Find the increase in its gravitational potential energy.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{\mathrm{p}} & =m g h \\
& =(35)(9.8)(1200) \\
& =411600 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 10

## Question

How far above the surface of the Earth must 1 kg be raised so that its potential energy is increased by 1 MJ ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{\rho} & =m g h \\
1 \times 10^{6} & =(1)(9.8) h \\
h & =\frac{1 \times 10^{6}}{9.8} \\
& =102041 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Energy changes in a body moving under the influence of gravity

If friction is absent, or if it is so small that it can be neglected:

- A freely falling object gains kinetic energy as it speeds up. The gain in kinetic energy is equal to the loss in potential energy, as its height decreases.
- Likewise, if an object is thrown vertically upwards, it gains potential energy as it gets higher. The gain in potential energy is equal to the loss in kinetic energy, as it slows down.


## Worked Example 11

## Question

A stone of mass 4 kg is dropped from a height of 200 m . Find its kinetic energy and speed just before it hits the ground.

## Solution

You could use the equations of motion here. However, it is easier to use energy methods. At the top: kinetic energy $E_{\mathrm{k}}=0$ and potential energy $E_{\mathrm{p}}=m g h=(4)(9.8)(200)=7840 \mathrm{~J}$ At the bottom, the potential energy has transferred to kinetic energy ( $E_{\mathrm{k}}=7840 \mathrm{~J}$ ), so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} & =7840 \\
\frac{1}{2}(4) v^{2} & =7840 \\
v & =\sqrt{\frac{(7840)(2)}{4}} \\
& =62.61 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 12

## Question

A stone is projected vertically upwards with an initial speed of $40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Find the greatest height reached by the stone.

## Solution

Let $m$ be the mass of stone.
As it leaves the ground, its kinetic energy is $E_{\mathrm{k}}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}=\frac{1}{2} m(40)^{2}$ and its potential energy is $E_{\rho}=0$
At its greatest height $h$, its speed is zero, so:
$E_{\mathrm{k}}=0$ and $E_{\mathrm{p}}=m g h$
On the upward journey, the gain in $E_{\mathrm{p}}=$ loss in $E_{k^{\prime}}$ that is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m g h & =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \\
m(9.8) h & =\frac{1}{2} m(40)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the greatest height reached:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h & =\frac{40^{2}}{(2)(9.8)} \\
& =81.63 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 13

## Question

A mass, at the end of a string, is released at position A in Figure 10.8. Find the speed of the mass as it passes through the vertical position B.

## Solution

In going from A to B : gain in $E_{\mathrm{k}}=$ loss in $E_{\mathrm{p}}$; that is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m g h & =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \\
m g h & =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \\
v^{2} & =2 g h \\
v & =\sqrt{(2)(9.8)(0.4)} \\
& =2.8 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-202.jpg?height=701&width=828&top_left_y=1849&top_left_x=1354)
Figure 10.8

Note that the loss in potential energy depends only on the vertical height through which the object falls - in this case 40 cm - and it does not depend on the actual path taken. This result is generally true.

## Worked Example 14

## Question

A mass of 2 kg is released at position $A$ in Figure 10.9. It swings downward in a circular path and passes through point $B$, which is vertically below the point of suspension.
Find:
a) The vertical height through which it falls in going from $A$ to $B$
b) The potential energy it loses as it moves from $A$ to $B$
c) The speed, $v$, of the mass as it passes through $B$.
(Acceleration due to gravity, $g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ )

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-203.jpg?height=705&width=1580&top_left_y=992&top_left_x=371)
Figure 10.9

## Solution

a) From Figure 10.9:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos 45^{\circ} & =\frac{x}{4} \\
x & =4 \cos 45^{\circ} \\
& =(4)\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\
& =2.83 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, vertical height fallen: $h=4-x=4-2.83=1.17 \mathrm{~m}$
b) Potential energy lost:

$$
E_{\mathrm{p}}=m g h=(2)(9.8)(1.17)=22.93 \mathrm{~J}
$$

c) In going from $A$ to $B$, gain in $E_{\mathrm{k}}=$ loss in $E_{\mathrm{p}}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} & =m g h \\
\frac{1}{2}(2) v^{2} & =22.93 \\
v^{2} & =22.93 \\
v & =\sqrt{22.93} \\
& =4.79 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Student Experiment 10.1

This experiment is to investigate the principle of conservation of energy for a trolley that is being accelerated along a runway by a scale pan of weights falling vertically. The investigation is to show that the value of the potential energy + kinetic energy of the system remains constant as the system moves.

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will exert a force $F$ on a trolley using a scale pan of weights hanging vertically (Figure 10.10). Using a motion sensor and data logger, you will measure the distance moved by the trolley (which is also the distance $h$ fallen by the scale pan), and the velocity of the trolley (which is also the velocity of the scale pan) a number of different times as it falls.

## Equipment

A trolley, a runway, a motion sensor, a data logger, a computer or laptop (depending on the data logger), a lowfriction pulley, a scale pan, a set of masses (e.g. 0-800 g) and some string.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-204.jpg?height=864&width=1382&top_left_y=1269&top_left_x=240)
Figure 10.10

## Method

1. Find the mass of the trolley, the scale pan, weight and the string, i.e. find the total mass of the system ( $m_{s y s}$ ).
2. Raise one end of the runway slightly, so that the trolley will move along the runway at constant speed when given a gentle push and released.
3. Connect the motion sensor to the data logger (or computer).
4. Set the data logging software to measure distance and velocity.
5. Connect the scale pan to the trolley and place a mass on it (say, 200 g ).
6. Place the trolley in front of the motion sensor and hold the trolley in place.
7. Release the trolley and turn on the motion sensor. Allow the trolley to move down the runway.
8. Before the trolley reaches the end of the runway or the scale pan hits the ground, switch off the motion sensor and stop the trolley.
9. Measure and record the total mass ( $m_{s}$ ) of the scale pan and contents.
10. Measure and record the total mass ( $m_{\mathrm{t}}$ ) of the trolley and string (and any masses on it).
11. Record the value of the distance travelled (the height fallen by the scale pan) and the speed of the trolley at five different times during the fall.
12. Complete the table below:
a) Calculating the loss in potential energy of the scale pan and contents
b) Calculating the total kinetic energy of the moving system

## Handling the data

1. Copy and complete the table, using your results.

| Mass of scale pan and contents $m_{5}$ (kg) | Mass of trolley and any weights on it $m_{\mathrm{t}}$ (kg) | Heights fallen by scale pan $h(\mathrm{~m})$ | Velocity of trolley $v\left(\mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right)$ | Loss in potential energy $E_{p}(\mathrm{~J}) m_{g} g h$ | Gain in kinetic energy of system $E_{k}(\mathrm{~J}) \frac{1}{2}\left(m_{s}+m_{t}\right) v^{2}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  | $h_{1}$ | $v_{1}$ |  |  |
|  |  | $h_{2}$ | $v_{2}$ |  |  |
|  |  | $h_{3}$ | $v_{3}$ |  |  |
|  |  | $h_{4}$ | $v_{4}$ |  |  |
|  |  | $h_{\mathrm{s}}$ | $v_{\mathrm{s}}$ |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |

## Results

You should find that the loss in potential energy is equal to the gain in potential energy for each height, therefore verifying the principle of conservation of energy for the system.
The experiment may be repeated a number of times with different masses on the scale pan and different masses on the trolley.

## Loss of kinetic energy in collisions

When two objects collide, momentum is always conserved, provided no external forces act. Usually, however, kinetic energy is not conserved. The total kinetic energy of the objects after the collision will usually be less than the total before.
The lost kinetic energy is converted into other forms such as heat energy and sound energy. How much kinetic energy is lost depends on the elastic properties of the colliding bodies. In pool, when one ball hits another ball, almost no kinetic energy is lost and almost all the first ball's energy is shared between the two balls as kinetic energy (Figure 10.11). On the other hand, in a collision between a lump of plasticine and a tennis ball, a considerable amount of kinetic energy is lost.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-205.jpg?height=883&width=2013&top_left_y=2552&top_left_x=325)
Figure 10.11

## Worked Example 15

## Question

A mass of 5 kg travelling at $20 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ collides with and sticks to a mass of 2 kg , which is initially at rest.
a) Find the velocity of the combined mass after the collision.
b) Find the loss in kinetic energy.
c) Where did the lost kinetic energy go?

## Solution

a) Let $v$ be the speed of the combined mass after the collision (Figure 10.12).

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { momentum before collision }=\text { momentum after collision } \\
& \qquad \begin{aligned}
(5)(20)+(2)(0) & =7 v \\
7 v & =100+0 \\
v & =\frac{100}{7} \\
& =14.29 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

b)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-206.jpg?height=604&width=746&top_left_y=878&top_left_x=1634)
Figure 10.12

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { total } E_{\mathrm{k}} \text { before collision } & =\frac{1}{2}(5)(20)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(2)(0)^{2} \\
& =1000+0 \\
& =1000 \mathrm{~J} \\
\text { total } E_{\mathrm{k}} \text { after collision } & =\frac{1}{2}(7)(14.29)^{2} \\
& =714.7 \mathrm{~J} \\
\text { loss in } E_{\mathrm{k}} & =1000=714.7 \\
& =285.3 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

c) The lost kinetic energy is converted into other forms of energy such as heat or sound.

### 10.6 Renewable and non-renewable sources of energy

Every day people use energy for many purposes, such as transport and heating. The sources of this energy are many, including oil, coal, wind and hydroelectricity. Sources of energy are classified as renewable or non-renewable.

A source of energy that does not get used up is called a renewable source of energy.

Examples of renewable energy sources are wind (Figure 10.16), solar (Figure 10.17), hydroelectric, wave, tidal, geothermal and biomass. Non-renewable sources include oil, coal, peat and natural gas.
In recent years, there has been increasing concern about the overuse and depletion

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-208.jpg?height=948&width=1423&top_left_y=436&top_left_x=1198)
Figure 10.16 Wind turbines

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-208.jpg?height=974&width=1423&top_left_y=1536&top_left_x=1198)
Figure 10.17 Solar panels

of natural resources, and the subsequent damage to the natural environment. People are dependent on the natural environment for survival and wellbeing. Humans therefore need to regulate and modify practices so that valuable resources do not run out with irreparable damage to the environment.
Sustainability is a word used to refer to the use of a natural resource in such a manner that it does not run out. This is particularly important in the energy sources you use, and there is an urgent need to reduce the use of non-renewable sources of energy and increase the use of renewable, or sustainable, sources. As you progress through your physics course, you need to become aware of societal and environmental implications of energy technologies, based on the principles of physics you will learn.

## Efficient use of energy in the home

There are many good reasons for using energy efficiently in the home, but in particular, it reduces energy costs and it slows down the rate at which non-renewable sources are used.
Increasing energy efficiency can be done, for example, by:

- Insulating walls, attics and floors
- Installing double or triple glazing in windows and draught-proofing in doors and windows
- Using energy efficient LED bulbs, which use considerably less energy than a conventional filament bulb to produce the same amount of light (see pages 413-414).


### 10.7 Power

An LED bulb in a desk lamp may convert electrical energy into heat and light at the rate of 7 joules per second; a bulb in a floodlight may convert electrical energy to heat and light at the rate of 500 joules per second. The second bulb is more powerful than the first.
A builder brings 1000 blocks, each of mass 20 kg , up a ladder to the top of a house. It takes him 5 hours to do so. A crane lifts all the blocks together from the ground to the top in a time of 10 seconds. Even though the man and the crane do the same work on the blocks, the crane does it in a much shorter time. The crane is much more powerful than the man.
In physics, power is defined as the rate at which work is done or the rate at which energy is converted from one form to another. These two definitions are really the same thing. Whenever energy is converted, work is always done.
The symbol for power is $P$.
Power is a scalar quantity.

## Average power

The average power developed in a time $t$ is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average power } & =\frac{\text { work done }}{\text { time taken }} \\
P & =\frac{W}{t}
\end{aligned}
$$

(F\&T page 55)
or

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Average power } & =\frac{\text { energy transferred }}{E} \text { time taken } \\
P & =\frac{E}{l}
\end{aligned}
$$

If the power is being developed at a constant rate, each of these formulae represent the power at any instant.

## Sl unit of power

Since $P=\frac{W}{t}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Sl unit of power } & =\frac{\text { Sl unit of work }}{\text { SI unit of time }} \\
& =\frac{\text { joule }}{\text { second }} \\
& =\text { joule per second } \\
& =\mathrm{Js}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## James Watt

James Watt (1736-1819) was a Scottish inventor, chemist and mechanical engineer. He significantly improved the operation and efficiency of the steam engines available at the time. He was the first to use the term 'horsepower'.

This unit is called the watt (W) in honour of the English scientist James Watt (1736-1819).
Power is the rate at which work is done.
or
Power is the rate at which energy is converted from one form to another.
The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
1 watt = 1 joule per second
Note: Dimensional (Unit) Analysis
The watt in base units:

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \mathrm{~W} & =1 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \\
& =1\left(\mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right) \mathrm{s}^{-1} \\
& =1 \mathbf{k g ~ m}^{2} \mathbf{s}^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

( $1 \mathrm{~J}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$; page 17)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-209.jpg?height=789&width=1466&top_left_y=3027&top_left_x=1279)

## Worked Example 16

## Question

A woman raises an object of mass 40 kg through a vertical height of 20 m in 4 seconds. Find her average power.

## Solution

First, calculate work done (= energy transferred):

$$
\begin{aligned}
W & =m g h \\
& =(40)(9.8)(20) \\
& =7840 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =\frac{W}{t} \\
& =\frac{7840}{4} \\
& =1960 \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 17

## Question

A weightlifter raises a mass of 30 kg through a height of 0.6 m . He does this 25 times in half a minute. Find the average power he develops.

## Solution

Work done in one lift:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{\text {one }} & =m g h \\
& =(30)(9.8)(0.6) \\
& =176.4 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, total work done:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{\text {total }} & =(25)(176.4) \\
& =4410 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

Average power:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =\frac{W}{t} \\
& =\frac{4410}{30} \\
& =147 \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 18

## Question

A woman of mass 80 kg runs up a flight of 120 stairs in 30 seconds. If the height of each stair is 15 cm , find her average power.

## Solution

Vertical height through which woman runs $=(0.15)(120)=18 \mathrm{~m}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =\frac{W}{t} \\
& =\frac{m g h}{t} \\
& =\frac{(80)(9.8)(18)}{30} \\
& =470 \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 10.8 Efficiency

In machines and motors of all types, energy is input and output. For example, in an electric motor, electrical energy is supplied to the motor, which converts it to kinetic energy.
In all such devices, there are always some energy losses, in which energy is converted to nonuseful forms (usually heat). Thus, the useful energy output is always less than the energy input. Such devices are therefore not $100 \%$ efficient. In terms of power, the useful power output is less than the power input.

$$
\begin{equation*}
\text { Percentage efficiency }=\frac{\text { useful power output }}{\text { power input }} \times 100 \tag{F\&Tpage55}
\end{equation*}
$$

## Worked Example 20

## Question

An engine has an input power of 4500 W . The useful power output is 3000 W . Calculate its percentage efficiency.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Percentage efficiency } & =\frac{\text { useful power output }}{\text { power input }} \times 100 \\
& =\frac{(3000)(100)}{4500} \times 100 \\
& =66.67 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 21

## Question

A 60 kW motor in a crane lifts a mass of 4000 kg through a height of 10 m in 20 s . Calculate the efficiency \% of the motor if it is working at full power.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =\frac{W}{t} \\
& =\frac{m g h}{t} \\
& =\frac{(4000)(9.8)(10)}{20} \\
& =19600 \mathrm{~W} \\
\text { Percentage efficiency } & =\frac{\text { useful power output }}{\text { power input }} \\
& =\frac{(19600)(100)}{60000} \\
& =32.67 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 22

## Question

A petrol car engine is $30 \%$ efficient. Kinetic energy is produced at the rate of 105 kW . The rest of the energy input is dissipated as heat. Calculate the rate at which heat is dissipated.

## Solution

$30 \%$ of the input power is 105 kW
Therefore, 70\% of the power is dissipated as heat.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{(105)(70)}{30} \\
& =245 \mathrm{~kW}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Summary What I should know

- The work done $W$ when a force $F$ moves a body through a displacement $s$ in the direction of the force is equal to the force multiplied by the displacement: $W=F s$
- The SI unit of work is the joule (J)
- One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton acts for a distance of 1 metre in the direction of the force. $1 \mathrm{~J}=1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}$
- Energy, $\boldsymbol{E}$ is the ability to do work. The amount of energy something has is the amount of work it can do.
- The SI unit of energy is the joule (J).
- The principle of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be converted from one form to another.
- The kinetic energy, $E_{\mathrm{k}}$ of a body is the energy that body has due to its motion:

$$
E_{\mathrm{k}}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}
$$

- The potential energy, $E_{p}$ of a body is the energy it has due to its position in a force field.
- In a gravitational field: $E_{\mathrm{p}}=m g h$
- Power is the rate at which work is done: $P=\frac{W}{t}$
- Power is the rate at which energy is converted from one form to another.
- The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
- $\mathbf{1}$ watt = 1 joule per second. $1 \mathrm{~W}=1 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
- Percentage efficiency $=\frac{\text { useful power output }}{\text { power input }} \times 100$
- Whenever work is done, energy is transferred.
- The potential energy plus the kinetic energy of a freely falling body is a constant (in the absence of air resistance).
- Kinetic energy is not always conserved in collisions; momentum is always conserved, provided no external forces act.

# 11 Circular Motion

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand tangential speed, linear speed, angular velocity, centripetal force, and centripetal acceleration.
- To ensure students appreciate how centripetal force depends on the speed and mass of the object moving in a circle, as well as on the radius of the circle.
- To make students appreciate that the force of gravity is the centripetal force that keeps the planets orbiting the Sun and satellites orbiting the Earth.
- To ensure students understand Kepler's third law.
- To ensure students can apply Kepler's third law.
- To ensure students can model situations involving the orbits of planets and satellites in near-Earth and geostationary orbits


## Keywords

- Tangential speed (linear speed)
- (Constant) angular velocity
- Centripetal force
- Centripetal acceleration
- Orbit
- Period of an orbit
- Kepler's third law
- Geostationary orbit
- Low-Earth Orbit (Near-Earth Orbit)


### 11.1 Particle moving in a circle

A small object $P$ is moving at a constant speed of $v$ metres per second in an anticlockwise direction around the circle in Figure 11.1.
At any instant, $P$ is moving along a tangent to the circle, i.e. when it is at $A$ it is moving along the tangent at $A$, and when it is at $B$ it is moving along the tangent at $B$.
$v$ is called the tangential speed or the linear speed of the small object.
Since the direction of the velocity of $P$ is continually changing, $P$ is accelerating. The magnitude of $P^{\prime}$ s velocity, i.e. its speed, is constant.
Suppose point $P$ moves from $X$ to the position shown in $t$ seconds, covering a distance of $s$ metres along the circle.
Since the speed, $v$, of $P$ is constant, we have $v=\frac{s}{t}$.
During this time, the radius $O P$ traces out an angle $\theta$ with the line $O X$. As $t$ increases, the angle $\theta$ also increases.

## Angular velocity

In Figure 11.1, the rate at which the angle $\theta$ is changing with respect to time is called the angular velocity of $P$ about $O$. It can be measured in degrees per second. Since $P$ is moving at a constant speed, the angle $\theta$ is also changing at a steady rate. So, $P$ has a constant angular velocity.

Angular velocity is the rate of change of angle with respect to time.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-216.jpg?height=785&width=874&top_left_y=2923&top_left_x=1744)
Figure 11.1

In Figure 11.2, $A, B$, and $C$ are three points on a wheel that is rotating about its centre with constant angular velocity.
Since the points $A, B$ and $C$ take the same time to undergo a full circle, they all have the same angular velocity. However, since the point $C$ must travel a longer path than $A$ or $B$ to trace out the full circle, it has the greatest linear speed $v$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-217.jpg?height=757&width=854&top_left_y=634&top_left_x=755)

Figure 11.2 $A, B$ and $C$ take the same time to complete a full circle. $C$ travels the longest path and $A$ travels the shortest. $C$, therefore, has the greatest linear speed of the three, and $A$ the least

## Worked Example 1

## Question

A stone on a string, moving at a steady speed in a circle of radius 2.0 m , performs 10 complete revolutions of the circle per second. Find its tangential (linear) speed.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { circumference of a circle }=2 \pi r \\
& 10 \text { revolutions per second }=10 \times 2 \pi r \text { metres per second } \\
& \text { angential or linear speed, } \begin{aligned}
v & =10 \times 2 \pi r \\
& =40 \pi \\
& =125.7 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A flywheel of diameter 2.2 m rotates with 4000 revolutions per minute. Calculate:
a) The length of the circumference of the flywheel
b) How long it takes the flywheel to make one complete revolution
c) The speed of a particle at the circumference of the flywheel

## Solution

a) circumference length $=2 \pi r$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =2 \pi(1.1) \\
& =6.91 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

b)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { time for one revolution } & =\frac{\text { time for } 4000 \text { revolutions }}{4000} \\
& =\frac{60}{4000} \\
& =0.015 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

c)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { speed } & =\frac{\text { distance }}{\text { time }} \\
& =\frac{6.91}{0.015} \\
& =461 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

The radius of the Earth at the equator is $6.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$. If the Earth rotates once about its polar axis every 24 hours, find the linear speed of a point on the equator (Figure 11.3).

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
24 \text { hours } & =(24)(60)(60) \text { seconds } \\
& =86400 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

distance travelled in one full revolution = circumference of Earth

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =2 \pi r \\
& =2 \pi\left(6.4 \times 10^{6}\right) \mathrm{m} \\
\text { speed } & =\frac{\text { distance travelled }}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{2 \pi\left(6.4 \times 10^{6}\right)}{86400} \\
& =465 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 11.2 Centripetal force

- You have just seen that when a particle moves at a constant speed around a circle, the direction of its velocity is always changing. The particle is therefore accelerating.
- By Newton's second law, the particle must therefore have a resultant force acting on it.
- Since the particle moves at a constant speed, this force must always be at right angles to the direction of motion. If the force had a component parallel to the direction of the motion, the particle would speed up or slow down.
- The force must therefore be acting towards the centre of the circle rather than in the opposite direction. This force is called centripetal force.
This can easily be demonstrated in the lab. A light rubber bung is tied to the end of about 0.5 m of thread, and is then whirled in a circle. The centripetal force acting on the bung is the tension in the thread, which is always acting towards the centre of the circle. If the string is released from your hand, the tension immediately disappears and the bung moves off in a direction along the tangent of the circle. Be careful - the flying bung could do damage.
Since centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circle, the body on which it acts must also have an acceleration towards the centre of that circle. This acceleration is called centripetal acceleration.

Centripetal force is the force towards the centre of a circle, needed to keep a body moving in that circle.

Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration towards the centre of a circle that a body has, if it is moving in that circle.

## Factors on which centripetal force depends

To keep an object moving in a circular path, there are three factors that affect the force needed. They are:

- The mass of the object (the greater the mass, the greater the force needed)
- The speed of the object (the faster the object is moving, the greater the force needed)
- The radius of the circular path (the smaller the radius, the greater the force needed)

The exact relationship between these three factors and the force is given in the following formula:
To keep an object of mass $m$ moving at a constant speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$, a force $F$ acting towards the centre of the circle is needed, where $F$ is given by:

Centripetal force, $F=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}$
(F\&T, page 51)
Since acceleration $=\frac{\text { force }}{\text { mass }}$, it follows that:
Centripetal acceleration, $a=\frac{v^{2}}{r}$
(F\&T, page 51)

Note: Centripetal force is not a new type of force you have not yet come across. It is the name given to some real force (or the resultant of several forces) that is causing an object to move in a circle.
For example, for a car going round a bend, it's the friction force between the tyres and the road.
For satellites or other objects orbiting a planet, it's the force of gravity.
For objects being whirled in a horizontal circle on a string, it is the tension in the string.
In each problem, you must be able to spot which real force (or forces) is supplying the centripetal force needed to keep an object moving in a circle

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A 2 kg stone moves in a circle of radius 3 m with a constant speed of $4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Find:
a) Its centripetal acceleration
b) The resultant force acting on it

## Solution

a) Centripetal acceleration, $a=\frac{v^{2}}{r}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{4^{2}}{3} \\
& =\frac{16}{3} \\
& =5.3 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) Resultant force acts towards the centre:

$$
F=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}=\frac{(2)\left(4^{2}\right)}{3}=10.7 \mathrm{~N}
$$

Alternative solution to (b):

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =m a \\
& =(2)(5.333) \\
& =10.7 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A flywheel of radius 1.4 m rotates with 5000 revolutions per minute.
Calculate:
a) The speed of a particle at the circumference of the flywheel
b) The centripetal acceleration of a particle at the circumference of the flywheel

## Solution

a) If the flywheel does 5000 rpm , a particle on its circumference travels at a speed of $(5000)(2 \pi)(1.4)$ metres per minute

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{(5000)(2 \pi)(1.4)}{60} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \\
& =733.0 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) centripetal acceleration, $a=\frac{v^{2}}{r}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{733^{2}}{1.4} \\
& =3.84 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 6

## Question

An electron in a magnetic field moves in a circular path of radius 1 cm . If its speed is $2 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, find the centripetal force on the electron. (mass of electron $=9.1 \times 10^{-3 t} \mathrm{~kg}$ )

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =\frac{m v^{2}}{r} \\
& =\frac{\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{6}\right)^{2}}{1 \times 10^{-2}} \\
& =3.6 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 7

## Question

A car of mass 1500 kg is travelling in a straight line at a speed $30 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. It comes to a bend in the road which is in an arc of a circle of radius 50 m .
Find the centripetal force needed to enable the car to travel around the bend.

## Solution

Required centripetal force:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =\frac{m v^{2}}{r} \\
& =\frac{(1500)\left(30^{2}\right)}{50} \\
& =27000 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

towards the centre of the arc of the circle.

## Some more challenging problems

Suppose an object is moving in a circular path, but its speed is changing. To remain on this path it still must have a force acting on it towards the centre of the circular path. This force, $F$, is given, as before, by:

$$
F=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}
$$

where $v$ is its speed at any instant.
Its centripetal acceleration at any instant is also given by:

$$
a=\frac{v^{2}}{r}
$$

## Worked Example 8

## Question

A mass hanging at the end of a string is released at position $A$ in Figure 11.4. The mass swings downwards and passes point $B$, where its speed is $v$.
Find:
a) The linear speed, $v$, of the mass as it passes through the vertical position $B$
b) The centripetal acceleration of the mass when at $B$.

## Solution

a) In going from $A$ to $B$, gain in $E_{\mathrm{k}}=$ loss in $E_{\mathrm{p}}$; that is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} & =m g h \Rightarrow v^{2}=2 g h \\
\Rightarrow v & =\sqrt{(2)(9.8)(0.4)} \\
& =\sqrt{7.84} \\
& =2.8 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-221.jpg?height=604&width=672&top_left_y=2675&top_left_x=2034)
Figure 11.4

b) centripetal acceleration, $a=\frac{y^{2}}{r}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{(2.82)^{2}}{1.0} \\
& =7.8 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 9

## Question

A mass of 5.0 kg hanging at the end of a string of length 10 m is displaced through an angle of $50^{\circ}$ from the vertical (position $A$ ) and is then held in position $B$, as shown in Figure 11.5.
a) Calculate:
i) The height through which the mass has been raised
iii) The potential energy that it has gained

The mass is then released and allowed to swing freely.
b) What is the maximum velocity it attains?
c) Calculate the centripetal force on the mass when it reaches position $A$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-222.jpg?height=704&width=681&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1504)
Figure 11.5

(acceleration due to gravity, $g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$ )

## Solution

a) i) From Figure 11.6:

$$
\cos 50^{\circ}=\frac{x}{10} \Rightarrow x=10 \cos 50^{\circ}=6.43 \mathrm{~m}
$$

Therefore, height, $h$ through which it is raised is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h & =10-x \\
& =10-6.43 \\
& =3.56=3.6 \mathrm{~m}

$$

ii) potential energy gained, $E_{\mathrm{p}}=m g h$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(5.0)(9.8)(3.57) \\
& =174.93=175 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-222.jpg?height=692&width=789&top_left_y=1337&top_left_x=1380)
Figure 11.6

b) Maximum velocity occurs when the mass is back in position $A$.
In moving from $B$ to $A$ :
gain in kinetic energy = loss in potential energy

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} & =174.93 \\
\frac{1}{2}(5.0) v^{2} & =174.93 \\
v^{2} & =\frac{(2)(174.93)}{5} \\
& =69.972 \\
v & =\sqrt{69.972} \\
& =8.36=8.4 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

c) Centripetal force at position $A$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =\frac{m v^{2}}{r} \\
& =\frac{(5)(8.36)^{2}}{10} \\
& =34.94=35 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

a) i) See Figure 11.7(A)
ii) See Figure 11.7(B)

Figure 11.7(C)

b) i) At its highest point, the weight of the object and the tension in the string both act towards the centre of the circle (Figure 11.7(A)). Their resultant provides the necessary centripetal force; that is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { centripetal force } & =W+T \\
& =(0.1)(9.8)+T
\end{aligned}
$$

Also:
centripetal force, $F=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}$
So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(0.1)(9.8)+T & =\frac{(0.1)(14)^{2}}{1.2} \\
T & =16.33-0.98 \\
& =15 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

ii) At its lowest point, the resultant force towards the centre is $T-W$ (Figure 11.7 (B)). This provides the necessary centripetal force.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { centripetal force } & =T-W \\
& =T-(0.1)(9.8)
\end{aligned}
$$

Also:
centripetal force, $F=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}$
So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T-(0.1)(9.8) & =\frac{(0.1)(14)^{2}}{1.2} \\
& =16.33+0.98 \\
& =17 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

iii) At the instant it is moving vertically (Figure $11.7(\mathrm{C})$ ), all the centripetal force is supplied by the tension in the string.

$$
\begin{aligned}
T & =\frac{m v^{2}}{r} \\
& =\frac{(0.1)(14)^{2}}{1.2} \\
& =16 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 11.3 Circular satellite orbits

The Earth and the other planets of the Solar System orbit the Sun, some with orbits that are approximately circular. The Moon orbits the Earth. The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, but there are also many artificial satellites orbiting the Earth (Figure 11.10). What supplies the necessary centripetal force to keep these satellites in their orbits?

Note: The force of gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps the planets orbiting the Sun and satellites orbiting the Earth.

Newton's law of universal gravitation tells you that the gravitational force $F$ of attraction between two spherical bodies is given by:

$$
F=\frac{G m_{1} m_{2}}{d^{2}}
$$

where $G$ is the universal gravitation constant, $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are the masses of the bodies and $d$ is the distance between their centres.

So, in Figure 11.11 there is a satellite of mass $m$ moving with speed $v$ in an orbit of radius $R$ about a central body of mass $M$, then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { centripetal force }=\text { force of gravity } \\
& \qquad \frac{m v^{2}}{R}=\frac{G M m}{R^{2}} \\
& \Rightarrow v^{2}=\frac{G M}{R}
\end{aligned}
$$

From this equation you can see that:

- If you know the height of the orbit, and hence its radius, this equation tells you the speed of the satellite.
- If you know the speed of the satellite, this equation gives you the radius of the orbit and hence its height.
- The speed of the satellite does not depend on the mass of the satellite.
- $v=\sqrt{\frac{G M}{R}} \Rightarrow v=\frac{\sqrt{G} \sqrt{M}}{\sqrt{R}}$

Thus, since $G$ is constant, the speed of a satellite is directly proportional to the square root of the mass of the body it orbits and inversely proportional to the square root of the radius of the orbit.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-225.jpg?height=675&width=1160&top_left_y=1572&top_left_x=322)
Figure 11.10 The International Space Station orbits the Earth at an average height of 400 km and takes about 93 minutes to go once around the Earth.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-225.jpg?height=789&width=821&top_left_y=1565&top_left_x=1517)
Figure 11.11

## Worked Example 11

## Question

A military spy satellite orbits the Earth at a height of 40000 km above the Earth's surface. At what speed is it travelling?
( $G=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$; radius of Earth $=6.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$; mass of Earth $=6 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$ )

## Solution

radius of orbit = radius of Earth + height of satellite above Earth

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\left(6.4 \times 10^{6}\right)+\left(40 \times 10^{6}\right) \mathrm{m} \\
\frac{m v^{2}}{R} & =\frac{G M m}{R^{2}} \\
v^{2} & =\frac{G M}{R} \\
v & =\sqrt{\frac{\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{24}\right)}{\left(6.4 \times 10^{6}\right)+\left(40 \times 10^{6}\right)}} \\
& =2943.4 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

In Figure 11.12, the time $T$ taken to go from $P$ around the orbit once and back again to $P$ is the period of the orbit.

The period, $\boldsymbol{T}$, of an orbit is the time taken for a satellite to go once around the central body.

$$
\begin{aligned}
T & =\text { time for one revolution } \\
& =\frac{\text { length of orbit }}{\text { speed }} \\
& =\frac{2 \pi R}{v}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T=\frac{2 \pi R}{v}
$$

## Question

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-226.jpg?height=717&width=720&top_left_y=302&top_left_x=1852)
Figure 11.12

What is the period of the satellite in Worked Example 11?

## Solution

$$
\text { period, } \begin{aligned}
T & =\frac{2 \pi R}{v} \\
& =\frac{2 \pi\left(6.4 \times 10^{6}+40 \times 10^{6}\right)}{2943.4} \\
& =99048.65 \mathrm{~s}=27.5 \text { hours }
\end{aligned}
$$

## HL Kepler's third law: The relationship between the period of an orbit and its radius

Before Newton discovered his law of gravity, it was already known that for any planet orbiting the Sun, the square of the period of its orbit was directly proportional to the cube of the radius of its orbit. This is Kepler's third law.

Kepler's third law states that for a planet orbiting the Sun, the square of the period of its orbit is directly proportional to the cube of the radius of its orbit.

$$
T^{2} \propto R^{3} \text { or } T \propto \sqrt{R^{3}}
$$

Newton was able to show that Kepler's third law followed mathematically from his law of gravity, showing that his law was most likely correct. This was a surprising prediction at the time, especially since direct verification of the law of gravitation was not yet possible.
The orbits of some of the planets are not perfectly circular; instead they are elliptical. It can still be shown, using Newton's law of gravity, that $T^{2} \propto R^{3}$ for an elliptical orbit. In any questions you may encounter, assume that the orbits are circular.

## Johannes Kepler

Johannes Kepler (1571-1630) was a German
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-226.jpg?height=274&width=320&top_left_y=2295&top_left_x=2298)
natural philosopher, mathematician and astronomer. By number-crunching a large data set of measurements taken by the deceased astronomer Tycho Brahe, for whom he was an assistant, he discovered three laws of planetary motion that now bear his name. Keppler saw these laws as celestial harmonies that reflected God's design for the universe. In optics, he proposed the theory that when we see something, an upside-down image of that thing is formed on the retina of our eye. Therefore vision occurs through a picture of the visible things on the white, concave surface of the retina.'

## Worked Example 13

## Question

The radius of the orbit of the planet Neptune around the Sun is 30 times longer than the Earth's radius of orbit around the Sun. Calculate the time it takes Neptune to complete one orbit of the Sun.

## Solution

$T^{2} \propto R^{3} \quad \Rightarrow T^{2}=k R^{3} \quad$ where $k$ is a constant
$T_{\mathrm{N}}^{2}=k R_{\mathrm{N}}^{3} \quad$ and $\quad T_{\mathrm{E}}^{2}=k R_{\mathrm{E}}^{3}, \mathrm{so}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T_{\mathrm{N}}^{2}}{T_{\mathrm{E}}^{2}} & =\frac{k R_{\mathrm{N}}^{3}}{k R_{\mathrm{E}}^{3}} \\
& =\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{N}}}{R_{\mathrm{E}}}\right)^{3} \\
\text { Since } \quad R_{\mathrm{N}} & =30 R_{\mathrm{E}}: \\
\frac{T_{\mathrm{N}}^{2}}{T_{\mathrm{E}}^{2}} & =30^{3} \\
\frac{T_{\mathrm{N}}}{T_{\mathrm{E}}} & =\sqrt{30^{3}} \\
T_{\mathrm{N}} & =T_{\mathrm{E}} \times\left(\sqrt{30^{3}}\right) \\
& =164 \text { years }
\end{aligned}
$$

(since the period of Earth's orbit = 1 year)

## Worked Example 14

## Question

Calculate the period of the Moon's orbit around the Earth.
( $G=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{Nm}^{2} \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$; radius of Earth $=6.4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$; distance from centre of Earth to centre of Moon $=3.85 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m}$ )

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
T^{2} & =\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M} \\
& =\frac{4 \pi^{2}\left(3.85 \times 10^{8}\right)^{3}}{\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{24}\right)} \\
& =5.604 \times 10^{12} \\
T & =\sqrt{5.604 \times 10^{12}} \\
& =2.367 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~s} \\
& =27.4 \text { days }
\end{aligned}
$$

## SEC examination question (HL)

Saturn, the second-largest planet in our solar system, is orbited by at least 83 moons. A group of students researched the orbits of these moons to try to verify Kepler's third law.
Kepler's third law can be modelled by the equation $T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}$
The table below shows the period of orbit $T$ and the radius of orbit $R$ for three of Saturn's moons.

| Name of Moon | Period of orbit $T(\mathrm{~s})$ | Radius of orbit $\boldsymbol{R}(\mathrm{m})$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mimas | $8.14 \times 10^{4}$ | $1.85 \times 10^{8}$ |
| Enceladus | $1.18 \times 10^{5}$ | $2.37 \times 10^{8}$ |
| Dione | $2.36 \times 10^{5}$ | $3.77 \times 10^{8}$ |

a) Use the data in the table to verify Kepler's third law.
b) Calculate an average value for the mass of Saturn.
c) Given that the mass of Saturn is $5.683 \times 10^{26} \mathrm{~kg}$, calculate the percentage error in your calculated value for the mass of Saturn.
d) State one assumption made when working with the model $T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}$ that may account for the error.

## Solution

a) Kepler's third law: $T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}$

Rearranging gives: $\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}}=\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{G M}$
So, for all moons orbiting the same planet, $\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}}$ should be constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}} \text { for Mimas } & =\frac{\left(8.14 \times 10^{4}\right)^{2}}{\left(1.85 \times 10^{8}\right)^{3}}=1.04649 \times 10^{-15} \\
\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}} \text { for Enceladus } & =\frac{\left(1.18 \times 10^{5}\right)^{2}}{\left(2.37 \times 10^{8}\right)^{3}}=1.04597 \times 10^{-15} \\
\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}} \text { for Dione } & =\frac{\left(2.36 \times 10^{5}\right)^{2}}{\left(3.77 \times 10^{8}\right)^{3}}=1.03944 \times 10^{-15}
\end{aligned}
$$

These three values are very close to each other, which verifies that $\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}}$ is a constant.
Hence, this verifies Kepler's third law.
b) First, find the average value $\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}}$ from part (a):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}}\right)_{\text {avg }} & =\frac{\left(1.04649 \times 10^{-15}+1.04597 \times 10^{-15}+1.03944 \times 10^{-15}\right)}{3} \\
& =1.04396 \times 10^{-15}
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearrange Kepler's third law to make $M$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T^{2} & =\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M} \\
G M T^{2} & =4 \pi^{2} R^{3} \\
M & =\left(\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{G}\right)\left(\frac{R^{3}}{T^{2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute the known values:
$\left(\frac{R^{3}}{T^{2}}\right)_{\text {avg }}$ is equal to $\frac{1}{\left(\frac{T^{2}}{R^{3}}\right)_{\text {avg }}}$, so $\left(\frac{R^{3}}{T^{2}}\right)_{\text {avg }}=\frac{1}{1.04396 \times 10^{-15}}$

$$
G=6.674 \times 10^{-11}
$$

(F\&T, page 46).

So:
Average mass of Saturn $M_{\text {satum }}=\left(\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{6.674 \times 10^{-11}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{1.04396 \times 10^{-15}}\right)$

$$
=5.666 \times 10^{26} \mathrm{~kg}
$$

c)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { percentage error } & =\frac{\text { error }}{\text { true value }} \times 100 \\
& =\frac{5.683 \times 10^{26}-5.666 \times 10^{26}}{5.683 \times 10^{26}} \times 100 \\
& =0.2991 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

d) The model $T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}$ assumes the orbit of the satellite is circular.

Note: In reality, the path of a satellite is an ellipse that is not perfectly circular. Also, the model assumes the satellite orbits around the centre of the central body. A satellite and the central body actually orbit around their common centre of mass. If the central body is much more massive than the satellite, this point is close to the centre of the central body, but it is not its centre.

## Weightlessness

You saw on page 138 that if a plane (or a lift) is falling freely, a person in that plane experiences weightlessness This is because both the person and the plane have the same acceleration in the Earth's gravitational field.
Therefore:

- Relative to the plane, the person has no acceleration
- Relative to the plane, there are no forces acting on the person
- The person experiences weightlessness relative to the plane.

The same thing happens for a person in a satellite that is orbiting the Earth. Both the person and the satellite are in free fall in the Earth's gravitational field. They therefore have the same acceleration and the person experiences weightlessness. You might have seen videos of astronauts floating around the International Space Station, and this is why they float rather than walk - it is not because there is no gravity where they are (there is gravity holding them in orbit), but rather it is because they are constantly in free fall.

### 11.4 Near-Earth and geostationary orbits

## Near-Earth orbit

More than $3 / 4$ of the satellites that orbit the Earth are in what is called Near-Earth Orbit (NEO) or Low-Earth Orbit (LEO). Such satellites orbit the Earth more than 11 times daily. Most are around 800 km above the Earth's surface, the furthest being 2000 km . Such satellites are easy to reach, and communication signals get to them in a short amount of time. The International Space Station, the Hubble Telescope, and most imaging satellites are in this category.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-230.jpg?height=704&width=1371&top_left_y=1780&top_left_x=1250)
Figure 11.14 A satellite in a geostationary orbit

## Geostationary orbit

In Figure 11.14, a satellite is orbiting the Earth vertically above the equator and is therefore moving in the equatorial plane.
The Earth rotates once about its polar axis every 24 hours. Suppose the period of the orbit of the satellite is also 24 hours, and suppose that it also moves in the same direction as the Earth.
The satellite will remain stationary above the same point on the equator. Such a satellite is said to be in a geostationary orbit.
Many weather and communication satellites are geostationary, as they can benefit from always being in the same position above the Earth. Since the period of the orbit is fixed at 24 hours, the equation $T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}$ gives only one value of $R$ for which this can occur. Therefore, there is only one possible height above the Earth for a geostationary orbit.

If a satellite is in a geostationary orbit then:

- The satellite orbits in the equatorial plane
- Its period is 24 hours
- The satellite moves in the same direction as the Earth rotates
- There is only one height at which this can occur

| Orbit | Satellite uses | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Low-Earth orbit <br> (Near-Earth Orbit) <br> Height above Earth is between 160 km and about 2000 km . Most around 800 km . <br> Over $\frac{3}{4}$ of the satellites that orbit the Earth are in LEO | Earth observation satellites, e.g. monitoring agriculture, forestry, natural disasters, armed conflicts. <br> International Space Station, Hubble Telescope. <br> Some communication satellites. | Relatively near the Earth. Highdetail photos of Earth's surface can be taken. <br> Short distance to travel to satellites. <br> Short communication time and strong data signals. | Needs many satellites to give good coverage. |


| Orbit | Satellite uses | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mid-Earth orbit <br> $2000-37000 \mathrm{~km}$ | Navigation systems, e.g. GPS, Galileo | Higher vantage point, fewer satellites needed for coverage | Many satellites needed to give global coverage |
| Geostationary orbit <br> 37000 km above equator | Weather, telecommunications, TV, satellite phone, internet | Large areas of the Earth can be viewed. Three well-placed satellites cover almost all of the Earth. Satellites in fixed positions, so aerials on Earth can be pointed to a fixed position. | Poor real-time communication due to distance. |

## Worked Example 15

## Question

Calculate the height above the equator of a satellite in a geostationary orbit.

## Solution

Solving $T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}$ gives $R=\sqrt[3]{\frac{T^{2} G M}{4 \pi^{2}}}$
The period of a stationary orbit is 24 hours $=86400$ seconds. The values of all the other quantities in the equation are known. Thus, $R$ can be found.

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{(86400)^{2}\left(6.7 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{24}\right)}{4 \pi^{2}}} \\
& =4.24 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{~m} \\
\text { height of satellite above Earth } & =R-\text { radius of Earth } \\
& =4.24 \times 10^{7}-6.4 \times 10^{6} \\
& =3.6 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{~m} \\
& =36000 \mathrm{~km}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this height is significantly greater than near-Earth orbit heights.

## Exam and problem-solving tip

When solving problems involving satellite orbits, it is useful to

- Write down the equations:

$$
v^{2}=\frac{G M}{R} \quad T=\frac{2 \pi R}{v} \quad T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}
$$

- List the quantities you know and the ones which you need to calculate
- Decide which of the three equations has only one unknown in it
- Substitute in the known values in this equation and solve for the unknown
- Continue this process until you have the desired solution

## Summary What I should know

- Angular velocity is the rate at which an angle is changing with respect to time.
- When a particle moves at constant speed around a circle, the direction of its velocity is changing and hence it is accelerating.
- Centripetal force is the force towards the centre of a circle that's needed to keep a body moving in that circle.
- Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration towards the centre of a circle that a body has if it is moving in that circle.
- To keep an object of mass $m$ moving at a constant speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$, a force $F$ acting towards the centre of the circle is needed, where $F$ is given by:

$$
F=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}
$$

- Centripetal acceleration $a=\frac{v^{2}}{r}$
- The force of gravity supplies the necessary centripetal force to keep the planets orbiting the Sun and satellites orbiting the Earth.
- The period ( $T$ ) of an orbit is the time taken for a satellite to go once around the central body.

$$
T=\frac{2 \pi R}{V}
$$

- Kepler's third law states that, for a planet orbiting the Sun, the square of the period of the orbit is directly proportional to the cube of the radius of the orbit, i.e. $\quad T^{2} \propto R^{3}$

$$
T^{2}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} R^{3}}{G M}
$$

- An orbit is geostationary if the satellite orbits in the equatorial plane, its period is 24 hours, and the satellite moves in the same direction as the Earth rotates.

# 12 Elasticity and Hooke's Law

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand that if you try to compress or stretch an object, the object exerts a force trying to restore itself to its original length
- To ensure students understand Hooke's law
- To ensure students can apply Hooke's law to model real world situations
- To ensure students understand that a stretched or compressed object stores elastic potential energy
- To ensure students can model real world situations involving elastic potential energy
- To ensure students appreciate the energy conversions that take place when a body is oscillating in a system that obeys Hooke's law


## Keywords

- Elastic
- Elastic limit
- Natural length
- Restoring force
- Elastic constant
- Elastic potential energy
- Equililbrium position
- Cycle (oscillation)


### 12.1 Elasticity

Any object will change shape when a large enough force is applied to it. For example, an elastic band stretches, a rod bends and a spring stretches or gets compressed. When the force is removed, the object may return to its original shape. If this happens, the object is said to be elastic.
If the applied force is too great, however, even an elastic object may not return to its original shape when the force is removed (Figure 12.1). It becomes permanently strained. If this happens, the object has exceeded its elastic limit.

An object is said to behave elastically if after being compressed or stretched, it returns to its original shape when the force that compressed or stretched it is removed.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-234.jpg?height=776&width=1202&top_left_y=1979&top_left_x=1419)
Figure 12.1 If the spring is stretched too far, it will not return to its original length when released. It has exceeded its elastic limit.

## Student Experiment 12.1

To investigate the force needed to:
a) Compress an object
b) Stretch an object

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will place a force on a rubber block to try to compress it. You will qualitatively see that the bigger the force applied, the more the block compresses. Similarly, you will place a force on a rubber cord to try to stretch it. Again, you will see that the bigger the force applied, the more the rubber cord stretches.

## Equipment

A rectangular piece of rubber, a metre stick, elastic cord, a clamp, and a newton meter.

## Method (a)

1. Place a rectangular rubber eraser on the bench (Figure 12.2).
2. Place a metre stick (or a piece of wood) across the top of the rubber and push it downwards.
3. As you push down, you will see that the rubber will become compressed, i.e. its vertical length will become smaller.
4. The greater the downward force you exert, the more it will become compressed.
5. When you remove the force, the rubber comes back to its original length.
6. If a data logger and force meter are available you could see numerically how the force and the compression are related.

## Method (b)

1. Clamp an elastic band or an elastic cord to a fixed point on the bench (Figure 12.3).
2. Attach a newton meter to the other end of the cord.
3. Measure the length of the unstretched elastic cord.
4. By pulling the newton meter, stretch the cord.
5. Record the length of the cord and the size of the stretching force several times as you increase the force.
6. You will again find that the greater the force, the greater the amount by which the cord stretches.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-235.jpg?height=728&width=1207&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=1501)
