### 12.2 Hooke's law

Figure 12.4(A) shows a spring hanging vertically. The unstretched length of the spring is called its natural length.
In Figure 12.4(B), the end of the spring is pulled downwards through a distance $s_{1}$, by a weight $W_{1}$ hanging off the spring. When it is pulled down, the spring exerts an upwards force trying to pull it back to its original length. This force is called the restoring force $\boldsymbol{F}_{1}$. The size of the restoring force is the same as the applied force when the spring comes to rest.
If you increase the applied force, the spring stretches further (by an overall distance $s_{2}$ beyond its natural length, in Figure 12.4(C)). Again, the restoring force increases and equals the applied force.
For a spring like this, experiment shows that the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement undergone by the end of the spring.
If the spring is compressed smaller than its natural length (provided the coils don't jam up on each other), it also exerts a force that tries to restore it to its natural length. This force is also directly proportional to the displacement.
This example is a particular case of Hooke's law.
Hooke's law states that when an object is stretched or compressed by a displacement $s$, the restoring force $F$ is directly proportional to the displacement, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-235.jpg?height=1356&width=828&top_left_y=2457&top_left_x=1832)
Figure 12.4

Hooke's law applies to many objects when they are compressed or stretched, but sometimes only if the amount of stretch or compression is small.
Mathematically, Hooke's law states that:

$$
F \propto-s \Rightarrow F=-k s
$$

where $k$ is a constant, called the elastic constant. The negative sign indicates that the displacement and the restoring force are always in the opposite direction to each other.

## Hooke's law:

Restoring force $\alpha$ displacement

$$
\Rightarrow F=-k s
$$

(F\&T, page 57)

The elastic constant of an object that obeys Hooke's law is the number $k$, in the equation
$F=-k s$
Its unit is the newton per metre ( $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^{-1}$ ).

## Robert Hooke

Robert Hooke (1635-1703) was an English astronomer, geologist, meteorologist and physicist. In 1660 he discovered the law of elasticity that now bears his name. From his studies of microscopic fossils, using a compound microscope that he designed, he became an early proponent of a theory of evolution in biology.
He observed the diffraction of light and proposed a wave theory to explain it. He also proposed an inverse square law to account for the motion of the planets around the Sun. Using a type of reflecting telescope, which he also designed, he showed that both Mars and Jupiter rotate. He offered an explanation as to why matter usually expands when heated.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

When a spring is stretched 10 cm beyond its natural length, the restoring force is 50 N . Assuming that the spring obeys Hooke's law, find the restoring force when the extension is 12 cm .

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =-k s \\
50 & =k(0.1) \\
k & =500
\end{aligned}
$$

(in most calculations, you can ignore the negative sign)
So, $F=-k s$ becomes $F=500 s$
When $s=12 \mathrm{~cm}=0.12 \mathrm{~m}$, the restoring force:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =(500)(0.12) \\
& =60 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A helical spring, with a spring constant of $200 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$, hangs vertically. A 0.8 kg mass is then attached to its free end and the length of the spring increases to 40 cm .
a) What is the natural length of the spring?
b) If an additional 0.5 kg is added to the end of the spring, what would its length become?

## Solution

a) Force stretching spring = weight of the 0.8 kg mass

$$
\begin{aligned}
&=(0.8)(9.8)=7.84 \mathrm{~N} \\
& \Rightarrow \text { Restoring force } F=7.84 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

The length of the spring is now $40 \mathrm{~cm}=0.4 \mathrm{~m}$ (Figure 12.5).
If $l$ is the natural length of the spring, then the extension caused by $\mathbf{7 . 8 4} \mathbf{~ N}=\mathbf{0 . 4 - l}$.
Applying $F=-k s \quad$ gives: $\quad 7.84=(200)(0.4-l)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow 7.84 & =80-200 l \\
\Rightarrow 200 l & =72.16 \\
\Rightarrow l & =0.3608 \mathrm{~m} \\
& =36.08 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) When 0.5 kg is added, the new force is the weight of ( $0.8+0.5$ ) kg

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(1.3)(9.8) \mathrm{N} \\
& =12.74 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying $F=-k s \quad$ gives: $\quad 12.74=(200) s$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow s & =\frac{12.74}{200} \\
& =0.0637 \mathrm{~m} \\
& =6.37 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

New length of spring $=$ natural length + new extension

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =36.08+6.37 \\
& =42.45 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-237.jpg?height=1512&width=1046&top_left_y=2210&top_left_x=1028)
Figure 12.5

## Student Experiment 12.2

To verify Hooke＇s law by showing that the restoring force is directly proportional to the extension for a helical spring； that is $F \propto s$ ．

## Summary of method

In this experiment，you will progressively stretch a helical spring by hanging weights of increasing values off its end．For each weight，you will measure the extension produced in the spring．You will then plot a graph of the restoring force against the extension．

## Equipment

Helical spring，metre stick，retort stand and two clamps，set of slotted weights with a holder，and a pointer．

## Method

1. Set up the equipment as shown in Figure 12.6(A).
2. Ensure both clamps are tightened securely. Allow the system to settle.
3. Take, and record, the reading $l_{0}$ of the pointer on the metre stick, with no weights on the holder. Take this as the natural length of the spring.
4. Add a weight to the holder and allow the system to settle. Record the total weight on the holder and record the reading on the metre stick.
5. Repeat this step several times, each time adding an extra weight to the holder.

## Handling the data

Copy and complete the table by calculating the extension for each set of values.

| Restoring force, $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{N})$ | 0 |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Length of spring, $l(\mathrm{~cm})$ | $l_{0}=$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Extension of spring, $s(\mathrm{~cm})$ <br> $\left(s=l-l_{0}\right)$ | 0 |  |  |  |  |  |  |

On graph paper, plot a graph of restoring force $F(y$-axis) against the extension $s$ ( $x$-axis). The points should be very close to lying on a straight line that passes through the origin. Draw the best straight line that fits the points (like in Figure 12.7). This shows that the force is directly proportional to the extension ( $F \propto s$ ), verifying Hooke's law.
Calculate the slope of the graph.

## Sources of error

1. Make sure the pointer remains horizontal and doesn't start pointing upwards or downwards as the spring stretches.
2. Avoid parallax error when reading the metre stick.
3. Ensure the slotted weights actually have the weight written on them. Check with a weighing scale if needed.

### 12.3 Work done in stretching or compressing

Figure 12.8 shows a spring of length $l$. A small force is applied to the end of the spring and starts to stretch the spring. If you want to keep stretching the spring, you must increase the strength of the applied force to overcome the restoring force of the spring.
According to Hooke's law, this is directly proportional to the extension and, therefore, increases as the extension does.
If you stretch it a distance $s$, hold it there and the value of the force is $F$, it can be shown that the work done by the increasing force is equal to $\frac{1}{2} k s^{2}$.
This work done is the elastic potential energy stored by the spring:

$$
E_{p}=\frac{1}{2} k s^{2}
$$

A similar result holds if the spring is compressed, and also note that this

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-240.jpg?height=844&width=766&top_left_y=423&top_left_x=1855)
Figure 12.8

result will hold for any object that stretches or compresses while obeying Hooke's law; it doesn't have to be a spring.

If an object that obeys Hooke's law is stretched or compressed by a distance $s$, the elastic potential energy stored in it is given by:

$$
E_{p}=\frac{1}{2} k s^{2}
$$

This is also the work done in stretching or compressing the object.

## Worked example 3

## Question

A spring has an elastic constant of $400 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$. It is stretched until it has been extended by 7 cm .
a) Calculate the increase in the potential energy stored in the spring.
b) Calculate the work done in stretching the spring.

## Solution

a) $\quad k=400, \quad s=7 \times 10^{-2}, \quad E_{\rho}=?$

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{p} & =\frac{1}{2} k s^{2} \\
& =\frac{1}{2}(400)\left(7 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{2} \\
& =0.98 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) work done = potential energy gained

$$
=0.98 \mathrm{j}
$$

### 12.4 Energy changes in an oscillating body that obeys Hooke's law

Figure 12.9 shows a mass, on a smooth frictionless surface, attached by a spring to a rigid wall. If the spring is neither compressed nor stretched (i.e. it is at its natural length), there is one position $O$ where the mass will remain at rest. $O$ is called the equilibrium position.
If the mass is pulled horizontally, stretching the spring, and released at point $A$, it vibrates (or oscillates) back and forth between $A$ and $B$.
A cycle or an oscillation is the movement from $A$ to $B$ and back again to $A$.
A cycle or oscillation is the complete motion of an oscillating body to return to an initial position after having passed through every other position along its path of motion.

For an oscillating body obeying Hooke's law, equilibrium position is the position at which no resultant force acts on it.

The maximum distance of the mass from the equilibrium position is the length $|O A|$ or $|O B|$, which are the same. As the mass moves, its energy changes continually from elastic potential ( $E_{\mathrm{p}}$ ) to kinetic ( $E_{\mathrm{k}}$ ) and back again to elastic potential. Figure 12.10 shows how the energy changes as the body moves.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-241.jpg?height=724&width=1205&top_left_y=1754&top_left_x=319)
Figure 12.10

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-241.jpg?height=955&width=1144&top_left_y=1354&top_left_x=1601)
Figure 12.9

At $O$, the mass has maximum kinetic energy and zero elastic potential energy. Suppose it undergoes a displacement $s$ to the right from $O$. Displacements to the right are given a positive sign (the spring is stretched).
The work done, and hence the potential energy gained by the mass, when at displacement $s$, is given by the formula:

$$
E_{p}=\frac{1}{2} k s^{2}
$$

The same is true if the mass is displaced to the left of $O$. Displacements to the left are given a negative sign (the spring is compressed).
Figure 12.11 is a graph of the potential energy, $\frac{1}{2} k s^{2}$ against displacement, $s$ of the mass at any point on its path as it moves from $A$ to $B$ and back.
At any point during the motion, the kinetic energy + elastic potential is always the same fixed number. This number is equal to the total energy of the mass. Its value is the same as the maximum potential energy of the mass.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-241.jpg?height=747&width=932&top_left_y=2975&top_left_x=1666)
Figure 12.11

## Summary What I should know

- An elastic object is one that, after being compressed or stretched, returns to its original shape when the force that compressed or stretched it is removed.
- An elastic object reaches its elastic limit when it has been stretched (or compressed) so much that it does not return to its original shape after the stretching (or compressing) force is removed.
- Hooke's law states that when an object is stretched or compressed by a displacement $s$, the restoring force $F$ is directly proportional to the displacement, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
- The elastic constant of an object that obeys Hooke's law is the number $k$ in the equation:

$$
F=-k s
$$

Its unit is the newton per metre ( $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^{-1}$ ).

- The elastic potential energy stored in an object that obeys Hooke's law is given by:

$$
E_{p}=\frac{1}{2} k s^{2}
$$

where $s$ is the displacement by which it is compressed or stretched.

- The work done in stretching or compressing an object that obeys Hooke's law is also equal to $\frac{1}{2} k s^{2}$
- If an object is attached to a spring that obeys Hooke's law and is set oscillating, then:
- The equilibrium position of the object is the position where the resultant force on the object is zero.
- The energy of the body changes continually from potential to kinetic and back again to potential. The total energy of the body is the same at any point during the motion.


## Learning outcomes

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-243.jpg?height=746&width=2410&top_left_y=2233&top_left_x=319)

# 13 Temperature and Thermometers

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the concept of temperature
- To ensure students appreciate what a thermometric property is
- To ensure students are familiar with the Celsius and kelvin scales of temperature
- To ensure students are familiar with different types of thermometers
- To ensure students appreciate which characteristics of thermometric properties make them more suitable for measuring temperature.


## Keywords

- Temperature
- The kelvin (K)
- Kelvin scale
- Degrees Celsius
- Celsius scale
- Thermometric property
- Thermometer


### 13.1 Concept of temperature

We all know the difference between hot and cold. We can often tell if one object is hotter or colder than another - that is, to recognise different degrees of hotness. A scientist would say this is the ability to recognise differences in temperature. Temperature is the measure of the hotness or coldness of a body.

Temperature is the measure of the hotness or coldness of a body.

## Units of temperature

The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K). Temperatures expressed in kelvin are symbolised by $T$. You don't need to know the exact definition of the kelvin.
In practice though, and in most everyday situations, temperature is usually measured in degrees Celsius. The Celsius scale is the practical scale of temperature. Temperatures in degrees Celsius are typically symbolised by $\theta$.

The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K).
The kelvin is one of the seven base units.

## Relationship between the degree Celsius and the kelvin

The size of 1 kelvin $(K)$ is the same as the size of 1 degree Celsius $\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$.
The only difference between the two scales is that 0 K is equal to $-273.15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, or put another way, $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is equal to 273.15 K .
So, to convert from degrees Celsius to kelvin, you add 273.15, and to convert from kelvin to degrees Celsius, you subtract 273.15 (Figure 13.1).

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Temperature in degrees Celsius }=\text { temperature in kelvin }-273.15 \\
& \qquad \theta\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=T(\mathrm{~K})-273.15
\end{aligned}
$$

(F\&T, page 58)

### 13.2 Thermometric properties

To measure temperature accurately, scientists use a physical property that changes measurably as temperature changes. They use the changing value of this property to indicate the temperature. Such a property is called a thermometric property. An instrument based on a particular thermometric property and used to measure temperature is called a thermometer.

A thermometric property is any physical property that changes measurably with temperature.

A thermometer is an instrument based on a particular thermometric property and used to measure temperature.

## Thermometric properties

Some thermometric properties used in thermometers include the following.

## Length of a column of liquid

When a liquid is heated, it expands (in other words, its volume increases). If the liquid is put in a thin capillary tube, the length of the column of liquid will increase as the temperature increases. This is the thermometric property on which a mercury-in-glass or an alcohol-in-glass thermometer is based (Figure 13.2).

## Electrical resistance

The electrical resistance of a conductor changes with temperature (page 381). For a metal, the resistance increases with increasing temperature, whereas for a semiconductor or carbon the resistance decreases with increasing temperature. Resistance is the thermometric property on which the resistance thermometer is based. A thermistor (page 381) is a semiconductor whose electrical resistance decreases rapidly with a small rise in temperature. The resistance is measured with an ohmmeter (page 370).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-246.jpg?height=1261&width=743&top_left_y=688&top_left_x=1878)
Figure 13.2 The thermometric property on which an alcohol-in-glass thermometer is based is the length of the column of alcohol.

## Emf of a thermocouple

If two different metals are joined together to form a complete circuit (Figure 13.3) and the two junctions are maintained at different temperatures, a small emf (voltage) of a few millivolts appears across the circuit. The size of the emf depends on the temperature difference between the junctions. The emf can be measured with a very sensitive voltmeter. This device is called a thermocouple and it can be used to measure temperature.

## Colour

The colour of certain crystals changes with temperature. This is the basis of one form of thermometer used to measure the temperature of your body (Figure 13.4).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-246.jpg?height=678&width=1323&top_left_y=3167&top_left_x=198)
Figure 13.4

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-246.jpg?height=1164&width=1072&top_left_y=2317&top_left_x=1549)
Figure 13.3 The thermometric property on which the thermocouple is based is emf (voltage). The cold junction is kept at a fixed temperature and the temperature of the other junction is varied. The emf produced as a result of this is measured.

The colour of a very hot object also changes as its temperature rises. For example, if a piece of iron is heated, its colour changes from grey to a dull brown, then to red, then bright red, then yellow, then white. Similarly, increasing the current through the filament of a bulb causes its colour to change (Figure 13.5). The colour can be used to indicate temperature inside furnaces or volcanoes, from a safe distance.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-247.jpg?height=707&width=1935&top_left_y=638&top_left_x=367)
Figure 13.5

## Characteristics of a good thermometric property

There are certain characteristics of thermometric properties that make them more useful for measuring temperature. An ideal thermometric property:

- Is accurately measurable
- Varies continuously with temperature
- Is measurable over a wide range of temperatures
- Is very sensitive to temperature change (i.e. its value varies noticeably even for a small change in temperature)
- Does not take much heat from the object whose temperature is being measured (i.e. it should have a small heat capacity (see Chapter 14)
- Changes quickly in response to a temperature change
- Ideally varies linearly with temperature, and in sync with other types of thermometers

The thermometric property used in any real thermometer will have some or all these desirable properties to a greater or lesser extent. The following table shows details of some types of thermometers.

| Type of thermometer | Thermometric property | Typical temperature range | Comments |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mercury-in-glass thermometer | Length of column of liquid | -39 to $356^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ | Cheap, portable, but not extremely accurate. Mercury is dangerous if the thermometer breaks |
| Alcohol (spirit)-inglass thermometer | Length of column of liquid | -114 to $78^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ | Cheap, portable, but not extremely accurate |
| Platinum resistance thermometer | Electrical resistance | -200 to $1200^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ | Very accurate. Heat capacity is too large to allow it to follow rapidly changing temperatures |
| Thermocouple thermometer | Voltage (emf) | -250 to $1500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ | Compact. Used to measure rapidly changing temperatures. The junction can be extremely small and can fit into very small spaces. Commonly used in a digital thermometer with a probe |

## Student Experiment 13.1

To analyse the suitability of alcohol in glass for use as a thermometer

## Summary

In this experiment, you will place an ungraduated alcohol-in-glass thermometer in melting ice and measure the length of the alcohol column. You will have a laboratory standard thermometer in the ice also. You will read the temperature from the standard thermometer. By gently heating the water, you will repeat the above at several different temperatures. You will plot a graph of the 'length of alcohol' column against 'temperature'.

## Equipment

An ungraduated alcohol-in-glass thermometer, a standard laboratory thermometer, some ice, a beaker $(250 \mathrm{ml})$, a retort stand and clamp, a Bunsen burner, and a tripod and gauze.

## Method

1. Place the ungraduated alcohol thermometer and the standard lab thermometer in the beaker of melting ice. Leave them there until the column of alcohol stops rising and the lab thermometer gives a steady reading.
2. Read and record the temperature on the lab thermometer. Mark the position of the alcohol on the glass. Remove the alcohol thermometer from the beaker and measure the length of the column of alcohol. Record its value.
3. Set up the Bunsen, tripod, gauze and beaker of ice/water as in Figure 13.6.
4. Heat the water by about $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
5. Read and record the temperature on the lab thermometer. Simultaneously mark the position of the alcohol on the glass. Remove the alcohol thermometer from the water and measure the length of the column of alcohol. Record its value.
6. Repeat steps 3 and 4 at least six times, raising the temperature by about $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ each time.
7. On graph paper, plot a graph of the length of the alcohol column against temperature. This graph shows you how the thermometric property (the length of the column of alcohol) changes with temperature.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-248.jpg?height=1290&width=1531&top_left_y=2171&top_left_x=244)
Figure 13.6

## Analysis of results

Based on your results, consider the following:

- Was the length of the column of alcohol measurable?
- Was the length of the column of alcohol accurately measurable?
- Did the length of the column of alcohol vary continuously with temperature?
- What range of temperatures do you think it could measure?
- From your graph, can you estimate the sensitivity of the alcohol-in-glass thermometer by finding the increase in length per degree rise in temperature?
- Did the length of the column of alcohol increase linearly with temperature? And would it be an advantage if it did? Explain your answer.
- In your opinion, is alcohol in glass suitable for use as a thermometer?
- How could you now use the alcohol-in-glass thermometer to measure the temperature of tap water, without using the lab thermometer?

Note: The temperature of any environment can be read with the alcohol-in-glass thermometer, by measuring its length at the unknown temperature and using the calibration curve to determine the temperature.
A calibration curve for any other type of thermometer, such as a thermocouple or a resistance thermometer, can also be made by the above method. The graph plotted is then the value of the thermometric property of that given thermometer against the reading of temperature on the commercial thermometer.

## Summary What I should know

- Temperature is the measure of the hotness or coldness of a body.
- The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K).
- The degree Celsius is the practical unit of temperature, used for most everyday situations.
- temperature in degrees Celsius = temperature in kelvin - 273.15 $\theta\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=T(\mathrm{~K})-273.15$
- A thermometric property is any physical property that changes measurably with temperature.
- A thermometer is an instrument based on a particular thermometric property and used to measure temperature.
- Length of a column of liquid, electrical resistance, emf and colour are examples of thermometric properties.

- Latent heat
- The joule (J)

## Keywords

### 14.1 The states of matter

Matter can exist in three different states, solid, liquid or gas. You should already be familiar with the terms used in Figure 14.1.

## Particle model for changes of state

## Solids

- In a solid, the molecules are packed closely together. This makes it very difficult to compress a solid into a smaller volume (Figure 14.2).
- There are large forces attracting each molecule to its neighbouring molecules.
- The molecules have fixed positions, and they cannot move through the solid. This gives the solid a fixed shape and means it cannot flow like a liquid or a gas. However, the molecules can vibrate about these fixed positions.
- The higher the temperature, the greater the size and speed of these vibrations. This increases slightly the average distance between neighbouring molecules and means a solid usually expands when heated.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-251.jpg?height=1033&width=883&top_left_y=2021&top_left_x=1862)
Figure 14.1

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-251.jpg?height=584&width=1645&top_left_y=3203&top_left_x=325)
Figure 14.2

## Liquids

- If sufficient heat energy is added to a solid, it reaches a temperature called its melting point, where some of the molecules get sufficient energy to break free from the strong forces attracting them to their neighbouring molecules.
- These molecules become able to slide freely around each other. As more heat is added, eventually all the molecules have enough energy to do this. All of the solid has melted and has turned into a liquid (Figure 14.2).
- There are still forces between the molecules, but they are weaker than in a solid. The molecules are still quite close to each other, and a liquid is also very difficult to compress into a smaller volume.
- In a liquid, the molecules can move anywhere in the liquid, and they collide with each other. The speed of an individual molecule varies as it collides with other molecules. If a molecule gets a high enough velocity, it may leave the surface of the liquid. This is evaporation.


## Gases

- As further heat energy is added, the molecules move faster and faster. Evaporation increases, and eventually a temperature is reached where evaporation starts to occur throughout the liquid. This temperature is called the boiling point.
- If energy continues to be added at this temperature, all the molecules will eventually get enough energy to escape, and the substance will turn into a gas (Figure 14.2).
- In a gas, there are large distances between molecules, so a gas is much easier to compress than a liquid or solid. The forces between the molecules are negligible, except when a molecule is temporarily close to another molecule.
- The molecules move in random directions at random speeds, which are very high. For example, the average speed of a nitrogen molecule in the atmosphere, near the surface of the Earth at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, is about $492 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
- The molecules collide with each other and with the walls of their container, so a gas will expand to fill that container.


### 14.2 Heat capacity

If a substance is at its melting point or boiling point and is changing state, then as you add or remove heat energy, the temperature of the substance does not change.
If the substance is not at its melting or boiling point, then when you add heat energy, its temperature rises, and when you take heat energy away, its temperature falls. Experimentally, it is found that:

- The heat energy $Q$ needed to produce a given rise in temperature $\Delta \theta$ is directly proportional to the rise in temperature (Figure 14.3).
- The amount of heat energy taken in by an object to produce a given rise in temperature is the same as the amount given out to produce the same fall in temperature.
Therefore, the amount of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of an object by $1^{\circ} \mathrm{C} (1 \mathrm{~K})$ is the same as the amount of heat energy given out if its temperature falls by $1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. This amount of heat energy is called the heat capacity of the object. Its value is different for different objects.

The heat capacity of an object is the heat energy needed to change its temperature by $1 \mathrm{~K}\left(1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$.

- The symbol for heat capacity is $C$ (uppercase C).
- The SI unit of heat capacity is the joule per kelvin ( $\mathbf{J} \mathbf{K}^{\mathbf{- 1}}$ ).

If an object has heat capacity $C$, the heat energy $Q$ needed to change its temperature by $\Delta \theta$ degrees Celsius is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Heat }=\text { heat capacity × change in temperature, i.e. } \\
& Q=C \Delta \theta \quad(F \& T, \text { page } 58, \text { where } Q \text { is referred to as } \Delta E)
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-253.jpg?height=606&width=2013&top_left_y=270&top_left_x=325)
Figure 14.3 For a given object, the rise in temperature is directly proportional to the amount of heat energy added.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

A beaker of water has a heat capacity of $2000 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$. How much heat energy must be added to raise its temperature from $4.0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $96^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q & =C \Delta \theta=(2000)(96-4) \\
& =184000 \mathrm{~J} \\
& =180000 \mathrm{~J} \text { (to two significant figures) }
\end{aligned}
$$

2. A metal block of heat capacity $600 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ loses 1 MJ of heat energy to its surroundings. Find the decrease in its temperature.

Water at $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ was placed in a container of negligible heat capacity. Energy $Q$ was supplied to heat the water, and $\theta$, the temperature which the water reached, was recorded. This was repeated several times with different values of $Q$ supplied to equal masses of water. The student was careful that the water had an initial temperature of $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ each time. The following data was recorded:

| $Q(\mathrm{~J})$ | 1273 | 2552 | 3823 | 5107 | 6376 | 7642 |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $\theta\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 | 35 | 40 |

Draw a graph, on graph paper, of $Q$ against $\Delta \theta$, the change in temperature of the water.
a) What conclusion can you draw from the graph?
b) What does the slope of the graph represent?

### 14.3 Specific heat capacity

To compare the heat energy needed to produce a given temperature change in different substances, scientists use the amount of heat necessary to change the temperature of $\mathbf{1}$ kilogram of that substance by $1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}(1 \mathrm{~K})$. This amount is called the specific heat capacity $\boldsymbol{c}$ (lowercase $\boldsymbol{c}$ ) of that substance. For example, it takes 4180 J to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by $1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, but only 390 J to do the same for copper.

The specific heat capacity of a substance is the heat energy needed to change the temperature of 1 kilogram of that substance by 1 kelvin.

- The symbol for specific heat capacity is $c$ (lowercase c).
- The SI unit of specific heat capacity is the joule per kilogram per kelvin ( $\mathbf{J} \mathbf{k g}^{-\mathbf{1}} \mathbf{K}^{-\mathbf{1}}$ ).


## Specific heat capacity formula

Experimentally, it is found that:

- The heat energy $Q$ needed to produce a given rise in temperature is directly proportional to the rise in temperature.
- The heat energy needed to produce a given rise in temperature in a body is directly proportional to the mass of that body (Figure 14.4).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-254.jpg?height=789&width=1697&top_left_y=377&top_left_x=924)
Figure 14.4 For a given rise in temperature, the heat energy required is directly proportional to the mass of the body being heated.

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q \propto \Delta \theta \text { and } \quad Q \propto m & \Rightarrow Q \propto m \Delta \theta \\
& \Rightarrow Q=c m \Delta \theta \quad \text { where } c \text { is a constant. }
\end{aligned}
$$

If, in this formula $m=1 \mathrm{~kg}$ and $\Delta \theta=1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then $Q=c$, i.e. $c$ is the heat energy needed to change the temperature of 1 kilogram of that substance by 1 kelvin, i.e. the specific heat capacity.
It follows that, provided a substance does not change state:

|  | Heat energy added | $=$ mass × specific heat capacity × rise in temperature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Heat energy lost | $=$ mass × specific heat capacity × fall in temperature |  |
| In either case: | $Q$ | $=m c \Delta \theta \quad$ |
| (F\& $T$, page 58, where $Q$ is referred to as $\Delta E$ ) |  |  |

## The SI unit of specific heat capacity is the joule per kilogram per kelvin ( $\mathbf{J ~ k g}^{\mathbf{- 1}} \mathbf{K}^{\mathbf{- 1}}$ ).

Table 14.1 shows the specific heat capacities of some common substances.
| Substance | Specific heat capacity ( $\mathbf{J ~ k g}^{-\mathbf{1}} \mathbf{K}^{-\mathbf{1}}$ ) | Substance | Specific heat capacity ( $\mathbf{J ~ k g}^{\boldsymbol{-} \mathbf{1}} \mathbf{K}^{\boldsymbol{-} \mathbf{1}}$ ) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Water | 4180 | Paraffin oil | 2100 |
| Copper | 390 | Alcohol | 2500 |
| Iron | 451 | Wood | 1700 |
| Glass | 674 | Ice | 2100 |
| Aluminium | 910 | Air | 1000 |


## Table 14.1

In the following worked examples: Specific heat capacity of water $=4180 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ and specific heat capacity of copper $=390 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$.

## Worked Example 2

## Question

How much heat energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2.00 kg of water from $5.00^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q & =m c \Delta \theta=(2)(4180)(100-5) \\
& =794200 \mathrm{~J} \\
& =794000 \mathrm{~J} \text { (to three significant figures) }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

5544 J of heat energy are given out when the temperature of 800 grams of copper cools from $25.0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $7.00^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Calculate the specific heat capacity of copper.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q & =m c \Delta \theta \quad \Rightarrow 5544=(0.8)(c)(25-7) \\
\Rightarrow c & =\frac{5544}{(0.8)(18)} \\
& =385 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \\
& =390 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \text { (to two significant figures) }
\end{aligned}
$$

Note: Mass must be in kilograms when using $Q=m c \Delta \theta .800$ grams $=0.8 \mathrm{~kg}$.

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A 2.0 kW electric heater raises the temperature of 10 kg of water from $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If there is no heat loss to the surroundings, how long does it take?

## Solution

Heat needed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q & =m c \Delta \theta=(10)(4180)(80-15) \\
& =2717000 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

The heat is supplied at the rate of $2 \mathrm{~kW}=2000$ joules per second.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Time taken } & =\frac{\text { energy supplied }}{\text { energy supplied per second }}=\frac{2717000}{2000} \\
& =1358.5 \mathrm{~s} \\
& =1400 \mathrm{~s} \text { (to two significant figures) }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

20 grams of copper at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is added to 150 grams of water at $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. There is no loss of heat to the surroundings. Find the final temperature of the mixture.

## Solution

Let $\theta=$ final temperature of mixture. Then:
Rise in temperature of water: $\quad \Delta \theta \uparrow=\theta-15$
Fall in temperature of the copper: $\Delta \theta \downarrow=100-\theta$
Since there is no heat loss to the surroundings:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Heat lost by copper } & =\text { Heat gained by water, } \\
\text { i.e. } \quad m_{c} c_{c} \Delta \theta \downarrow & =m_{w} c_{w} \Delta \theta \uparrow \\
\Rightarrow(20 \times 10-3)(390)(100-\theta) & =(150 \times 10-3)(4180)(\theta-15) \\
\Rightarrow 7.8(100-\theta) & =627(\theta-15) \\
\Rightarrow 780-7.8 \theta & =627 \theta-9405 \\
\Rightarrow 780+9405 & =627 \theta+7.8 \theta \\
\Rightarrow \theta & =\frac{10185}{634.8} \\
& =16.04^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\
& =16^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { (to two significant figures) }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Exercise 14.2

Where needed, specific heat capacities: copper $=390 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$; water $=4180 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$; iron $=451 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$; aluminium $=910 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$

1. How much heat energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water from $12^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?
2. How much heat energy is needed to raise the temperature of 12 kg of copper from $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $120^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?
3. 11088 J of heat energy are needed to raise the temperature of 1.6 kg of copper from $7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Calculate the specific heat capacity of copper.
4. One megajoule of heat energy is supplied to a piece of iron and raises its temperature from $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $200^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Find the mass of the piece of iron.
5. 4000 J of heat energy are added to 400 grams of water at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. What is the resulting temperature of the water?

## Student Experiment 14.1

To determine the specific heat capacity of a liquid by an electrical method

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will send an electric current through a heating coil that is immersed in a copper calorimeter of water. With a joulemeter, you will measure the amount of energy supplied. The rise in temperature is measured with a thermometer. Knowing the mass of the water, the mass of the calorimeter and the specific heat capacity of copper, you will calculate the specific heat capacity of water.

## Equipment

A copper calorimeter, a stirrer and an insulating lid, some insulating material (e.g. cotton wool or polystyrene beads), a container (e.g. a large beaker) to hold the calorimeter and insulating material, a heating coil and a thermometer (0-50 ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in steps of $0.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), a DC power supply unit and connecting leads, a joulemeter and a weighing scale.

## Method

1. Find the mass of the empty calorimeter $m_{c}$.
2. Fill the calorimeter with enough water to fully cover the heating coil when the coil is placed in it, then find the mass of the calorimeter and water. By subtraction, find the mass of the water $m_{\mathrm{w}}$.
3. Place the calorimeter of water in the insulating material and set up the equipment as in Figure 14.5.
4. Wait a minute or two, then measure the temperature of the cold water and the

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-257.jpg?height=1117&width=1290&top_left_y=1406&top_left_x=1009)
Figure 14.5

calorimeter $\theta_{1}$.
5. Switch on the joulemeter and the electric current. Allow the current to flow until a temperature rise of about $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ has occurred. Stir the water continuously throughout the experiment.
6. Switch off the current and joulemeter. Take the reading on the joulemeter, $Q$.
7. Stir the water and wait until the temperature stops rising. Then read the final and highest temperature of the water and the calorimeter $\theta_{2}$.
8. Complete Table 14.2.

| Mass of empty calorimeter | $m_{\mathrm{c}}=$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mass of calorimeter and water | $m_{2}=$ |
| Mass of water | $m_{\mathrm{w}}=$ |
| Temp. of cold water and calorimeter | $\theta_{1}=$ |
| Reading on joulemeter | $Q=$ |
| Final temperature of water and calorimeter | $\theta_{2}=$ |

Table 14.2

## Calculations

On the assumption that no heat is given to or taken from the surroundings:
Electrical energy supplied = heat gained by water + heat gained by calorimeter

$$
Q=m_{\mathrm{w}} c_{\mathrm{w}}\left(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}\right)+m_{\mathrm{c}} c_{\mathrm{c}}\left(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}\right)
$$

Since you now know the values of all these quantities except the specific heat capacity of water ( $c_{w}$ ), you can now calculate its value.

## Sources of error

A major source of error in this experiment is heat loss to the surroundings from the calorimeter and warm water. This is a systematic error causing the value of $Q$ used in the calculations to be too big, and consequently causing the calculated value of $c$ to also be too big. Heat loss to the surroundings may be reduced by:
a) Insulating the sides and bottom of the calorimeter
b) Polishing the calorimeter, which reduces losses by radiation (see page 257-258)
c) Placing a lid on the calorimeter
d) Ensuring that the temperature rise is not much higher than $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and that the experiment doesn't take much longer than 10 minutes
To further minimise errors due to heat loss to the surroundings, you may pre-cool the water to about $7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ below room temperature (e.g. by allowing some ice to melt in it). Allow the current to raise the temperature to about $7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ above room temperature. The heat flowing into the calorimeter and water from the surroundings during the first part of the experiment almost cancels out the heat leaving during the remainder of the experiment.

1. Too high a current can cause the water next to the coil to boil, producing steam and resulting in a systematic error. To avoid this, check the coil's specifications for the maximum suitable current.
2. Ensure that the coil is completely immersed in the water or it may burn out when the current is switched on.
3. Errors in measuring the masses are usually small compared with those that you might make in measuring the temperature. To keep these to a minimum, use a sensitive thermometer. One that reads in steps of $0.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is suitable. The thermometer should also have a small heat capacity so that it takes very little heat from the system.
4. The water is stirred during the experiment to ensure that it is all at the same temperature and consequently that the temperature read on the thermometer is correct.

## Questions

1. Why must the heating coil be completely covered with water?
2. Explain how a poorly insulated calorimeter will affect the accuracy of the results.
3. Why is the water stirred throughout the experiment?
4. How would the accuracy of the experiment be affected if the rise in temperature produced was very large, say $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?
5. How would the accuracy of the experiment be affected if the current used was very small, thus causing the experiment to take a very long time to produce a $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ rise in temperature?
6. What is the advantage in pre-cooling the water in the calorimeter to about $7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ below room temperature?
7. Why is it more important in this experiment to use a thermometer graduated in steps of $0.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ than to use a very high precision balance to measure the various masses?
8. List three precautions you should take in this experiment to minimise heat loss to the surroundings.
9. What in this experiment - other than the water and the calorimeter - receives heat? Why can these heat losses be neglected?
10. Why should the calorimeter be polished?
11. Why would using more water and supplying the same amount of energy be less accurate?

### 14.4 Latent heat

## Heat change without a change in temperature

When a substance is changing state, it can take in or give out heat energy without its temperature changing.
For example, to keep a beaker of boiling water boiling, heat energy must continually be added to it. A thermometer will show that the water remains at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ while it is boiling, even though heat energy is being added.
Likewise, a beaker of melting ice will stay at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ as it melts, even though heat energy is being added to it.
Or in reverse, heat energy will have to be continually removed from a beaker of water at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to turn the water into ice at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
Figure 14.6 shows how the temperature of a pure substance changes as heat energy is added to that substance.
The heat energy that needs to be added or removed to change the state of a substance, without a change in temperature, is called its

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-259.jpg?height=785&width=857&top_left_y=537&top_left_x=1888)
Figure 14.6 How temperature changes as heat energy is added

The latent heat ( $\boldsymbol{L}$ ) of a substance is the heat energy needed to change its state without a change in temperature.

$$
L=Q \quad(\text { F\&T, page 58, where } Q \text { is referred to as } \Delta E)
$$

- The latent heat needed to change from a solid to a liquid is called the latent heat of fusion.
- The latent heat needed to change from a liquid to a gas is called the latent heat of vaporisation.
- The symbol for latent heat is $\boldsymbol{L}$.
- The SI unit of latent heat is the joule (J).


## Worked Example 6

## Question

The graph in Figure 14.7 shows the variation in the temperature of 150 g of crushed ice when it was supplied with energy $Q$ at a constant rate.
a) Explain the shape of the graph.
b) Using the graph, estimate the energy taken in by the ice as it melts without changing temperature, i.e. calculate its latent heat of fusion.

## Solution

a) As the energy is added, the temperature of the ice rises from $-3^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
The temperature stays at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ while the ice is melting (or changing state).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-259.jpg?height=766&width=933&top_left_y=2317&top_left_x=1770)
Figure 14.7

While the ice is melting, the energy being added is absorbed as the latent heat of fusion of ice. When all the ice is melted, the temperature of the liquid water rises from $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ as energy continues to be supplied.
b) From the graph, the energy $Q$ needed to melt 150 g of ice $=59-10 \mathrm{~kJ}=49 \mathrm{~kJ}$. This is $L$, the latent heat of fusion of the ice.

### 14.5 Specific latent heat

To compare the amounts of heat energy needed to change the state of various substances, scientists use the amount of heat energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of the substance without a change in temperature. This is called the specific latent heat of the substance.

The specific latent heat ( $l$ ) of a substance is the amount of heat energy needed to change the state of $\mathbf{1}$ kg of that substance without a change in temperature.

- The symbol for specific latent heat is $\boldsymbol{l}$.
- The SI unit of specific latent heat is the joule per kilogram ( $\mathbf{~ k g} \mathbf{~ g}^{-1}$ ).

The specific latent heat of fusion of a substance is the amount of heat energy needed to change 1 kg of that substance from a solid to a liquid without a change in temperature (i.e. at its melting point). The same amount of heat energy is given out when the substance changes from a liquid to a solid at its melting point.

The specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance is the amount of heat energy needed to change $\mathbf{1}$ kg of that substance from a liquid to a gas without a change in temperature (i.e. at its boiling point). The same amount of heat energy is given out when the substance changes from a gas to a liquid at its boiling point.

The SI unit of specific latent heat of vaporisation and of fusion is the joule per kilogram ( $\mathbf{~} \mathbf{~ k g}^{\mathbf{- 1}}$ ).
Note that the specific latent heat of fusion of a substance and specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance are not the same value. The specific latent heat of vaporisation is usually significantly larger.

## Formula for specific latent heat

Since the heat energy $Q$ needed to change the state of a given mass $m$ of a substance is directly proportional to that mass, it follows that:

```
Heat needed to change from solid to liquid or vice versa = specific latent heat of fusion
leat needed to change from = mass * specific latent heat of vaporisation
In either case: (F&T, page 58, where Q is referred to as \DeltaE)
```

In the following worked examples, take:

- Specific heat capacity of: water $=4180 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ copper $=390 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ aluminium $=910 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$
- Specific latent heat of: vaporisation of water $=2.3 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1}$ fusion of ice $=3.3 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1}$

## Question

How much heat energy is needed to completely convert 50 grams of water at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to 50 grams of steam at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\binom{\text { heat }}{\text { needed }} & =\binom{\text { heat needed to bring } 50 \mathrm{~g} \text { of }}{\text { water from } 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { to } 100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}} \\
& =\binom{\text { heat needed to convert } 50 \mathrm{~g} \text { of water }}{\text { at } 100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { to } 50 \mathrm{~g} \text { of steam at } 100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}} \\
& =\left(\begin{array}{c}
\left.m_{\mathrm{w}}\right)\left(c_{\mathrm{w}}\right)(\Delta \theta) \\
\\
=(0.05)(4180)(80)
\end{array}\right. \\
& +(0.05)(2300000) \\

## Worked Example 9

## Question

20 grams of ice at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is added to 80 grams of water in a copper calorimeter of mass 50 grams. The temperature of the calorimeter and water is $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Find the final temperature of the calorimeter and water, assuming that no heat is transferred to or from the surroundings and that all the ice melts.

## Solution

Let the final temperature of the water and calorimeter be $\theta^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Since no heat is transferred to or from the surroundings:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\binom{\text { heat lost }}{\text { by water }}+\binom{\text { heat lost by }}{\text { calorimeter }} & =\left(\begin{array}{l}
\text { heat needed to } \\
\text { melt ice at } 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\
\text { to water at } 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}
\end{array}\right)+\left(\begin{array}{c}
\text { heat needed to raise temp. } \\
\text { of melted ice from } 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\
\text { to final temp. } \theta^{\circ} \mathrm{C}
\end{array}\right) \\
m_{w} c_{w}(\text { temp. } \downarrow)+m_{\mathrm{c}} c_{\mathrm{c}}(\text { temp. } \downarrow) & =\quad m_{\text {ice }} l
\end{aligned}+\begin{gathered}
m_{\text {ice }} c_{w}(\text { temp. } \uparrow) \\
\Rightarrow(0.08)(4180)(25-\theta)+(0.05)(390)(25-\theta) \\
=(0.02)(330000)+\quad(0.02)(4180)(\theta-0) \\
\Rightarrow 8360-334.4 \theta+487.5-19.5 \theta \\
\Rightarrow \quad 6600+83.6 \theta \\
\Rightarrow 437.5 \theta \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2247.5 \\
\Rightarrow \text { final temperature } \theta \\
=5.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}
\end{gathered}
$$

## Student Experiment 14.2(A)

To determine: a) The latent heat of fusion of a quantity of ice ( $L$ )
b) The specific latent heat of fusion of ice (l) (Higher Level only)

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will add ice at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to a calorimeter of warm water and allow the ice to melt fully. The water in the calorimeter will be about $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ above room temperature, and you will add sufficient ice to bring the final temperature to about $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ below room temperature. Knowing the mass of the calorimeter, water and ice, as well as the temperature of the calorimeter before and after adding the ice, the latent heat of fusion of the ice and the specific latent heat of fusion of ice can be found.

## Equipment

Some ice cubes and a clean cloth, a thermometer ( $0-50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in steps of $0.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), a Bunsen burner, tripod and gauze, some insulating material (e.g. cotton wool or polystyrene beads), copper calorimeter, a beaker ( $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ ), a heavy object with which to crush the ice, a container to hold the calorimeter (e.g. a large beaker).

## Method

1. Crush the ice, place it in a beaker and leave it there for a few minutes until it is noticeably melting. The thermometer should then read $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, i.e. initial temperature of ice $=0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
2. Find the mass of the empty calorimeter $\boldsymbol{m}_{\mathrm{e}^{\cdot}}$.
3. Heat some water to about $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in a beaker using the Bunsen burner. Fill the calorimeter about $2 / 3$ full of this water. Find the combined mass of the calorimeter and the warm water $\boldsymbol{m}_{2}$.
4. Note the value of room temperature, then place the thermometer in the calorimeter of hot water, stirring it occasionally until its temperature is about $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ above room temperature.
5. Dry some of the crushed ice thoroughly with the cloth.
6. Place the calorimeter into the container of insulating material as shown in Figure 14.10, and measure the temperature of the water in the calorimeter $\theta_{1}$.
7. Add some of the dried ice to the water, and stir it with the thermometer until it melts. Keep adding further pieces of ice, and allow them to melt until the temperature of the water is about $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ below room temperature.
8. Record this temperature, i.e. the lowest temperature reached $\theta_{2}$.
9. Find the combined mass of the calorimeter, water and melted ice $m_{3}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-263.jpg?height=720&width=985&top_left_y=2168&top_left_x=1565)
Figure 14.10

10. Complete the other rows in Table 14.3.

| Mass of empty calorimeter | $m_{\mathrm{c}} \quad=$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mass of calorimeter and warm water | $m_{2} \quad=$ |
| Mass of calorimeter, water and melted ice | $m_{3} \quad=$ |
| Mass of water | $\left(m_{\mathrm{w}}=m_{2}-m_{\mathrm{c}}\right) \quad=$ |
| Mass of melted ice | $\left(m_{\text {ice }}=m_{3}-m_{2}\right)=$ |
| Temp. of water and calorimeter before ice is added | $\theta_{1} \quad=$ |
| Final temp. of calorimeter, water and melted ice | $\theta_{2}=$ |
| Fall in temperature | ( $\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}$ ) |

Table 14.3

## Calculations

a) On the assumption that no heat is given to or taken from the surroundings:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\binom{\text { heat lost }}{\text { by water }}+\binom{\text { heat lost by }}{\text { calorimeter }} & =\left(\begin{array}{l}
\text { heat needed to } \\
\text { melt ice at } 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\
\text { to water at } 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}
\end{array}\right)+\left(\begin{array}{c}
\text { heat needed to raise temperature } \\
\text { of melted ice from } 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { to } \\
\text { final temperature } \theta_{2}
\end{array}\right) \\
m_{w} c_{w}\left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)+m_{c} c_{c}\left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right) & =+\quad L \quad m_{\text {ice }} c_{w}\left(\theta_{2}-0\right) \\
\Rightarrow L & =\left(\left(m_{w} c_{w}+m_{c} c_{c}\right)\left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)-m_{\text {ice }} c_{w} \theta_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

By substituting the values for the variables on the right-hand side of this formula, the latent heat of fusion of ice $L$ can be found.
b) Dividing the calculated value of $L$ by the mass of the ice ( $m_{\mathrm{ice}}$ ) gives the specific latent heat of fusion of ice ( $l$ ).
i.e. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice $l=\frac{L}{m_{\text {ice }}}$

## Sources of error

1. Heat loss to the surroundings from the calorimeter and warm water is a systematic error in this experiment. Heat loss may be reduced by:
a) Insulating the calorimeter, which reduces losses by conduction
b) Polishing the calorimeter, which reduces losses by radiation
c) Placing a lid on the calorimeter, which reduces losses by conduction and convection

To further minimise errors due to heat loss to the surroundings, warm water is used in the calorimeter so that heat loss from the calorimeter when it is above room temperature is more or less compensated by heat entering the calorimeter when it is cooler than the surroundings.
The warm water also allows the ice to melt quickly and a larger mass of ice to be used; again reducing percentage errors in measuring its mass and in measuring the temperature change.
2. The calorimeter must not be allowed to reach more than 5 or $6^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ below room temperature. If it does, water vapour in the air may condense on it, giving errors in the final weighing.
3. The theory for the experiment assumes that only ice at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (and not water) is added to the calorimeter.

Therefore:
a) When you get ice from the freezer, it will be at a temperature below $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. You must allow it to reach $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ before adding it to the water. Check this with a thermometer.
b) The ice must be crushed so that it is at the same temperature throughout. A large lump could have its surface at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and its centre much cooler.
c) The ice must be dried before adding it to the calorimeter.
4. To minimise errors in measuring temperature, use a sensitive thermometer. One that reads in steps of $0.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is suitable. The thermometer should also have a small heat capacity so that it takes very little heat from the system.

## Questions

1. Why is the ice crushed?
2. Why is the ice allowed to start to melt?
3. Why is the ice dried before adding it to the water?
4. List three other precautions you would take to ensure an accurate result.

## Student Experiment 14.2(B)

To determine: a) The latent heat of vaporisation of some steam ( $L$ )
b) The specific latent heat of vaporisation of steam (l) (Higher Level only)

## Summary of method

In this experiment, you will pass steam into cold water in a copper calorimeter. There the steam will condense back into water. By measuring the rise in temperature produced and the mass of steam added, the latent heat of vaporisation $(L)$ of the steam and the specific latent heat of vaporisation $(l)$ of steam can be calculated.

WARNING! The steam emerging from the delivery tube is very hot and will scald you. Be careful not to knock the flask of boiling water or sit anywhere near it.

## Equipment

A hotplate, a flat-bottomed flask, a stopper and glass tubing, two retort stands and two clamps, a steam trap (if available), a copper calorimeter, a stirrer and insulating lid, insulating material, a container to hold the calorimeter and insulating material (e.g. a large beaker), a thermometer (0-50 ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in steps of $0.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )

## Method

1. Find the mass of the empty calorimeter $\boldsymbol{m}_{\mathrm{c}}$.
2. Fill the calorimeter about $3 / 4$ full of cold water (about $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ below room temperature).
3. Find the mass of the calorimeter and cold water $m_{1}$.
4. By subtraction, find the mass of the cold water $\boldsymbol{m}_{\mathbf{w}}$. Place the calorimeter in the container of insulating material.
5. Set up the round-bottomed flask as in Figure 14.11. Connect the steam trap to it. Fill the flask about $\frac{1}{3}$ with water and bring it to the boil. Adjust the hotplate so that steam is emerging from the trap at a steady rate. If no steam trap is available, insulate the delivery tube by surrounding it with cotton wool.
6. Note the temperature of the cold water in the calorimeter $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}$. Dry the exit tube from the steam trap with a cloth and place it deep into the cold water.
7. Leave it there until there is a rise in temperature of about $12^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ as shown on the thermometer. Turn off the hotplate, and remove the steam delivery tube from the calorimeter.
8. Stir the water in the calorimeter with the thermometer, and note and record the highest temperature reached $\theta_{2}$.
9. Find the combined mass of the calorimeter, water and condensed steam $\boldsymbol{m}_{2}$. Hence, by subtraction, find the mass of the condensed steam $\boldsymbol{m}_{s}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-265.jpg?height=1066&width=1577&top_left_y=2721&top_left_x=442)
Figure 14.11

## Calculations

a) On the assumption that no heat is given to or taken from the surroundings:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \binom{\text { heat gained }}{\text { by water }}+\binom{\text { heat gained by }}{\text { calorimeter }}=\left(\begin{array}{c}
\text { heat given out by } \\
\text { steam in turning } \\
\text { to water at } 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}
\end{array}\right)+\left(\begin{array}{c}
\text { heat lost by condensed } \\
\text { steam in cooling from } \\
100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \text { to final temperature }
\end{array}\right) \\
& \left.m_{\mathrm{w}} c_{\mathrm{w}}\left(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}\right)+m_{\mathrm{c}} c_{\mathrm{c}}\left(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}\right)=\begin{array}{c}
m_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{w}}\left(100-\theta_{2}\right)
\end{array}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The values of all the variables in this formula, except $L$ (the latent heat of vaporisation of the steam) are known, hence $L$ can be calculated (Table 14.4).

| Mass of empty calorimeter | $m_{\mathrm{c}} \quad=$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mass of calorimeter and cold water | $m_{1} \quad=$ |
| Mass of cold water | $m_{\mathrm{w}} \quad=$ |
| Temperature of cold water | $\theta_{1} \quad=$ |
| Final temperature of water and calorimeter | $\theta_{2} \quad=$ |
| Mass of calorimeter, water and steam | $m_{2} \quad=$ |
| Mass of condensed steam | $m_{\mathrm{s}}=m_{2}-m_{1}=$ |

Table 14.4

b) Dividing the calculated value of $L$ by the mass of the steam ( $m_{s}$ ) gives the specific latent heat of vaporisation of steam ( $l$ ).
i.e. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of steam $l=\frac{L}{m_{5}}$

## Sources of error

1. Heat loss to the surroundings when the calorimeter and water are above room temperature is a systematic error in this experiment. Heat loss may be reduced by:
a) Insulating the calorimeter, which reduces losses by conduction
b) Polishing the calorimeter, which reduces losses by radiation
c) Placing a lid on the calorimeter, which reduces losses by conduction and convection
2. To further minimise errors due to heat loss to the surroundings during the experiment, precool the water in the calorimeter with some ice to about $5{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ below room temperature before putting the steam into it. Allow the steam to raise the temperature to about $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ above room temperature. By doing this, heat energy flowing into the system at the start of the experiment will almost cancel heat leaving at the end of the experiment.
Pre-cooling the water also allows a greater mass of steam to be used, which reduces \% errors in measuring its mass. It also causes the steam to condense faster, again reducing heat loss.
3. The steam trap ensures that only steam and not water enters the calorimeter (preventing systematic error). If a trap is not available, the delivery tube must be insulated to prevent steam condensing in it, and sloped downwards towards the flat-bottomed flask.
4. To minimise errors in measuring temperature, use a sensitive thermometer. One that reads in steps of $0.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is suitable. The thermometer should also have a small heat capacity so that it takes very little heat from the system.
5. The water in the calorimeter is stirred during the experiment to ensure it is all at the same temperature and consequently the temperature read on the thermometer is correct.

## Questions

1. Why should the end of the delivery tube be dried before putting it into the calorimeter?
2. How would the accuracy of the experiment be affected if the rise in temperature were very large (e.g. $70^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )?
3. What would be the effect on the value of the final result if steam was seen to be leaving the calorimeter of water?
4. What is the function of the steam trap?
5. Why must the delivery tube be insulated if no steam trap is available?
6. How would the accuracy of the experiment be affected if only a very small rise in temperature were produced (e.g. $2^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )?
7. What is the advantage in cooling the water before adding the steam?

### 14.6 The heat pump

A heat pump transfers heat energy from a cooler region to a warmer one. Work must be done to bring this about. It is used in refrigerators and in air conditioning systems in buildings and cars. Figure 14.12 shows a simple diagram of a heat pump in a refrigerator. This makes use of the fact that a change in pressure can cause a change in state from liquid to gas, or gas to liquid.

A heat pump is a device that uses electricity to transfer heat from a cooler region to a warmer one.

- The circulating liquid has a high specific latent heat of vaporisation and a low boiling point.
- The liquid is pumped around a closed circuit.
- On reaching the expansion valve, pressure drops. The liquid vaporises and takes in its latent heat from the inside of the

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-267.jpg?height=805&width=1020&top_left_y=911&top_left_x=1725)
Figure 14.12 A heat pump in a refrigerator

fridge, thus cooling the fridge.

- When the vapour reaches the compressor, its pressure is increased and it turns back into a liquid, giving out its latent heat as it does so.
- This heat is given off to the surroundings from the black pipes and cooling fins at the back of the fridge.


### 14.7 Heat transfer

Heat can be transferred from one place to another by conduction, convection and radiation.

## Conduction

If one end of an object is at a higher temperature than the other, the molecules at the hotter end vibrate more than those at the cooler end. This molecular vibration is passed on from the hotter end to the cooler end. Thus, heat energy flows through the object.
Substances in which this occurs easily are called good thermal conductors, e.g. metals.
Substances in which it only occurs a little are called thermal insulators, e.g. wood.
Conduction is the movement of heat energy through a substance by the passing on of molecular vibration from molecule to molecule. There is no overall motion of the substance.

Figure 14.13 shows a simple experiment that compares the rates of heat conduction through different materials. Equal amounts of melted candle wax stick an identical coin to the end of each rod. The wax is allowed to solidify. Boiling water is then placed in the trough, and heat from it is conducted along each rod towards the coins.
The better the conductor, the less time it takes before the coin falls off.
Figure 14.14 shows a simple experiment to show that water is not a very good conductor of heat. The water at the top of the tube boils, but very little heat is

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-267.jpg?height=636&width=815&top_left_y=2229&top_left_x=1930)
Figure 14.13

conducted to the ice at the bottom and it does not melt.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-267.jpg?height=785&width=688&top_left_y=3005&top_left_x=2063)
Figure 14.14

## Radiation

The electrons at the surface of a substance vibrating with thermal energies emit electromagnetic waves. The higher the temperature, the shorter the wavelengths emitted. The waves travel at the speed of light, i.e. $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

Radiation is the transfer of heat energy from one place to another in the form of electromagnetic waves.

Note: Heat from the Sun is radiated heat.

The darker the colour of an object, the better it is at emitting heat energy as radiation. Figure 14.18 shows two cans; one is black, and the other is bright-coloured shiny metallic. Hot water at the same temperature is placed in each. The black can shows a quicker fall in temperature because heat energy radiates from it at a greater rate.
The darker can will also absorb heat radiation falling on it better than the shiny one. If both cans containing cold water are placed in direct sunlight

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-269.jpg?height=922&width=838&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1907)
Figure 14.18

(or radiated heat from a heater), the black can will show a greater rise in temperature because it absorbs radiation better.

## Energy efficiency

You already met the concept of energy efficiency on page 200. You saw how to calculate percentage efficiency, using the formula:

$$
\text { Percentage efficiency }=\frac{\text { useful power output }}{\text { power input }} \times 100
$$

In a building such as a domestic house, becoming more energy efficient means using less energy to perform the same task. In any activity or application that uses energy, the goal is to reduce energy consumption and minimise energy waste.

## The impact of insulation on energy consumption

If there is a temperature difference between two adjacent living spaces in a building, heat will flow from the hotter to the cooler space. For example, if a room is heated, heat will flow from it to unheated areas, such as an attic, unheated adjacent rooms, the ground and the outdoors. In the summer the reverse may be the case.
To maintain a higher temperature in any living space, heat must be provided to it at the same rate at which the heat is escaping to cooler regions.

Figure 14.19 shows typical energy losses from a house. Using insulation to reduce heat losses results in less energy being required to maintain the desired temperature.
Attic insulation, ceiling insulation, wall insulation and floor insulation, as well as double- or tripleglazed windows and doors, can dramatically reduce the heat loss from a building. This helps to make our energy use more efficient and sustainable.
You saw in Worked Example 10 and Exercise 14.5, Q4, that an uninsulated roof has a U-value of $2.5 \mathrm{~W} \mathrm{~m}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ and that insulating the roof to the recommended building regulations standard reduces the U -value to $0.18 \mathrm{~W} \mathrm{~m}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$. This reduces the heat loss through the roof by more than $90 \%$.

## Summary What I should know

- The heat capacity of an object is the heat energy needed to change its temperature by $1 \mathrm{~K}\left(1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$.
- The SI unit of heat capacity is the joule per kelvin (J $\left.\mathrm{K}^{-1}\right)$.
- The specific heat capacity (c) of a substance is the heat energy needed to change the temperature of 1 kilogram of that substance by 1 kelvin.
- The SI unit of specific heat capacity is the joule per kilogram per kelvin $\left(\mathrm{Kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right)$.
- The latent heat ( $L$ ) of a substance is the heat energy needed to change its state without a change in temperature.
- The SI unit of latent heat is the joule (J).
- The specific latent heat ( $l$ ) of a substance is the amount of heat energy needed to change the state of $\mathbf{1}$ kg of that substance without a change in temperature.
- The SI unit of specific latent heat is the joule per kilogram $\left(\mathrm{J} \mathrm{kg}^{-1}\right)$.
- The specific latent heat of fusion of a substance is the amount of heat energy needed to change $\mathbf{1}$ kg of that substance from a solid to a liquid without a change in temperature (i.e. at its melting point).
- The specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance is the amount of heat energy needed to change $\mathbf{1}$ kg of that substance from a liquid to a gas without a change in temperature (i.e. at its boiling point).
- The SI unit of specific latent heat of vaporisation and of fusion is the joule per kilogram ( $\mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ )
- A heat pump transfers heat energy from a cooler region to a warmer one.
- Conduction, convection and radiation are three means by which heat can be transferred from one place to another.
- Conduction is the movement of heat energy through a substance by the passing on of molecular vibration from molecule to molecule. There is no overall motion of the substance.
- Convection is the transfer of heat through a fluid by means of circulating currents of fluid caused by the heat.
- Radiation is the transfer of heat energy from one place to another in the form of electromagnetic waves.
- The U-value of a structure is the amount of heat energy conducted per second through $1 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ of that structure when a temperature difference of $1{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (i.e. 1 K ) is maintained between its ends.
- The Sl unit of U -value is the $\mathrm{W} \mathrm{m}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$.

# 15 Waves and Wave Motion

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the meaning of all the keywords for this chapter

- To ensure students can model wave motion and wave behaviour

### 15.1 Travelling waves

You may already know about different types of waves. Water waves (Figure 15.1), radio waves, waves on a string or rope, and seismic waves from earthquakes are all examples. You may also know that both light and sound travel as waves.

Waves play an important part in all branches of physics. The waves you will study in this course can be classified as either mechanical or electromagnetic.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-275.jpg?height=811&width=1590&top_left_y=2565&top_left_x=325)
Figure 15.1 Water waves are an example of a travelling mechanical wave.
