## Mechanical waves

Mechanical waves must have a substance (a solid, a liquid or a gas) to travel through. They cannot travel in a vacuum. The substance through which they travel is called a medium (plural: media). A mechanical wave passing through a medium is a vibration being passed on from molecule to molecule within that medium.
Examples of mechanical waves include water waves, waves on a rope, waves on a spring, and sound waves.

## Electromagnetic waves

Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum. They do not need a medium to travel through, though they can travel through various media. In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves travel at the incredibly fast speed of $3 \times 10^{8}$ metres per second. This speed is sometimes called the speed of light. In other media, their speed is always less.
Electromagnetic waves are also called electromagnetic radiation. Examples of electromagnetic waves include radio waves, microwaves, infra-red waves, visible light waves, ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays.

## Travelling waves

In the following examples, the waves move from one place to another.
They are, therefore, called travelling waves.

## Waves on a rope

In Figure 15.2, the hand moves one end of the rope up and down once. This causes a disturbance on the rope, which travels along the rope. You can try this at home or in the laboratory. The disturbance is called a wave (or more correctly a wave pulse). The same type of wave can also be formed on a spring (called a slinky) as in Figure 15.3.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-276.jpg?height=541&width=1202&top_left_y=1517&top_left_x=195)
Figure 15.2 A wave pulse travelling on a rope.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-276.jpg?height=548&width=1199&top_left_y=1513&top_left_x=1422)
Figure 15.3 A wave pulse travelling on a slinky.

## Waves on water

If you drop something into a calm pool of water, a disturbance is produced. The disturbance moves away from the point where the object entered the water. This moving disturbance is a water wave. Water waves are also caused by the action of wind on the water.

## Compression waves on a spring

Figure 15.4(A) shows a stretched slinky. If you hold several of the coils together, called a compression, and let them go, the compression begins to move along the spring (Figure 15.4(B), (C)). You can try this in the laboratory. After the compression passes a point on the spring, the coils in that part become more stretched apart than normal, creating a region called a rarefaction. The rarefaction follows the compression along the spring. This disturbance travelling along the spring is another type of travelling wave.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-276.jpg?height=1089&width=1290&top_left_y=2584&top_left_x=1331)
Figure 15.4 A compression wave on a spring.

### 15.2 Waves are a means of transferring energy from one place to another

When waves move along water, a rope or a slinky, there is no overall motion of the medium as the wave passes. Energy gets transferred through the medium, but as the wave pulse passes a point, the medium around that point is disturbed before returning to its original rest position. In other words, the rope itself does not move away from the hand, and the water does not move away from the point where the object falls into it.
If a small object is attached to the rope at some point ( $B$ in Figure 15.2), this object is at rest until the wave pulse reaches it. Thus, it has no kinetic energy. When the wave pulse passes $B$, the object gains kinetic energy and begins to move around its rest position. The same phenomenon can be seen in waves on water or springs.

## Electromagnetic waves

When an electromagnetic wave passes through a region of space, there is a rapidly changing electric and magnetic field in that region. In this way, energy gets transferred from one place to another by the wave. For example, heat and light energy from the Sun travel to Earth this way. The following is, therefore, true:

A travelling wave, either mechanical or electromagnetic, is a disturbance that travels out from the source producing it, transferring energy from the source to other places through which it passes, without transferring matter.

## Periodic travelling waves

If the hand in Figure 15.5 repeatedly and regularly moves the end of the rope up and down, a continuous series of identical wave pulses moves along the rope. Such a disturbance is called a periodic travelling wave.
In Figure 15.6, as the hand moves to the right, it forms a compression. This compression immediately moves out along the spring. As the hand then moves to the left, it forms a rarefaction. This also moves out along the spring. If the hand therefore continues to move back and forth, a series of evenly spaced compressions and rarefactions move out along the spring. This is also a periodic travelling wave.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-277.jpg?height=1163&width=1062&top_left_y=2715&top_left_x=325)
Figure 15.5

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-277.jpg?height=1759&width=916&top_left_y=1813&top_left_x=1484)
Figure 15.5

Figure 15.6

### 15.3 Transverse and longitudinal waves

Look at Figure 15.5 on the previous page. As the wave on the rope passes, the particles of the rope vibrate (or oscillate) up and down. In other words, they vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave is travelling. Such a wave is called a transverse wave.

A transverse wave is a wave where the direction of vibration is perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels.

Examples of transverse waves include:

- Waves on a rope
- Waves on a spring as in Figure 15.3
- Water waves

It can also be shown that all electromagnetic waves are transverse waves.
In the compression-rarefaction wave on the slinky (Figure 15.6), you can see that as the waves pass, the particles of the spring vibrate (oscillate) parallel to the direction in which the wave is travelling. Such a wave is called a longitudinal wave.

A longitudinal wave is a wave where the direction of vibration is parallel to the direction in which the wave travels.

Examples of longitudinal waves include:

- Compression waves on a spring
- Sound waves in a solid, liquid or a gas
- Ultrasonic waves


## Describing a transverse periodic travelling wave

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-278.jpg?height=552&width=1938&top_left_y=2050&top_left_x=195)
Figure 15.7 A periodic transverse wave.

In Figure 15.7:

- The top of a wave is called the crest of the wave. The bottom of a wave is called the trough.
- The maximum displacement of any particle from its rest position is called the amplitude (A). Thus the perpendicular distance from the crest (or trough) to the undisturbed position is the amplitude.
- The disturbance produced by one complete vibration of the source (one crest and one trough) is called an oscillation or a cycle.
- The distance from any point on one cycle to the corresponding point on the next cycle is called the wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of the wave. The distance from one crest to the next is therefore given by the wavelength, as is the distance from one trough to the next. Wavelength is measured in metres.
- The distance travelled by one wave cycle in one second is called the velocity $(\boldsymbol{v})$ of the wave. This is also the distance travelled in one second by a crest, a trough or any other point on a wave.
- The number of wave cycles passing any point per second is called the frequency (f). Frequency is measured in number of cycles per second. 1 cycle per second is called $\mathbf{1}$ hertz (Hz).
- The time period ( $\boldsymbol{T}$ ) is the time taken for one oscillation to pass. $T$ is measured in seconds.


## Energy carried by a wave

Suppose you have two identical ropes carrying waves of the same frequency, velocity and wavelength. Their amplitudes are different. Which wave is carrying the most energy?
As you might expect, it is the one with the greater amplitude. In fact, the energy carried by a wave is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude. This means that:

- If the amplitude is doubled, the energy is four times bigger.
- If the amplitude is made three times bigger, the energy is nine times bigger.
- If the amplitude is made four times bigger, the energy is sixteen times bigger,
- If the amplitude is halved, the energy is four times smaller.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-280.jpg?height=542&width=1043&top_left_y=302&top_left_x=1562)
Figure 15.9 The energy carried by a wave is directly proportional to the square of its amplitude.

... and so on
Energy carried by a wave $\propto$ (amplitude) ${ }^{2}$

### 15.4 The relationship $\nu=f \lambda$

Suppose a wave of wavelength $\lambda$ and frequency $f$ moves with a speed $v$.
Figure 15.7 shows such a wave at a particular instant. Consider the complete cycle that is shaded. If you start a clock as this cycle begins to pass, one second later $f$ cycles will have passed.
Each cycle has a length $\lambda$, therefore the first moves a distance $f \lambda$ in this second.
So, the speed of the waves is $f \lambda$; that is, $v=f \lambda$. The same argument applies to longitudinal waves.
If a periodic wave has frequency $f$, wavelength $\lambda$ and velocity $v$ then:

$$
v=f \lambda
$$

Note: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in a vacuum. This speed is called the speed of light and is usually denoted by $c$.

If an electromagnetic wave has frequency $f$, wavelength $\lambda$ and velocity $c$ then:

$$
c=f \lambda
$$

(F\&T, page 59)

## Worked Example 1

## Question

The frequency of a wave is 20 Hz .
a) How many full cycles pass a given point per second?
b) How long does it take one cycle to pass?

## Solution

a) $20 \mathrm{~Hz}=20$ cycles passing per second.
b) Time for one cycle to pass:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T & =\frac{1}{f} \\
& =\frac{1}{20} \\
& =0.05 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

If the wavelength of a sound wave emitted from a whistle is 4 m and the speed of sound in air is $340 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, find the frequency of the wave.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
v & =f \lambda \\
f & =\frac{v}{\lambda} \\
& =\frac{340}{4} \\
& =85 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

If the frequency of a radio station is 92.2 MHz and its wavelength is 3.254 metres, find the velocity of the radio waves.

## Solution

First convert MHz to Hz :

$$
\begin{aligned}
92.2 \mathrm{MHz} & =92.2 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~Hz} \\
v & =f \lambda \\
& =(92.2 \times 10.6)(3.254) \\
& =3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

The wavelength of visible light varies from $3.7 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ to $7.0 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$. Find the lowest frequency that an electromagnetic wave can have and still be in the visible range.

## Solution

Since $c=f \lambda$ it follows that $f$ is smallest when $\lambda$ is biggest. Therefore, the required frequency is the one corresponding to a wavelength of $7.0 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{\min } & =\frac{c}{\lambda_{\max }} \\
& =\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{7.0 \times 10^{-7}} \\
& =4.3 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A wave of amplitude 0.4 m carries energy at the rate of 3 joules per second. To what value should the amplitude be increased so that it carries 6 joules per second?

## Solution

When $E=3, A=0.4$
$E \propto A^{2} \Rightarrow E=k A^{2}$
Find the constant $k$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
3 & =k(0.4)^{2} \\
k & =\frac{3}{(0.4)^{2}} \\
& =18.75
\end{aligned}
$$

Use $k$ to find the new amplitude when $E=6$;

$$
\begin{aligned}
6 & =(18.75) A^{2} \\
A & =\sqrt{\frac{6}{18.75}} \\
& =0.57 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

Alternatively:
Since $E \propto A^{2}$, it follows that $A \propto \sqrt{E}$
So, if $E$ doubles to $2 E$, then $A$ is multiplied by $\sqrt{2}$ :

$$
(0.4) \sqrt{2}=0.57 \mathrm{~m}
$$

### 15.5 Wave behaviour

The different types of waves you meet in physics behave similarly when they interact with their environment. Different kinds of waves can undergo reflection, refraction, interference and diffraction. Transverse waves can also undergo polarisation.
By looking at each of these in turn, you can build up a model of wave behaviour. In Chapter 16 you will apply this model to sound. In Chapter 17 you will see that the geometrical optics model of light cannot fully explain many properties of light, and so the more sophisticated wave model is needed to do so.

## Reflection

When a wave meets an obstacle in its path, it bounces off that obstacle. This is called reflection.

> The bouncing of waves off of an obstacle in their path is called reflection of waves

Figure 15.10 shows a wave pulse on a rope being reflected from a wall to which it is tied. You can try this with a rope or a slinky. You will have also seen the reflection of water waves in the sea, a lake or in a sink, and reflection of water waves can easily be demonstrated with a ripple tank. The reflection of light waves from a mirror was discussed in Chapter 2.

## Longitudinal waves also undergo reflection. A

compression sent along a slinky that is fixed at one end will be reflected from the fixed end. You will see in Chapter 16 that an echo is a sound wave (a longitudinal wave) being reflected.
When a series of parallel waves, called plane waves, strike a flat obstacle, they are reflected at the same angle at which they strike the obstacle. So, in Figure 15.11, angles $A$ and $B$ are the same. In this figure, the blue parallel lines represent the crests of the waves, and they are known as wavefronts. Wavefronts can theoretically be any part of a wave (not just crests), as long as it is the exact same position on each cycle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-283.jpg?height=822&width=818&top_left_y=1868&top_left_x=1523)
Figure 15.10 A wave pulse on a rope being reflected from a fixed end.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-283.jpg?height=581&width=1199&top_left_y=3053&top_left_x=1139)
Figure 15.11

## Waves changing speed

The speed, $v$, at which a wave travels depends on the properties of the medium through which it travels. When waves travel from one medium to another, their speed generally changes on entering the second medium.
The frequency, $f$, of a wave depends on the source producing it. If a wave moves from one medium to another, or through regions of the same medium where its speed changes, its frequency remains the same.
Since $v=f \lambda$ and $f$ remains the same, it follows that:
The wavelength increases if the wave speeds up and the wavelength decreases if the waves slow down
(Figure 15.12, Figure 15.13 and Figure 15.14).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-284.jpg?height=503&width=1173&top_left_y=354&top_left_x=1429)
Figure 15.12 When the wave slows down, its frequency remains the same but its wavelength decreases.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-284.jpg?height=512&width=1075&top_left_y=1204&top_left_x=195)
Figure 15.13 The change in speed causes the waves to change direction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-284.jpg?height=512&width=610&top_left_y=1204&top_left_x=1308)
Figure 15.14 Refraction in a ripple tank.

## Refraction of waves

In Figure 15.13, the waves enter the second medium at an angle other than $90^{\circ}$. As the wave speed changes on entering this medium, the waves also change direction. This phenomenon is called refraction. Figure 15.14 shows the refraction of water waves in a ripple tank. The refraction of light waves is discussed in Chapter 3.

## Explanation of refraction

In Figure 15.13, point A on the wavefront meets the boundary with a slower medium before point $B$. One side of the wavefront therefore travels slower than the other until the other side also reaches the boundary, at the point labelled $\mathrm{B}_{1}$. By this time, the side that crossed the boundary first will have travelled less distance, and so the wavefront has turned as the distance $B$ to $B_{1}$ must be larger than the distance $A$ to $A_{1}$. The wave then continues perpendicular to $A_{1} B_{1}$

The changing of direction of a wave when it enters a region where its speed changes is called refraction.

## Diffraction

- Figure $15.15(\mathrm{~A})$ shows parallel water waves meeting a flat obstacle with a gap in it. The waves pass through the gap. At the other side of the gap, the waves spread out sideways slightly, but mostly the waves pass straight through.
- However, if the size of the gap is near in size to the wavelength $\lambda$ of the waves, the waves spread into the whole region beyond the gap (Figure 15.15(B)). This phenomenon is called diffraction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-284.jpg?height=776&width=890&top_left_y=3004&top_left_x=1331)
Figure 15.15

Diffraction can be easily observed in water waves in a ripple tank (Figure 15.16). Waves can also spread around an obstacle in their path, though the effect is only significant if the object is small relative to the wavelength of the wave.
You will see in Chapter 16 and Chapter 17 that, under the right conditions, diffraction occurs for both sound and light waves.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-285.jpg?height=480&width=1284&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=1461)
Figure 15.16 Diffraction of water waves in a ripple tank.

The sideways spreading of waves into the region beyond a gap or around an obstacle is called diffraction.

## Principle of superposition of waves

What happens when waves from two sources meet each other?
The waves from the two sources pass through each other and come out the other side unchanged. However, while the waves are overlapping, they combine to produce a new wave.
In this new wave, the displacement of any particle of the medium, at a given instant, is the algebraic sum of the displacements that each wave on its own would cause. This is known as the principle of superposition of waves.
This can be demonstrated in the lab with a slinky, as in Figure 15.17, which shows two pulses heading towards each other. At the instant the pulses are in the same place, a pulse with twice the height is produced, but then the pulses continue to move as they were.
In Figure 15.18, the pulses cancel out the instant they are in the same place, but after that, they continue to move on as they were before meeting.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-285.jpg?height=906&width=893&top_left_y=1904&top_left_x=325)
Figure 15.17

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-285.jpg?height=909&width=906&top_left_y=1901&top_left_x=1243)
Figure 15.18

When waves from two sources meet, a new wave is produced. The displacement produced at any point by this wave is the algebraic sum of the displacements that each wave would produce on its own. This is the principle of superposition of waves.

Consider two sources of water waves $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ (Figure 15.19) that have the same frequency and amplitude. Suppose that crests from $S_{1}$ and crests from $S_{2}$ arrive together at $X$. The troughs from each source will also arrive together. The waves arrive perfectly in step and are said to be in phase with each other
By the principle of superposition, a new wave is formed as shown in Figure 15.19. The amplitude of the resulting waves is bigger than the amplitude of each of the individual waves. The waves are said to undergo constructive interference.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-285.jpg?height=460&width=825&top_left_y=3288&top_left_x=1920)
Figure 15.19 Constructive interference

When waves from two sources meet and the amplitude of the resulting wave is greater than the amplitudes of each of the individual waves, the waves are said to undergo constructive interference.

Suppose the crests from one source arrive at X together with troughs from the other source. The waves arrive fully out of step and are said to be completely out of phase with each other. By the principle of superposition, a new wave is formed as in Figure 15.20. The waves completely cancel each other and the water between $X$ and $Y$ remains undisturbed. This phenomenon is called destructive interference. Waves are completely out of phase when one set is one half wavelength $\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)$ ahead of the other.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-286.jpg?height=300&width=831&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 15.20 Destructive interference.

When waves from two sources meet and the amplitude of the resulting wave is less than the amplitude of each of the individual waves, the waves are undergoing destructive interference.

Note: Waves of all types will undergo interference.
If two sources are emitting waves that are a definite fixed amount out of step with each other, there is said to be a constant phase difference between them.

Two sources of periodic waves are said to be coherent if they are in phase, or if there is a constant phase difference between waves from each of the sources.
If follows that the sources must also have the same frequency.

When waves from two (or more) coherent sources meet, the resulting wave pattern formed is called an interference pattern.

## Interference pattern from two point sources

A very important interference pattern occurs when waves of equal amplitude from two coherent point sources meet. This can be shown in the laboratory using a ripple tank and two vibrating dippers (Figure 15.21 and Figure 15.22). Here, two point sources $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are producing circular water waves. Suppose that the circles drawn represent crests from each source. Then, halfway between two consecutive crests from the same source is a trough.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-286.jpg?height=792&width=1102&top_left_y=2682&top_left_x=250)
Figure 15.21

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-286.jpg?height=831&width=873&top_left_y=2571&top_left_x=1416)
Figure 15.22 Interference from two point sources in a ripple tank. The regions of maximum disturbance and zero disturbance can be clearly seen.

## Constructive interference

Consider the situation along a line such as $C_{0}$ or $C_{1}$ (Figure 15.21). Along each of these lines, you can see that crests from one source always meet crests from the other.
Likewise, troughs from one source meet troughs from the other, resulting in constructive interference along these lines. Such lines are called antinodal lines.

## Destructive interference

Along the lines $D_{1}, D_{2}$, and so on. you can see that crests from one of the sources arrive together with troughs from the other. So destructive interference occurs. The water remains calm and undisturbed along these lines. Such lines are called nodal lines.
Between the nodal and antinodal lines, the waves still interfere. Near the nodal lines the interference is almost completely destructive, and as you move towards the antinodal lines, the amplitude of the resultant wave increases.
This kind of interference pattern also occurs for sound waves (page 290) and for light waves (page 308).

## Polarisation

Figure 15.7 (page 266) shows a transverse wave on a rope. The rope is vibrating up and down in a vertical plane. This wave is said to be vertically polarised. Figure 15.23 shows a horizontally polarised wave on a rope. The plane in which a transverse wave is vibrating is called its plane of polarisation.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-287.jpg?height=190&width=713&top_left_y=1435&top_left_x=1517)
Figure 15.23 A horizontally polarised wave.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-287.jpg?height=717&width=1831&top_left_y=1894&top_left_x=325)
Figure 15.24

In Figure 15.24, the end $A$ of the rope is moved back and forth in various planes to produce a series of wave pulses on the rope, vibrating in different planes: unpolarised waves travel between $A$ and the vertical slit at $X$.
At the slit, only the waves that are vibrating in a vertical plane pass through. So, at the other side of the slit, a vertically polarised wave is produced on the rope. These waves are said to be plane polarised (in the vertical plane). This can easily be demonstrated in the laboratory.
If this vertically polarised wave then meets another slit ( $Y$ ), it will fully pass through this slit only if the slit is vertical. If the slit is horizontal, the vertically polarised waves will not get through at all.

Note: Only transverse waves can be polarised.

If the vibrations of a transverse wave are confined to one plane only, that wave is said to be polarised.

You will study the polarisation of light on page 319.

### 15.6 Stationary waves

If a rope or a slinky is held fixed at one end and the other end is shaken up and down, there are certain frequencies at which the vibrations will look fixed in position and are not travelling along the rope (or the slinky). You can try this in the laboratory.

- Some points on the rope will be at rest. These points are called nodes (Figure 15.25)
- Other points will be vibrating with maximum amplitude. These points are called antinodes.
- Points between the nodes and the antinodes vibrate up and down with the amplitude decreasing as you move from an antinode to a node.
- The frequency of all vibrating particles is the same.
- Energy does not travel along the rope, but remains at the same position on it.

Such waves are called stationary waves or standing waves.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-288.jpg?height=428&width=1183&top_left_y=1184&top_left_x=195)
Figure 15.25

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-288.jpg?height=424&width=1202&top_left_y=1188&top_left_x=1419)
Figure 15.26 Stationary waves on a rubber band.

Figure 15.26 shows a thick rubber band attached to a vibration generator. With the frequency at about 50 Hz , and by varying the tension in the band, several stationary waves can be set up on it.

## How stationary waves occur

Stationary waves are formed when two periodic travelling waves of the same frequency and amplitude but travelling in opposite directions, meet. The two wave trains interfere, producing a stationary wave.
In Figure 15.26, the vibrating source produces a travelling wave that moves along the rubber band and is reflected from the fixed hand. The reflected wave and the original wave then interfere to produce the stationary wave.
Figure 15.27 shows how this happens. At each instant, the resultant of the two waves is found by the principle of superposition of waves.
In (A) and (E), crests from one travelling wave coincide with crests from the other. Likewise, troughs from each coincide, giving the resultant wave shown by the purple (lower) line.
In (B) and (D), the purple line again shows the resultant of the two waves.
In (C), crests from one wave coincide with troughs from the other. Destructive interference occurs at this instant.
By drawing the travelling waves at any instant and finding their resultant, the position of the stationary wave at that instant can be found. If you do this, you will see that a stationary wave with nodes and antinodes will result.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-288.jpg?height=565&width=1906&top_left_y=3183&top_left_x=263)
Figure 15.27 Two travelling waves of the same frequency and amplitude moving in opposite directions produce a stationary wave.

When two periodic travelling waves, of the same frequency and amplitude but moving in opposite directions meet, they interfere with each other.
The resulting wave formed is called a stationary wave or a standing wave.
There is no net transfer of energy through the medium

## Frequency and wavelength of a stationary wave

In a standing wave, the frequency of every vibrating particle in a stationary wave is the same.
The frequency of a stationary wave is the same as the frequency of the travelling wave producing it.
If $\lambda$ is the wavelength of travelling waves causing the stationary wave, then:

- The distance between 2 consecutive nodes $=\frac{\lambda}{2}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-289.jpg?height=382&width=1208&top_left_y=768&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 15.28

- The distance between 2 consecutive antinodes $=\frac{\lambda}{2}$
- The distance between an antinode and the next node $=\frac{\lambda}{4}$
(see Figure 15.28)


## Worked Example 6

## Question

Waves on a rope travel at a speed of $3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. When a stationary wave is set up on the rope, the distance between an antinode and the nearest node is 60 cm . What is the frequency of the wave?

## Solution

Distance between antinode and adjacent node $=\frac{\lambda}{4}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.6 & =\frac{\lambda}{4} \\
\lambda & =(0.6)(4) \\
& =2.4 \mathrm{~m} \\
v & =f \lambda \\
f & =\frac{v}{\lambda} \\
& =\frac{3}{2.4} \\
& =1.25 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 15.7 The Doppler effect

## Change in wavelength of waves from a moving source

Figure 15.29 shows a source of periodic circular water waves of frequency $f$. The source is not moving.
Let $c$ be the speed of the waves through the water and $\lambda$ their wavelength.
Figure 15.30 shows the same source moving to the right with a constant speed of $u \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-290.jpg?height=870&width=837&top_left_y=755&top_left_x=195)
Figure 15.29 Waves from a source that is not moving.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-290.jpg?height=867&width=951&top_left_y=755&top_left_x=1061)
Figure 15.30 Waves from a source moving to the right at speed $u \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

Look what happens ahead of the moving source:

- The crests are closer together than crests from the stationary source.
- This means the wavelength is less than the wavelength of waves from the stationary source.
- Since the speed of the waves is the same, it follows that, to a stationary observer (e.g. at A), the frequency of the waves from the approaching source must be greater than the frequency from the stationary source.
Behind the moving source, the opposite happens.
- The crests are further apart than crests from the stationary source.
- Therefore the wavelength is greater than the wavelength of the waves from the stationary source.
- Thus, the frequency is less than the frequency from the stationary source.
A change in observed frequency also occurs if the source is stationary and the observer moves away from or towards the source. In this case, the wavelength does not change, but the speed of the wave relative to the observer and hence the observed frequency does change. This change in frequency occurs for all kinds of waves and is called the Doppler effect.


## Christian Andreas Doppler

Christian Andreas Doppler
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-290.jpg?height=271&width=317&top_left_y=3125&top_left_x=1171)
(1803-1853) was an Austrian mathematician and physicist. In 1842 he published a paper where he first described the Doppler effect. He also studied and wrote about magnetism, electricity, light and astronomy.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-290.jpg?height=811&width=1088&top_left_y=2243&top_left_x=1530)
Figure 15.31 The change in wavelength for water waves in a ripple tank produced by a source moving to the right.

The apparent change in the frequency of waves due to the motion of the source or the observer is called the Doppler effect.
If a source emits waves of frequency $f$, the observed frequency $f^{\prime}$ will be:

- Greater than $f$ if the source moves towards the observer or the observer moves towards the source.
- Less than $f$ if the source moves away from the observer or the observer moves away from the source.


## Doppler effect for sound waves

The higher the frequency of a sound wave, the higher its pitch. Or in other words, high notes have high frequency and low notes have low frequency. If you have ever heard an ambulance go past with its siren on, you will have experienced the Doppler effect. When it passes, there is an abrupt decrease in its pitch. Another common example is in racing cars speeding past, and their engine sound changing pitch from high to low.
The Doppler effect can easily be demonstrated in the lab if an electronic buzzer is whirled in a horizontal or vertical circle. The pitch of the note from the buzzer is increased as it moves towards you and it is decreased as it moves away.

## The Doppler effect and electromagnetic waves

The Doppler effect also occurs for light waves and other electromagnetic waves. It can be used to determine the speeds at which stars or galaxies are moving towards or away from us. If a star is moving away from us, the wavelength of the light emitted from it will appear longer than light from a similar stationary source. The wavelength is thus shifted towards the red (red light has the longest wavelength). This is known as red shift. The wavelength of light from a source moving towards Earth is shifted towards the violet.

## Applications of the Doppler effect Medical applications

A Doppler ultrasound (or Doppler echocardiography) of the heart sends ultrasound waves, which are waves of inaudible high frequency sound, to your heart. The waves bounce off your heart and blood vessels. The returning sound waves (echoes) are picked up and turned into pictures showing blood flow through the arteries and the heart itself (Figure 15.32). Different colours represent different speeds,
Doppler ultrasound testing allows doctors to clearly see how blood flows through the heart and blood vessels, and to measure flow speeds. It also lets them see and measure obstructions in arteries and measure the degree of narrowing or leakage of heart valves.
Doppler ultrasound is the standard method used for monitoring fetal wellbeing (Figure 15.33). It is used in pregnancy to study blood circulation in

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-291.jpg?height=581&width=763&top_left_y=2190&top_left_x=1979)
Figure 15.32 Doppler ultrasound images of the heart

the baby, uterus and placenta, and to see how they're developing.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-291.jpg?height=867&width=1355&top_left_y=3008&top_left_x=322)
Figure 15.33 Fetal monitoring using Doppler ultrasound

## Weather applications

Doppler radar is a radar system that can detect different types of precipitation, the rotation of thunderstorm clouds, airborne debris, and wind strength and direction.
Doppler radars work by sending short pulses of microwaves towards moving targets like raindrops or snowflakes, then detecting returning signals that are reflected back to the radar antenna (Figure 15.34). The change in frequency from the moving targets is calculated.
By measuring this change, meteorologists and researchers can tell if the targets are moving towards or away from the radar and build up a picture of the weather systems.
The Doppler effect for microwaves is used by the Gardai to measure the speed of cars
(Figure 15.35). Radar guns based on microwaves have now been replaced by infrared laser speed guns. Both types rely on the Doppler effect to

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-292.jpg?height=525&width=848&top_left_y=690&top_left_x=1295)
Figure 15.35 A laser speed gun

calculate the speed of vehicles.

## Formula for the frequency of waves from a moving source

The observed frequency $f^{\prime}$ of the waves from a moving source of mechanical waves, as observed by a stationary observer, depends on:

- The actual frequency $f$ of the source
- The speed of the source $u$
- The speed of the waves in the medium $c$
- Whether the source is approaching or moving away

If the source is moving towards the observer, the observed frequency $f^{\prime}$ is given by:

$$
f^{\prime}=\frac{f c}{(c-u)}
$$

If the source is moving away from the observer, the observed frequency $f^{\prime}$ is given by:

$$
f^{\prime}=\frac{f c}{(c+u)}
$$

A combined formula showing both of the above formulae,

$$
\text { i.e. } \quad f^{\prime}=\frac{f c}{(c \pm u)}
$$

is given in F\&T, page 59.

For the following Worked Examples, assume that speed of sound in air $=340 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and speed of light $=3.00 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, unless otherwise stated.

## Worked Example 7

a) When the car is approaching:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{f c}{(c-u)} \\
& =\frac{(1000)(336)}{(336-30)} \\
& =1098 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) When the car is moving away:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{f c}{(c+w)} \\
& =\frac{(1000)(336)}{(336+30)} \\
& =918 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Question

A police car travelling at $30 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ passes a stationary observer. Its siren emits a note of frequency 1 kHz . If the velocity of sound is $336 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, what is the frequency heard by the observer when the car is:
a) Approaching the observer
b) Moving away from the observer

## Solution

Here: $u=30 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \quad c=336 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \quad f=1000 \mathrm{~Hz} \quad f^{\prime}=$ ?

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-292.jpg?height=577&width=447&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=2171)
Figure 15.34
Doppler radar image of the precipitation in a storm over Ireland (Source: Met Éireann)

Note: The increase in frequency ( 98 Hz ) when the source is approaching the observer is different from the decrease in frequency $(82 \mathrm{~Hz})$ when it is moving away.

## Worked Example 8

## Question

A train's whistle emits a continuous note of frequency 800 Hz as it approaches a person standing near the track. To the person, the frequency of the note appears to be 920 Hz . Find the speed of the train.

## Solution

$f=800 \mathrm{~Hz} \quad f^{\prime}=920 \mathrm{~Hz} \quad c=340 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \quad u=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime}=\frac{f c}{c-u} \Rightarrow 920=\frac{(800)(340)}{340-u} & \Rightarrow(920)(340-u)=272000 \\
\Rightarrow 312800-920 u & =272000 \\
\Rightarrow u & =44.35 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 9

## Question

A train, travelling at a constant velocity, emits a sound of constant frequency. An observer, standing at the side of the track, measures the frequency of the sound to be 1216 Hz as the train approaches and 960 Hz as the train moves away.
a) Find the speed at which the train was travelling.
b) Calculate frequency of the sound heard by the driver of the train.

## Solution

a) Let $f$ be the actual frequency of the sound emitted by the train. This is also the frequency heard by the driver of the train.
Let $u$ be the speed of the train. Then:
For approaching train:

$$
\begin{align*}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{f c}{c-u} \\
\Rightarrow 1216 & =\frac{340 f}{340-u} \\
\Rightarrow(1216)(340-u) & =340 f \tag{1}
\end{align*}
$$

For train moving away:

$$
\begin{align*}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{f c}{c+u} \\
\Rightarrow 960 & =\frac{340 f}{340+u} \\
\Rightarrow(960)(340+u) & =340 f \tag{2}
\end{align*}
$$

From these equations we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1216)(340-u) & =(960)(340+u) \\
\Rightarrow 413440-1216 u & =326400+960 u
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. speed of train $u=40 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$
b) Substituting this value for $u$ into equation (1) gives:

$$
(1216)(340-40)=340 f
$$

Solving this for $f$ gives:

$$
\text { frequency heard by the driver of the train } \begin{aligned}
=f & =1072.9 \mathrm{~Hz} \\
& =1073 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 10

## Question

A source emitting a sound wave of a certain frequency is approaching an observer. The frequency observed is $15 \%$ greater than the frequency of the sound wave emitted. Find the speed of the source.

## Solution

The observed frequency is 15\% greater than the emitted frequency, so the observed frequency is 1.15 times greater (since $100 \%+15 \%=115 \%$ or 1.15 )
$f^{\prime}=1.15 f$
Since the source is approaching, use $f^{\prime}=\frac{f c}{(c-u)}$ and solve for $u$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
1.15 f & =\frac{f(340)}{340-u} \\
1.15 & =\frac{(340)}{340-u} \\
1.15(340-u) & =340 \\
391-1.15 u & =340 \\
51 & =1.15 u \\
u & =\frac{51}{1.15} \\
& =44.3 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 11

## Question

A whistle emitting a note of 2 kHz is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 0.86 m at a constant speed (see Figure 15.36).
If the highest note heard by a person a large distance away is 2100 Hz , find:
a) The speed of the whistle
b) The lowest note heard by the observer

## Solution

a) The highest note occurs when the source is moving towards the observer (at point $A$ ).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-294.jpg?height=705&width=724&top_left_y=1998&top_left_x=1461)
Figure 15.36

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{f c}{(c-u)} \\
2100 & =\frac{(2000)(340)}{340-u} \\
2100(340-u) & =(2000)(340) \\
714000-2100 u & =680000 \\
714000-680000 & =2100 u \\
u & =\frac{714000-680000}{2100} \\
& =16.19 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) Lowest frequency occurs when source is moving away from observer at speed 16.19 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ (at point $B$ ).

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{f c}{(c+u)} \\
& =\frac{(2000)(340)}{340+16.19} \\
& =1909.1 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 12

## Question

The wavelength of the yellow line in the emission line spectrum of helium was measured in the laboratory as 587 nm . The same yellow line in the helium spectrum of a star has a measured wavelength of 592 nm .
a) What can you deduce about the motion of the star?
b) Calculate the speed of the moving star.

## Solution

a) The wavelength of the light from the star is different to the same light from a stationary source (the lab).
So, the frequency of the light from the star is different.
Therefore, by the Doppler effect, the star is moving.
Since the wavelength has increased, the frequency has decreased.
This means the star is moving away from the Earth.
b) Wavelength of yellow line from lab $=587 \mathrm{~nm}=587 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}$

Frequency of yellow line from lab:

$$
\begin{aligned}
c & =f \lambda \\
f & =\frac{c}{\lambda} \\
& =\frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{587 \times 10^{-9}} \\
& =5.11073 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

Frequency of yellow line in helium spectrum of star:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{592 \times 10^{-9}} \\
& =5.06757 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the frequency of the light from the star is less, the source (the star) is moving away:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime} & =\frac{f c}{(c+u)} \\
f^{\prime}(c+u) & =f c \\
f^{\prime} u & =f c-f^{\prime} c \\
u & =\frac{c\left(f-f^{\prime}\right)}{f^{\prime}} \\
& =\frac{\left(3.00 \times 10^{8}\right)\left(5.11073 \times 10^{14}-5.06757 \times 10^{14}\right)}{5.06757 \times 10^{14}} \\
& =2.5551 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the velocity of the star is $2.5551 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ away from the Earth

## Summary What I should know

- A travelling mechanical wave is a disturbance that carries energy through a medium without any overall motion of that medium.
- A travelling wave, either mechanical or electromagnetic, is a disturbance that travels out from the source producing it, transferring energy from the source to other places through which it passes, without transferring matter.
- A transverse wave is a wave where the direction of vibration is perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels.
- All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves.
- A longitudinal wave is a wave where the direction of vibration is parallel to the direction in which the wave travels.
- The SI unit of frequency is the hertz (Hz), where: 1 hertz = 1 cycle per second or $1 \mathrm{~Hz}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
Energy carried by a wave $\propto$ (amplitude) ${ }^{2}$.
- If a periodic wave has frequency $f$, wavelength $\lambda$ and velocity $v$, then: $v=f \lambda$
- Reflection of waves is the bouncing of waves off an obstacle in their path.
- Refraction is the changing of direction of a wave when it enters a region where its speed changes.
- Diffraction is the sideways spreading of waves into the region beyond a gap or around an obstacle.
- When waves from two sources meet, a new wave is produced. The displacement produced at any point by this wave is the algebraic sum of the displacements that each wave would produce on its own. This is called the principle of superposition of waves.
- Constructive interference occurs when waves from two sources meet and the amplitude of the resulting wave is greater than the amplitudes of each of the individual waves.
- Destructive interference occurs when waves from two sources meet and the amplitude of the resulting wave is less than the amplitude of each of the individual waves.
- Two sources of periodic waves are said to be coherent if they are in phase, or if there is a constant phase difference between waves from each of the sources. The sources must also have the same frequency.
- When waves from two (or more) coherent sources meet, the resulting wave pattern formed is called an interference pattern.
- If the vibrations of a transverse wave are confined to one plane only, that wave is said to be polarised.
- Polarisation can only occur for transverse waves.
- A stationary wave (a standing wave) occurs when two periodic travelling waves, of the same frequency and amplitude and moving in opposite directions, meet. When this happens, there is no net transfer of energy through the medium.
- The frequency of vibration of every vibrating particle in a stationary wave is the same.
- The frequency of a stationary wave is the same as the frequency of the travelling wave producing it.
- If $\lambda$ is the wavelength of travelling waves causing the stationary wave then:
- The distance between 2 consecutive nodes $=\frac{\lambda}{2}$
- The distance between 2 consecutive antinodes $=\frac{\lambda}{2}$
- The distance between an antinode and the next node $=\frac{\lambda}{4}$
- The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency of waves due to the motion of the source or the observer.
- If a source emits waves of frequency $f$, the observed frequency $f^{\prime}$ will be:
- Greater than $f$ if the source moves towards the observer or the observer moves towards the source
- Less than $f$ if the source moves away from the observer or the observer moves away from the source

### 16.1 Every source of sound is a vibrating object

## Vibrating objects

Figure 16.1 shows a ruler clamped to a bench. If the free end of the ruler is pulled down and released, it vibrates up

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-299.jpg?height=467&width=850&top_left_y=2317&top_left_x=1048)
Figure 16.1

and down. The motion from $A$ to $B$ and back again to $A$ is one cycle. The number of cycles per second is the frequency of the vibration. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz).
If you adjust the length of the ruler so that it vibrates with a frequency of 20 Hz or more, the ruler gives off an audible sound.
Every sound, no matter what its source, is produced by something that is vibrating. A string on a guitar or piano, the paper cone in a loud speaker, a tuning fork or your vocal cords (Figure 16.2) all produce sound when they are vibrating.
For the sound to be audible to humans, the frequency of vibration must be between 20 Hz and 20000 Hz .

## \subsection*{16.2 Sound travels as a mechanical wave <br> <br> 16.2 Sound travels as a mechanical wave}

The sound produced by a vibrating object travels away from that object as a mechanical wave. Evidence for this is that sound undergoes reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference. These are standard properties of all waves.

Figure 16.2 Human vocal cords

## Reflection of sound - echoes

Stand at least 20 m away from a large high wall or a large cliff face and clap your hands. You will hear an echo. The echo is sound reflected from the wall or cliff and returned to you. If you are close to the wall, you will hear the echo at almost the same time as the original sound. The further you are from the wall, the greater the time between the clap and the echo.

## Refraction of sound

The refraction of sound waves is responsible for the fact that sounds can be heard more clearly on a cold night or over water (which is cool) than on a hot day or over land. This is explained fully on page 291.

## Diffraction of sound

The fact that sound travels around corners is evidence that sound undergoes diffraction. When sound reaches an obstacle with a gap in it, such as a wall with an open door or window, it travels through the gap and then spreads into the region on the other side of the obstacle. The width of doorways and windows is near to that of the wavelength of sound, meaning the diffraction is significant and we can hear around corners.

## Interference of sound

In the next experiment, you will see that sound can undergo interference.
Only waves undergo interference, so this demonstration is strong evidence to support the mechanical wave nature of sound.

## Demonstration Experiment 16.1

To show the interference of sound and hence that sound travels as a wave.

- Set up the equipment shown in Figure 16.3 and turn on the signal generator.
- Walk slowly from A to B.
- You will hear the loudness of the sound increase and decrease regularly as you move from $A$ to B.
- This is because the sound from each source produces constructive and destructive interference between $A$ and $B$ (producing an interference pattern similar to that on page 274).
- Interference is evidence that sound is a wave.

### 16.3 How a vibrating object produces a sound wave

Figure 16.5 shows a simplified diagram of a sound wave being emitted from a vibrating prong of a tuning fork.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-301.jpg?height=889&width=1205&top_left_y=511&top_left_x=322)
Figure 16.5 A sound wave being emitted from a vibrating prong of a tuning fork.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-301.jpg?height=734&width=980&top_left_y=507&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 16.6 The sound wave is moving from left to right. The wavelength $\lambda=$ distance between centres of two adjacent compressions or between the centres of two adjacent rarefactions.

Between the fork and the listener's ear, the air consists of billions of gas molecules (and some individual atoms).
As the prong moves to the right, it pushes nearby molecules closer together, forming a compression, where the pressure and density of the air are slightly increased. This region of compression moves forward, compressing the molecules ahead of it. This process continues and the compression travels along the rest of the molecules away from the prong.
As the prong moves to the left, it pulls nearby molecules apart from each other, forming a rarefaction, where the pressure and density of the air are slightly decreased. This rarefaction also travels along the rest of the molecules, away from the prong.
As the prong continues to move left and right, a series of evenly-spaced compressions and rarefactions travel along the molecules away from the prong. The moving compressions and rarefactions cause the molecules in the air to vibrate as they pass.
When this vibration reaches the molecules next to the eardrum, the eardrum vibrates with the same frequency, and the listener hears a sound.
The frequency of the vibrating source and the frequency of the vibrating molecules are the same. Therefore, the frequency of a sound wave is the same as the frequency of the vibrating source producing it.

## Sound travels as a longitudinal wave

In Figure 16.5, the molecules vibrate parallel to the direction in which the compressions and rarefactions are travelling (i.e. parallel to the direction in which the wave is travelling). Therefore, a sound wave is a longitudinal wave.
As with other longitudinal waves (page 267), the wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of a sound wave is the distance between corresponding points on adjacent cycles. For example, $\lambda=$ distance between centres of two adjacent compressions (Figure 16.6).
The amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum displacement of any molecule from its rest position (Figure 16.7).

Sound travels as a longitudinal wave.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-301.jpg?height=610&width=994&top_left_y=2744&top_left_x=1754)
Figure 16.7 As a molecule vibrates between X and Y (as the wave passes), its maximum distance from its original rest position is the amplitude.

## A tuning fork also shows interference of sound

If a vibrating tuning fork is rotated near your ear, a louder sound will be heard in four positions and a much quieter sound will be heard in four others.
As the prongs move apart, a compression leaves the fork and moves along $O A$ and $O B$, while a rarefaction is produced between the prongs and moves along $O X$ and $O Y$ (Figure 16.8). As the prongs move towards each other the reverse happens.
In either case, compressions always arrive with rarefactions along each of the directions $O Z$ and destructive interference occurs. In other words, very little sound can be heard along $O Z$. Conversely, the sound is loud along $O A, O B, O X$ or $O Y$.
Since only waves undergo interference, this also shows that sound travels as a wave motion.

## Sound waves need a medium to travel through

Sound is the passing of a vibration from molecule to molecule, so it obviously needs a medium to travel through.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-302.jpg?height=799&width=743&top_left_y=292&top_left_x=1875)
Figure 16.8 As the prongs move apart, a region of compression leaves the fork and moves along $O A$ and $O B$, while a rarefaction is produced between the prongs and moves along $O X$ and $O Y$.

## Demonstration Experiment 16.2

To show that sound waves need a medium to travel through.

## Method

1. Set up the equipment in Figure 16.9, with the bell ringing.
2. As the air is removed from the bell jar with a vacuum pump, the sound becomes quieter and quieter until it is eventually barely audible. A small amount of sound can still be heard as vibrations escape through the supporting wires.
3. If the air is let back in, the sound can be heard again.

## Conclusion

- Sound waves need a medium to travel through.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-302.jpg?height=848&width=916&top_left_y=1881&top_left_x=1686)

### 16.4 The speed of sound

Usually sound travels slowest in gases, faster in liquids and fastest in solids. In general, the more dense the medium, the greater the speed, but as you can see from Table 16.1, not always. It also depends on the elastic properties (e.g. how compressible and how stiff the medium is). Diamond is less dense than copper or steel, but sound travels much faster in diamond, due to its very high stiffness.

| Material | Approximate Speed ( $\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ ) | Density ( $\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ ) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Dry air $\left(0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ | 331 | 1.28 |
| Water | 1500 | 1000 |
| Copper | 3400 | 8940 |
| Steel | 4800 | 7850 |
| Diamond | 12000 | 3500 |

Table 16.1 Speed of sound in some materials.

Also, in a gas, as the temperature increases, so does the speed of sound.

| Temperature $\left(0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ | Approximate Speed $\left(\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\right)$ |
| :---: | :---: |
| 0 | 331 |
| 20 | 344 |
| 100 | 384 |

Table 16.2 Speed of sound in air at various temperatures.
The fact that the speed of sound in a gas increases with temperature sometimes causes refraction, e.g. sounds can be heard more clearly on a cold night than on a warm day.
On a warm day, the air near the ground is warmer than the air higher up, so sound travels faster near the ground. This causes it to be refracted upwards (Figure 16.10(A)).
At night, the air near the ground is colder and the sound is refracted down (Figure 16.10(B)), so it appears to travel better over the ground.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-303.jpg?height=570&width=2305&top_left_y=1273&top_left_x=389)
Figure 16.10

### 16.5 Characteristics of sounds

Two characteristics of a sound are its loudness and its pitch.
The loudness of a sound depends on the amount of sound energy entering your ear per second. The greater the amplitude of a sound wave, the greater the energy it carries. So, the loudness of a sound depends on the amplitude of the sound wave.

The loudness of a sound wave depends on the amplitude of the sound wave. The greater the amplitude the greater the loudness.

You can think about the pitch of a sound in terms of musical notes. A high note is said to have high pitch, and a low note is said to have low pitch.
The pitch of a sound depends on the frequency of the sound wave. To see this, vibrate a number of tuning forks and place them in order of increasing pitch. Then, check the frequency written on each fork. You will see that a higher frequency corresponds with a higher pitch.

The pitch of a sound depends on the frequency of the sound wave. The higher the frequency the higher the pitch, and the lower the frequency the lower the pitch.

## Demonstration Experiment 16.3

To relate the pitch and loudness of a sound to their wave characteristics using observation

## Part 1. Pitch

1. Connect a microphone to an oscilloscope (Figure 16.11).
2. Sound the tuning fork of lowest pitch and observe the trace on the oscilloscope.
3. Repeat this with other tuning forks of higher pitch and observe the trace on the oscilloscope.

Result: You will see that as the pitch increases, so does the frequency.

## Conclusion

This shows that the pitch of the sound is related to the wave property frequency and that a higher frequency corresponds with a higher pitch.

## Part 2. Loudness

1. Tap one of the tuning forks gently so that it produces a quiet sound. Observe the trace on the oscilloscope.
2. Tap the same tuning fork more vigorously, producing a louder sound. Observe the trace on the oscilloscope.
3. Repeat this for progressively louder sounds.

Result: You will find that the louder the sound, the greater the amplitude of the trace on the oscilloscope.

## Conclusion

This shows that the loudness of the sound is related to the wave property amplitude and that a greater amplitude corresponds with a louder sound. This can be repeated with different frequencies and the result for the amplitude will still hold.

### 16.6 Frequency limits of audibility and ultrasound

For a sound wave to be audible to humans, its frequency must be between 20 Hz and 20000 Hz . These values are known as the frequency limits of audibility. However, the upper frequency limit decreases with age, and most adults cannot hear frequencies of 20000 Hz .

The frequency limits of audibility are the highest and lowest frequencies that can be heard by a normal human ear. The range is $\mathbf{2 0 ~ H z - 2 0 0 0 0 ~ H z}$.

Frequencies above 20000 Hz are called ultrasonic and are inaudible to humans. However, dogs and bats can hear sounds of frequencies up to about 35000 Hz , and some dog whistles operate at a frequency above 20000 Hz .

## Uses of ultrasound in medical and technological contexts

Ultrasound is a very important tool in medicine. It can be used to diagnose issues or used as a therapy for certain conditions.
Diagnostic ultrasound can be used to produce images of internal features of the human body, such as organs, other structures or fetuses (Figure 16.13). Also, Doppler ultrasound uses the Doppler effect to provide information about moving parts or liquids, for example the velocity of blood flow.
Ultrasound can be used therapeutically for many issues such as pains, sprains and musculoskeletal conditions. Very high frequency ultrasound can be used to dissolve blood clots or heat up tissue and stop it performing a function that it shouldn't be performing (ultrasound ablation). The

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-305.jpg?height=665&width=1082&top_left_y=2373&top_left_x=1660)
Figure 16.13 Diagnostic ultrasound of a fetus

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-305.jpg?height=584&width=955&top_left_y=3164&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 16.14 Ultrasonic cleaners used for cleaning dental equipment.

advantages of ultrasound in all medical applications is the fact that it is non-invasive and non-ionising (unlike X-rays).
In the world of manufacturing and industry, ultrasound can be used as:

- A non-contact sensor
- Motion sensors and flow measurement sensors
- Non-destructive testing, to test for cracks and flaws in welded materials
Ultrasonic cleaners can be used for cleaning objects such as jewellery, watches, dental equipment (Figure 16.14), surgical equipment and industrial parts. The ultrasound creates cavitation bubbles near the dirty surface, which form tiny shockwaves that clean the surface.


### 16.7 Resonance

## Natural frequency

Objects tend to vibrate at certain frequencies, and there is usually one frequency they are more likely to vibrate at than the others. This frequency is the object's natural frequency of vibration.
Figure 16.15 shows a person sitting on a swing. If given a push and released, the swing will vibrate forwards and backwards with its own natural frequency.
If the person on the swing is pushed every time it is about to move away, the size of the swings will increase. When this happens, the natural frequency of the swing and the frequency of the applied force (the driving frequency) are the same. This is an example of resonance.

If the frequency of a periodic force applied to a body (the driving frequency) is the same as or very near to its

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-306.jpg?height=837&width=1091&top_left_y=462&top_left_x=1530)
Figure 16.15

natural frequency, then the body will vibrate with a very large amplitude. This phenomenon is called resonance.

Resonance will only occur if the frequency of the driving force is the same as (or very near to) the natural frequency of vibration of the object. When this happens, the amplitude of the vibration can get very large.
If the frequency of the driving force is not the same as or not near to the natural frequency, the amount of vibrational kinetic energy picked up by the object is small. In the swing example, a push at the wrong time will result in much less energy transferred, and the size of the swings will not increase as much or could even decrease.

## Demonstration Experiment 16.4

## To show resonance

## Method

1. Strike a tuning fork to set it vibrating.
2. Hold this tuning fork near, but not touching, another tuning fork of the same frequency.
3. The second tuning fork will start vibrating and can be heard even if you stop the first fork from vibrating.
4. Repeat with two forks of different frequencies and the effect is much less noticeable.

## Conclusion

- The first tuning fork exerts a periodic driving force on the second tuning fork. The second fork only vibrates with large amplitude if its frequency is the same as or very near to that of the first. This demonstrates resonance.


## Other examples of resonance in real life situations

- If several pendulums are set up as in Figure 16.16 (known as Barton's pendulums) and pendulum 1 is set vibrating, the other pendulums will gain some vibrational energy. However, pendulum 2 (which has the same length and hence the same natural frequency as pendulum 1) starts to swing violently as pendulum 1 slows down. If left swinging, the energy goes from pendulum 1 to 2 and back to 1 again. When swinging, pendulum 1 causes periodic forces in the string which are the same as the natural frequency of pendulum 2 and so resonance occurs.
- Some drinking glasses have natural frequencies that are the same as some high-pitched notes. Opera singers singing high-pitched notes have been known to shatter glasses due to resonance (Figure 16.17).

The fixed ends of the string are nodes since these cannot undergo any displacement.
If the string is plucked at its centre, an antinode is formed there and the string vibrates as shown in Figure 16.20.
The frequency at which this string is vibrating is called its fundamental frequency $f$. The vibrating string causes a sound wave of the same frequency $f$ in the surrounding air.

A string vibrating with an antinode at its centre and a node at each end (and no other nodes or antinodes) is vibrating at its fundamental frequency.

If the same string is held lightly at its centre and bowed a quarter of the way along its length, it will vibrate as shown in Figure 16.21. Other modes of vibration can also occur (for example Figure 16.22) by bowing or plucking at different positions.
In general, when a string is plucked or bowed, it vibrates with some or all of these modes of vibration together. The amplitude of the fundamental mode is usually greatest with the other modes having lesser amplitudes. The sound you hear from the string will have a pitch corresponding to its fundamental frequency.
If a note of the same pitch (and frequency) is produced by two different stretched strings, the notes may not sound exactly the same. We say they have different quality. The quality of a musical note depends on the number and the amplitudes of the other modes of vibration present.

## Worked Example 1

A stretched string of length 80 cm is vibrating at its fundamental frequency of vibration. The speed of sound in the string is $400 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ? What is the frequency of vibration of the string?
Solution:
length of string = distance between two adjacent nodes

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.8 & =\frac{\lambda}{2} \\
\lambda & =(0.8)(2) \\
& =1.6 \mathrm{~m} \\
c & =f \lambda \\
f & =\frac{c}{\lambda} \\
& =\frac{400}{1.6} \\
& =250 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Harmonics

Figure 16.24 shows different stationary waves on a string of fixed length. Remember that the distance between two adjacent nodes is half a wavelength.
The wavelength of the standing wave in Figure 16.24(B) is therefore half of the wavelength of that in Figure 16.24(A).
Its frequency is therefore twice that in Figure 16.24(A).
The wavelength of the standing wave in Figure 16.24(C) is one third of the wavelength in Figure 16.24(A), so its frequency is three times that in Figure 16.24(A).

Frequencies that are multiples of a certain frequency $f$ are called harmonics.
$f$ is the fundamental frequency or the first harmonic.
$2 f$ is the second harmonic.
$3 f$ is the third harmonic, and so on.

| (A) A string vibrating at its first harmonic; that is, at its fundamental frequency $f$ | (B) The same string vibrating at its second harmonic; that is, at a frequency $2 f$ | (C) The same string vibrating at its third harmonic; that is, at a frequency $3 f$ |

## Factors that determine the fundamental frequency of a stretched string

Experimentally it is found that the greater the length of the string, the lower its fundamental frequency. More precisely, it is found that:

The fundamental frequency of a string is inversely proportional to its length, i.e.

$$
f \propto \frac{1}{l}
$$

This means that, for example, doubling the length causes its frequency to halve, tripling the length causes its frequency to become three times smaller and halving the length causes its frequency to double.

In string musical instruments, such as the violin or the guitar, the frequency of the note emitted can be varied by changing the length of the vibrating string: long strings give low notes and short strings give high notes (Figure 16.25).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-310.jpg?height=871&width=1121&top_left_y=481&top_left_x=195)
Figure 16.25 String section of an orchestra.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-310.jpg?height=805&width=867&top_left_y=488&top_left_x=1344)
Figure 16.26 Graph of frequency vs length of string

Experimentally it is also found that the higher the tension, $T$, of the string, the higher the fundamental frequency. More precisely it is found that

The fundamental frequency of string is directly proportional to the square root of its tension, i.e.

$$
f \propto \sqrt{T}
$$

This means that, for example, increasing the tension by 4 times causes its frequency to double, doubling the tension causes its frequency to be $\sqrt{2}$ times bigger and halving the tension causes its frequency to be $\sqrt{2}$ times smaller.
Experimentally it is found that the greater its mass per unit length (i.e. its linear density) $\mu$, the lower its fundamental frequency. More precisely:

The fundamental frequency of a string is inversely proportional to the square root of its mass per unit length (linear density), that is:

$$
f \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}
$$

This means that, for example, doubling the mass per unit length causes its frequency to be $\sqrt{2}$ times smaller and making the mass per unit length 4 times bigger causes its frequency to halve.

If $T$ is the tension in the string, $\mu$ is its mass per unit length, $l$ its length and if $f$ is its fundamental frequency of vibration, then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f \propto \frac{1}{l} & T \\
f \propto \sqrt{T} & l \\
f & \text { and } \mu \text { fixed } \mu \text { fixed } \\
f \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}} & T \\
\text { and } & l \text { fixed }
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-310.jpg?height=785&width=887&top_left_y=1504&top_left_x=1731)
Figure 16.27 Graph showing frequency vs tension

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-310.jpg?height=812&width=886&top_left_y=2464&top_left_x=1735)
Figure 16.28 Graph of fundamental frequency vs mass per unit length

| Quantity | Unit |
| :---: | :---: |
| length $l$ | metre (m) |
| tension $T$ | newton (N) |
| mass per unit length $\mu$ | kilogram per metre $\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-1}\right)$ |

It follows that:

$$
f \propto \frac{1}{l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \Rightarrow f=\frac{k}{l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \quad \text { where } k \text { is a constant. }
$$

It can be proved that $k=\frac{1}{2}$ (you do not need to know the proof), so:
The fundamental frequency $f$ of a stretched string is given by:

$$
f=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
$$

(F\&T, page 59)

## Worked Example 2

A wire of length 3 m and mass 0.6 kg is stretched between two points so that the tension in the wire is 200 N . Calculate its fundamental frequency of vibration.

## Solution

$l=3 \mathrm{~m}$; mass $=0.6 \mathrm{~kg} ; T=200 \mathrm{~N} ; f=$ ?
First calculate $\mu$, the mass per unit length of the wire:

$$
\mu=\frac{\text { mass }}{\text { length }}=\frac{0.6}{3}=0.2 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}
$$

All variables, except $f$, in the formula $f=\frac{1}{2 i} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ are now known. So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f & =\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \\
& =\frac{1}{(2)(3)} \sqrt{\frac{200}{0.2}} \\
& =5.27 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

a) If the length of a stretched string is doubled, with the tension remaining constant, how does the fundamental frequency of vibration change?
b) If the tension $T$ of a stretched string of fundamental frequency $f$ is increased to $9 T$, what is the new fundamental frequency?

## Solution

a) $f \propto \frac{1}{l}$, so if the length is doubled, the frequency is halved.
b) $f \propto \sqrt{T} \quad \Rightarrow f=k \sqrt{T}, \quad f_{\text {new }}=k \sqrt{T_{\text {new }}}$

$$
\text { i.e. } \begin{aligned}
f_{\text {new }} & =k \sqrt{9 T} \\
& =3 k \sqrt{T} \\
& =3 f
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. the new fundamental frequency is $3 f$.
OR
The tension becomes 9 times bigger, so the square root of the tension becomes $\sqrt{9}=3$ times bigger.
Since $f \propto \sqrt{T}$, the frequency also becomes 3 times bigger, i.e. the new fundamental frequency is $3 f$.

## Worked Example 4

What effect does increasing the tension of a stretched string from 16 N to 49 N have on the frequency of the string?

## Solution

$\sqrt{16}=4$ and $\sqrt{49}=7$, so the square root of the tension has increased by a factor of $\frac{7}{4}$.
The frequency is directly proportional to the square root of the tension. Therefore, the frequency also increases by a factor of $\frac{7}{4}$.
Or:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f \propto \sqrt{T} \Rightarrow f & =k \sqrt{T} \\
f_{\text {old }} & =k \sqrt{16} \\
& =4 k \\
k & =\frac{f_{\text {old }}}{4} \\
f_{\text {new }} & =k \sqrt{49} \\
& =7 k \\
k & =7\left(\frac{f_{\text {old }}}{4}\right) \\
& =\frac{7}{4} f_{\text {old }}
\end{aligned}
$$

That is, the frequency increases by a factor of $\frac{7}{4}$.

## Worked Example 5

By expressing the units of each side of the equation $f=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ in base units, show that the equation is dimensionally correct.

## Solution

## LHS:

Unit of $f=\mathrm{Hz}=\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

RHS:
Unit of $l=\mathrm{m}$
Unit of $T=\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-2}$
Unit of $\mu=\mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}=\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Unit of } \mathrm{RHS} & =\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{~m}}\right) \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{kgm} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}}{\mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}}} \\
& =\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{~m}}\right) \sqrt{\mathrm{ms}^{-2} \mathrm{~m}} \\
& =\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{~m}}\right) \sqrt{\mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}} \\
& =\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{~m}}\right)\left(\mathrm{ms}^{-1}\right) \\
& =\mathrm{s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

(1) = (2), so both sides have the same dimensions.

### 16.9 The sonometer

A sonometer consists of a wooden sounding board with a wire stretched between two movable bridges (Figure 16.29). The wire is fixed at one end and the tension in the wire is adjusted by means of a winder. The size of the tension is read on a newton balance. In another type, the tension is produced by hanging masses and the tension is the weight of the hanging masses.

## Measuring the frequency of vibration of the wire on a sonometer

To measure the frequency of vibration of the wire, pluck the wire and strike a tuning fork. Adjust the length or tension of the wire until it sounds to be near to or at the same pitch as the tuning fork. Then place a small piece of paper on the centre of the wire. Place the stem of the vibrating tuning fork on one of the bridges. If they are at the same frequency, resonance will occur, and the wire will start vibrating. The wire will then have an antinode at its centre and the small paper rider will be agitated and jump off

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-314.jpg?height=616&width=1264&top_left_y=325&top_left_x=1354)
Figure 16.29 A sonometer.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-314.jpg?height=580&width=1267&top_left_y=1100&top_left_x=1354)
Figure 16.30 lis the distance from the top of one bridge to the top of the other.

the wire (Figure 16.30). Vary the length or the tension until this occurs. The frequency of the wire is then the same as the frequency of the tuning fork, which is usually written on the fork.

## Student Experiment 16.1

To verify the model: $f=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ for a particular stretched string

## Summary of method

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-314.jpg?height=382&width=301&top_left_y=2018&top_left_x=1855)

In this experiment, you will measure the length $l$ of the wire on a sonometer and its tension $T$ when it vibrates at the same frequency as a tuning fork of known frequency $f$. If the mass per unit length, $\mu$, of the wire is not already known, you will also have to measure its value. Finally, to verify the model, you will substitute these values into the formula $f=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$. You will find that they satisfy the formula.
You may repeat the experiment using different tuning forks and the same wire, but at different lengths and tensions.

## Equipment needed

A set of tuning forks of known frequencies, a sonometer (with a newton balance), a metre stick, a weighing scale.

## Method

1. By moving the bridges on the sonometer, make the wire as long as possible.
2. Strike the tuning fork of lowest frequency, $f$, on a wooden block and place its stem on one of the bridges.
3. Adjust the tension in the wire until it resonates with the tuning fork. Resonance occurs when the paper rider jumps off the wire when the tuning fork is vibrating. It may take a little practice to find this.
4. Measure the length, $l$, of the wire between the tops of the two bridges with the metre stick.
5. Measure the tension, $T$, in the wire using the newton balance.
6. Record these values and the frequency of the tuning fork in the table.
7. Repeat steps 2 to 6 with tuning forks of progressively higher frequencies. You may need to shorten the length of the string to get resonance with the higher frequency tuning forks.
8. If the mass per unit length, $\mu$, of the wire is not already known, it must be measured as follows. Carefully remove the wire from the sonometer and measure its mass and its total length.

$$
\mu=\frac{\text { total mass of wire }}{\text { total length of wire }}
$$

Record this value.
9. Substitute the values for $l, T$ and $\mu$ into the expression: $\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, and evaluate the expression.

## Result

The value of $\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ should be equal to the value of $f$ on the tuning fork in each case. This verifies that $f=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ models the stretched string very well.

| Frequency <br> $f(\mathrm{~Hz})$ | Length <br> $l(\mathrm{~m})$ | $T(\mathrm{~N})$ | $\mu\left(\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^{-1}\right)$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
|  |  |  |  |

## Sources of error:

1. Random errors occur when using the metre stick to measure the length of the string. Avoid the error of parallax to reduce these.
2. Ensure no systematic error occurs when using the newton balance, i.e. ensure that the newton balance reads zero when no tension is applied to it. Also avoid the error of parallax.
