## Summary What I should know

- Sound travels as a mechanical wave.
- The frequency of a sound wave is the same as that of the vibrating source producing it.
- A sound wave is a longitudinal wave.
- Sound needs a medium to travel through.
- The speed of sound is different in different materials. In a gas the speed increases as the temperature does.
- The loudness of a sound wave depends on the amplitude of the sound wave. The greater the amplitude, the louder the sound.
- The pitch of a sound depends on the frequency of the sound wave. The higher the frequency, the higher the pitch. The lower the frequency, the lower the pitch.
- For a sound to be audible, the frequency of vibration must be between 20 Hz and 20000 Hz .
- Sounds with frequencies above 20000 Hz are called ultrasonic or ultrasound.
- If the frequency of a periodic force applied to a body (the driving frequency) is the same as or very near to its natural frequency, the body will vibrate with a very large amplitude. This phenomenon is called resonance.
- A string vibrating with an antinode at its centre and a node at each end (and no other nodes or antinodes) is vibrating at its fundamental frequency.
- Frequencies that are multiples of a certain frequency $f$ are called harmonics.
- If $f$ is the fundamental frequency or first harmonic, $2 f$ is the second harmonic, $3 f$ is the third harmonic, and so on.
- The fundamental frequency of string is inversely proportional to its length, i.e. $f \propto \frac{1}{l}$
- The fundamental frequency of string is directly proportional to the square root of its tension, i.e. $f \propto \sqrt{T}$
- The fundamental frequency of string is inversely proportional to its mass per unit length, i.e. $f \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}$

# 17 The Wave Nature of Light

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the wave properties of light
- To ensure students can demonstrate the wave nature of light
- To ensure students understand the relationship between the wavelength of light and its colour
- To ensure students understand the behaviour of a diffraction grating
- To ensure students can determine the wavelength of light in the laboratory
- To ensure students appreciate how the polarisation of light is evidence that light travels as a transverse wave
- To ensure students can explain how and why a prism and a diffraction grating can cause dispersion of light
- To ensure students can categorise electromagnetic waves by their wavelength, frequency, ionising ability and everyday use
- To ensure students understand the impact of solar irradiance on life on Earth


### 17.1 The wave nature of light

You saw in Chapters 2, 3 and 4 that the geometrical optics model of light (the ray model of light) is a very useful model in optics. However, like any model, its assumptions are approximations and can become invalid in certain circumstances. In this chapter, you will see that a more sophisticated model is needed to explain the behaviour of light when it passes through a very narrow gap. This model of light is known as the wave model of light.
In Chapter 15, you saw that when waves meet an obstacle with a gap approximately the same size as the wavelength of the wave, diffraction occurs. This diffraction becomes more pronounced as the width of the gap decreases (Figure 17.1)
The Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens (1629-95) first proposed that light travels as a wave. At the time, others - in particular, Isaac Newton - considered light to be a stream of very fast-moving particles. This view predominated, even though Newton was aware that light could undergo diffraction.

- Wave model of light

Figure 17.5 Young's experiment using the telescope of a spectrometer

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-321.jpg?height=717&width=1147&top_left_y=319&top_left_x=1549)
Figure 17.6 How the interference pattern is produced

## Explanation

- In Figure 17.6, light from $M$ shines onto the first narrow slit. The light undergoes diffraction here because the width of the slit is approximately the same size as the wavelength of the light.
- The diffracted light then illuminates the pair of slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$. These two slits are known as Young's slits and their width is also approximately the same size as the wavelength of the light.
- Diffraction occurs at each of the Young's slits and the diffracted waves overlap, producing an interference pattern.
- The light passing through $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ originates from one source, so is coherent and the resulting interference pattern is similar to that shown on page 274.
- Since the sources are line sources, the interference pattern consists of a series of parallel bright and dark lines, known as interference fringes.
- In 1801, Young used the results of this experiment to estimate that the wavelength of light was in the region of $10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$.

Two sources of waves are said to be coherent if they are in phase, or if there is a constant phase difference between waves from each of the sources. This means the sources must also have the same frequency.
When waves from two (or more) coherent sources meet, the resulting wave pattern formed is called an interference pattern.

If $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ were not coherent sources, there would not be an interference pattern.

## Conclusion

The fact that light undergoes interference indicates that light travels as a wave.

## Young's experiment using a laser

Young's experiment may be demonstrated much more clearly using a laser, as shown in Figure 17.7(A). The interference pattern produced by a laser can be easily observed on a screen or on a wall as the fringes are brighter and sharper Figure 17.7(B). Dust motes in the air can sometimes show up the beams of light, or smoke can be used.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-321.jpg?height=584&width=2013&top_left_y=3232&top_left_x=325)
Figure 17.7(A) Young's experiment demonstrated using a laser and (B) the interference pattern produced

## Formula for Young's slits

Consider point $P$ on the screen in Figure 17.8. If the light from each slit arrives at point $P$ with the same phase, constructive interference will occur, producing a bright image (an interference fringe).
The phase of the light at slit 1 and slit 2 is the same. At $P$, the waves may be out of phase because light from slit 2 must travel an extra distance to reach $P$.
If this extra distance is 1 wavelength $(1 \lambda)$, then the light arriving at $P$ from the two slits will be in phase and constructive interference occurs.
If this extra distance is 2 wavelengths ( $2 \lambda$ ), then the light arriving at $P$ from the two slits will again be in phase, and constructive interference occurs (Figure 17.9).
This is how the bright images are formed.
In general, if the extra distance (called the path difference) is a whole number of wavelengths $(n \lambda)$, then the light arriving at $P$ from the two slits will be in phase, and constructive interference occurs.
If $\theta$ is the angle between the straight-through position and the $n^{\text {th }}$ bright image (Figure 17.10), and $d$ is the distance from the centre of one slit to the centre of the other it can be shown that:

$$
n \lambda=d \sin \theta
$$

where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the light.
Also from the diagram:

$$
\tan \theta=\frac{x}{D}
$$

where $D$ is the distance from the Young's slits to the screen.
The wavelength of the light, $\lambda$, can be calculated using these formulae.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

Young's experiment was repeated in a school laboratory, as shown in Figure 17.11. The slits were 0.6 mm apart and were placed at a distance of 2.0 m from the screen. The distance across nine bright fringes on the screen was found to be 1.45 cm .
Calculate the wavelength of the monochromatic light.

## Solution

From Figure 17.11:

$$
\begin{aligned}
n & =4 ; \quad d=0.6 \mathrm{~mm}=0.6 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} ; \quad D=2.0 \mathrm{~m} \\
x & =\frac{1.45}{2}=7.25 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} \\
\tan \theta & =\frac{x}{D}=\frac{7.25 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0}=3.625 \times 10^{-3} \\
\theta & =\tan ^{-1}\left(3.625 \times 10^{-3}\right) \\
& =2.077 \times 10^{-1} \text { degrees } \\
n \lambda & =d \sin \theta \\
\lambda & =\frac{d \sin \theta}{n} \\
& =\frac{\left(0.6 \times 10^{-3}\right)(\sin 0.2077)}{4} \\
& =5.44 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Exercise 17.1

1. Young's experiment was carried out in a school laboratory. The slits were 0.7 mm apart and were placed at a distance of 1.8 m from the screen. The distance across 11 bright fringes on the screen was found to be 1.80 cm . Calculate the wavelength of the monochromatic light.

### 17.2 Wavelength and colour

- Light is an example of an electromagnetic wave.
- You will see on page 323 that it is a transverse wave.
- If the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave is between $3.8 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ and $7 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$, the wave affects the human eye and is called visible light.
- Different colours are seen when light of different wavelengths strikes the eye (Figure 17.12).
- The range of wavelengths that can be seen by the human eye is called

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-323.jpg?height=470&width=838&top_left_y=745&top_left_x=1910)
Figure 17.12 The visible spectrum of light

the visible spectrum of light.

- Normal white light is a mixture of different wavelengths.
- Light that is not a mixture of different wavelengths is called monochromatic light (it cannot be broken down into different colours).
- The light from the sodium vapour lamp used in Young's experiment is monochromatic. It has a wavelength of $5.9 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ and is orange/yellow in colour. The light from a laser is also monochromatic.
By convention, the different colours of light in the visible spectrum are:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-323.jpg?height=89&width=2013&top_left_y=1933&top_left_x=325)

Note: Monochromatic light is light of only one wavelength and its colour depends on its wavelength.
Light from a laser is monochromatic, coherent and collimated (that is, a parallel beam).
Light from most vapour lamps is not monochromatic, but sodium vapour lamps are an exception.

## Colours produced by interference in soap bubbles and petrol films

The colours sometimes seen in soap bubbles (Figure 17.13) or in a film of petrol on water (Figure 17.14) are due to interference of light waves. When light falls on a petrol film, some is reflected from the top surface of the film and some is reflected from the surface of the water. When light from each surface meets, interference occurs. Different wavelengths are refracted at different angles in the petrol. Depending on the angle at which you view the film or on the thickness of the film, different wavelengths interfere constructively. The colour of the light that is constructively interfering is the colour seen. A similar situation occurs in soap bubbles.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-323.jpg?height=590&width=1691&top_left_y=3115&top_left_x=325)
Figure 17.13 Interference colour on a 32 -metre-long soap bubble. The bubble was created by Alan McKay (New Zealand) on 9 August 1996, and he holds the world record for longest soap bubble.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-323.jpg?height=577&width=711&top_left_y=3118&top_left_x=2034)
Figure 17.14 Formation of interference colour on a film of petrol on water

### 17.3 Diffraction grating

It is difficult to measure the wavelength of light accurately with Young's slits because the interference fringes are diffuse and the bands are very close together. If, however, the number of slits is increased from two to a few hundred per millimetre, a much clearer pattern is formed. Many slits arranged like this is called a diffraction grating.
A typical diffraction grating consists of a piece of a transparent medium on which a very large number of parallel lines are engraved. Light cannot pass through these lines. The spaces between the lines behave as slits and allow the light to pass through. The width of each slit is close to the wavelength of light, so diffraction occurs at each slit.

The distance $d$ between two adjacent slits (so, the width of one line and one slit) on the grating is called the grating constant or the grating spacing (Figure 17.15).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-324.jpg?height=773&width=880&top_left_y=292&top_left_x=1738)
Figure 17.15 A diffraction grating showing the distance $d$, the grating constant, between two adjacent slits

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A fine diffraction grating has 400 engraved lines per mm . Find the grating constant $d$.

## Solution

From Figure 17.15, we can see that if the grating has 400 lines per mm it also has 400 slits per mm.
So, one line and one slit take up $\frac{1}{400} \mathrm{~mm}$.
So, the grating constant $d=\frac{1}{400} \mathrm{~mm}=0.0025 \mathrm{~mm}=2.5 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}$

$$
\text { The grating constant } d \text { (in } \mathrm{mm})=\frac{1}{\text { number of lines per } \mathrm{mm}}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

Red light falls normally (at right angles) on a diffraction grating. The grating has 500 engraved lines per mm and the second order diffracted image is at $30^{\circ}$ from the straight-through position. Find the wavelength of the light.

## Solution

For a grating of 500 lines per mm

$$
d=\frac{1}{500} \mathrm{~mm}=0.0025 \mathrm{~mm}=2 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}
$$

So, $d=2 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m} ; \quad n=2 ; \quad \theta=30^{\circ} ; \quad \lambda=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
n \lambda & =d \sin \theta \\
\lambda & =\frac{d \sin \theta}{n} \\
& =\frac{\left(2 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}\right)\left(\sin 30^{\circ}\right)}{2} \\
& =5 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Is this answer reasonable?

First, check the units on both sides of the formula, $\lambda=\frac{d \sin \theta}{n}$ :
On the left-hand side, the unit of $\lambda$ is the metre.
On the right-hand side, the unit of $d$ is the metre, $\sin \theta$ has no unit (it is the ratio of two lengths) and $n$ has no unit (it is just a number).
Therefore, both sides have the same unit, the metre.
Next, check the order of magnitude:
$5.00 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ has an order of magnitude of $10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$. The wavelength range of visible light is from $3.8 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ to $7.0 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$. Therefore, the order of magnitude is correct and, so, the answer is reasonable.

## HL

## The number of diffracted images

How many diffracted images are found at each side of the central image?
Rearranging the equation $n \lambda=d \sin \theta$ to make $n$ the subject gives $n=\frac{d \sin \theta}{\lambda}$
The maximum value of $\sin \theta$ is 1 . Therefore, the maximum value of $n$ is $n \frac{d}{\lambda_{\text {max }}}$
So, for a given $\lambda$, the larger the distance $(d)$ the larger the number of diffracted images $(n)$.
Typically, there will be two, three or four images on each side of the straight-through position, depending on the grating being used.

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A diffraction grating has 350 lines per mm . Monochromatic light of wavelength $5.2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ is incident normally. What is the highest order diffracted image formed?

## Solution

For a diffraction grating of 350 lines per mm:

$$
\begin{aligned}
d & =\frac{1}{350} \mathrm{~mm}=2.857 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m} \\
n \lambda & =d \sin \theta
\end{aligned}
$$

The maximum value of $n$ occurs when $\sin \theta$ is maximum, so when $\sin \theta=1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{\max } & =\frac{d}{\lambda} \\
& =\frac{2.857 \times 10^{-6}}{5.2 \times 10^{-7}} \\
& =5.49
\end{aligned}
$$

The maximum value of $n$ is 5 , so the $5^{\text {th }}$ order is the highest order of image observed.

## Worked Example 6

## Question

A diffraction grating with 100 lines per mm is placed between a light source (a laser) which gives out parallel coherent light and a screen (Figure 17.19). The distance from the grating to the screen is 2 m . Bright spots are seen on the screen at the points $A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H$ and I. If the distance $|A I|=80 \mathrm{~cm}$, calculate the wavelength of the source.

## Solution

For a diffraction grating with 100 lines per mm:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-327.jpg?height=629&width=884&top_left_y=410&top_left_x=1412)
Figure 17.19

$$
\begin{aligned}
d & =\frac{1}{100} \mathrm{~mm}=1 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m} \\
\sin \theta & =\frac{|A E|}{O A} \\
& =\frac{0.4}{0.4^{2}} \\
& =0.1961
\end{aligned}
$$

For the fourth order image ( $A$ or $I), n=4$

$$
\begin{aligned}
n \lambda & =d \sin \theta \\
\lambda & =\frac{d \sin \theta}{n} \\
& =\frac{\left(1 \times 10^{-5}\right)(0.1961)}{4} \\
& =4.90 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 7

## Question

Sodium emits visible light with a wavelength of 589 nm . This light passes through a diffraction grating of 300 lines per mm . Calculate the angular separation between the first line to the left of the central image and the first line to the right of the central image.

## Solution

For a diffraction grating of 300 lines per mm:

$$
d=\frac{1}{300} \mathrm{~mm}=0.00333 \mathrm{~mm}=3.33 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}
$$

So, $d=3.33 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m} ; \quad n=1 \quad \lambda=589 \mathrm{~nm} ; \quad \theta=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
n \lambda & =d \sin \theta \\
\sin \theta & =\frac{n \lambda}{d} \\
& =\frac{(1)\left(589 \times 10^{-9}\right)}{3.33 \times 10^{-6}} \\
& =0.1796 \\
\theta & =\sin ^{-1}(0.1769)=10.2^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

The angular separation between the two images $=2 \theta=2 \times 10.2=20.4^{\circ}$

## Student Experiment 17.1

To measure the wavelength of monochromatic light

## Summary of method

In this experiment，a light shines from a laser normally（at right angles）onto a diffraction grating．A series of images appears on a screen placed at a measurable distance on the other side of the diffraction grating．By calculating the angle，$\theta$ ，that each image makes with the straight－through position，and knowing the grating constant $d$ ，it is possible to calculate the wavelength of the sodium light using the formula $n \lambda=d \sin \theta$

## Equipment

A diffraction grating with a known grating constant（grating spacing，grating separation）$d$ ， a grating holder，a laser，a metre stick and a screen（such as a wall）

WARNING！Laser light is hazardous to the eyes．Do not look directly at the laser light or at a reflection of it．If laser light shines into your eyes，immediately close your eyes and look away．

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-329.jpg?height=949&width=1160&top_left_y=1425&top_left_x=367)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-329.jpg?height=945&width=1157&top_left_y=1432&top_left_x=1546)
Figure 17.22

## Method

1．Set up the equipment as shown in Figure 17．21．The larger the distance，$D$ ，between the grating and the screen，the better（Figure 17．22）．A suitable distance would be between 1 m and 3 m ．
2．Make sure that：
－The grating and the screen are vertical and parallel to each other
－The lines of the grating are vertical
－The grating is perpendicular to the light from the laser
3．Turn on the laser．The row of images on the screen should be horizontal．If not，adjust the equipment until it is．
4．With the metre stick，carefully measure the distance，$D$ ，between the diffraction grating and the screen．
5．Locate the first order diffracted image at each side of the central image．
6．With the metre stick，carefully measure the distance，$Y$ ，between the centres of both first order images．Record this value．
7．Repeat steps 5 and 6 for the second and third order diffracted images．Continue for further order images．
8．Find the grating constant，$d$ ．It should be written somewhere on the grating or its surrounds．
9．Complete the table，calculating the wavelength of the light for each value of $n$ ．
10. Calculate the average value of the wavelength.

Grating constant $d=$ $\_\_\_\_$ metres
Distance from grating to screen $D=$ $\_\_\_\_$ metres

| Order of image n | Distance between centres of corresponding images (m) $Y$ | $\frac{Y}{2}$ | $\boldsymbol{\operatorname { t a n }} \theta=\frac{\left(\frac{Y}{\mathbf{2}}\right)}{D}$ | $\boldsymbol{\operatorname { s i n }} \theta$ | Wavelength $\lambda$ (m) ( $\lambda=\frac{d \boldsymbol{\operatorname { s i n }} \theta}{n}$ ) |

## Sources of error

- The grating may not be exactly at right angles to the light from the laser.
- The grating may not be parallel to the screen.
- When measuring the distances avoid the error of parallax.

Note that if $D$ is large and a diffraction grating with many lines per mm is used (for example, 600 ), $Y$ will be large. The percentage errors in measuring $D$ and $Y$ will be small and a very accurate value for $\lambda$ can be obtained.

### 17.4 Polarisation of light

A transverse wave that is vibrating in one plane only is said to be polarised (or plane polarised, page 275). Only transverse waves can be polarised. Light waves, being transverse waves can be polarised.

Polarised light is light with waves that are vibrating in one plane only.
When a filament light bulb gives out light, electrons in the filament emit electromagnetic waves (vibrations in electric and magnetic fields). Light from a particular point on the filament is emitted as a pulse that lasts for about $10^{-9}$ seconds. In that pulse, the electric field component is vibrating in a particular direction. The direction in which the electric field of the next pulse vibrates is different and changes randomly with each pulse.
Other points on the filament are also emitting pulses, which are all vibrating in different directions. So, light from a filament bulb is unpolarised. This means the electric and magnetic fields are vibrating in many different planes.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-331.jpg?height=857&width=1704&top_left_y=2155&top_left_x=325)
Figure 17.23(A) and (B)

If unpolarised light is passed through a polarising filter, it becomes plane polarised (Fig 17.23). This means that the light is vibrating in one plane only. A polarising filter does to light waves what the slit did to waves on a rope on page 275 . The polarising filter absorbs light vibrating at right angles to its axis and only allows light that is vibrating parallel to its axis to pass through. If this light is then passed through another polarising filter, it only gets through if the axis of the second filter is parallel to that of the first (Figure 17.23(A)). If the second polarising filter is rotated through $90^{\circ}$, virtually no light gets through (Figure 17.23(B)).
Since only transverse waves can be polarised, this shows that light is a transverse wave.

## Polarisation by reflection

Light reflected from glass or water surfaces is partially plane-polarised. Reflections from horizontal surfaces tend to be horizontally polarised. A polaroid filter - a material that only allows light vibrating in one direction to pass through - can block much of this reflected light when its transmission axis is aligned vertically.
Reflected light can be a nuisance - for example, sunlight reflecting off water can obscure objects beneath the surface, reflections on windows can reduce visibility, clock face glare can make it difficult to read the time, and glare from whiteboards can interfere with viewing in a classroom. Viewing these reflections through a polarising filter can reduce glare and improve visibility. This effect can be observed with a simple experiment using a polarising filter. Try this yourself.
Polaroid sunglasses, as the name suggests, have polarising coatings, and as well as reducing the brightness of light, they also reduce glare (Figure 17.24). Polarising filters can be used on cameras with the same effect (Figure 17.25).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-332.jpg?height=600&width=2442&top_left_y=1201&top_left_x=192)
Figure 17.24(A) if a piece of polaroid is held in front of polaroid sunglasses, light only gets through if the axes of both polaroids are parallel. (B) If the piece of polaroid is rotated through $90^{\circ}$, no light gets through.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-332.jpg?height=603&width=2436&top_left_y=2005&top_left_x=192)
Figure 17.25 (A) Light reflecting off a window is plane polarised. The reflection makes it almost impossible to see in through the window. (B) A piece of polaroid placed in front of the camera blocks out most of the reflection, giving a clear view into the room

### 17.5 Dispersion

Dispersion of light can be brought about using a prism, as in Figure 17.26.

Dispersion is the separating out of the different wavelengths (colours) present in light.

Dispersion with a prism occurs because the refractive index of a medium is slightly different for different wavelengths. So, the different wavelengths (colours) are turned through different

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-332.jpg?height=428&width=1013&top_left_y=3053&top_left_x=1608)
Figure 17.26 Dispersion of light in a prism

angles by the prism and become separated. When light is dispersed by a prism, red is refracted the least and violet the most.

## Worked Example 8

## Question

The refractive index of a particular glass for red light is 1.51 and the refractive index for violet light is 1.53 .
In Figure 17.27, two parallel rays of light, one red and one violet, strike the side of a rectangular block of this glass at an angle of incidence of $45^{\circ}$.
Calculate the angle of refraction for each ray.

## Solution

For red light: $n=1.51$
Therefore, $\frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{\sin r}=1.51$

$$
\sin r=\frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{1.51}=0.4683
$$

The angle of refraction $r=\sin ^{-1}(0.4683)=27.92^{\circ}$ (Figure 17.27)

For violet light: $\sin r=\frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{1.53}=0.4622$
The angle of refraction $r=\sin ^{-1}(0.4622)=27.53^{\circ}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-333.jpg?height=753&width=828&top_left_y=416&top_left_x=1871)
Figure 17.27 Refractive index varies with wavelength. Therefore, different colours are turned through different angles. The red is refracted least.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-333.jpg?height=506&width=1287&top_left_y=1705&top_left_x=325)
Figure 17.28

A second prism, as in Figure 17.28, will recombine the constituents of white light to again form white light.
Dispersion is responsible for the colours in a rainbow. When white sunlight enters raindrops (or other fine drops of water) it is both refracted and internally reflected. The refraction causes the different wavelengths to be dispersed, and a spectrum of colours is

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-333.jpg?height=583&width=1398&top_left_y=2233&top_left_x=1347)
Figure 17.29

seen (Figure 17.29). A similar situation occurs when light enters and leaves polished gemstones, such as diamonds, giving them their characteristically coloured sparkle.
Dispersion can also be brought about using a diffraction grating, as in Figure 17.30.
A spectrum is formed for each value of $n$ other than $n=0$.
This happens because, in the formula $n \lambda=d \sin \theta$, for a given value of $n$, the angle $\theta$ varies with the wavelength $\lambda$. As a result, different colours appear at different angles from the straightthrough position.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-333.jpg?height=753&width=1040&top_left_y=2942&top_left_x=1718)
Figure 17.30 Dispersion of white light by a diffraction grating

## Worked Example 9

## Question

An average human eye can see light with wavelengths ranging from $3.8 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ (violet light) to about $7.0 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ (red light). White light falls normally on a diffraction grating. The grating has 400 engraved lines per mm . Find the angle between the straight-through position and the second order image of:
a) Diffracted violet light
b) Diffracted red light

## Solution

For a diffraction grating with 400 lines per mm:
$d=\frac{1}{400} \mathrm{~mm}=0.0025 \mathrm{~mm}=2.5 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}$
And for a second order image, $n=2$
a) For violet light:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda & =3.8 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m} \\
n \lambda & =d \sin \theta \\
\sin \theta & =\frac{n \lambda}{d} \\
& =\frac{(2)\left(3.8 \times 10^{-7}\right)}{2.5 \times 10^{-6}} \\
& =0.304 \\
\theta & =\sin ^{-1}(0.304)=17.70^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) For red light:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda & =7.0 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m} \\
n \lambda & =d \sin \theta \\
\sin \theta & =\frac{n \lambda}{d} \\
& =\frac{(2)\left(7.0 \times 10^{-7}\right)}{2.5 \times 10^{-6}} \\
& =0.560 \\
\theta & =\sin ^{-1}(0.560)=34.06^{\circ}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, red light deviates more than violet when light is dispersed by a diffraction grating. Looking at the equation $n \lambda=d \sin \theta, \theta$ is largest for the longest wavelength ( $\lambda$ ), which is red light.
When white light is dispersed by a prism, blue light deviates the most and red the least.
When $n=0$, light of all the wavelengths present in the white light are in phase when brought together (the path difference from each slit is the same) and so a white line is formed.

### 17.6 The electromagnetic spectrum

Electromagnetic waves were discussed briefly in Chapter 15, where you learned that:

- Electromagnetic waves (or electromagnetic radiation) are transverse waves with a speed of $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ in a vacuum (referred to as the 'speed of light'). Their speed is lower in other media.
- Electromagnetic waves show all typical wave properties, in particular they undergo interference and diffraction under the right conditions.
- The frequencies and wavelengths of electromagnetic waves are related by the equation: $c= f \lambda$, where $c=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.
Figure 17.31 shows the full range of electromagnetic waves in order of increasing frequency and decreasing wavelength.
This is called the electromagnetic spectrum.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-335.jpg?height=1000&width=2514&top_left_y=1175&top_left_x=322)
Figure 17.31 The electromagnetic spectrum

There are no exactly defined boundaries between the different types of electromagnetic radiation - they gradually blend from one region into the next. For example, high frequency ultraviolet radiation is very similar to low frequency X-ray radiation.
Also, in some cases, the naming of the radiation depends on its source. For example, high frequency electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus is called gamma rays but radiation identical in frequency and wavelength coming from electron transitions in atoms is known as X-rays (Chapters 28 and 29). So, there is significant overlap between X-rays and gamma rays.

## Radio waves

Radio waves are used in radio broadcasting, television broadcasting and VHF two-way communication.

## Microwaves

Microwaves are used to heat objects and cook food, as in a microwave oven. They are used in Wi-Fi, radar and satellite communication.

## Infra-red

Infra-red radiation (IR radiation) is just below the red end of the visible spectrum and so has longer wavelengths than visible light. IR radiation is the radiated heat discussed in Chapter 14. It is also the radiation is emitted from the Sun and from an ordinary filament lamp.
All objects emit some IR radiation. As the temperature of an object increases, it emits more IR radiation of shorter wavelengths. At about $500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, most objects start to emit visible red light as well.
Infra-red radiation can be detected by its heating effect using a blackened thermometer bulb or by the effect it has on a photographic plate. IR radiation also causes substances to heat up.
Infra-red light is used:

- As a heater, for cooking and in some saunas
- In remote controls, Wi-Fi and other wireless communication, such as headphones, keyboards and computers mouses
- In night vision devices (Figure 17.32). It can pass through fog and mist, meaning photographs can be taken in such conditions. Infrared images are used in weather forecasting.
- In medical imaging (Figure 17.33)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-336.jpg?height=467&width=815&top_left_y=2317&top_left_x=1005)
Figure 17.32 A photograph taken with an infra-red camera. The same photograph taken with an ordinary camera is almost useless due to the lack of visible light. The military and marine search and rescue use infrared goggles, which enable them to see in the dark.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-336.jpg?height=469&width=760&top_left_y=2321&top_left_x=1842)
Figure 17.33 Body heat emitted by the skin can be photographed and thermal images of the body produced. These can be used to diagnose abnormalities or other problems under the skin that cannot be detected on X-rays.

## Ultraviolet

Ultraviolet light (UV light) is just above the violet end of the visible spectrum and so has shorter wavelengths than visible light.

- UV light is emitted from the Sun.
- An ordinary filament lamp emits a small amount of UV light.
- A UV lamp used in the laboratory is usually a mercury vapour lamp.

UV light can cause certain substances (such as Vaseline) to fluoresce. Fluorescence is when a substance absorbs UV light and then re-emits this light as visible light. This characteristic can be used to detect the presence of UV radiation.
UV light can also be used for photography, as it affects photographic plates and digital camera sensors. This has applications in medical, scientific and forensic investigations, and photography can also be used to detect the presence of UV radiation
Some other uses of UV light are as follows:

- It is used to detect counterfeit currency or forgery of documents such as passports. Genuine examples have an invisible watermark that fluoresces when UV light shines on it.
- It is used in forensics and can be used to detect blood and urine, and fake artworks.
- It stimulates the production of vitamin D in the skin.
- It can cause photoemission and, therefore, is used in many applications of photo-sensing devices (Chapter 28).
- It is an ionising radiation and kills microbes. A germicidal UV lamp can be used to sanitise objects.
- Fluorescent light bulbs are basically mercury vapor tubes that give out UV light, which is reabsorbed by fluorescent material on the inside of the bulb and re-emitted as visible light.
- Ultraviolet light can be used in medicine to treat certain skin conditions, such as psoriasis.
- Certain colourless fluorescent dyes emit blue light when they are exposed to lower-level UV light. This can make colours appear more vibrant, and white to appear brighter. When exposed to UV light, a white shirt washed in modern detergents will glow due to fluorescent material in the detergent.
However, UV light can also be harmful. UV radiation from the Sun can cause burns on the skin, it is harmful to the eyes and it can cause skin cancer.


## X-rays

- X-rays are used in medical and dental imaging for diagnostic purposes.
- CT scans use X-rays.
- Radiation therapy, for destruction of cancer tumours, can use X-rays. The high ionising ability of X-ray radiation enables the light to destroy the DNA in cancer cells.
- X-rays are also used in airport security and can be used to detect counterfeit artwork.


## Gamma rays

- Gamma rays are used in industry to measure levels of liquids and powders in containers.
- Being the most ionising type of radiation, gamma rays are used to kill bacteria, for example in the sterilisation of medical equipment or of food to delay spoilage and maintain freshness and flavour.
- Gamma rays are used in medicine to treat some kinds of cancer, since cancer cells are more sensitive to gamma rays than healthy cells.
- They are used for diagnostic purposes in medicine. For example, a PET scan uses gamma rays for imaging purposes. They are also used as tracers in the body.


### 17.7 Solar irradiance

The solar irradiance at a place on the Earth's surface is the amount of the Sun's energy falling per second on one square metre of that surface, perpendicular to the Sun's rays. It is measured in watts per metre squared.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { solar irradiance } & =\frac{\text { power }}{\text { area }} \\
I & =\frac{P}{A}
\end{aligned}
$$

If $I$ is the solar irradiance (in $\mathrm{W} \mathrm{m}^{-2}$ ), $P$ is the power (in Watts) falling on an area $A$ (in $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ ), then:
Of all the electromagnetic radiation arriving at the Earth's upper atmosphere from the Sun, only a limited amount gets through to the Earth's surface. Only some bands of radio waves and microwaves get through, as well as some infrared, visible light, and the lower energy bands of ultraviolet radiation. X-rays, gamma rays, and higher energy microwaves do not get through.
The actual amount of solar radiation arriving at a point on the Earth's surface depends on a number of factors such as the time of the day, the season, the geographical location and the condition of the atmosphere at that location.
A significant amount of ultraviolet light arrives on the Earth's surface from the Sun, and this can and does affect living organisms in various ways. The effect of solar irradiance on life on Earth is predominantly due to the ionising effect UV light has on molecules in living organisms. Ultraviolet light can be divided into three bands, UVA, UVB and UVC (Figure 17.34).
The UVC band has the highest frequencies and, hence, the most energy. It is the most dangerous to life on Earth. However, none of this reaches the Earth's surface as it is absorbed by the atmosphere.
The middle energy band, the UVB band, is significantly absorbed by the ozone $\left(\mathrm{O}_{3}\right)$ layer in the atmosphere. However, some does get through, and this is highly damaging to the DNA in mammals' skin. It causes sunburn on

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-338.jpg?height=974&width=1365&top_left_y=1549&top_left_x=1256)
Figure 17.34 The ultraviolet light spectrum

exposed skin and, over time, skin aging and the promotion of skin cancers of different types. It is also damaging to the eyes. A benefit of UVB exposure is that it is required for vitamin D synthesis in the skin of mammals.
UVA is the lowest energy band of ultraviolet radiation. It is not as dangerous as UVB, but it still does cause skin damage and can cause skin cancer through damage to DNA, though not to the same degree as UVB.
It is, therefore, sensible to limit our exposure to UV radiation from the Sun. This can be done by using sunscreen, covering up with suitable clothing or by staying in the shade when the sun is most intense (usually for two hours before and after local noon). Also, wearing sunglasses, or ordinary glasses that have coatings that block UV light, is good practice.
As well as posing problems for mammals, high levels of UV light affect plants. It reduces photosynthesis and lessens growth, leading to reduced crop yields in commercial horticulture, for example.

## Summary What I should know

- Young's experiment showed that light undergoes interference, therefore firmly establishing that light travels as a wave.
- The formula $n \lambda=d \sin \theta$ can be used with Young's slits, where $n$ is the order of the image, $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the light, $d$ is the distance between the slits and $\theta$ is the angle the $n^{\text {th }}$ order image makes with the straight-through position.
- Light is an example of an electromagnetic wave.
- In typical vision, different colours are seen when light of different wavelengths strikes the eye.
- Monochromatic light is light of only one wavelength and, hence, only one colour when dispersed. The colour of monochromatic light depends on its wavelength.
- The distance $d$ between two adjacent slits (that is the width of one line and one slit) on the grating is called the grating constant or the grating spacing, where $d$ (in mm ) $=\frac{1}{\text { number of lines per } \mathrm{mm}}$
- For a diffraction grating, the $n^{\text {th }}$ bright line either side, $n \lambda=d \sin \theta$
- Polarised light is light with waves that are vibrating in one plane only.
- Since only transverse waves can be polarised, the fact that light can be polarised shows that light is a transverse wave.
- Dispersion is the separating out of the different wavelengths (colours) present in light. It can be brought about by using a prism or a diffraction grating.
- When white light is dispersed by a prism, blue light is deviated the most and red the least.
- When white light is dispersed by a diffraction grating, blue light is deviated the least and red the most.

# 18 Static Electricity

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the nature of electric charge at the subatomic level
- To ensure students appreciate how objects can become charged by friction and by induction
- To ensure students appreciate the conservation of electric charge in interactions
- To ensure students know how charge is distributed on a conductor and on an insulator
- To ensure students understand Coulomb's law and can use it to solve problems
- To ensure students understand how electric field lines can be used to represent an electric field
- To ensure students understand what electric field strength is and can use it to solve problems
- To ensure students can solve numerical problems using Coulomb's law and electric field strength (HL only)


### 18.1 Static electricity

Some of the effects of static electricity have been known for thousands of years. The ancient Greeks observed that rubbing amber with cloth caused it to attract small objects like dust or hair - this phenomenon is now understood to be static electricity. One of the most dramatic natural examples is lightning, which occurs when static charge builds up in storm clouds.

Today, static electricity is used in technologies such as photocopiers, laser printers and air purifiers. It is also used in industrial processes to reduce pollution by removing dust and smoke particles from exhaust gases. However, it can be hazardous too - sparks caused by static discharge can ignite flammable gases, vapours or fine dust, leading to fires or explosions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-340.jpg?height=913&width=1600&top_left_y=2903&top_left_x=201)
Figure 18.1 An interesting effect of static electricity

### 18.4 Conductors and insulators


#### Abstract

In some substances, electrons - called bound electrons - are strongly bound to their atoms and cannot easily move from one atom to another. If such a substance becomes electrically charged, the charge stays where it is placed, as it cannot flow through the substance. These substances are called electrical insulators. Examples are glass, Perspex and most plastics. Other substances - such as metals contain free electrons that are not strongly bonded to their atoms and can move easily throughout the substance. These substances allow electric charge to flow and are called electrical conductors.


![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-343.jpg?height=795&width=1495&top_left_y=426&top_left_x=1250)
Figure 18.6 In the insulator, all electrons are bound to their atoms. In the conductor, some electrons are not bound to their atoms and are free to move from atom to atom.

Any substance through which electric charge cannot flow is called an insulator.
Any substance through which electric charge can flow is called a conductor.
Both insulators and conductors can be charged by friction. However, if you want to charge a conductor, you must hold it with an insulating handle, otherwise the charge produced will flow from it through you (the human body is a conductor) to Earth (which is also a conductor).
A conductor from which charge cannot escape because it is insulated is called an insulated conductor.

## Earthing or grounding

If a conducting object is connected to the ground using another conductor, it is said to be earthed or grounded.
When a charged conducting object is connected to the Earth using another conductor, its charge is transferred to the Earth. Because the Earth is so large, it receives most of the charge that was on the object. As a result, the object becomes effectively discharged.

Grounding (or earthing) a conductor means connecting it to the Earth with a conducting path. If the conductor is charged, it will transfer its excess charge to the Earth.

### 18.5 Charging objects by induction

Usually, in a metal, one (or more) electron from each atom is not strongly bound to that atom, but is free to move throughout the metal, from atom to atom. Suppose a negatively charged rod (an insulator) is brought near to - but not touching - a metal conductor (Figure 18.7).
The electrons in the metal that are free to move are repelled by the negative charge on the rod and move to the opposite side of the metal. Therefore, a negative charge appears on one side of the metal and a positive charge on the other (from where the electrons have moved).
If the charged rod is taken away, the electrons move back again.
The charges produced on the metal are called induced charges. The amount of negative charge induced is equal to the amount of positive charge induced (as stated in the conservation of electric charge).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-343.jpg?height=509&width=958&top_left_y=2952&top_left_x=1787)
Figure 18.7 Left: A metal conductor; Right: A negatively charged rod is brought near, but not touching, the metal conductor. This causes a negative charge on one side of the metal and a positive charge on the other.

## Charging an insulated conductor by induction

A single insulated conductor can be charged by induction by:

- Bringing a negatively charged rod near the conductor (Figure 18.8)
- Allowing positive and negative charges to become induced on the conductor
- Touching the conductor while keeping the charged rod in place, so that the induced negative charge will flow through you to Earth
- Removing your finger and then removing the rod, leaving the conductor positively charged.

To charge the conductor negatively, a positive charge must be brought near it. Try drawing the steps involved as a diagram to check your understanding.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-344.jpg?height=756&width=1104&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1517)
Figure 18.8 Charging a single object by induction

## How a charged object exerts a force on a neutral object

Figure 18.9 shows a charged rod inducing charges on a small piece of aluminium foil. The rod exerts an attractive force on the induced negative charges on the foil and a repulsive force on the induced positive charges. Since the induced positive charge is further from the rod, the repulsive force on it is less. This means, overall, the foil is attracted to the rod.
Figure 18.10 is a simplified picture of the molecules in a piece of insulating material. When the positively charged rod is brought near it, electrons in the molecules nearest the rod are attracted

Figure 18.9 A charged rod inducing charges on a small piece of aluminium foil

This sets up a situation similar to that in
Figure 18.9 and, again, the material is attracted to the rod.

### 18.6 The gold leaf electroscope

Figure 18.11 shows a gold leaf electroscope. It consists of a very thin gold leaf attached to one end of a metal rod. The other end of the rod has a metal disc, called the cap, attached to it. The leaf and rod are in a metal case with a window, which stops draughts from causing the leaf to move. The rod is insulated from the case so that any charge put on the rod does not flow away.
A gold leaf electroscope can be used to detect charge, indicate the approximate size of a charge, or test if an object is an insulator or a conductor.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-344.jpg?height=827&width=922&top_left_y=2995&top_left_x=1699)
Figure 18.11 A gold leaf electroscope

## Detecting charge

If a charged object is brought near an electroscope (Figure 18.12), induced charges appear on the electroscope. Due to the force of repulsion between like charges, the leaf diverges. Therefore, the electroscope detects electric charge.
If objects with different charges are placed the same distance from the electroscope, the leaf will diverge by different amounts for each object. The larger the charge on the object, the greater the divergence produced.

## Testing if an object is an insulator or a conductor

Charge the electroscope. Then, holding the object in your hand, touch the cap of the electroscope with the object. If the leaf collapses, the object is a conductor; otherwise, it is an insulator. If the object is a conductor, the charge flows from it through you to the Earth, discharging the electroscope. This does not happen with the insulator.
A gold leaf electroscope can be given a charge of known sign by induction (Figure 18.13) in the same manner as the sphere earlier.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-345.jpg?height=583&width=1606&top_left_y=1302&top_left_x=325)
Figure 18.13 Charging a gold leaf electroscope by induction

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-345.jpg?height=948&width=584&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=2161)
Figure 18.12 A gold leaf electroscope detecting charge

### 18.7 The distribution of charge on an insulated conductor

When static charge is put on an insulator, it remains where it is put.
However, if an insulated conductor is charged, the like charges repel each other and spread around the conductor, moving as far apart as possible. They reach their maximum separation when they are on the outside surface of the conductor. Therefore:

All static charge resides on the outside surface of a conductor.

- If static charge is placed on a spherical conductor, it is found to be distributed uniformly over the surface sphere.
- If static charge is placed on a pear-shaped conductor, extra charge accumulates at the pointed end (Figure 18.14).
In general, the following is true:
Static charge on a conductor tends to accumulate where the conductor is most pointed.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-345.jpg?height=724&width=558&top_left_y=2122&top_left_x=2138)
Figure 18.14 A static charge placed on a spherical conductor is distributed uniformly over the surface of the sphere. A static charge placed on a pear-shaped conductor accumulates at the pointed end

## Point discharge

The air is made up mainly of nitrogen and oxygen molecules, argon atoms, and small amounts or other gases, such as carbon dioxide.
Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun, ionising radiation from natural radioactive minerals in the Earth's crust, and cosmic rays can knock electrons from molecules in the air, producing electrically charged molecules and atoms called ions. Lightning also creates ions in the surrounding air.

An ion is an atom or a molecule that has lost or gained one or more electrons.

Ions in the air are responsible for the phenomenon called point discharge. It occurs as follows:

- If a charged conductor has a very sharp point (Figure 18.15), a large accumulation of charge builds up around the point, resulting in a high charge density (charge per unit area).
- This creates very strong electric forces on any charges in the region around the point - in other words, a very strong electric field is formed around the point, see page 338)
- There are always some ions in the air near the point.
- Ions with opposite charge to that on the point are strongly attracted to, and accelerate towards, the point; as they move, they produce more ions by colliding with air molecules.
- The ions with opposite charge to that on the point head towards the point and neutralise the charge on it.
- Ions with the same charge are repelled by, and accelerate away from, the point, creating an 'electric wind'. from, the point, creating an 'electric wind'. from, the point, creating an 'electric wind'.
- This continuous movement of ions effectively removes charge from the point.
- The loss of charge from a point by this manner is called point discharge or the point effect.

Point discharge can be demonstrated in the laboratory using a Van de Graaff generator, a pointed object, and a candle flame (Figure 18.16). The generator builds up static electricity on its hollow metal dome, and a small version is ideal for electrostatic experiments in a school setting.
Any charged object will lose its charge more quickly if there are any points on it. For example, if you place a pin on the cap of a charged electroscope, it will lose its charge quickly. For the same reason, the dome of a Van de Graaff generator is smooth so that any charge stays on the surface and does not leak off.

## Some everyday effects of static electricity

The crackling and clinging of clothes made from synthetic materials is due to static electricity. The crackling heard is due to small sparks which you can see in the dark.
Sparks produced by static electricity can be dangerous if fine dust, flammable vapours or gases are present. In oil refineries, flour mills and in the chemical industry, special precautions must be taken to minimise the risk of explosion with these substances due to static electricity.
An aeroplane (or a helicopter) in flight can build up considerable amounts of static electricity due to friction with the air. When in flight, almost all commercial aircraft discharge most of this static charge in a controlled manner using small thin metal rods mounted on the trailing edges of the wings (Figure 18.17). These rods are called static discharge wicks, and they work by point discharge. When the plane lands, any remaining static must be discharged. Aeroplane tyres are made of conducting rubber to do this. If a plane in flight is struck by lightning, the charge remains on the outside of the metal plane and is safely discharged through the static wicks.
Large amounts of static charge can build up in clouds. Lightning is the discharge of this static charge from one cloud to another or from a cloud to the ground (Figure 18.18). It is a huge flow of electrons (an electric current). Such a flow can do considerable damage to buildings. To protect them, a metal rod called a lightning conductor is mounted on the top of the building and connected by a thick copper conducting strip to a large copper plate buried in the ground (Figure 18.19). Lightning is significantly more likely to strike the rod rather than the building itself, and it can flow harmlessly to the ground through the lightning conductor.

### 18.8 The size of the force between two static electric charges

A static electric charge will exert a force of attraction or repulsion on another static charge that is close by. The size of the force that each charge exerts on the other depends on:

- The size of each charge
- The distance between the charges

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-347.jpg?height=220&width=688&top_left_y=533&top_left_x=2057)
Figure 18.20

- The material surrounding the charges

Suppose two charges of $q_{1}$ coulombs and $q_{2}$ coulombs are placed a distance $d$ apart (Figure 18.20). Let $F$ be the force that one exerts on the other. Then, by experiment, it is found that:

$$
F \propto q_{1} ; \quad F \propto q_{2} \quad \text { and } \quad F \propto \frac{1}{d^{2}}
$$

It follows that: $F \propto \frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{d^{2}}$

$$
\Rightarrow F=k \frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{d^{2}} \quad \text { where } k \text { is a constant. }
$$

This result is known as Coulomb's law.
For reasons that you do need to understand at this stage, $k$ is written as:

$$
k=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon}
$$

where $\varepsilon$ is a constant that depends on the medium surrounding the charges.
Coulomb's law states that the force of attraction or repulsion between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

If the charges are $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ and the distance between them is $d$, Coulomb's law states:

$$
F=\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{d^{2}}\right)
$$

(F\&T, page 61)

Coulomb's law is an example of an inverse square law since the force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the charges. This means that, for example, if the distance between the charges is:

- Doubled, the size of the force is four times smaller
- Made three times bigger, the size of the force is nine times smaller
- Halved, the size of the force is four times bigger

The size of the force also depends on the medium surrounding the charges. The force is greatest when the charges are in a vacuum. In any other medium the force is less. Therefore, the value of $\varepsilon$ is different for different media.

- $\varepsilon$ is called the permittivity of the medium.
- If the charges are in a vacuum, the value of the permittivity is written as $\varepsilon_{0}, \varepsilon_{0}$ is called the permittivity of free space or the permittivity of a vacuum, and it is also approximately the permittivity of air.
- The SI unit of permittivity is the Farad per metre (F $\mathbf{m}^{-1}$ ). (You do not need to know why at this stage.)
- $\varepsilon_{0}=8.9 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{Fm}^{-1}$ (F\&T, page 47).


## Note:

- The size of the force on each charge is the same - even if one charge is greater than the other. This follows from Newton's third law.
- The direction of the force is always along the line joining the two charges.
- The force is attractive if they are unlike charges and repulsive if they are like charges.
- If the charges are not point charges, and if the distance between the charges is large compared to the dimensions of the charges, Coulomb's law still holds to a high degree of accuracy.
- If the charges are spherical, or if they are on a conducting sphere, Coulomb's law still holds, where $d$ is the distance between the centres of the spheres.
- Coulomb's law has the same mathematical form as Newton's law of universal gravitation. Both are inverse square laws. However, gravitational forces are only attractive and are much smaller.
- If a point charge $q$ is placed near several other point charges, the resultant force on $q$ is the vector sum of the forces that each of the other charges on its own would exert on $q$.

In the following Worked Examples, assume the charges are in air or in a vacuum and take $\varepsilon_{0}=8.9 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{Fm}^{-1}$.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

Calculate the force that a charge of +5 C exerts on a charge of +6 C placed 4 m from it (Figure 18.21).

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{d^{2}}\right) \\
& =\frac{(5)(6)}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)(4)^{2}} \\
& =\frac{30}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)(16)} \\
& =1.68 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-348.jpg?height=154&width=652&top_left_y=1165&top_left_x=1461)
Figure 18.21

The direction of the force is away from the $5 \mu \mathrm{C}$, since like charges repel.
Note the huge size of this force. In practice, static charges of this size are rarely found. In the following Worked Examples, the charges are usually in the order of microcoulombs $(\mu \mathrm{C})$, where $1 \mu \mathrm{C}=1$ millionth of a coulomb $=1 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{C}$

## HL

## Worked Example 2

## Question

Two-point charges of $+2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ and $-3 \mu \mathrm{C}$ are 50 cm apart in air (Figure 18.22). Find the magnitude and direction of the force on the $2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge.

## Solution

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-348.jpg?height=148&width=640&top_left_y=2480&top_left_x=1477)
Figure 18.22

The values of the charges must be expressed in coulombs and distances in metres before using Coulomb's law.
$2 \mu \mathrm{C}=2 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{C}$
$3 \mu \mathrm{C}=3 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{C}$
$50 \mathrm{~cm}=50 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{d^{2}}\right) \\
& =\frac{\left(2 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(3 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)(0.5)^{2}} \\
& =\frac{6 \times 10^{-12}}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)(0.25)} \\
& =0.215 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

The direction of the force is towards the $-3 \mu \mathrm{C}$, since unlike charges attract.

Figure 18.23

## Solution

Figure 18.24 shows the two forces acting on the $+2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge.
They are a force $F_{1}$ due to the $-1 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge and a force $F_{2}$ due to the $-3 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-349.jpg?height=134&width=831&top_left_y=905&top_left_x=1406)
Figure 18.24

Use Coulomb's law to find the magnitude of each of these forces:
$F_{2}=0.215 \mathrm{~N}$ towards the $-3 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge (from Worked Example 2).

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{1} & =\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{d^{2}}\right) \\
& =\frac{\left(1 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)(0.30)^{2}} \\

The resultant force on the $+2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge is $0.215-0.200=0.015 \mathrm{~N}$ towards the $-3 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge.

### 18.9 Electric fields

Another way to understand electrostatic force is through the concept of an electric field.
When a static electric charge exists in space, it affects the region around it. If another charge is placed nearby, it experiences a non-contact electrostatic force. This indicates that the original charge has modified the space around it, creating what is known as an electric field.
The electric field extends outward from the charge and exerts a force on any other charges within that space. The field is strongest close to the original charge and becomes weaker with increasing distance.

An electric field is any region of space where a static electric charge experiences a force other than the force of gravity.
An electric field is caused by other static charges nearby.

An electric field can be represented on a diagram by lines, called electric field lines. Arrow heads on the electric field lines show the direction of the force that would be exerted on a positive charge if it were placed in the field (Figures 18.27 and 18.28).

An electric field line is a line drawn on a diagram of an electric field showing the direction of the force on a positive charge placed in the field.

Where the electric field is strong, the field lines are closer together. Where the field is weak, the lines are further apart. Figure 18.29 shows the shape of other electric fields.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-350.jpg?height=476&width=1362&top_left_y=2972&top_left_x=195)
Figure 18.29 The shapes of electric fields

If two parallel metal plates are connected to a high-voltage source (Figure 18.30), positive charge appears on one plate and an equal amount of negative charge appears on the other. This produces an almost-uniform electric field in the space between the plates.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-350.jpg?height=571&width=580&top_left_y=2044&top_left_x=1432)
Figure 18.27 The electric field due to an isolated positive charge

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-350.jpg?height=567&width=584&top_left_y=2041&top_left_x=2037)
Figure 18.28 The electric field due to an isolated negative charge

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-350.jpg?height=636&width=1020&top_left_y=3053&top_left_x=1601)
Figure 18.30 The almost uniform electric field between two oppositely charged parallel plates

### 18.10 Electric field strength

To represent the strength of the electric field in various places we introduce a new vector quantity called electric field strength. It is defined as follows:

The electric field strength, $E$, at a point in an electric field is the force per unit charge at that point; that is, electric field strength is the force per coulomb.

The SI unit of electric field strength is the newton per coulomb ( $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$ ).
This is the equal to the volt per metre $\left(\mathrm{V} \mathrm{m}^{-1}\right)$.
Suppose a charge of +1 C experiences a force of 6000 N at a particular point in an electric field. The electric field strength at this point is 6000 newtons per coulomb.
If a charge of +4 C experiences a force of 80000 N at a point, the electric field strength at that point is:

$$
E=\frac{80000}{4}=20000 \mathrm{NC}^{-1}
$$

In general, if a charge $q$ experiences a force $F$ when placed in an electric field, the field strength $E$ is given by:

$$
\text { Electric field strength } \quad E=\frac{F}{q}
$$

(F\&T, page 61)

- Electric field strength is a vector.
- The magnitude of $\boldsymbol{E}$ at a point in an electric field, is the size of the force that would be exerted on a charge of +1 C placed at that point.
- The direction of $\boldsymbol{E}$ is the direction of the force that would be exerted on a charge of +1 C placed at that point.
In the following, take it that $\varepsilon_{0}=8.9 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{Fm}^{-1}$ and all charges are in a vacuum or air.


## Worked Example 4

## Question

A charge of $2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ experiences a force of 34 N when placed at a point in an electric field. Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength at that point.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
E & =\frac{F}{q} \\
& =\frac{34}{2 \times 10^{-6}} \\
& =1.7 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{NC}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

Find the magnitude of the force on a charge of $5 \mu \mathrm{C}$ when placed in an electric field of strength $2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
E & =\frac{F}{q} \\
F & =E q \\
& =\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right) \\
& =1 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 6

## Question

Find the electric field strength $E$ at point $P$, a distance $d$ from a point charge $+q$.

## Solution

The direction of $E$ is radially out from $+q$
(Figure 18.31)
(If $q$ was negatively charged it would be in the opposite direction.)
Force $F$ on +1 C at point $P$ is:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-352.jpg?height=596&width=831&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1354)
Figure 18.31

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}\right)\left(\frac{(q)(1)}{d^{2}}\right) \\
\Rightarrow E & =\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} d^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 7

## Question

What is the electric field strength halfway between a charge of $+2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ and a charge of $+9 \mu \mathrm{C}$, if the charges are separated by a distance of 60 cm ?

## Solution

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-352.jpg?height=245&width=750&top_left_y=1653&top_left_x=1367)
Figure 18.32

Figure 18.32 shows the situation. First calculate the field strength at $P$ due to each charge individually, and then find the resultant field strength.
Field strength $E_{1}$ at $P$ due to $+2 \mu \mathrm{C}=$ Force on +1 C placed at $P$ due to $+2 \mu \mathrm{C}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{1} & =\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^{2}}\right) \\
& =\frac{\left(2 \times 10^{-6}\right)(1)}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)(0.3)^{2}} \\
& =1.9869 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{NC}^{-1} \text { to the right }
\end{aligned}
$$

Field strength $E_{2}$ at $P$ due to $+9 \mu \mathrm{C}=$ Force on +1 C placed at $P$ due to $+9 \mu \mathrm{C}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{2} & =\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^{2}}\right) \\
& =\frac{\left(9 \times 10^{-6}\right)(1)}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)(0.3)^{2}} \\
& =8.941 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{NC}^{-1} \text { to the left }
\end{aligned}
$$

Resultant electric field strength:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{\text {net }} \text { at } \begin{aligned}
P & =8.941 \times 10^{5}-1.9869 \times 10^{5} \\
& =6.954 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{NC}^{-1} \text { to the left }
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 8

## Question

The spherical dome of a Van de Graaff generator is charged. The dome has a diameter of 20 cm and it has a charge of 88 nC . A $10 \mu \mathrm{C}$ point charge is placed 12 cm from the surface of the dome.
a) Calculate:
i) The electric field strength at a point 12 cm from the surface of the dome
ii) The electrostatic force exerted on the $10 \mu \mathrm{C}$ point charge
b) All the charge resides on the surface of a Van de Graaff generator's dome. Explain why.

## Solution

a) i) The dome is spherical. Therefore, for calculation purposes, we will assume all its charge is at its centre.

The distance from the centre to the surface of the dome is half of the diameter $\frac{20}{2}=10 \mathrm{~cm}$
Since the point charge is placed 12 cm from the surface, you must calculate the electric field strength $10+12=22 \mathrm{~cm}$ from the dome's centre.

$$
\begin{aligned}
E & =\text { force on }+1 \mathrm{C} \text { at } 22 \mathrm{~cm} \text { from centre } \\
& =\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^{2}}\right) \\
& =\frac{\left(88 \times 10^{-9}\right)(1)}{4 \pi\left(8.9 \times 10^{-12}\right)\left(22 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{2}} \\
& =1.626 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{NC}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

ii) $\quad E=\frac{F}{q}$
$F=E q$

$$
=\left(1.626 \times 10^{4}\right)\left(10 \times 10^{-6}\right)
$$

$=0.1626 \mathrm{~N}$
b) Since like charges repel each other, they move to maximise their distance apart. They are the maximum distance apart when on the outside of the dome.

## Summary What I should know

- If an object is negatively charged (-) it has gained electrons. If an object is positively charged (+) it has lost electrons. It is only the electrons that move when objects become charged.
- The unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C).
- Any substance through which electric charge cannot flow is called an insulator.
- Any substance through which electric charge can flow is called a conductor.
- All static charge resides on the outside of a conductor.
- An ion is an atom or a molecule that has lost or gained one or more electrons.
- Static charge on a conductor tends to accumulate where the conductor is most pointed.
- Coulomb's law states that the force of attraction or repulsion between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them:

$$
F=\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\right)\left(\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{d^{2}}\right)
$$

- An electric field is any region of space where a static electric charge experiences a force other than the force of gravity.
- An electric field is usually caused by other nearby static charges.
- An electric field line is a line drawn in an electric field showing the direction of the force on a positive charge placed in the field.
- The electric field strength $\boldsymbol{E}$ at a point in an electric field is the force per unit charge at that point, i.e. electric field strength is the force per coulomb $E=\frac{F}{q}$.
- The SI unit of electric field strength is the newton per coulomb ( $\mathbf{N ~ C}^{-\mathbf{1}}$ ). You will see on page 339 that this is the same as the volt per metre ( $\mathbf{V ~ m}^{-\mathbf{1}}$ ).

# 19 Potential Difference

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the concept of potential difference
- To ensure students appreciate the relationship between potential difference and electric field strength
- To ensure students know what an electric current is
- To ensure students understand why all points on a conductor carrying static charge are at the same potential


## Keywords

- Potential difference ( $V$ )
- Potential ( $V$ )
- Voltage (V)
- The volt (V)
- Electric current ( $I$ )
- The ampere (A)
- Electric charge ( $q$ )
- The coulomb (C)
- Electric field
- Electric field strength ( $E$ )
- The newton per coulomb ( $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$ )


### 19.1 Potential difference

To understand potential difference, it is helpful to first think about how the energy of an object changes in a more familiar context - such as in a gravitational field.

## Potential energy in a gravitational field

Imagine an object thrown upwards near the surface of the Earth.

- As the object rises, it slows down, losing kinetic energy. As it does so, it gains an equal amount of gravitational potential energy.
- At its highest point, its energy is entirely gravitational potential; as it falls, its energy changes from gravitational potential energy back to kinetic energy - the object speeds up as it descends.


## Potential energy in an electric field

Something similar happens for a charged particle in an electric field.
In Figure 19.1, if a positive charge is released at point $A$, the electric field will exert a force on it and it will accelerate in the direction of the electric field.

- As it gains speed, its energy changes from electrical potential energy to kinetic energy - the field does work on the charge.
- If a positive charge is projected from $B$ to $A$ (against the direction of the field), its energy changes from kinetic energy to electrical potential energy as the charge slows down.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-358.jpg?height=847&width=1013&top_left_y=2770&top_left_x=1602)
Figure 19.1 The electric field does work on the charge as it 'falls' from $A$ to $B$.

To move a positive charge from $B$ to $A$, a force must be applied to it. In other words, work must be done on the charge to move it against the electric field (Figure 19.2).
It can be shown experimentally that the work done (that is, the amount by which the potential energy changes) in bringing a charge from one point to another in an electric field does not depend on the path taken.
For example, the work done in going from $A$ to $B$ by any of the paths shown in Figure 19.1 is the same.
The amount of work that must be done to bring a charge of one coulomb from $A$ to $B$ is, therefore, a fixed number. It is called the potential difference between $A$ and $B$.

- The symbol for potential difference is $V$.
- Potential difference is a scalar quantity, since work and

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-359.jpg?height=760&width=1017&top_left_y=276&top_left_x=1728)
Figure 19.2 The girl does work in pushing the charge from $A$ to $B$ against the field.

energy are scalar quantities.

- Potential difference is sometimes called voltage.
- Potential difference is the amount by which the potential energy of a +1 C charge changes in going from one point to the other.
- The SI unit of potential difference is the joule per coulomb ( $\mathbf{J ~ C}^{-\mathbf{1}}$ ). This unit is also called the volt (V).

The potential difference ( $V$ ) between two points in an electric field is the work done in bringing a charge of +1 C from one point to the other.

The volt is defined as follows:
The $\mathbf{S I}$ unit of potential difference is the joule per coulomb ( $\mathrm{J} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$ ).
This unit is also called the volt (V).
$\mathbf{1 ~ v o l t}=\mathbf{1}$ joule per coulomb $\quad \mathbf{1 ~ V}=\mathbf{1 ~ J ~ C}{ }^{-\mathbf{1}}$
If the work done in bringing a charge of 1 C from $A$ to $B$ is $V$ joules, then the work done in bringing a charge of 2 C from $A$ to $B$ is $2 V$ joules. For 3 C , it is $3 V$ joules, and so on.
Therefore, the work done in bringing a charge of $\boldsymbol{q}$ coulombs from $A$ to $B$ is $q V$ joules.
Work done $=$ charge transferred × voltage

$$
W=q V \quad \Rightarrow V=\frac{W}{q}
$$

(F\&T, page 61)

## Measuring potential difference

Potential difference can be measured with a voltmeter (page 365). Potential difference can also be measured approximately with an electroscope (Figure 19.3). When the cap is connected to one point and the metal case to another, the size of the divergence of the leaf is a measure of the potential difference between the two points.
The size of the divergence of the leaf indicates the size of the potential difference between the charged conductor and the ground.

## Alessandro Volta

Alessandro Volta (1745-1827) was an Italian

chemist and physicist. He contributed to the knowledge of static electricity. He invented the electric battery (called a voltaic pile), which was able to provide a steady electric current. He also discovered methane gas.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-359.jpg?height=988&width=760&top_left_y=2760&top_left_x=1985)
