## Worked Example 1

## Question

The potential difference between two points is 12 V . Find the work done in transferring a charge of 8 C between the two points.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{W}{q} \\
\Rightarrow W & =q V \\
& =(8)(12) \\
& =96 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

The work done in bringing a charge of 4 C from one point to another is 10 J . What is the potential difference between the two points?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{W}{q} \\
& =\frac{10}{4} \\
& =2.5 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

The potential difference between two points is 100 kV . Find the work done when a charge of $3 \mu \mathrm{C}$ is moved from one point to the other.

## Solution

Note: $100 \mathrm{kV}=100 \times 10^{3}=1.00 \times 10^{5}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{W}{q} \\
\Rightarrow W & =q V \\
& =\left(3 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(1.00 \times 10^{5}\right) \\
& =0.3 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

An electron of charge $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ transfers $4 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~J}$ of energy as it moves from one point to another. What is the potential difference between the two points?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{W}{q} \\
& =\frac{4 \times 10^{-16}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \\
& =2500 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

[^2]
## Worked Example 5

## Question

Two oppositely charged plates are 3 cm apart. There is a uniform electric field of strength $2 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$ between them.
a) What is the force on a charge of +1 C if it is placed between the plates?
b) Find the work done in bringing a charge of 1 C from one plate to the other.
c) What is the potential difference between the plates?

## Solution

a) $E=\frac{F}{q}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow F & =E q \\
& =\left(2 \times 10^{3}\right)(1) \\
& =2 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) Work $=$ force × distance $=\left(2 \times 10^{3}\right)\left(3 \times 10^{-2}\right)=60 \mathrm{~J}$
c) Potential difference = work done in bringing 1C from one plate to the other $=60 \mathrm{~V}$

## Worked Example 6

## Question

The potential difference between two points is 2000 V . An electron (of charge $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ and mass $9 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$ ) is released at one of the points and moves towards the other under the action of the field. Find its speed when it arrives at the second point.

## Solution

Potential energy lost by electron = work done on it by field and is given by $W=q V$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
W & =q V \\
& =\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)(2000) \\
& =3.2 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

The decrease in electrical potential energy becomes the kinetic energy gained by the electron.
Let $v=$ speed of electron on reaching the second point.
Its kinetic energy at that point $=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}=3.2 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~J}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\left(9 \times 10^{-31}\right) v^{2} & =3.2 \times 10^{-16} \\
\Rightarrow v^{2} & =\frac{(2)\left(3.2 \times 10^{-16}\right)}{9 \times 10^{-31}}=7.111 \times 10^{14} \\
\Rightarrow v & =2.7 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 7

## Question

Show that the SI unit of electric field strength, the $\mathrm{NC}^{-1}$, is equivalent to the unit volts per metre, $\mathrm{V} \mathrm{m}^{-1}$.

## Solution

1 volt (V) = 1 joule per coulomb = $1 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{C}{ }^{-1}$
1 joule $(\mathrm{J})=1$ newton metre $=1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}$
Therefore, $1 \mathrm{~V} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}=1 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{C}-1 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =1 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{C}^{-1} \mathrm{~m}^{-1} \\
& =1 \mathrm{NC}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 19.2 Relationship between potential difference and electric field strength

Suppose the point $A$ and $B$ in Figure 19.1 (page 346) are a fixed distance apart.
Suppose the electric field between $A$ and $B$ is weak and the work done in bringing +1 C from $A$ to $B$ is $W$ joules. The potential difference between $A$ and $B$ is $W$ volts.
On the other hand, if the electric field strength between $A$ and $B$ is much larger, then the work done in bringing +1 C from $A$ to $B$ is going to be much larger than $W$ joules, and so the potential difference between $A$ and $B$ will be much larger than $W$ volts.

Figure 19.4 shows a battery and its circuit symbol. It has two places on it called its terminals. For now, you can assume that:

- The negative terminal has an excess of negative charge
- The positive terminal has an excess of positive charge There is therefore an electric field in the space between the terminals. The higher the voltage between the terminals of the battery, the stronger this electric field is.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-362.jpg?height=1010&width=864&top_left_y=2708&top_left_x=1757)
Figure 19.4

## Electric current

If the terminals of the battery in Figure 19.4 are connected with a conductor (e.g. a piece of copper wire), there will be an electric field in the conductor. Free electrons in the conductor will therefore move under the influence of this field. The electrons move from the negative terminal, through the wire, back to the positive terminal. The battery continually maintains an excess of electrons on the negative terminal.
This flow of electrons, which is also a flow of electric charge, is called an electric current. You will study this in more detail in Chapter 21.

An electric current is a flow of electric charge.

## Potential at a point

Up to this point, potential differences have been considered between two points. However, it is sometimes useful to talk about the potential at a single point. To do this, there must be an agreed reference point of zero potential for comparison.
By convention, scientists use the Earth as this reference point, and measure the potential difference between other points and the Earth. The potential difference between a point and the Earth is called the potential of that point.
With this definition, the Earth is at zero potential.
Note also that as you add positive (+) charge to a conductor, it becomes more difficult to bring a charge of +1 C from Earth to it, which means the potential of the conductor increases.

## All points on a conductor carrying static charge are at the same potential

If two points on a conductor were not at the same potential, there would be a potential difference between them. There would thus be an electric field in the conductor and the charges on the conductor would move under its influence.
But in a conductor carrying a static charge, the charges are not moving. Therefore, there is no electric field in the conductor and all points on the conductor must be at the same potential, called the potential of the conductor.

The potential difference between a point and the Earth is called the potential of that point.

Note: All points on a conductor carrying static charge are at the same potential.

## Summary What I should know

- The potential difference $(V)$ between two points in an electric field is the work done in bringing a charge of +1 C from one point to the other.
- The SI unit of potential difference is the joule per coulomb ( $\mathrm{J} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$ ). This unit is also called the volt (V).
- The potential difference between two points is 1 volt if 1 joule of work is done when 1 coulomb is brought from one point to the other.
- $\mathbf{1}$ volt = $\mathbf{1}$ joule per coulomb or $\mathbf{1} \mathbf{~ V}=\mathbf{1} \mathbf{~ J ~ C}^{-\mathbf{1}}$
- An electric current is a flow of electric charge.
- The potential at a point is the potential difference between that point and the Earth.
- All points on a conductor carrying static charge are at the same potential.

# 20 Current and Charge

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the keywords listed (right)
- To ensure students appreciate the relationship between current and charge
- To ensure students can solve problems involving the charge on the electron and size of an electric current
- To ensure students appreciate why the current is the same at all points in a series circuit
- To ensure that students can model electric current in parallel circuits
- To make students aware that electric charge is conserved in an electric circuit


### 20.1 Three effects of an electric current

When a bulb, a battery, a switch, and a beaker of dilute sulfuric acid are connected using copper wire as shown in Figure 20.1, and the switch is closed, three effects can be observed:

- Heating effect: Heat is given out from the bulb. Some heat is also given out from the wires and from the inside of the battery. However, the heat produced in the wires and the battery is small and difficult to detect.
- Magnetic effect: A magnetic compass needle, which normally lines up north-south, deflects from its north-south position when it is brought near the wire, indicating the presence of a magnetic field around the wire.
- Chemical effect: A chemical reaction occurs in the beaker and bubbles of gas are seen coming from the wires dipped in the acid.
If the wire is cut, or the switch is opened or the acid is removed from the beaker, the three effects stop. If the break is repaired, they start again. This indicates that something flows through the copper wire, through the bulb and through the acid. That something is called electric charge.
A flow of electric charge is called an electric current. The path around which the charge flows is called a circuit.

An electric current is a flow of electric charge.

Figure 20.1

## Conductors and insulators

Any substance through which electric charge can flow is called an electrical conductor. In Figure 20.1, the wire and the acid are conductors. Copper, aluminium (as well as all other metals) and the human body are conductors too.
A substance through which electric charge cannot flow is called an electrical insulator. Plastic, glass and rubber are good insulators. If one of the pieces of wire in Figure 20.1 was replaced with a piece of plastic, the current would not flow and the three effects would stop.

A substance through which electric charge can flow is called a conductor.

A substance through which electric charge cannot flow is called an insulator.

### 20.2 What is electric charge?

Matter is made up of atoms. Every atom has a central part called the nucleus which contains particles called protons and neutrons. Particles called electrons orbit in the space surrounding the nucleus (Figure 20.2).
Electrons are attracted to the protons and are repelled by other electrons. Protons repel protons.
These forces of attraction and repulsion are much stronger than gravitational forces; they are called electrostatic forces (See page 335).
Particles that exert electrostatic forces on each other are said to be electrically charged. Protons and electrons have the same amount of charge, but electrons are negatively charged, and protons are positively charged. Remember, an electric current is a flow of charges, so an electric current is charged particles moving.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-366.jpg?height=682&width=766&top_left_y=1269&top_left_x=1849)
Figure 20.2

In a metal conductor, some electrons are not stuck to any particular atom and are free to move. So, when connected to a battery, electrons move through the metal conductor. This means that:

An electric current in a metal conductor is a flow of electrons.

## SI unit of electric charge

The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C). One coulomb is the amount of charge on about $6.24 \times 10^{18}$ electrons. You do not need to remember this number.

The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C).
Each electron has a charge of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulombs, which is a very small amount of charge.

$$
\text { Charge on one electron, } \begin{aligned}
e & =1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text { coulombs } \\
& =0.00000000000000000016 \text { coulombs }
\end{aligned}
$$

### 20.3 Size of an electric current

The size of an electric current in a conductor is, by definition, the amount of charge passing any point of that conductor per second.

- The letter $I$ is the symbol for electric current.
- The SI unit of current is the ampere(A).

For example, if in Figure 20.1 two coulombs of charge pass any point in the circuit per second, the current is 2 amperes.

The size of an electric current in a conductor is the amount of charge passing any point of that conductor per second.

The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A).

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \text { ampere } & =1 \text { coulomb per second } \\
1 \mathrm{~A} & =1 \mathrm{C} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

It follows that, if a steady current of $I$ amperes flows for a time of $t$ seconds, the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) that passes is given by: $\quad q=I t$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Charge that passes a point }=\text { steady current × time taken } \\
& \qquad q=I t
\end{aligned}
$$

Or

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { steady current } & =\frac{\text { charge that passes }}{\text { time taken }} \\
I & =\frac{q}{t}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 1

## Question

If a charge of 10 C passes a point in a circuit at a steady rate in a time of 5 s , what current flows in the wire?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
I & =\frac{q}{t} \\
& =\frac{10}{5} \\
& =2 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A steady current of 5 A flows in a circuit. How much charge passes a point in the circuit in:
a) 1 s ?
b) 12 s ?
c) 2 hours?

## Solution

a)

$$
\begin{aligned}
q & =I t \\
& =(5)(1) \\
& =5 \mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}
$$

b)

$$
\begin{aligned}
q & =I t \\
& =(5)(12) \\
& =60 \mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}
$$

c) First, convert 2 hours to seconds:
$2 \mathrm{~h}=(2)(60)(60)=7200 \mathrm{~s} q=I t$
$=(5)(7200)$
$=36000 \mathrm{C}$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

The charge on one electron is $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$.
a) How many electrons are needed to give a charge of 1 coulomb?
b) Find the number of electrons passing any point in a circuit, per second, in which a current of 10 A is flowing.

## Solution

a) Let $n=$ the number of electrons needed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Total charge on } n \text { electrons } & =(n)(\text { charge on } 1 \text { electron }) \\
& =(n)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

If this is one coulomb, then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(n)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right) & =1 \\
n & =\frac{1}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \\
& =6 \times 10^{18} \text { electrons }
\end{aligned}
$$

b) $10 \mathrm{~A}=10 \mathrm{C} \mathrm{s}^{-1} \Rightarrow(10)\left(6.25 \times 10^{18}\right)$ electrons passing per second

Therefore, in a 10 A current, $6.25 \times 10^{19}$ electrons pass any point per second.

### 20.4 Conventional current

A battery has two places to connect the wires. One is called the positive terminal (+) and the other the negative terminal (-). Figure 20.3 shows the circuit symbol for a battery. Note that the longer thin vertical line (on the left) is the positive terminal and the shorter thicker vertical line (on the right) is the negative terminal.
Scientists knew a lot about electric current even before they knew about the existence of electrons. Over 150 years ago, they knew that something flowed in a circuit like that in Figure 20.1, but they did not know the direction in which an electric current flowed in a metal conductor and unfortunately guessed incorrectly. They said an electric current flowed from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
Today, electric current (called conventional current) is still described as flowing from + to -, even though the actual flow of electrons in a metal is in the opposite direction, from - to + (Figure 20.4). The size of an electric current in amperes - the amount of charge passing per second remains the same whether it is described as conventional current or as electrons moving in the opposite direction.

Whenever the direction of an electric current is mentioned, it will always mean conventional current (unless otherwise stated).

Conventional current is said to flow from + to In a metal, electrons actually flow in the opposite direction.

### 20.5 Direct current (DC) and alternating current (AC)

A current that always flows in one direction is a direct current (DC). An electric current caused by a chemical cell or a battery is a direct current. If an electric current in a circuit reverses direction every so often, it is an alternating current (AC). For example, the current that flows through an ordinary domestic light bulb when connected to the mains electricity supply reverses direction 100 times every second and is, therefore, an alternating current (Figure 20.5). For now, only direct current will be considered.

Direct current (DC) is a current that flows in one direction only.
Alternating current (AC) is an electric current that periodically reverses the direction in which it flows.

## Measuring direct current

An ammeter (Figure 20.6) can be used to measure the size of a current in amperes. Smaller currents are measured using meters called milliammeters or microammeters. A galvanometer is another word for a milliammeter or microammeter (Figure 20.7). These are often different current ranges on a multimeter.

### 20.6 Series and parallel circuits

## Series circuit

In the circuit in Figure 20.8, the circuit components (the battery, the two bulbs and the switch) are connected end-to-end to form a single path. The moving charges pass through the circuit components one after another in a particular order. A circuit like this, in which there is only one path for the current to follow, is called a series circuit.
Charge does not appear or disappear at any point in the circuit, so the same amount of charge passes any point every second. The size of the current flowing out of the battery is the same size as the current flowing back into the battery, and is the same as the current in the bulb. The current is the same at every point in a series circuit.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-370.jpg?height=590&width=665&top_left_y=436&top_left_x=1959)
Figure 20.8

The fact that charge does not appear or disappear at any point in the circuit is an example of the conservation of electric charge in a circuit.

The current is the same at every point in a series circuit.

## Current at a junction of conductors

In Figure 20.9, five conductors meet at a junction, labelled $O$. If the wires $A$ and $B$ are carrying currents $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ towards $O$, and if wires $C, D$ and $E$ carry currents $I_{3}, I_{4}$ and $I_{5}$ away from $O$, then since charge is conserved, it follows that:

$$
I_{1}+I_{2}=I_{3}+I_{4}+I_{5}
$$

The sum of the currents flowing into a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving the junction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-370.jpg?height=711&width=798&top_left_y=1311&top_left_x=1823)
Figure 20.9

Find the current flowing through wire $W$.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
1+4+x & =6+3 \\
x & =4 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Measuring current with an ammeter

To measure the current flowing in a circuit such as that in Figure 20.11(A) with an ammeter, the circuit must be broken at some point and the ammeter inserted. In other words, an ammeter must be connected in series with the circuit in which the current to be measured is flowing. It does not matter where in a series circuit an ammeter is inserted since the current is the same everywhere. In Figure 20.11(B), each ammeter gives the same reading.

An ammeter must be connected in series with the part of the circuit in which the current

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-371.jpg?height=552&width=1290&top_left_y=406&top_left_x=1430)
Figure 20.11(A) and (B)

to be measured is flowing.

## Parallel circuits

At the point $B$ in Figure 20.12, the current splits, with some going through path 1 and some going through path $2 . \mathrm{A}_{1}$ reads the same current as $\mathrm{A}_{4}$.
The sum of the values on $A_{2}$ and $A_{3}$ is equal to the value on $A_{1}$ (and $\mathrm{A}_{4}$ ) that is: $I=I_{1}+I_{2}$
Path 1 and path 2 are said to be in parallel with each other. The same current does not necessarily pass through each parallel path, but it would be the same if the paths were made from identical pieces of wire.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-371.jpg?height=584&width=733&top_left_y=1321&top_left_x=1901)
Figure 20.12 Path 1 and path 2 are said to be in parallel with each other: $I=I_{1}+I_{2}$

## Summary What I should know

- An electric current is a flow of electric charge.
- A conductor is a substance through which electric charge can flow.
- An insulator is a substance through which electric charge cannot flow.
- An electric current in a metal conductor is a flow of electrons.
- The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C).
- The size of an electric current in a conductor is the amount of charge passing any point of that conductor per second.
- The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A).
- 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second; $1 \mathrm{~A}=1 \mathrm{C} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$
- Charge that passes a point $=$ steady current × time taken; $q=I t$
- Conventional current is said to flow from positive (+) to negative (-).
- In a metal, electrons actually flow from negative (-) to positive (+).
- Direct current (DC) is a current that flows in one direction only.
- Alternating current (AC) is an electric current that periodically reverses the direction in which it flows.
- An ammeter is used to measure the size of an electric current.
- Conservation of electric charge in a circuit means that electric charge does not appear or disappear at any point in the circuit.
- The current is the same at every point in a series circuit.
- An ammeter must be connected in series with the part of the circuit in which the current to be measured is flowing.
- The sum of the currents flowing into a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving the junction.
- If several conductors are connected in parallel with each other, the current entering the combination is equal to the sum of the currents in each conductor which is equal to the current leaving the combination. The currents in the parallel conductors may not be the same.

# 21 Potential Difference and Electromotive Force

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the energy changes that occur in a simple circuit
- To ensure students understand the meaning of the potential difference between two points in a circuit
- To ensure students can model the relationship between work, charge and potential difference
- To ensure students can model the relationship between power, current and potential difference
- To ensure students appreciate the difference between voltages in series and voltages in parallel
- To ensure students know what is meant by emf


## Keywords

- Potential difference $(V)$
- Voltage ( $V$ )
- Electromotive force ( $E$ )
- The volt (V)
- Power
- The watt (W)
- Voltages in series
- Voltages in parallel
- Voltmeter


### 21.1 Energy changes in a simple electric circuit

When current flows in a conductor, heat energy is given out at every point in that conductor. Where does this heat energy come from? It comes from the battery (or other source, such as a generator) that is driving the current through the conductor. In a battery, stored chemical energy is converted to electrical potential energy. When the electric charges (electrons) pass through the battery, they gain electric potential energy.
Then, as they move around the circuit, their average speed and average kinetic energy remain constant, but they lose electrical potential energy. The lost potential energy appears as heat energy. (Figure 21.1).
Note that some of this electrical potential energy can also be converted to light (if the conductor gets hot enough, as in a filament bulb) or to kinetic energy (if the conductor is placed in a suitable magnetic field, as in an electric motor). For the following discussion, It is assumed that all the wasted ('lost') energy is in the form of heat.

### 21.2 Potential difference between two points in a circuit

The amount of electrical potential energy 'lost' by one coulomb as it moves 'from one point to another in a circuit is called the potential difference, $V$, between those two points (Figure 21.2).

- The SI unit of potential difference is the joule per coulomb $\left(\mathrm{J} \mathrm{C}^{-1}\right)$.
- The joule per coulomb is also called the volt (V).
- Since potential difference is measured in volts, potential difference is also called voltage.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-374.jpg?height=740&width=1017&top_left_y=1953&top_left_x=1604)
Figure 21.1 The average kinetic energy of the moving charges remains the same. Electrical potential energy is converted to heat as the charges move around the circuit.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-374.jpg?height=486&width=734&top_left_y=3001&top_left_x=1881)
Figure 21.2 If the potential difference between $A$ and $B$ is 4 volts, then 4 joules of electrical potential energy are lost by each coulomb as it moves from $A$ to $B$. This energy is converted to other forms, mainly heat, between $A$ and $B$.

The potential difference, $V$ between two points in a circuit is the energy lost by one coulomb as it moves from one point to the other.

The SI unit of potential difference is the joule per coulomb ( $\mathbf{J C}^{-1}$ ).
The joule per coulomb is also called the volt (V).

Figure 21.3 shows electrons flowing through a metal conductor.
Suppose the thin slice of electrons (slice 1 ) that is just about to pass $A$ in Figure 21.3 has $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons in it. This number of electrons has a charge of 1 coulomb. While this slice flows from $A$ to $B$, the potential energy that it loses, and consequently the heat energy produced by this slice between $A$ and $B$ is by definition, the potential difference between $A$ and $B$.
Suppose there are 20 such slices between $A$ and $B$, each giving out heat at the same rate as slice 1 . If all 20 slices move a short distance such that slice 1 takes up the position of slice 2 , the total energy given out between $A$ and $B$ would be equal to the energy given out by slice 1 if it travelled on its own from $A$ to $B$. Therefore:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-375.jpg?height=577&width=1189&top_left_y=674&top_left_x=1554)
Figure 21.3

The potential difference between two points in a circuit is also the amount of energy converted from electrical to other forms between those two points when 1 coulomb of charge passes anywhere between those two points.

For example, suppose the potential difference between $A$ and $B$ in Figure 21.4 is 4 volts.
This means that 4 joules of potential energy are 'lost' (and 4 joules of heat given out) by each coulomb as it moves from $A$ to $B$.
It also means that the total heat energy given out between $A$ and $B$ is 4 joules, in the time it takes one coulomb to just pass $A$ (or any other point in the circuit).
This means that if the potential difference between two points in a circuit is $V$ volts, and $W$ joules of energy is given out between the two points, then, when

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-375.jpg?height=489&width=763&top_left_y=1875&top_left_x=1982)
Figure 21.4

a charge of $q$ coulombs passes any point in the circuit:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{W}{q} \\
& =\frac{\text { energy given out }}{\text { charge gone past }}
\end{aligned}
$$

(F\&T, page 61)

## Worked Example 1

## Question

In Figure 21.5, the potential difference between $A$ and $B$ is 20 volts. In a certain time, 40 C of charge passes $A$. How much energy is given out as heat between $A$ and $B$ ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{W}{q} \\
W & =q V \\
& =(40)(20) \\
& =800 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-375.jpg?height=531&width=743&top_left_y=3073&top_left_x=1559)
Figure 21.5

## Worked example 2

## Question

300 J of heat is given off from a wire when a charge of 60 C passes a point in the wire. What is the potential difference across the wire?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{W}{q} \\
& =\frac{300}{60} \\
& =5 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 21.3 The rate at which heat is produced in a current-carrying conductor

## Note:

- Power is the rate at which work is done and is also the rate at which energy is converted from one form to another
- If $W$ joules of work are done (or if $W$ joules of energy are converted from one form to another at a constant rate) in time $t$ seconds, then:
- Power $=\frac{\text { work done }}{\text { time taken }}$, or $P=\frac{W}{t}$
(F\&T, page 55)
- Power $=\frac{\text { energy transferred from one form to another }}{\text { time taken }}$, or $P=\frac{W}{t}$
- The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 watt = 1 joule per second

In Figure 21.6, suppose that in a time of $t$ seconds:

- $W$ joules of energy is given out between $A$ and $B$
- $q$ coulombs of charge passes point $A$
- The potential difference between $A$ and $B$ is $V$ volts

Rearrange $V=\frac{W}{q}$ to make $W$ the subject: $W=V q$
Divide both sides by $t$ :

$$
\frac{W}{t}=V \frac{q}{t}
$$

$\frac{W}{t}$ is the power, $P$ produced between $A$ and $B$; i.e. $P=\frac{W}{t}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-376.jpg?height=512&width=798&top_left_y=2080&top_left_x=1824)
Figure 21.6

$\frac{q}{t}$ is the current, $I$ that flows; i.e. $I=\frac{q}{t}$
Therefore, $P=V I$
Power produced between $A$ and $B=$ (voltage between $A$ and $B$ ) × (current flowing)

$$
P=V I
$$

(F\&T page 62)
Note that the power, $P$, in this equation is the total energy converted from electrical energy to any other type between $A$ and $B$ per second.

## Worked example 3

## Question

The current in a bulb is 2 A when the potential difference across it is 230 V . What is the power dissipated in the bulb?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =V I \\
& =(230)(2) \\
& =460 \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked example 4

## Question

What current flows through a 60 W bulb when connected to 230 V mains supply?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =V I \\
I & =\frac{P}{V} \\
& =\frac{60}{230} \\
& =0.261 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 21.4 Voltages in series and parallel

## Voltages in series

In Figure 21.7, the total energy 'lost' per coulomb between $A$ and $B$ is equal to the energy 'lost' per coulomb between $A$ and $X$ plus the energy 'lost' between $X$ and $Y$ plus the energy 'lost' between $Y$ and $B$.

$$
V=V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3}
$$

This follows from the principle of conservation of energy.
The potential difference across two (or more) consecutive parts of a series circuit is equal to the sum of the potential differences across each part; for example, in Figure 21.7:

$$
V=V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3}
$$

## Voltages in parallel

In Figure 21.8, the voltages across each of the three paths are the same. This is because the change in potential energy in bringing a charge from one point to another in an electric field does not depend on the path taken (Page 347).

The potential difference is the same across each of several conductors connected in parallel. For example, in Figure 21.8:
voltage across path $1=$ voltage across path $2=$ voltage across path 3

$$
V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}
$$

## Measuring potential difference

A voltmeter is used to measure potential difference (Figure 21.9).
A voltmeter is always connected in parallel with the part of the circuit across which the potential difference is being measured.

For example, in Figure 21.10, to measure the potential difference between $A$ and $B$ (across the bulb), the voltmeter is connected as shown. The meter is connected between two points without breaking the circuit between them. The above results for voltages in series and parallel can be easily verified in the laboratory using bulbs and voltmeters.

### 21.5 Electromotive force (emf)

To keep a current flowing in a circuit, an electric field must be maintained in that circuit. This means that there must be a potential difference (voltage) maintained between the ends of the circuit. This voltage, applied to a circuit, is called an electromotive force or an emf. The symbol for emf is $E$ and its unit is the volt.

A voltage when applied to a circuit is called an emf.
A source of electrical energy, such as a cell, battery, a generator or a solar panel converts energy from some other form to electrical potential energy. Its emf is the amount of electrical potential energy it gives to each coulomb of charge as it passes through the source.

A cell usually is made up of two different metals separated by various chemicals in a container. Chemical reactions in the cell cause a voltage to be maintained between the two metals. For example a 1.5 volt AAA 'battery' is actually a cell. Strictly speaking the word "battery" refers to a number of sells connected together.

## Sources of emf connected in series

If several batteries (or other sources of emf) are connected in series, with the positive terminal of one connected to the negative terminal of the next as in Figure 21.11, then the total voltage of the combination is the sum of the individual voltages.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-378.jpg?height=252&width=766&top_left_y=1331&top_left_x=1855)
Figure 21.11 Total voltage of battery $=V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3}$

Many everyday applications make use of this fact. For example, in the torch in Figure 21.12, three cells, each of voltage 1.5 V , are connected in series, giving an overall voltage of 4.5 V .

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-378.jpg?height=428&width=916&top_left_y=1770&top_left_x=1705)
Figure 21.12

## Summary What I should know

- The potential difference, V, between two points in a circuit is the energy lost by one coulomb as it moves from one point to the other: $V=\frac{W}{q}$
- The SI unit of potential difference is the volt (V).
- 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb $\left(1 \mathrm{~V}=1 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{C}^{-1}\right)$
- The potential difference between two points in a circuit is the amount of energy converted from electrical to other forms between the two points when 1 coulomb of charge passes any point of that circuit: $V=\frac{W}{q}$
- Power dissipated between $A$ and $B=$ (potential difference between $A$ and $B$ ) × (current flowing between $A$ and $B$ )

$$
P=V I
$$

- The potential difference across two (or more) consecutive parts of a series circuit is equal to the sum of the potential differences across each part:

$$
V=V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3} \text { for voltages in series. }
$$

- The potential difference is the same across each of several conductors connected in parallel:

$$
V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3} \text { for voltages in parallel. }
$$

- A voltmeter is always connected in parallel with the part of the circuit across which the potential difference is being measured.
- An emf is a voltage when applied to a circuit.

# 22 Resistance

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand resistance, ohmic conductor, resistivity
- To ensure students appreciate how the current in a circuit depends on its resistance and the voltage across it
- To ensure students understand Ohm's law
- To ensure students can derive (HL) and use the formulae for resistors in series and parallel
- To ensure students understand the potential divider circuit
- To ensure students understand why the resistance of a metal increases as the temperature does and the resistance of an insulator or a semiconductor decreases as the temperature increases

### 22.1 Resistance

## Conductors oppose the flow of electric charge

As electrons move through a metal, they continually collide with atoms in the metal and lose energy. This energy appears as heat. In this way, the material of the metal resists the movement of the electric charges through it. Different conductors oppose current by different amounts.

- If you increase the potential difference across most conductors, the current flowing through them increases.
- If a conductor opposes current by a large amount, a large potential difference causes only a small current and the ratio of $V$ to $I$, i.e. $\frac{V}{I}$ is large.
- If a conductor opposes current by a small amount, a large potential difference causes a large current and the ratio $\frac{V}{I}$ is small.
The last two facts are used to define a new quantity called the resistance $(R)$ of a conductor.
- The resistance $(R)$ of a conductor is the ratio of the potential difference across it to the current flowing through it, i.e. $R=\frac{V}{I}$
- Resistance is a scalar quantity.
- The SI unit of resistance is the ohm $(\Omega)$.
- From $R=\frac{V}{I}$, the resistance of a conductor is 1 ohm if a potential difference of 1 volt across it causes a current of 1 ampere through it.

The resistance, $R$ of a conductor is the ratio of the potential difference across it to the current flowing through it:

$$
R=\frac{V}{I}
$$

(F\&T page 61)

[^3]A conductor has a resistance of $\mathbf{1}$ ohm if the current through it is 1 ampere when the potential difference across it is 1 volt.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

Find the resistance of a conductor if it carries a current of 4 A when the potential difference across it is 20 V .

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & =\frac{V}{I} \\
& =\frac{20}{4} \\
& =5 \Omega
\end{aligned}
$$

### 22.2 Measuring resistance

## Using an ammeter and a voltmeter

A simple way to measure the resistance of a conductor is to pass an electric current through it, then measure the potential difference across it with a voltmeter and the current through it with an ammeter. Divide the voltage by the current to find its resistance $\left(R=\frac{V}{I}\right)$.

## Using an ohmmeter

An ohmmeter is often part of a digital multimeter. By selecting one of the resistance-measuring scales, it directly reads the resistance of whatever is connected across the ends of its probes.

## Fixed and variable resistors

Some conductors are made to have a resistance of a specific value. These are known as fixed resistors.
Other conductors have a resistance that can be changed. These are known as variable resistors.
Figure 22.3 shows one type of variable resistor (also called a rheostat), through which current flows as shown. Moving the sliding contact along the bar causes the current to pass through all the wire, some of the wire or none of the wire in the coil. Doing this changes the total resistance of the circuit, which you can check with an ohmmeter (Figure 22.4)

### 22.4 Ohm's law

The resistance of some conductors changes as the potential difference across them (or the current through them) changes. For other conductors - mainly metals and some liquids - the resistance remains the same as the voltage across them changes. These are called Ohmic conductors and they obey Ohm's law which states:

For certain conductors (mainly metals), at a constant temperature, the current flowing through them is directly proportional to the potential difference across them:

$$
V \propto I \quad \Rightarrow \frac{V}{I}=\mathrm{a} \text { constant }
$$

The constant of proportionality is the resistance ( $R$ ) of the conductor. So, in other words, the resistance of an ohmic conductor remains constant as the size of the current passing through them or potential difference across them changes. This fact was discovered by Georg Simon Ohm in 1826.

## Student Experiment 22.1

## Georg Simon Ohm

Georg Simon Ohm (1789-1854) was a
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-383.jpg?height=274&width=317&top_left_y=1901&top_left_x=2428)
German mathematician and physicist. In 1827 he published the results of his investigations on electrical circuits, stating what is now known as Ohm's law.

To verify the relationship between the current flowing through and voltage across an ohmic conductor

## Summary

In this experiment, you will measure the current flowing through and the voltage across a length of resistance wire, for a series of different values of the voltage. You will plot a graph of current against voltage. It will be a straight line through the origin, verifying that the current is directly proportional to the voltage, i.e. $I \propto V$

## Equipment

DC power supply, a variable resistor, a length of resistance wire (e.g. nichrome), an ammeter, a voltmeter, connecting leads.

## Method

1. Set up the equipment as shown in Figure 22.6.
2. Adjust the variable resistor so that the voltage across the resistance wire is small.
3. Measure and record the current flowing through and the voltage across the resistance wire.
4. Adjust the variable resistor to increase the voltage and hence the current. Measure and record $I$ and $V$ again.
5. Repeat Step 4 several times, recording all values.
6. On graph paper, plot a graph of $I$ (on the $y$-axis) against $V$. The graph will be a straight line through the origin (Figure 22.7), verifying that $I \propto V$; i.e. verifying Ohm's law.
7. Measure the slope of the graph, and hence calculate the resistance of the length of resistance wire.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-384.jpg?height=616&width=717&top_left_y=449&top_left_x=315)
Figure 22.6

## Sources of error

- Make sure your circuit is set up correctly, with the voltmeter in parallel with the coil of wire and the ammeter in series with the coil of wire.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-384.jpg?height=818&width=860&top_left_y=296&top_left_x=1722)
Figure 22.7 The current voltage characteristic of a metal, i.e. of a conductor that obeys Ohm's law

- Do not use large values of current, as the coil will heat up and its resistance will change.
- Use a sensitive and high-resistance voltmeter and a sensitive ammeter to get accurate readings.


### 22.5 Resistors in series and parallel

## Resistors in series

Figure 22.8 shows three resistors of resistances $R_{1}, R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$ ohms connected in series. The total resistance, $R$, of the combination (i.e. the resistance between $A$ and $B$ ) can be found using the formula:

$$
R=R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}
$$

If two or more resistors are connected in series, the total resistance of the combination is equal to the sum of the resistances of each resistor, i.e. in Figure 22.8, the resistance ( $R$ ) between $A$ and $B$ is given by:

$$
R=R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}
$$

(F\&T page 61)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-384.jpg?height=141&width=721&top_left_y=1972&top_left_x=1855)
Figure 22.8

## Worked Example 2

## Question

Find the resistance between $A$ and $B$ in Figure 22.9.

## Solution

Total resistance:

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & =R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3} \\
& =2+5+8 \\
& =15 \Omega
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-384.jpg?height=141&width=714&top_left_y=2955&top_left_x=1380)
Figure 22.9

## Derivation of formula

In Figure 22.8, let $V_{1}, V_{2}$ and $V_{3}$ be the voltages across each resistor. Let the current through each be $I$.
If $V$ is the voltage and $R$ is the total resistance between $A$ and $B$, the definition of resistance gives:

$$
\begin{equation*}
V=I R \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

For each resistor the definition of resistance gives:
$V_{1}=I R_{1}$ and $V_{2}=I R_{2}$ and $V_{3}=I R_{3}$
Now, $V=V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3}$ (voltages in series)
HL

$$
\begin{align*}
& \Rightarrow V=I R_{1}+I R_{2}+I R_{3} \\
& \Rightarrow V=I\left(R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}\right) \tag{2}
\end{align*}
$$

Comparing (1) and (2) gives:

$$
\begin{gathered}
I R=I\left(R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}\right) \\
R=R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}
\end{gathered}
$$

This result, clearly, will apply for any number of resistors in series; that is:

$$
R=R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}+\ldots
$$

## Resistors in parallel

Figure 22.10 shows three resistors, of resistances $R_{1}, R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$ ohms, connected in parallel. The overall resistance, $R$, of the combination (i.e. the resistance between $A$ and $B$ ) can be found from the following formula:

$$
\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}+\frac{1}{R_{3}}
$$

If resistors of resistances $R_{1}, R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$ ohms are connected in parallel with each other, the resistance of the combination can be calculated from the formula:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-385.jpg?height=402&width=730&top_left_y=1757&top_left_x=1995)
Figure 22.10

$$
\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}+\frac{1}{R_{3}}
$$

(F\&T page 61)

## Worked Example 3

## Question

Find the total resistance $R$ of the combination shown.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{R} & =\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}+\frac{1}{R_{3}} \\
& =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{10} \\
& =\frac{11}{20} \\
\frac{R}{1} & =\frac{20}{11} \\
R & =1.82 \Omega
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-385.jpg?height=464&width=817&top_left_y=2627&top_left_x=1478)
Figure 22.11

## Worked Example 5

## Question

Find the current flowing through each resistor.

## Solution

Let the currents be $I_{1}, I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ as indicated.
Resistance of the two resistors in parallel:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{p}}} & =\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}} \\
& =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{6} \\
R_{\mathrm{p}} & =2.4 \Omega
\end{aligned}
$$

Total resistance of circuit: $R=3+2.4=5.4 \Omega$
Calculate current from battery:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-387.jpg?height=785&width=889&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1429)
Figure 22.13

$$
\begin{aligned}
I & =\frac{V}{R} \\
& =\frac{12}{5.4} \\
& =2.22 \mathrm{~A}=\text { current through } 3 \Omega \text { resistor }
\end{aligned}
$$

Potential difference across $3 \Omega$ resistor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{1} & =I R \\
& =(2.22)(3) \\
& =6.667 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

Potential difference across parallel combination:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{2} & =12-V_{1} \\
& =12-6.667 \\
& =5.333 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the remaining currents using $I=\frac{V}{R}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& I_{1}=\frac{5.333}{4}=1.33 \mathrm{~A} \\
& I_{2}=\frac{5.333}{6}=0.89 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

To check, confirm that:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I & =I_{1}+I_{2} \\
& =1.33+0.89 \\
& =2.22 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Student Experiment 22.2

To investigate, by experimentation, the behaviour of resistors connected in series and in parallel, in electrical circuits

## Summary

In this experiment, you will set up resistors (a) in series, (b) in parallel and (c) in a combination of series and parallel.
In each case, you will:

- Try to predict and justify what you think the resistance of the combination will be
- Measure the individual resistances and the resistance of the combination with an ohmmeter
- Use the relevant formulae to calculate the resistance of the combination
- Compare your answers


## Equipment

Several resistors, ohmmeter, connecting leads.

## Method

## (a) Resistors in series

1. Measure the resistances of two or three individual resistors.
2. Connect the resistors in series.
3. Would you expect the resistance of the combination to be less than, equal to or greater than:
a) The resistance of any one of the resistors?
b) The sum of the resistances of the resistors?
4. Measure the resistance of the combination using an ohmmeter.
5. Calculate the expected resistance of the combination using the relevant formula.
6. Compare your results from Steps 3, 4 and 5.
7. Repeat the above steps with different resistors.

## (b) Resistors in parallel

1. Measure the resistances of two identical resistors.
2. Connect the resistors in parallel.
3. Would you expect the resistance of the combination to be less than, equal to or greater than the resistance of either one of the resistors?
4. Measure the resistance of the combination using an ohmmeter.
5. Calculate the expected resistance of the combination using the relevant formula.
6. Compare your results from Steps 3, 4 and 5.
7. Repeat the above steps with two or three resistors of different resistances.

## (c) Resistors in parallel connected in series with another resistor

1. Measure the resistances of three individual resistors.
2. Connect the resistors as shown in Figure 22.23.
3. Which of the three resistors is the resistance of the combination always greater than?

## Result

## Sources of error

- Heat the water slowly, otherwise the temperature of the coil will change too quickly and it will be difficult to read the temperature and resistance of the coil.
- Stir the water continuously, so that it will have a uniform temperature. The temperature of the glycerol should then also be uniform.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-392.jpg?height=824&width=903&top_left_y=319&top_left_x=1673)
Figure 22.25 Variation of the resistance of a metal with temperature

## Metallic conductors

In a metal, some electrons are not stuck to any particular atom, and are free to move around the metal. For example, in copper, there is usually one 'free electron' from every copper atom. An electric current is the movement of these free electrons through the metal. As the electrons move, they collide with the atoms, which provides resistance to their motion. The greater the number of collisions, the greater the resistance.

## Effect of increasing temperature

As the temperature of the metal is increased, the metal atoms vibrate at a greater rate. So, as the electrons move through the metal, they collide more frequently with the atoms, which means there is more resistance to their movement. In other words, the resistance of a metallic conductor increases as the temperature increases.

- For moderate changes in temperature (less than $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ) it is found that the change in resistance is proportional to the change in temperature.
- Figure 22.25 shows graphically how the resistance of a metal changes with temperature. Note that the graph is a straight line, but it does not pass through the origin. The resistance changes linearly with temperature.
- Note that the increase is not very great. For example, a piece of copper wire that has a resistance of $10 \Omega$ at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ might have a resistance of $13 \Omega$ at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Note: The resistance of a metal increases as the temperature does.
For moderate changes in temperature, (less than $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), the resistance changes linearly with temperature (Figure 22.25).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-393.jpg?height=932&width=893&top_left_y=1855&top_left_x=1813)
Figure 22.27 Variation of the resistance of a thermistor with temperature

Note: The thermistor is immersed in glycerol (or oil) rather than water because glycerol is a better conductor of heat and makes better thermal contact with the wire and it also doesn't conduct electricity.

## The thermistor

'Thermistor' is an abbreviation for the word 'thermal resistor'. A thermistor (Figure 22.28) is a semiconductor whose resistance decreases rapidly with increasing temperature (Figure 22.27 ). Such a thermistor might have a resistance of $800 \Omega$ at $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and a resistance of $80 \Omega$ at $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

## Insulators and semiconductors

In an insulator or semiconductor, most electrons are attached to particular atoms. Only a few (in semiconductors) or almost none (in insulators) are free to move

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-393.jpg?height=486&width=529&top_left_y=3314&top_left_x=2216)
Figure 22.28 A thermistor

## Effect of increasing temperature

When the temperature of an insulator or semiconductor is increased, more electrons are freed from their atoms. If a potential difference is put across the material, these free electrons can form an electric current. This means the resistance of an insulator or semiconductor decreases as the temperature increases.
The atoms still vibrate more as the temperature increases, but the increase in the number of conduction electrons totally masks this effect, meaning the resistance decreases overall. In a metal, virtually no extra conduction electrons are produced when the metal's temperature increases.

### 22.7 Resistivity

As well as temperature, the resistance of a conductor also depends on:

- Its length
- Its cross-sectional area
- The material from which it is made

Figure 22.29 shows a wire conductor. If the wire is cut at right angles to its length, as shown, the exposed ends are circular. The circles all have the same area, so the wire has a uniform cross-sectional area.

## Resistance and length

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-395.jpg?height=636&width=698&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=2047)
Figure 22.29

Figure 22.30(A) shows a piece of wire of uniform circular cross-section and length $l$ metres. Suppose its resistance is $R$ ohms.
Figure 22.30 (B) shows two such pieces of wire connected in series. The resistance of this piece must be $2 R$ ohms since it is made of two pieces of resistance $R$ connected in series. If any other number of pieces of the same wire are added, the resistance would increase proportionally. This can be verified with an ohmmeter. So, the resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-395.jpg?height=356&width=1835&top_left_y=1513&top_left_x=324)
Figure 22.30 If the length is doubled, the resistance is doubled.

The resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length:
$R \propto I$ (for a fixed cross-sectional area $A$ )

## Resistance and cross-sectional area

By experiment, it is found that the resistance of a uniform conductor of fixed length is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, i.e. provided the length remains the same:

- If the cross-sectional area is doubled, the resistance is halved
- If the cross-sectional area is three times larger, the resistance is three times smaller
- If the cross-sectional area is four times smaller, the resistance is four times larger

This can be seen from the following. If two identical pieces of wire are connected in parallel, the resistance of the combination is half the resistance of each individual piece, using $\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}$. But, Figure 22.31 shows that connecting them in parallel is effectively doubling the crosssectional area through which the electric current can flow.

The resistance of a uniform conductor is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area:

$$
\begin{equation*}
R \propto \frac{1}{A} \text { (for a fixed length } l \text { ) } \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-395.jpg?height=284&width=538&top_left_y=2819&top_left_x=2057)
Figure 22.31 The cross-sectional area is doubled and the resistance is halved.

From (1) and (2) it follows that:

$$
R=\rho \frac{l}{A}
$$

where $\rho$ is a constant
(F\&T page 61)

- The constant of proportionality, $\rho$, is only a constant for the particular material in the conductor. For different materials, the value of $\rho$ is different.
- If the material is a good conductor, $\rho$ is small. If the material is a bad conductor, $\rho$ is large. Thus $\rho$ takes account of the fact that the resistance of a conductor depends on the material from which it is made.
- $\rho$ is called the resistivity of the material in the conductor.
- Solving $R=\rho \frac{l}{A}$ for $\rho$ gives:

$$
\rho=\frac{R A}{l}
$$

So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { unit of resistivity } & =\frac{(\text { unit of } R)(\text { unit of } A)}{\text { unit of } I} \\
& =\frac{\Omega \mathrm{m}^{2}}{\mathrm{~m}} \\
& =\Omega \mathrm{m}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the SI unit of resistivity is the ohm metre ( $\Omega$ m).

If a conductor of length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$ has a resistance $R$, the constant $\rho$ given by:

$$
\rho=\frac{R A}{l}
$$

is called the resistivity of the material in the conductor.
(F\&T page 61)
Resistivity of a material could also be defined as the resistance of a piece of that material of length 1 m and cross-sectional area $1 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$.

| Material | Resistivity ( $\Omega$ m) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Silver | $1.6 \times 10^{-8}$ |
| Copper | $1.7 \times 10^{-8}$ |
| Iron | $9.8 \times 10^{-8}$ |
| Manganin | $4.2 \times 10^{-7}$ |
| Nichrome | $1.12 \times 10^{-6}$ |
| Silicon | $1 \times 10^{3}$ approx. |
| Distilled water | $5 \times 10^{3}$ |
| Glass | $10^{12}$ approx. |

Table 22.1 Resistivities at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ of some common materials

## Worked Example 6

## Question

A uniform wire of length 2 m has a resistance of $12 \Omega$. Find the resistance of a piece of identical wire of length 11.4 m .

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { length of second wire } & =\frac{11.4}{2} \times \text { length of first wire } \\
& =5.7 \times \text { length of first wire }
\end{aligned}
$$

Since resistance is proportional to length, the resistance of the second wire will be 5.7 times that of the first.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { resistance of second wire } & =12 \times 5.7 \\
& =68.4 \Omega
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 7

## Question

What length of copper wire of cross-sectional area $2 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ is needed to make a resistor of resistance $10 \Omega$ ? Resistivity of copper $=1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \mathrm{~m}$

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\rho & =\frac{R A}{l} \\
l & =\frac{R A}{\rho} \\
& =\frac{(10)\left(2 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{1.7 \times 10^{-8}} \\
& =1176.5 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that length must be expressed in metres and cross-sectional area in metres squared when using this formula. Recall that $1 \mathrm{~m}^{2}=10^{6} \mathrm{~mm}^{2} \Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}=1 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$

## Worked Example 8

## Question

A coil of copper wire 20 m long has uniform composition and uniform cross-sectional area. The diameter of the wire is 0.055 mm . Taking the resistivity of copper to be $1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \mathrm{~m}$, calculate the resistance of the coil.

## Solution

First find the cross-sectional area of the coil:

$$
\begin{aligned}
d=0.055 \mathrm{~mm} & =0.055 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} \\
r & =\frac{d}{2} \\
& =\frac{0.055 \times 10^{-3}}{2} \\
& =2.75 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A & =\pi r^{2} \\
& =\pi r\left(2.75 \times 10^{-5}\right)^{2} \\
& =2.376 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & =\frac{\rho l}{A} \\
& =\frac{\left(1.7 \times 10^{-8}\right)(20)}{2.376 \times 10^{-9}} \\
& =143 \Omega
\end{aligned}
$$

### 22.8 The potential divider circuit

## Worked Example 9

## Question

Calculate the potential difference across each resistor in the given circuit.

## Solution

Total resistance of circuit: $2 \Omega+4 \Omega=6 \Omega$
Current flowing:

$$
I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{12}{6}=2 \mathrm{~A}
$$

Potential difference across top resistor:

$$
V_{1}=I R=(2)(2)=4 \mathrm{~V}
$$

Potential difference across bottom resistor:

$$
V_{2}=I R=(2)(4)=8 \mathrm{~V}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-398.jpg?height=542&width=583&top_left_y=1692&top_left_x=1735)
Figure 22.32

## Worked Example 10

## Question

Calculate the potential difference across each resistor in the given circuit.

## Solution

Total resistance of circuit: $1000 \Omega+2 \Omega=1002 \Omega$
Current flowing: $\quad I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{12}{1002}=0.11976 \mathrm{~A}$
Potential difference across $1000 \Omega$ resistor:

$$
V_{1}=I R=(0.011976)(1000)=11.976 \mathrm{~V}
$$

Potential difference across $2 \Omega$ resistor: $V_{2}=I R=(0.011976)(2)=0.023952 \mathrm{~V}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-398.jpg?height=545&width=617&top_left_y=2571&top_left_x=1959)
Figure 22.33

From the last two Worked Examples, if two resistors are connected across a fixed voltage supply:

- The greater voltage is across the greater resistor.
- The sum of the voltages is the supply voltage.
- If one resistance is much larger than the other, the voltage across the small resistor is approximately zero and the voltage across the larger resistance is almost the same as the supply voltage.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-398.jpg?height=558&width=688&top_left_y=3320&top_left_x=1933)
Figure 22.34 A variable potential divider

The circuits in Figures 22.32 and 22.33 are examples of potential divider circuits.
The circuit in Figure 22.34 is called a variable potential divider circuit. As the moving contact $C$ moves from $A$ to $B$, the resistance of $A C$ increases and so does the voltage across it. The voltage increases from zero volts, when the contact is at $A$, to 12 volts when it is at $B$. Set up this circuit in the laboratory and measure the output voltage with a voltmeter. See how the voltage varies as $C$ is moved.

## Summary What I should know

- The resistance $(R)$ of a conductor is the ratio of the potential difference across it to the current flowing through it: $\quad R=\frac{V}{I}$
- The SI unit of resistance is the ohm ( $\Omega$ ).
- Ohm's law states that for certain conductors (mainly metals), at a constant temperature, the current flowing through them is directly proportional to the potential difference across them:

$$
V \propto I \Rightarrow \frac{V}{I}=\mathrm{a} \text { constant }
$$

- If resistors of resistances $R_{1}, R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$ ohms are connected in series, the total resistance $R$ of the combination is equal to the sum of the resistances of each resistor, i.e.

$$
R=R_{1}+R_{2}+R_{3}
$$

- If resistors of resistances $R_{1}, R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$ ohms are connected in parallel, the resistance of the combination can be calculated from the formula:

$$
\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}+\frac{1}{R_{3}}
$$

- The resistance of a metallic conductor increases as the temperature increases.
- The resistance of most other substances (including carbon and semiconductors) decreases as the temperature increases.
- A thermistor is a semiconductor whose resistance decreases rapidly with increasing temperature.
- The resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length:

$$
R \propto I \text { (for a fixed cross-sectional area } A \text { ) }
$$

- The resistance of a uniform conductor is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area:

$$
\left.R \propto \frac{1}{A} \quad \text { (for a fixed length } l\right)
$$

- If a conductor of length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$ has a resistance $R$, the constant $\rho$ given by:

$$
\rho=\frac{R A}{l} \text { is called the resistivity of the material in the conductor. }
$$

- The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm metre ( $\Omega$ m).
- A variable resistor connected across a DC power source can be used to supply a voltage of any value from 0 volts to the value of the voltage of the power source. Such an arrangement is called a variable potential divider circuit.

# 23 Heating Effect of an Electric Current

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand the heating effect of an electric current
- To ensure students can model the rate of conversion of electrical energy in components of electric circuits
- To ensure students understand how the relationship between the current flowing through and the voltage across a non-ohmic conductor is related to temperature
- To ensure students can model fuses and circuit breakers in electricity supplies
- To ensure students appreciate the advantage of use of high voltage in the transmission of electrical energy


## Keywords

- $I-V$ graph
- Non-ohmic conductor
- Filament bulb
- Transformers
- Live
- Neutral
- Distribution box
- Earthing
- Fuse
- Miniature circuit breaker (MCB)
- Residual current device (RCD)
- Kilowatt-hour (kW h)


### 23.1 The heating effect of an electric current

The heating effect of an electric current has numerous applications, such as in electric heaters, cookers, hairdryers, kettles and so on. However, the unintended production of heat motivates engineers to improve designs of electromagnetic devices to make them more efficient and sustainable.
The amount of heat energy produced by an electric current depends on:

- The size of the current, $I$
- The resistance, $R$, of the conductor through which it flows
- The time, $t$, for which it flows

This result follows from equations in previous chapters:
Substitute $V=I R$ into $P=V I$ to give:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =(I R) I \\
& =I^{2} R
\end{aligned}
$$

Then rearrange $P=\frac{W}{t}$ to make work the subject:

$$
W=P t
$$

Finally, substitute $P=I^{2} R$ into $W=P t$ to give: $\quad W=I^{2} R t$
Based on this formula, heat energy changes in the following ways:

- $W \propto I^{2}$ if $t$ and $R$ are fixed
- $W \propto R$ if $I$ and $t$ are fixed
- $W \propto t$ if $I$ and $R$ are fixed

If a current, $I$, flows in a conductor of resistance, $R$, for a time, $t$, the heat energy, $W$, produced is given by:

$$
W=I^{2} R t
$$

If a current, $I$, flows in a conductor of resistance, $R$, the rate at which heat is produced, $P$ (that is, the power dissipated), is given by:

$$
P=I^{2} R
$$

Note that both these formulae only apply to heat energy produced.

## Worked example 1

## Question

Find the heat produced in a $20 \Omega$ resistor by a current of 3 A flowing for 40 s .

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
W & =I^{2} R t \\
& =(32)(20)(40) \\
& =7200 \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked example 2

## Question

Find the rate at which heat is produced (in other words, the power dissipated) by a current of 80 mA in a $2 \mathrm{k} \Omega$ resistor.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =I^{2} R \\
& =\left(80 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}(2000) \\
& =12.8 \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked example 3

## Question

When a current of 3 A flows in a wire, heat is produced at a rate of 60 W . What current would produce heat at a rate of 540 W in the same wire, assuming its resistance did not change?

## Solution

First work out the resistance in the wire:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =I^{2} R \\
60 & =(3)^{2} R \\
R & =\frac{60}{(3)^{2}} \\
& =6.66 \mathbf{\Omega}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then work out the current to produce heat at a rate of 540 W in the same wire:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =I^{2} R \\
I & =\sqrt{\frac{P}{R}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{540}{6.66}} \\
& =9 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Alternative solution

Since $P \propto I^{2}$ and 540 is 9 times 60, then the current must be three times larger: $3 \times 3=9 \mathrm{~A}$.

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A current of 4 A flows in an electric drill when it is connected to a 230 V mains supply. Some of the input energy is dissipated as heat in the coil of the motor.
The drill has an electrical resistance of $20 \Omega$. Calculate:
a) The power dissipated as heat in the drill
b) The input power supplied to the drill by the 230 V mains supply
c) The percentage efficiency of the drill.

## Solution

a)

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm{h}} & =I^{2} R \\
& =(4)^{2}(20) \\
& =320 \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}
$$

b)

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm{i}} & =V I \\
& =(230)(4) \\
& =920 \mathrm{~W}
\end{aligned}
$$

c) useful power output in drill:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm{o}} & =920-320 \\
& =600 \mathrm{~W} \\
\text { percentage efficiency } & =\frac{P_{\mathrm{o}}}{P_{\mathrm{i}}} \times 100 \\
& =\frac{600}{920} \times 100 \\
& =65.2 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

## Revision note

Recall from page 200 that:
Percentage efficiency $=\frac{\text { useful output power }}{\text { input power }} \times 100 \%$

### 23.3 Advantage of high voltage in the transmission of electrical energy

Figure 23.6 shows a simplified version of the national grid. The generating station sends electrical energy to homes through transmission wires with a total resistance of $R$ ohms. If the current flowing in the wires is $I$, then the heat energy wasted per second in the wires is given by $P=I^{2} R$. So, the larger the current, the larger the energy wasted as heat.
Transformers are devices that can change the voltage of the supply (see Chapter 27).
Since power $P=$ current $I \times$ voltage $V$ a bigger voltage produces a smaller current for a given power.
Transformer 1 increases the voltage to several hundred kilovolts, reducing the current and, therefore, minimising heat losses in the transmission wires. Transformer 2 then reduces the voltage to a safer value to use in homes and businesses.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-405.jpg?height=463&width=1756&top_left_y=1191&top_left_x=325)
Figure 23.6

### 23.4 Domestic electric circuits

Mains electricity is supplied at 230 V AC in Ireland and the EU. Figure 23.7 shows a simplified diagram of the electric wiring found in a typical house. You do not need to remember this diagram.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-405.jpg?height=740&width=1775&top_left_y=2194&top_left_x=325)
Figure 23.7

Two wires enter the house from the mains:

- The live wire has a voltage that varies from about +325 V to -325 V . It is very dangerous. Contact with this wire could be fatal.
- The neutral wire should be at or very near to zero volts. The neutral wire is at the same potential as the Earth.
When the live wire enters the house, it is first interrupted by a master switch and the house's main fuse. It then passes through a meter (similar to a joulemeter) which can measure the amount of electrical energy used. It then goes to the distribution box. The neutral wire follows a similar route.


## House wiring layout

To supply power to the various appliances in the house, a live wire and a neutral wire must be connected to each appliance. These wires come from the distribution box.

## Appliances that take a large current

Appliances that take a large current, such as an electric cooker, an immersion heater or an electric shower, have a separate live and neutral wire coming from the distribution box. Each circuit like this has its own fuse.

## Connections to lights

Since lights do not take much current, several of them may be connected to the same fuse. Each light has a separate switch in the live wire. The lights are connected in parallel with each other, so that if one bulb fails, the others are not affected.

## Connections to the sockets

The sockets are usually connected in a ring, with the live terminals of each socket connected together. Power is fed along both sides of the ring to each socket. The neutrals are also connected together and then connected back to the neutral at the distribution box. Each ring circuit has a fuse in its live wire.

## Switches

A switch should always be connected in the live wire, so that when the switch is open, the appliance is disconnected from the live.

## Danger of electrocution

The human body is an electrical conductor. If a person touches the live wire and the neutral wire at the same time, current will flow through their body. The same happens if a person touches the live wire while standing on the ground - current will flow between the live and the Earth, passing through the body.
The danger depends on the path the current takes. A current that flows across the chest - such as from one hand to the other or from hand to foot - can pass through the heart, which greatly increases the risk of death. A shock from one hand to the same-side foot may not be fatal, though still dangerous and potentially very painful.
Wearing insulating gloves and shoes (as professional electricians often do) increases resistance at entry and exit points, which reduces the amount of current that can flow. While this improves safety in some situations, it is not guaranteed protection, especially at higher voltages or with faulty equipment.

## Earthing

Suppose a fault occurs in an electric kettle causing the live wire to come into contact with the metal casing of the kettle. The metal casing is now at the potential of the live wire.
If the kettle is insulated from the ground, nothing happens.
But if someone touches the kettle, an electric current will pass through them to the ground (Figure 23.8), possibly killing them.
If, however, the metal of the kettle is earthed (Figure 23.9), current from the live wire will flow through the kettle to earth. Since this path has low resistance, a large current will flow. This will blow the fuse (see page 395) and disconnect the kettle from the live.
If the current is not large enough to blow the fuse, it is still safe to touch the kettle, since its potential is zero when earthed.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-406.jpg?height=1131&width=951&top_left_y=2734&top_left_x=1673)
Figure 23.8

All electrical equipment with exposed metal parts should be earthed (for example, by the yellow/green wires in Figures 23.9 and 23.11).
Likewise, all metal water pipes, metal taps, metal water tanks and so on in a house must be earthed (this is called bonding to earth). This means, for example, if the metal pipes become accidentally connected to live, they will not be at 230 V but will remain at zero potential and will not electrocute anyone.

## Fuses

If an excessive current passes through an appliance, it may cause it to overheat or catch on fire. A fuse is a piece of wire that will melt when a current of a certain size passes through it. The fuse is connected in series with the appliance. In this way, the fuse protects an appliance if a fault occurs, causing an excessive current to flow, by breaking the circuit and preventing the large current from flowing.

A fuse should be connected in the live wire, so that, as well as

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-407.jpg?height=1033&width=955&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=1793)
Figure 23.9

switching off the current if it blows, it also disconnects the appliance from the live. Figure 23.10 shows the circuit symbol for a fuse.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-407.jpg?height=919&width=1023&top_left_y=1572&top_left_x=322)
Figure 23.10

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-407.jpg?height=154&width=493&top_left_y=1582&top_left_x=1360)
Figure 23.10

Figure 23.11

Figure 23.11 shows a plug with the live wire connected to the pin with the fuse. Take note of the colours of the wires. Live is BROWN, neutral is BLUE and earth is GREEN/YELLOW.

## Note:

- The wire in a fuse melts, breaking the circuit, if an excessive current flows.
- A fuse protects against fire but may not respond or act fast enough to protect against electrocution.
- A fuse is always connected in the live wire. As well as switching off the current if it blows, it also disconnects the appliance from the live.
- When the fault is resolved, the fuse must be replaced with a similar fuse.
- Fuses are found in plugs, in some appliances and in the distribution box.
- Fuses have been replaced by miniature circuit breakers (MCBs) in most distribution boxes.


## Worked Example 5

## Question

Mains voltage is supplied at 230 V . An electric kettle has a power rating of 2 kW . Modern plugs contain a small fuse which comes with a rating of $1 \mathrm{~A}, 2 \mathrm{~A}, 3 \mathrm{~A}, 5 \mathrm{~A}$ or 13 A . Which is the most suitable fuse to use in the plug of the kettle?

## Solution

$$
\text { power, } \begin{aligned}
P & =2 \mathrm{~kW}=2000 \mathrm{~W} \\
P & =V I \\
I & =\frac{P}{V} \\
& =\frac{2000}{230} \\
& =8.7 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the 13 A fuse would be the only one suitable.

## Miniature circuit breakers (MCBs)

Miniature circuit breakers (MCBs) are usually used instead of fuses in the distribution box as they operate faster than fuses and can be reset by flicking a switch. They contain a bimetallic strip and an electromagnet. When the current is larger than a pre-set value, one of these pulls two contacts apart and breaks the circuit.

- If a small overload of current occurs, the increased current causes the bimetallic strip to heat up and bend; this releases a latch that causes the switch to trip.
- If a short circuit occurs, the rapid increase in current generates a very strong magnetic field in a solenoid. This immediately attracts an iron bar with large force that releases the latch, and the switch trips almost instantaneously, disconnecting the circuit.


## Residual current devices (RCDs)

Circuits connected to the sockets in a house are protected by residual current devices (RCDs). This is in addition to the protection offered by fuses in appliances and MCBs in the distribution box.
An RCD is designed to safeguard humans from electrocution. If someone touches a live wire, current will flow through them to earth and not back through the neutral wire. This means there will be a difference in the value of the current between the live wire and the neutral.
When this difference reaches a pre-set value (usually 30 mA ), the RCD trips very quickly (usually in less than 30 milliseconds), disconnecting the circuit from the live before injury or electrocution can occur. Fuses and MCBs cannot blow fast enough to protect people in this way.
An RCD will not protect you if you come in contact with live and neutral at the same time.

## Worked example 6

## Question

A lamp has a power rating of 100 W . It operates on 230 V mains.
a) What current does it draw?
b) What size fuse should be put in its plug, 3 A or 13 A ?

## Solution

a)

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =V I \\
I & =\frac{P}{V} \\
& =\frac{100}{230} \\
& =0.43 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) The 3 A fuse is much more suitable.

## Worked example 7

## Question

An electric cooker has four 500 W plates, a 2 kW grill and a 3 kW oven. It operates on 230 V mains. Is a 40 A fuse suitable for this cooker?

## Solution

Total power, $P=(4)(500)+2000+3000=7000 \mathrm{~W}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
P & =V I \\
I & =\frac{P}{V} \\
& =\frac{7000}{230} \\
& =30.4 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

The maximum current the cooker takes is 30.4 A , so a 40 A fuse is suitable.

## The kilowatt-hour

The joule is a very small unit of energy to use when dealing with domestic electricity. A unit of energy called the kilowatt-hour ( $\mathbf{k W} \mathbf{h}$ ) is used instead. This is the amount of energy used by a 1000 W appliance in one hour. The number of 'units' recorded in an electricity bill is the number of kilowatt-hours used.

The kilowatt-hour ( kWh ) is the amount of energy used by a 1000 W appliance in one hour.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Number of kilowatt-hours } & =\text { number of kilowatts × number of hours } \\
\text { Energy } & =\text { power } \text { × } \text { time }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked example 8

## Question

How many joules are there in a kilowatt-hour?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 1000 \mathrm{~W}=1000 \text { joules per second } \\
& 1 \text { hour }=(60)(60) \text { seconds } \\
& \text { energy }=\text { power } \text { × } \text { time }=(1000)(60)(60)=3.6 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~J}=3.6 \mathrm{MJ}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \text { kilowatt-hour } & =3600000 \mathrm{~J} \\
1 \mathrm{~kW} \mathrm{~h} & =3.6 \mathrm{MJ}
\end{aligned}
$$
