## Summary What I should know

- The heat energy, $W$, produced in a conductor of resistance, $R$, by a current, $l$, in a time, $t$, is given by: $W=I^{2} R t$
- The power, $P$, dissipated in a conductor of resistance, $R$, by a current, $I$, is given by: $P=I^{2} R$
- A switch should always be connected in the live wire.
- A fuse should always be connected in the live wire.
- A miniature circuit breaker (MCB) should be connected in the live wire.
- When the difference in the value of the current between the live and the neutral reaches a pre-set value (usually 30 mA ), a residual current device (RCD) trips very quickly (usually in less than 30 milliseconds), disconnecting the circuit from the live before injury or electrocution can occur.
- All electrical equipment with exposed metal parts should be earthed.
- All metal water pipes, metal taps, metal water tanks and so on in a house must be connected to earth.
- The kilowatt-hour $(\mathbf{k W} \mathbf{h})$ is the amount of energy used by a 1000 W appliance in one hour.

# 24 Semiconductors

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand conduction in a pure semiconductor, i.e. intrinsic conduction
- To ensure students understand doping and conduction in p-type and n-type semiconductors, i.e extrinsic conduction
- To ensure students can model the relationship between the current flowing through and the voltage across a semiconductor diode in forward and reverse bias
- To ensure students understand the operation of a diode, an LDR, an LED and a transistor
- To ensure students appreciate and understand the action of a transistor as a switch
- To ensure students are aware of the enormous impact semiconductors have on virtually all aspects our lives


### 24.1 Semiconductors

Virtually every electronic device now available is based on the conduction of electricity by materials known as semiconductors. What is a semiconductor?

A semiconductor is a substance whose resistivity is between that of a good conductor and a good insulator. The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases as its temperature increases.

## Keywords

- Semiconductor
- Valence electron
- Conduction electron
- Positive hole or hole
- Intrinsic conduction
- Thermistor
- Light-dependent resistor (LDR)
- Doping
- n-type semiconductor
- p-type semiconductor
- Extrinsic conduction
- p-n junction
- p-n diode or semiconductor diode
- Depletion layer
- Junction voltage
- Reverse-biased
- Leakage current
- Forward-biased
- Light-emitting diode (LED)
- Rectification
- npn junction transistor
- Base and base current $\left(I_{b}\right)$
- Collector and collector current ( $I$ )
- Emitter and emitter current (I)

Examples of semiconductors are silicon, gallium arsenide, germanium and cadmium sulphide.

### 24.2 Conduction in semiconductors

Figure 24.1 shows the outer electron arrangement in the semiconductor silicon at a temperature very near zero kelvin.

- Each silicon atom has its four outer electrons (called valence electrons) involved in covalent bonds with four other silicon atoms.
- These electrons are not free to wander from atom to atom.
- Silicon is therefore an insulator near zero kelvin.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-412.jpg?height=1287&width=1457&top_left_y=2513&top_left_x=1158)
Figure 24.1 The outer electron arrangement in pure silicon at a temperature very near zero kelvin. The orange circles are the outer electrons.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-413.jpg?height=1322&width=1671&top_left_y=270&top_left_x=328)
Figure 24.2 The outer electron arrangement in silicon at room temperature

Figure 24.2 shows the outer electron arrangement in silicon at room temperature. At this temperature, some of the valence electrons have enough thermal energy to break their covalent bonds and are free to move from atom to atom. These are called conduction electrons. The energy of a conduction electron is greater than the energy of a valence electron. When an electron breaks free from a covalent bond, it leaves behind a gap in the atom from which it came. This gap is called a positive hole or simply a hole. The atom has lost an electron, creating an imbalance in the numbers of protons and electrons, which leaves an overall positive charge on the atom. So, we say a hole is positively charged.

When an electron breaks free from a covalent bond, it leaves behind a gap in the atom from which it came. This gap is called a positive hole or simply a hole.

A valence electron from a neighbouring atom can move into this hole, producing another hole in the atom from which it came. So, as an electron moves into one hole it produces another. This process can continue and can be viewed as a movement of positive holes through the silicon.

If a potential difference is now put across the silicon, it will conduct electricity. The charge carriers are the conduction electrons moving in one direction and an equal number of positive holes moving the opposite direction. Conduction like this, in a pure semiconductor, is called intrinsic conduction. Intrinsic conduction has low conductivity.

Conduction in a pure semiconductor due to electrons moving from negative to positive (- to +) and an equal number of holes moving in the opposite direction is called intrinsic conduction.
The conductivity is low, and the semiconductor is called an intrinsic semiconductor.
The resistivity of an intrinsic semiconductor is quite large, e.g. a piece of pure silicon of diameter 1 mm and length 1 cm has a resistance of about 8 million ohms at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. To increase the conductivity (or reduce the resistivity) of a semiconductor, you must increase the number of mobile charge carriers present in it. This can be done in a number of ways.

## Increasing the temperature of a semiconductor increases its conductivity

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-414.jpg?height=662&width=1378&top_left_y=533&top_left_x=221)
Figure 24.3 (A) A thermistor and (B) its circuit symbol. (C) Thermistors are available in a variety of shapes and sizes.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-414.jpg?height=786&width=910&top_left_y=455&top_left_x=1666)
Figure 24.4 Variation of the resistance of a thermistor with temperature

By increasing the temperature of a semiconductor, more electrons get enough energy to break out of their covalent bonds. This means more conduction (free) electrons and holes are produced. Since these are charge carriers, the conductivity of the semiconductor is increased.
The thermistor (Figure 24.3) is a good example of a semiconductor whose conductivity increases rapidly with increasing temperature. This can be demonstrated by measuring the resistance of a thermistor with an ohmmeter at a number of different temperatures, giving a graph similar to Figure 24.4 (see Student Experiment 22.3(B) on page 380).

A thermistor is a semiconductor device whose resistance decreases rapidly with increasing temperature.

## Shining light on some semiconductors increases their conductivity

The conductivity of some semiconductors can be increased by shining light on them. For example, cadmium sulphide shows a notable increase in conductivity when light shines on it. Valence electrons in the material get enough energy from the light to become conduction electrons, therefore producing more conduction electrons and holes and reducing the resistivity of the material. Typically, the resistance of cadmium sulphide changes from several megaohms in darkness to a few hundred ohms in daylight. A semiconductor that behaves like this is called a light-dependent resistor (LDR) (Figure 24.5).
The behaviour of an LDR can be investigated by measuring its resistance in the dark and in varying degrees of brightness (by varying its distance from a bulb).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-414.jpg?height=789&width=1867&top_left_y=2812&top_left_x=263)
Figure 24.5 (A) A light-dependent resistor (LDR), (B) its circuit symbol and (C) a graph showing how its resistance varies with light intensity.

[^4]
## The conductivity of a semiconductor can be increased by the presence of certain impurities

The conductivity of a semiconductor may be increased by adding small amounts of certain impurities to it. This procedure is called doping.

Doping is the adding of controlled small amounts of certain impurities to a pure semiconductor to increase its conductivity.

In the case of silicon, small amounts of substances with a valency of either 5 or 3 are added, when it is in a molten state at manufacture. The more impurity added, the greater the increase in conductivity. The semiconductors formed are called $\boldsymbol{n}$-type or $\mathbf{p}$-type semiconductors.

## n-type semiconductor

Figure 24.6 shows an $n$-type semiconductor where some silicon atoms have been replaced with phosphorus atoms.

- A phosphorous atom has five valence electrons.
- Phosphorous atoms are roughly the same size as silicon atoms and fit into the crystal structure of silicon.
- Only four of the five valence electrons are needed to form the four covalent bonds keeping the phosphorous in the lattice.
- The other electron becomes free to wander throughout the crystal, i.e. it becomes a conduction electron. By having sufficient phosphorous atoms present, the conductivity of the material can be greatly increased due to these extra conduction electrons.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-415.jpg?height=932&width=2185&top_left_y=1823&top_left_x=325)
Figure 24.6 An n-type semiconductor. Each phosphorous atom introduces an extra electron for conduction.

In an n-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are negatively charged electrons.
An $\mathbf{n}$-type semiconductor is one in which the added impurity produces more free electrons available for conduction, e.g. phosphorous in silicon.

There is also some intrinsic conduction taking place with some electrons and an equal number of holes moving in the material. The holes are the minority charge carriers. Note that a piece of n-type semiconductor does not contain excess negative charge, so it is still neutral.

## p-type semiconductor

Figure 24.7 shows a p-type semiconductor where some silicon atoms have been replaced with boron atoms.

- A boron atom has only three valence electrons.
- Boron atoms are similar in size to silicon atoms and fit into the crystal structure of silicon.
- Since boron atoms have only three valence electrons, there is a vacancy or gap (a positive hole) in the crystal lattice at every boron atom.
- When a potential difference is put across this material, a valence electron from a nearby atom may move into the hole, causing a hole to appear in the atom from which it came. It is as if the hole moved from the boron atom to the other atom. This process will continue, and the hole appears to move through the silicon.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-416.jpg?height=704&width=1743&top_left_y=1061&top_left_x=201)
Figure 24.7 A p-type semiconductor. Each boron atom introduces an extra hole.

A p-type semiconductor is one in which the added impurity produces extra holes that are available for conduction, e.g. boron in silicon.

In a p-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are positively charged holes. There is also some intrinsic conduction taking place with some electrons and an equal number of holes moving in the material. The electrons are the minority charge carriers. Again, a p-type semiconductor does not contain excess positive charge, so it is still neutral.

Increased conduction in a semiconductor due to the addition of impurities is called extrinsic conduction. The semiconductor formed is called an extrinsic semiconductor.

### 24.3 The p-n junction

Figure 24.8 shows a semiconductor that was formed by doping one side of a piece of pure semiconductor p-type and the rest of it n-type.
The resulting semiconductor is called a $\mathbf{p}$-n junction. It is also called a p-n diode or a semiconductor diode.
Recall that:

- In a p-type semiconductor, there are several holes that behave as mobile positive ( + ) charge carriers.
- In an n-type semiconductor, there are several electrons not involved in bonding and are mobile negative ( - ) charge carriers.
- Both p-type and n-type semiconductors are electrically neutral, as they do not have excess charge.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-416.jpg?height=414&width=577&top_left_y=2767&top_left_x=1894)
Figure 24.8 A p-n junction and circuit symbol. On the symbol, the thicker black line represents the n-type side. The arrowhead represents the p-type side.

When the p-n junction is being formed (Figure 24.9), the following happens:

- Free electrons in the n-type material move into the p-type material. They do this since the mobile electron concentration is higher in the n-type material than the p-type material. Here they meet holes. When an electron meets a hole, it fills the hole. This means both the electron and the hole are no longer available for conduction.
- Similarly, holes in the p-type material move into the n-type material. They do this since the concentration of holes is higher in the p-type material than in the n-type material. Here they meet electrons, and an electron fills the hole. This means, again, both the electron and the hole are no longer available for conduction.
- In this way, a region forms near the junction containing virtually no free majority charge carriers (Figure 24.9). This region is called the depletion layer and it effectively behaves as an insulator.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-417.jpg?height=1574&width=1482&top_left_y=1054&top_left_x=325)
Figure 24.9

Not all the electrons from the n-type material nor all the holes from the p-type material move towards the junction. This is because as electrons leave the n-type material, it becomes positively charged. Likewise, holes entering the n-type material increase its positive charge. When enough positive charge accumulates in the n-type material, no more electrons leave it, since they are attracted to the positive charge. In a similar way, a negative charge accumulates in the p-type material as electrons enter it and holes leave it. The charge that accumulates across the junction causes a small voltage to appear across the

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-417.jpg?height=435&width=958&top_left_y=2811&top_left_x=1762)
Figure 24.10

junction called the junction voltage (Figure 24.10). For silicon, its value is about 0.6 volts, and for germanium, it is about 0.2 volts.

A p-n junction is a piece of semiconductor with part of it doped p-type and the rest doped n-type.

The depletion layer is the region at both sides of a p-n junction that contains no free majority charge carriers. It therefore behaves as an insulator.

The potential difference that exists across a p-n junction, caused by holes and electrons moving across the junction when it was formed, is called the junction voltage.

## Reverse-biased p-n junction

If a battery is connected to a diode, with the positive terminal of the battery connected to the n-type and the negative terminal connected to the p-type, the diode is said to be reverse-biased (Figure 24.11).
A reverse-biased p-n junction will not conduct current. This is because the positive terminal of the battery attracts electrons from the n-type and the negative terminal attracts holes from the p-type, making the depletion layer wider. Since the depletion layer is effectively an insulator, no current flows.
However, in reverse bias, a very small current (called the leakage current) may flow ( $1 \mu \mathrm{~A}$ or less). This is the intrinsic conduction discussed on page 401. It is a very small amount of conduction and is not due to the extra electrons or holes that were produced by doping.

## Forward-biased p-n junction

If the battery is connected with its positive terminal to the p-type and the negative terminal to the n-type, the diode is said to be forward-biased (Figure 24.12).
A forward-biased p-n junction will conduct current, provided the voltage of the battery is near to or greater than the junction voltage of the diode.
When the applied voltage is greater than the junction voltage, the negative terminal of the battery is able to force electrons into the depletion layer and the positive terminal can force holes into the depletion layer. In the depletion layer, these electrons recombine with the holes. As this happens, the negative terminal forces more electrons into the $n$-type, and electrons are drawn from the p-type by the positive terminal, producing more holes in the p-type. This process continues and the circuit conducts (Figure 24.13).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-418.jpg?height=381&width=591&top_left_y=332&top_left_x=1972)
Figure 24.11 A reversebiased p-n junction

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-418.jpg?height=919&width=1423&top_left_y=1982&top_left_x=195)
Figure 24.13

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-418.jpg?height=916&width=681&top_left_y=1985&top_left_x=1647)
Figure 24.14

When electrons and holes recombine in the depletion layer, the electrons lose energy. Remember that conduction electrons have higher energy than the holes, which are gaps in the valence layer. The energy lost by the electrons appears as heat in the junction (or light, as in an LED, page 401).

Current flow in a diode can be demonstrated with the equipment shown in Figure 24.14. When it is forward-biased, the bulb lights up, but when it is reverse-biased, the bulb does not light up.

A forward-biased p-n junction conducts current.
A reverse-biased p-n junction does not conduct current.

## Student Experiment 24.1

To investigate the relationship between the current flowing through and the voltage across a semiconductor diode，in forward and reverse bias

## Summary of method

SCAN ME
In this experiment，you will measure the voltage $V$ across and the current $I$ flowing through a semiconductor diode for several different values of the voltage．You will do this when the diode is forward－biased and then reverse－biased．You will then plot a graph of $I$ against $V$ ．

## Equipment

A semiconductor diode，a low－voltage DC power supply（ $0-20 \mathrm{~V}$ ），a variable resistor（ $0-2 \mathrm{k} \Omega$ ）， a milliammeter $(0-20 \mathrm{~mA})$ ，a microammeter $(0-10 \mu \mathrm{~A})$ ，a high－resistance voltmeter $(0-20 \mathrm{~V})$

## Method

1．Set up the circuit shown in Figure 24．15，where the diode is forward－biased．
2．With the movable terminal of the variable resistor at $A$ ，read the value of the potential difference across the diode from the voltmeter and the corresponding current on the milliammeter． Record these values．
3．By adjusting the variable resistor towards $B$ ，increase the voltage across the diode by about 0.2 V ．Measure and record the new values of $V$ and of $I$ ．

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-419.jpg?height=450&width=835&top_left_y=1162&top_left_x=1868)
Figure 24.15

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-419.jpg?height=456&width=832&top_left_y=1810&top_left_x=1871)
Figure 24.16

4．Repeat Step 3 until the current or the voltage is just less than the maximum recommended by the manufacturer of the diode （typically 50 mA ）．
5．Reverse the connections on the diode．In the circuit，the diode is now reverse－biased．
6．Remove the milliammeter and connect the microammeter in the circuit as shown in Figure 24．16．Note that the microammeter is not in the same position as the milliammeter was in Figure 24．15．
7．Starting with the movable terminal of the variable resistor at $A$ again，measure and record a series of values for $I$ and $V$ ．This time， $V$ can be increased in larger steps than before．
8．On graph paper，plot a graph of $I$（on the $y$－axis）against values of $V$（on the $x$－axis）．A graph similar to Figure 24.17 will result．Note that the scales on the $y$－axis are different for forward and reverse bias．

| Forward－biased |  | Reverse－biased |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Voltage $V(\mathrm{~V})$ | Current $I(\mathrm{~mA})$ | Voltage $V(\mathrm{~V})$ | Current $I(\mu \mathrm{~A})$ |
|  |  |  |  |


![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-419.jpg?height=909&width=899&top_left_y=2474&top_left_x=1764)
Figure 24．17 The variation of current $(I)$ with potential difference（ $V$ ）for a semiconductor diode

## Experimental notes

- When the diode is forward-biased, you may connect a resistor in series with the milliammeter at C . The value of the resistor is chosen so that if the full supply voltage is put across the diode, the size of the current in the circuit will not exceed the safe maximum for the diode.
- A forward-biased diode has a very low resistance, and a reverse-biased diode has a very high resistance. The position of the voltmeter in relation to the current-reading meter must be arranged to allow for this.
- In Figure 24.15, the diode is forward-biased. The voltmeter reads the potential difference across the diode. The milliammeter reads the sum of the currents through the voltmeter and the diode.
- The resistance of the voltmeter is huge and thus takes almost no current. Therefore, the reading on the milliammeter is the current through the diode to a high degree of accuracy.
- If the diode is reverse-biased, it has a very high resistance. This means that if the same circuit is used, the current through the diode and voltmeter may be similar in size. So, the reading on the microammeter will not be the current through the diode.
- With the circuit in Figure 24.16, the microammeter reads the current flowing through the diode correctly.
- The voltmeter reads the sum of the potential differences across the diode and microammeter. The resistance of the microammeter is tiny compared with the resistance of the reverse-biased diode, so virtually all the potential difference is across the diode. This means the reading on the voltmeter is the potential difference across the diode to a high degree of accuracy.


## Questions

1. Why is a milliammeter used when the diode is forward-biased but a microammeter is used when it is reverse-biased?
2. Why is the position of the current-reading meter changed during the experiment?
3. When the diode is forward-biased, why is the current small until the voltage reaches about 0.6 V for a silicon diode or about 0.2 V for a germanium diode?
4. Does a forward-biased diode obey Ohm's law?
5. What will happen if the forward current is allowed to get too large?
6. Why might a resistor be connected in series with the milliammeter in the first part of the experiment?

## Explanation of the graph (Figure 24.17) Forward-biased

- In the region $C \rightarrow D$, the applied voltage is less than the junction voltage, so it is not large enough to force many electrons and holes across the junction. The current that flows is small.
- When the applied voltage exceeds the junction voltage (about 0.6 V for a silicon diode), a significant forward current flows. This current increases very rapidly with increasing forward voltage. If the voltage is increased too much, the current will be large enough to overheat and permanently damage the diode. Check with the manufacturer of the diode to find out the maximum safe forward current.


## Reverse-biased

In the region $B \rightarrow C$, the diode only allows an extremely small current to flow. As we have seen, this current is called the leakage current and is typically less than $1 \mu \mathrm{~A}$. Its value remains fairly steady over a large range of voltage. If the voltage is increased too much, suddenly the insulating properties of the diode break down and a large current flows. This current will destroy the diode.

### 24.4 The light-emitting diode (LED)

A light-emitting diode (LED) is a p-n diode that gives out light when it is forward-biased and conducting current (Figure 24.18).
LEDs are usually made of semiconductor materials containing gallium and have their junction very near the surface.

- When an LED is forward-biased, current flows through it.
- Electrons and holes recombine at the junction.
- When an electron recombines with a hole, it drops to a lower energy band and gives out energy in the form of light.
- The colour of the light emitted depends on the energy gap between the conduction electrons and the holes. This means the colour depends on the properties of the material from which the LED is made.
An LED can easily be damaged by a large current, so a protective

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-421.jpg?height=698&width=955&top_left_y=419&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 24.18 Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and their circuit symbol

resistor is normally connected in series with the LED to prevent large currents flowing. The value of the resistor is chosen so that if the full supply voltage is put across the diode, the size of the current in the circuit will not exceed the safe maximum for the diode.

A light-emitting diode is a p-n junction that gives out light when forward-biased and conducting current.

## SEC examination question (HL)

## Question

Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) are a more efficient source of light than filament bulbs. They can range from $80 \%$ to $90 \%$ efficient. An LED is in forward bias, and energy is emitted as photons of light. This happens as electrons lose energy and fill holes.
There is a potential difference of 2.1 V across a particular LED and a current of 20 mA flowing through it. The LED has an efficiency of $81 \%$.
Calculate the energy lost by an electron as it fills a hole.

## Solution

Energy produced in LED per second = input power =
$P=V I=(2.1)\left(20 \times 10^{-3}\right)=4.20 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

## Energy producing light in LED per second $=81 \%$ of $4.20 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~J}$

$P_{\text {light }}=(0.81)(0.042)=0.03402 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

Charge passing through LED per second = current = $20 \mathrm{~mA}=20 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}$
Charge on one electron $=1.602 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$

⇒ Number of electrons passing through LED per second $=\frac{\text { charge passing through LED per second }}{\text { charge on one electron }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{20 \times 10^{-3}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} \\
& =1.248 \times 10^{17}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Energy lost by one electron as it fills a hole } & =\frac{\text { energy producing light in LED per second }}{\text { number of electrons passing through LED per second }} \\
& =\frac{0.03402}{1.248 \times 10^{17}} \\
& =2.726 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Using a diode to convert AC to DC

In Figure 24.19, an alternating voltage source is connected in a circuit with a diode and a resistor. Will current flow

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-422.jpg?height=401&width=740&top_left_y=423&top_left_x=898)
Figure 24.19

through the resistor?

- When the alternating voltage causes the diode to be forward-biased, it will conduct, and current flows in the resistor.
- When the alternating voltage causes the diode to be reverse-biased, no current flows.
- The result is a pulsating direct current in the resistor (and the rest of the circuit) (Figure 24.20).
- This means a diode can be used to convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC). This is called rectification.


### 24.5 The transistor

Almost any piece of modern electronic equipment contains transistors of some form.

## The npn junction transistor

An npn junction transistor consists of a lightly doped piece of p-type semiconductor (called the base) sandwiched between two thicker, more heavily doped n-type pieces (called the collector and the emitter). These three layers are formed on the same crystal of semiconductor material.
There are three connections to a transistor: one to the collector, one to the base and the other to the emitter (Figure 24.21).

## Npn transistor in common emitter configuration

Figure 24.22 shows an npn transistor connected in common emitter configuration, where the emitter is connected to both the collector and the base via the batteries. In Figure 24.22 conventional current can flow in the paths shown.

- The current flowing in through the collector is the collector current ( $I_{\mathrm{c}}$ ).
- The current flowing out through the emitter is the emitter current ( $I_{\mathrm{e}}$ ).
- The current flowing in through the base is the base current ( $l_{\mathrm{b}}$ ).

$$
I_{\mathrm{e}}=I_{\mathrm{c}}+I_{\mathrm{b}}
$$

Emitter current = collector current + base current

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-422.jpg?height=610&width=793&top_left_y=475&top_left_x=1757)
Figure 24.20 The input voltage is alternating. The output current is pulsating DC.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-422.jpg?height=1105&width=932&top_left_y=1412&top_left_x=1686)
Figure 24.21 The npn transistor, its circuit symbol and a simplified diagram of its construction

Figure 24.22 An npn transistor connected in common emitter configuration

## Transistor action

Basic action of a transistor:

## A small current flowing in the base turns on or off and controls the size of a much larger current in the collector.

The following is found with the circuit in Figure 24.22:

- With $S_{1}$ open and $S_{2}$ closed, no current flows in either path. The collector current is zero if the base current is zero, even if there is a large voltage between the collector and the emitter (Battery 2).
i.e. $I_{\mathrm{b}}=0 \Rightarrow I_{\mathrm{c}}=0$
- When $S_{1}$ is closed, and if the value of the voltage between the emitter and the base is about 0.6 volts (for a silicon transistor), a small current $\left(I_{b}\right)$ will flow in through the base. (The base-emitter junction is a forward-biased p-n junction.) When base current flows, the collector current will also flow, provided $S_{2}$ is closed.
- $I_{c}$ is a lot bigger than $I_{b}$. Typically, $I_{c}$ is between 10 and 1000 times $I_{b}$ depending on the transistor.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-423.jpg?height=818&width=831&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=1907)
Figure 24.23 The collector current is much bigger than and directly proportional to the base current.

- $I_{c}$ is directly proportional to $I_{b}$ (Figure 24.23).

These results can easily be demonstrated in the laboratory by setting up a suitable circuit. If the base current exceeds a certain value, the transistor will be permanently damaged. A high resistance is normally connected in the base lead to limit the current if the potential difference across the base and the emitter is too high.

### 24.6 The transistor as a switch

In a transistor no collector current flows unless a base current flows, i.e. the base current turns on (or off) the larger collector current. In this sense, the transistor acts as a switch.

## Demonstration Experiment 24.1

## To demonstrate the transistor as a switch

Consider the circuit shown in Figure 24.24. Instead of using a separate battery to cause the base current, the variable resistor $R_{1}$ acts as a potential divider across the battery. The base emitter voltage then depends on the potential difference across the bottom piece of $R_{1}$ and can be varied. The resistor $R_{2}$ is the protective resistor mentioned above.

## Method

- By varying $R_{1}$, the input voltage $V_{1}$ can be increased or decreased.
- For values of $V_{1}$ less than about 0.4 V , no base current flows ( $V_{i}$ is less than the base emitter junction voltage). Observe that no collector current will be seen to flow either.
- Increasing $V_{\mathrm{i}}$ about 0.4 V causes $I_{\mathrm{b}}$ to flow, indicated on the microammeter.
- When this happens, $I_{\mathrm{c}}$ will also flow, indicated on the milliammeter.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-423.jpg?height=548&width=968&top_left_y=2581&top_left_x=1738)
Figure 24.24

- As $I_{b}$ is increased, $I_{c}$ will be seen to increase also.
- Note that $I_{\mathrm{c}}$ is much bigger than $I_{\mathrm{b}}$, $I_{\mathrm{b}}$ is in the order of microamperes whereas $I_{\mathrm{c}}$ is in milliamperes.
- If $V_{\mathrm{i}}$ is decreased below about $0.4 \mathrm{~V}, I_{\mathrm{b}}$ becomes zero and so does $I_{\mathrm{c}}$.
- Therefore the base current switches on or off the larger collector current.


## Applications of switching

In the following circuits, a sensor allows the base current to flow, turning on the collector current which then turns on a bulb in the collector circuit. Other devices, such as an LED, a bell or a buzzer could replace the bulb.

## A temperature-controlled switch

In Figure 24.25, the thermistor $T$ and the resistor $R$ form a potential divider across the battery. The resistances of $T$ and $R$ are chosen so that at low temperatures, most of the voltage is dropped across the thermistor. The voltage across $R$ is too small to cause a base current. As the temperature is increased, the resistance of the thermistor decreases and so does the voltage ( $V_{\mathrm{T}}$ ) across it. Hence, the voltage across $R\left(V_{\mathrm{R}}\right)$ increases. When $V_{\mathrm{R}}$ is large enough, the base emitter voltage becomes large enough to cause $I_{b}$ to flow. The transistor is turned on and $I_{\mathrm{c}}$ flows, causing the bulb to light up. The bulb lighting up indicates that the temperature has risen. The value of $R$ determines the temperature at which the bulb comes on.
In Figure 24.26, the positions of $R$ and $T$ are interchanged (the value of $R$ being suitably adjusted). The circuit is now a detector of a fall in temperature (e.g. a frost detector in a greenhouse). When the temperature drops, the resistance of the thermistor increases, increasing $V_{T}$ to a value that turns on the base current.

## A light-controlled switch

In Figure 24.27(A), the thermistor is replaced with a light-dependent resistor (LDR). This circuit will automatically turn on a light in the dark. The value of $R$ is chosen so that in daylight its resistance is much larger than that of the LDR. Hence, most of the voltage is dropped

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-424.jpg?height=463&width=808&top_left_y=690&top_left_x=1761)
Figure 24.25 A rise in temperature causes the bulb to light.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-424.jpg?height=463&width=808&top_left_y=1458&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 24.26 A fall in temperature causes the bulb to light.

across $R$ and no base current flows. When it gets dark, the resistance of the LDR increases and so does the potential difference across it, therefore increasing the potential difference across the base emitter junction. When this value is about 0.6 V , the base current flows, which turns on the transistor, causing the collector current to flow and the bulb to light.
In Figure 24.7(B), the positions of the LDR and $R$ (Figure 24.27(B)) are interchanged. This gives a circuit that comes on in brightness.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-424.jpg?height=645&width=1925&top_left_y=2591&top_left_x=192)
Figure 24.27

### 24.7 Real-world applications of semiconductors

Semiconductors are important because their unique electrical properties allow us to manipulate electrical current and voltage in useful ways. All digital devices are composed of electronic circuits and the components of these circuits are primarily made from semiconductors.

| Type of semiconductor | Significant feature(s) | Practical applications |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Diode | - Allows current to flow through it in one direction only <br> - Does not conduct significantly until the the forward voltage reaches a specific value | - Used to convert AC to DC <br> - Used to start conduction at a specific voltage |
| LED | - Emits light when forward-biased <br> - Has low energy consumption <br> - Low maintenance <br> - Small size <br> - Fast switching times | - Rapidly replacing conventional light bulbs and compact fluorescent bulbs for all forms of lighting; provides the efficient lighting needed for sustainability <br> - LEDs make up the individual pixels in many screens <br> - Produces the light pulses used to send data along fibre-optic cables |
| LDR | - Its resistance changes rapidly and sensitively with changes in illumination | - Used in light sensors to detect the presence or absence of light, control street lighting, in light metres and in security systems |
| Thermistor | - Its resistance is very sensitive to changes in temperature and reacts quickly | - Used in digital thermometers and temperature control <br> - Used in almost any system that needs a heating or cooling protection for safe operation. The thermistor detects the relevant temperature change and activates counter measures |
| Transistor | - A voltage (or a current) applied to one pair of the transistor's terminals controls the current flowing in another pair of its terminals | - It can be used as: <br> - An electronic switch <br> - An amplifier, which increases the strength of information signals <br> - It is the central component in logic gates, which are used in all computing |


![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-425.jpg?height=987&width=1765&top_left_y=2858&top_left_x=322)
Figure 24.28 Semiconductor manufacturing

## Diodes

You saw on page 406 that a p-n diode allows current to flow in one direction only and that it can be used to convert AC to DC. Why is this useful?
Almost all electronic appliances and electronic components need DC to operate. So, they need diodes to convert mains AC to DC. All phone and battery chargers also need DC and therefore have diodes in them.
Light-emitting diodes are rapidly replacing conventional light bulbs and compact fluorescent bulbs in all forms of lighting. Indoor lighting, street lighting, floodlighting, lights on cars and other forms of transport rely heavily on LED lighting. LEDs have low maintenance, small size and, more importantly, much lower energy consumption than conventional bulbs. They therefore play a major part in providing the efficient lighting

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-426.jpg?height=766&width=1053&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=1562)
Figure 24.29 LED lighting provides a more efficient light source than other light bulbs.

needed for sustainability.
LEDs are used for visual signals and for conveying information on screens of all forms. They are also used to create the light pulses needed to send data along fibre-optic cables. As well as this, almost any appliance with an on/off switch, except for the most simple, usually has an LED indicator light to tell when the appliance is on or off.

## Transistors

Page 413 detailed the basic action of a transistor and how it can be used as an electronic switch that uses a small voltage (or current) to turn another current on (or off).
In digital processing systems, the presence of a signal is represented by a 1 and the absence of a signal by a 0 . By arranging transistors (and other components) in integrated circuits (ICs), modern computers can perform huge numbers of complex logical operations and store massive amounts of information in binary form (0s and 1s) on memory chips. ICs contain massive numbers of transistors, diodes, resistors and capacitors on a very small chip of silicon, and they can function as microprocessors, amplifiers or as memory. A modern IC could have more than 100 billion transistors on a single chip.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-426.jpg?height=584&width=2426&top_left_y=2239&top_left_x=195)
Figure 24.30 Transistors are an essential component of any modern computer. As technology has developed, the size of the individual transistors has shrunk

Almost every piece of electrical equipment or device you use or know of, big or small, contains semiconductors: in your smartwatch, in your phone, in a clock (unless it is vintage and mechanical), any sound, music or entertainment system, computer, tablet, laptop, keyboard, mouse, phone charger, LED lighting bulbs, indicator lights, LED torch, printer, fan, air conditioner, thermometer, headphones, vacuum cleaner, cordless drill or other power tool, an exercise bike, an electric heater, and so on.
Other semiconductor uses:

- Temperature sensors and control systems in heaters, air conditioners, heating systems, kitchen appliances, cars, hybrid cars, electric cars, planes and ships
- Indoor lighting, street lights, flood lights, lighting anywhere
- Internet connectivity and global communication, satellites and satellite communication a navigation systems (e.g. GPS), wind turbines
- Solar farms, the National Grid and control of electricity distribution.

All modern societies rely on semiconductors for critical infrastructure.

## Summary What I should know

- A semiconductor is a substance whose resistivity is between that of a good conductor and a good insulator. The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases as its temperature increases.
- When an electron breaks free from a covalent bond, it leaves behind a gap in the atom from which it came. This gap is called a positive hole or simply a hole.
- Conduction in a pure semiconductor due to electrons moving from negative to positive (- to +) and an equal number of holes moving in the opposite direction is called intrinsic conduction.
- A thermistor is a semiconductor device whose resistance decreases rapidly with increasing temperature.
- A light-dependent resistor (LDR) is a semiconductor whose conductivity increases when light shines on it.
- The adding of small controlled amounts of certain impurities to a pure semiconductor to increase its conductivity is called doping.
- An $\boldsymbol{n}$-type semiconductor is one in which the impurity added produces more free electrons available for conduction, e.g. phosphorous in silicon.
- A p-type semiconductor is one in which the impurity added produces extra holes that are available for conduction, e.g. boron in silicon.
- Increased conduction in a semiconductor due to the addition of impurities is called extrinsic conduction. The semiconductor formed is called an extrinsic semiconductor.
- A p-n junction is a piece of semiconductor with part of it doped p-type and the rest doped n-type.
- The depletion layer is the region at both sides of a p-n junction that contains no free majority charge carriers. It therefore behaves as an insulator.
- The potential difference that exists across a p-n junction caused by holes and electrons moving across the junction when it was formed is called the junction voltage.
- A forward-biased p-n junction conducts current.
- A reverse-biased p-n junction does not conduct current.
- A light-emitting diode is a p-n junction that gives out light when forward-biased and conducting.
- In a transistor: $I_{\mathrm{e}}=I_{\mathrm{c}}+I_{\mathrm{b}} \quad$ emitter current = collector current + base current
- No collector current flows unless a base current flows, i.e. the base current turns on (or off) the larger collector current. So, the transistor acts as a switch.

# 25 Magnets and Magnetic Fields

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand what a magnetic field is
- To ensure students can model the relative strength and direction of magnetic fields around permanent magnets, a current carrying wire and a solenoid with and without a ferrous core
- To ensure students are aware of, and can describe, the many uses of permanent and temporary magnets in real life situations


## Keywords

- Magnet
- Ferromagnetic
- Magnetic pole
- North-seeking pole or north pole
- South-seeking pole or south pole
- Induced magnetism
- Permanent magnet
- Temporary magnet
- Magnetic field
- Magnetic field line
- Plotting compass
- Right-hand grip rule
- Solenoid
- Electromagnet


### 25.1 Basic properties of magnets

Over 2400 years ago, the Greeks knew that a particular ore of iron was able to attract small pieces of iron to it. Today this ore is called lodestone or magnetite.
They also knew that if a piece of lodestone was suspended by a string it would turn, until one particular end was pointing northwards.
Today scientists explain these properties by saying that the piece of lodestone is magnetised. You can investigate magnetic properties, like those of lodestone, using bar magnets.

## Demonstration Experiment 25.1

To demonstrate the main properties of magnets

## Property 1: A magnet attracts certain materials to it.

Test several different materials with a bar magnet by bringing it near them. The magnet will attract iron, steel, nickel, cobalt and some alloys of these. These materials are said to be ferromagnetic. The magnet will not have a noticeable effect on other materials.

## Property 2: A bar magnet is strongest at each end.

Dip the bar magnet into a jar of iron filings or a box of pins. It attracts the filings or pins, and most cling on at each end of the magnet (Figure 25.1).
The regions of greatest strength at each end are called magnetic poles.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-430.jpg?height=597&width=1007&top_left_y=2939&top_left_x=1569)
Figure 25.1(A) Iron filings attracted to a bar magnet.
(B) Drawing pins attached to a bar magnet.

## Property 3: If a bar magnet is suspended by a piece of thread, it will line up approximately north-south.

Make a paper stirrup and place the magnet in it. Suspend it from a wooden retort stand and note that it always comes to rest pointing roughly north-south (Figure 25.2).
The pole of the magnet that always points north is called the north-seeking pole or simply the north pole.
The pole that points south is called the south seeking pole or simply the south pole.
Experiments have always shown that:

- For every north pole there is always a south pole, i.e. magnetic poles exist in pairs
- The strength of the north pole is exactly the same as the strength of the south pole


## Property 4: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

Place the poles of different magnets near each other and see that like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-431.jpg?height=870&width=577&top_left_y=403&top_left_x=2129)
Figure 25.2 A suspended bar magnet comes to rest pointing roughly north-south.

- The north pole of one magnet repels the north pole of another.
- The south pole of one magnet repels the south pole of another.
- The north pole of one magnet is attracted to the south pole of another.

Note also that the force of repulsion or attraction between two magnets increases as the magnets are moved closer together and decreases as the magnets are placed further apart.

## Property 5: A magnet causes ferromagnetic material brought near or touching it to become magnetised.

Get some pins and notice that they do not stick to each other, i.e. they are not magnets.
Place a strong bar magnet into the heap of pins and see that, as well as being attracted to the magnet, the pins are also attracted to each other (Figure 25.1(B)). See also that the pins hold onto some of their magnetism when the bar magnet is removed.
This is called induced magnetism. If the original magnet is taken away, some materials (called permanent magnets) hold onto their magnetism, but others (called temporary magnets) lose most or all of it.

### 25.2 Magnetic fields

Just like we did with gravity and static electricity, we can introduce the idea of a magnetic field can be introduced.
Suppose you have a bar magnet. Due to the magnet, the surrounding space is now different to the space before the magnet was introduced. This magnet, in some way, has modified the space around it. We say the magnet has created a magnetic field in the space around it.
The field exerts a force on other magnets or pieces of ferromagnetic material that are brought close to the original magnet. The stronger the field the stronger the force. The magnetic field is strongest near the magnet and weaker further away from it.
The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction of the force on a north pole if it were placed at that point.

A magnetic field is any region of space where magnetic forces can be felt. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction of the force on a north pole if it were placed at that point.

## Magnetic field lines

Magnetic fields can be visually represented by lines called magnetic field lines. These have arrows to show the direction of the magnetic field.

A magnetic field line is a line drawn in a magnetic field showing the direction of the force on a north pole placed in the field.

A plotting compass can be used to show the direction of a magnetic field. This is a very small magnet, which can be suspended so that it can freely rotate about a vertical axis (Figure 25.5).
A plotting compass needle will point in the direction of the magnetic field present.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-432.jpg?height=733&width=1033&top_left_y=2285&top_left_x=1588)
Figure 25.5

If no other magnets are nearby, it will line up north-south.
If there is another magnetic field present, the compass needle will deflect from its north-south position. If the other field is strong enough, the compass needle will line up almost parallel to the other field. In this way, a plotting compass can be used to draw magnetic field lines around a magnet.

## Demonstration Experiment 25.2

To plot the magnetic field due to a bar magnet

## Method

1. Place a bar magnet on a sheet of paper.
2. Place a plotting compass next to one pole of the magnet and mark both ends of the compass needle with dots on the paper (Figure 25.6).
3. Move the compass so that one side is touching the previous dot (as in Figure 25.6). Mark the other end of the needle with a dot.
4. Repeat this step until you end up at the other pole of the magnet.
5. Join the dots with a smooth curved line.
6. Repeat this process drawing several lines at both sides of the magnet.
7. Mark each line with an arrowhead showing the direction of the magnetic field. A field pattern similar to that in Figure 25.7 will result.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-433.jpg?height=583&width=1003&top_left_y=1315&top_left_x=371)
Figure 25.6

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-433.jpg?height=597&width=1151&top_left_y=1308&top_left_x=1399)
Figure 25.7 The magnetic field around a bar magnet.

The magnetic field around a bar magnet may also be plotted with iron filings. A sheet of paper or cardboard is placed over the magnet and its outline is drawn in. Iron filings are sprinkled on the paper and it is shaken gently. The filings line up as in Figure 25.8. It must, however, be realised that the magnetic field around a magnet is, in reality, three-dimensional.

- The field lines in the space around a bar magnet start at the north pole and end at the south pole of the magnet.
- Near the poles, where the magnetic field is strongest, the lines are close together. Further away, where the field is weaker, the lines are far apart.
- The magnetic field lines never cross each other.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-433.jpg?height=580&width=857&top_left_y=2057&top_left_x=1842)
Figure 25.8 Iron filings showing the shape of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.

Figure 25.9 shows the magnetic field due to a horseshoe magnet. It can be plotted using a plotting compass or demonstrated with iron filings.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-433.jpg?height=685&width=1433&top_left_y=3082&top_left_x=374)
Figure 25.9 The magnetic field of a horseshoe magnet.

### 25.3 The magnetic effect of an electric current

In 1819, Hans Christian Oersted discovered that any current-carrying conductor has a magnetic field around it, as long as the current is flowing. When the current stops flowing, the magnetic field disappears.

## Demonstration Experiment 25.3

## To show the magnetic effect of an electric current

## Method

1. Align a piece of wire along the needle of a plotting

SCAN ME compass so that it points north-south (Figure 25.12(A)).
2. Send a steady current (e.g. 2 A) through the wire and the compass needle will deflect (Figure 25.12(B)). The direction in which it deflects depends on the direction of the current.
3. Reverse the direction of the current and the needle will deflect in the opposite direction.
4. Switch off the current. The magnetic field due to the current disappears and the needle lines up north-south again.
5. If the experiment is repeated and the size of the current is decreased, the compass needle will not deflect as much.

## Conclusion

- Every current-carrying conductor has a magnetic field around it caused by the current.
- As long as the current is flowing, the magnetic field exists.
- If the current stops flowing, the magnetic field disappears.
- The magnetic field due to a single current-carrying wire is weak unless the current is very large.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-435.jpg?height=861&width=766&top_left_y=670&top_left_x=1966)
Figure 25.12 Experiment to show the magnetic field of an electric current. (A) A piece of wire is aligned along the needle of a plotting compass so that it points north-south. (B) A steady current is sent through the wire so that the compass needle deflects.

## Demonstration Experiment 25.4

## To plot the magnetic field due to a current-carrying wire

## Method

1. Use the equipment in Figure 25.13 and send a current through the wire ( 2 A is suitable).
2. Place a plotting compass near the wire and mark both ends of the compass needle with dots on the paper.
3. Move the compass so that its south pole is at the dot that marked the previous north pole. Mark the north pole end of the needle with a dot.
4. Repeat this until you end up back at the point where you started.
5. Join the dots with a smooth curved line. This will be a circle.
6. Repeat this process at different points on the cardboard, drawing several circles around the wire.
7. Mark each circle with an arrowhead showing its direction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-435.jpg?height=570&width=1144&top_left_y=3021&top_left_x=377)
Figure 25.13 Magnetic field lines due to a long straight current-carrying conductor. In reality the lines should be progressively further apart as you move away from the wire, to indicate how the field gets weaker away from the wire.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-435.jpg?height=538&width=1163&top_left_y=3011&top_left_x=1543)
Figure 25.14 The magnetic field due to a currentcarrying wire may also be plotted with iron filings. The wire is passed through a sheet of cardboard and the current is switched on. Iron filings are sprinkled on the cardboard and it is shaken gently. The filings line up as in Figure 25.8.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-437.jpg?height=730&width=1626&top_left_y=263&top_left_x=325)
Figure 25.19 The magnetic field due to a current-carrying solenoid.

Using either of the methods used for the bar magnet, the magnetic field around a solenoid may be plotted. Figure 25.20 shows a solenoid wound on a Perspex plate specially for doing this.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-437.jpg?height=609&width=929&top_left_y=1289&top_left_x=325)
Figure 25.20

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-437.jpg?height=606&width=782&top_left_y=1292&top_left_x=1279)
Figure 25.21

Figure 25.21 shows an easy way to remember which side of a loop, coil or solenoid behaves like a north pole and which like a south pole. When looking into the loop, coil or solenoid, if the current is moving in a clockwise direction the end facing you is a South pole, and if the current is moving in an anticlockwise direction it is a North pole.
The strength of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid is not large unless there is a large number of turns of wire and a very large current.
An easier way to increase the strength is to place a core in the coil made of ferromagnetic material (a ferrous core). The core becomes magnetised, and produces a much stronger magnetic field in and around the solenoid, as shown in Figure 25.22.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-437.jpg?height=730&width=1853&top_left_y=2633&top_left_x=322)
Figure 25.22 The magnetic field of (A) a solenoid and (B) the same solenoid, carrying the same current, but with a ferrous core. The magnetic field produced is much stronger, represented by the greatly increased line density.

The solenoid and core together are sometimes called an electromagnet. When the current is switched off, the core loses its magnetism.

An electromagnet is a soft iron (ferrous) core surrounded by a solenoid. When current flows in the solenoid, the core becomes magnetised. When the current is switched off, the core loses its magnetism.

### 25.6 Uses of permanent and temporary magnets

Magnets have many uses in everyday life. Some magnets might be familiar to you, such as fridge magnets that can be used to stick shopping lists to the fridge door. Other magnets may be less visible, and you might not realise how they enable many everyday objects to function.
Uses of magnets in everyday life:
Fridges: As well as fridge magnets mentioned above, magnets also line fridge and freezer doors to keep them closed with a tight seal.
Children's toys: Many children's toys contain magnets to link parts together. Magnets of all shapes and sizes can themselves be used as toys to play with.
Securely storing objects: Many tools and instruments in home or workplaces use magnets to keep metal objects in place. For example, drills often have magnetic strips in the drill case to store spare drill bits until they are ready for use.
Enhancing objects' accessibility: Some objects, such as torches, contain magnets that allow them to be stuck to steel or iron while they are in use. Sometimes homes or workplaces may hang a magnetic strip on the wall to keep metal objects accessible, such as chef's knives in a kitchen.
Metal detectors and stud finders: Metal detectors and stud finders produce magnetic fields. If the magnetic field of a metal detector or stud finder passes through the magnetic field of another metal object, this will be detected and the user will be informed of its presence.
Pick-up tools: Magnetic pick-up tools can be used to retrieve small ferrous metal objects which may be difficult to pick up from the ground. These can be helpful when metal falls into hard-toreach places, or for individuals with mobility difficulties.
Magnetic compasses: The magnetic compass has been used for navigation for thousands of years, and continues to be used to this day in aircraft, ships and land vehicles.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-438.jpg?height=891&width=1204&top_left_y=1926&top_left_x=194)
Figure 25.23 The Earth's magnetic field.

Electric motors and generators: Electric motors and generators of all types operate using either permanent or temporary magnets or electromagnets. You will read about this in Chapter 27.
Scrap metal pick-up: Ferrous metals like steel and iron can be readily picked up, moved around and released by powerful electromagnets (Figure 25.25), which are commonly used in the metal industry.
Separation processes/Recycling: Electromagnets are used to separate ferrous metals from other materials during the recycling separation process. Aluminium, copper, plastics and other materials will not be affected by the magnet.
Loudspeakers and headphones: Loudspeakers, headphones and many microphones contain magnets that enable them to operate.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-438.jpg?height=724&width=1199&top_left_y=1930&top_left_x=1422)
Figure 25.24 The magnetic compass has been used for hundreds of years in marine navigation, since it always enables you to know the direction in which you are travelling.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-438.jpg?height=773&width=1091&top_left_y=2962&top_left_x=1530)
Figure 25.25 A powerful electromagnet lifting scrap iron and steel.

Smart phones, computers and televisions all contain magnetic components.
Memory storage: Hard drives, flash drives and other memory storage devices are built using magnets known as magnetic storage devices.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) machines: An MRI machine uses an extremely strong magnetic field to produce images of parts of the human body, which may be required in medical contexts.
Magnetic levitation of trains: Extremely strong electromagnets are used to raise the train above the train track, reducing friction to very low values. Trains are also powered by a linear electromagnetic motor, which allows them to reach high speeds.

## Summary What I should know

- The pole of a magnet that always points north is called the north-seeking pole or simply the north pole. The pole that points south is called the south-seeking pole or simply the south pole.
- Magnetic poles always occur in pairs.
- Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
- A magnetic field is any region of space where magnetic forces can be felt. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction of the force on a north pole if it were placed at that point.
- A magnetic field line is a line drawn in a magnetic field showing the direction of the force on a north pole placed in the field.
- The field lines in the space around a bar magnet start at the north pole and end at the south pole of the magnet.
- Near the poles, where the magnetic field is strongest, the lines are close together. Further away, where the field is weaker, the lines are far apart.
- The magnetic field lines never cross each other.
- Every current-carrying conductor has a magnetic field around it caused by the current.
- As long as the current is flowing, the magnetic field exists. If the current stops flowing, the magnetic field disappears.
- The right-hand grip rule states that: If a right-hand clasps a conductor, with the thumb pointing in the direction of the current, then the fingers give the direction of the magnetic field around the conductor. (Note that the thumb points in the direction of conventional current, i.e. from + to -)

# 26 Current in a Magnetic Field

## Objectives

- To ensure students understand that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force
- To ensure students can model the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field; that is, they can model the motor effect
- To ensure students can apply Fleming's left-hand rule to determine the direction of this force
- To ensure students understand that, and appreciate why, a magnetic field exerts a force on an electric charge moving in the field


## Keywords

- The motor effect
- Fleming's left-hand rule
- Magnetic flux density ( $B$ )
- The tesla ( $T$ )
- Simple DC motor
- Split ring commutator


### 26.1 Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field

A current-carrying conductor has a magnetic field around it due to the current (see page 353). If this conductor is placed in another magnetic field, the two fields interact, producing a force on the conductor. In simple terms, it can be imagined that the magnetic fields push off each other. If the conductor is free to move, it will do so under the influence of this force. This phenomenon is sometimes called the motor effect.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-440.jpg?height=1221&width=1151&top_left_y=2142&top_left_x=201)
Figure 26.1 The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-440.jpg?height=369&width=301&top_left_y=2148&top_left_x=1868)
2. Send a current through the aluminium foil (2 A is suitable).
3. The foil will be seen to move forwards or backwards depending on the direction in which the current is flowing.

## Conclusion

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force.

## Direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field

Experimentally, it is found that the direction of the force on the conductor is perpendicular to the current and perpendicular to the magnetic field. If the current-carrying conductor is placed parallel to the magnetic field, it experiences no force.

Note: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field will always experience a force unless the conductor is parallel to the magnetic field. The direction of the force is always:

- Perpendicular to the current
- Perpendicular to the magnetic field

However, there are two directions that are perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field.
In Figure 26.2, the magnetic field goes into the page (signified by the blue + signs), and the wire is carrying the current in the direction shown. The force is then either up the page or down the page.
Fleming's left-hand rule tells you which direction is correct.

## Fleming's left-hand rule states:

If the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand are held at right angles (Figure 26.3), with the first finger pointing in the direction of the magnetic field, and the second finger pointing in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of the force.
Note that the direction of the current is the direction of conventional current; that is, flowing from + to -.

Try applying this to Figure 26.2. You will find that the direction of the force is upwards.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-441.jpg?height=672&width=792&top_left_y=1982&top_left_x=325)
Figure 26.2

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-441.jpg?height=672&width=975&top_left_y=1982&top_left_x=1145)
Figure 26.3 Fleming's left-hand rule

## Worked Example 1

## Question

Figure 26.4 shows a magnetic field and a wire carrying an electric current into the page. In what direction is the force on the wire?

## Solution

Applying Fleming's left-hand rule:

- The first finger is in the direction of the magnetic field.
- The second finger is in the direction of the current (into page).
- The thumb gives the direction of the force, which is therefore downwards, as shown in Figure 26.5.

## Size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field

It can be shown, with equipment like that in Figure 26.1 (page 428), that the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field depends on:

- The size of the current, $I$
- The length of the conductor, $l$, in the magnetic field
- The strength of the magnetic field

The difference between a weak and a strong magnetic field has been discussed previously. However, in physics, it is important to assign a numerical value to the strength of a magnetic field.
Further accurate experiments show that if a conductor of length $l$, carrying a current $l$, is placed at right angles to a uniform magnetic field, it experiences a force $F$ where: $F \propto I$ and $F \propto L$ It follows that:

$$
F \propto I l \quad \Rightarrow \quad F=B I l \quad \text { where } B \text { is a constant }
$$

The value of $B$ depends on the strength of the magnetic field. In a strong magnetic field, $B$ is large, and in a weak field, $B$ is small. Therefore, $B$ is a measure of the strength of the magnetic field.
This new quantity, $B$, is called magnetic flux density.

- Magnetic flux density is a vector.
- At any point in the field, the direction of $B$ is the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point, i.e. the same as the direction of the magnetic field.
- Its magnitude is defined in terms of the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor placed at that point in the magnetic field, i.e. its magnitude is the value of $B$ from the equation $F=$ BII.


### 26.2 Magnetic flux density

To describe how magnetic fields affect current-carrying conductors, physicists use a quantity called magnetic flux density. It defines the strength of a magnetic field and allows the force it exerts on a conductor to be calculated.

The magnetic flux density (B) at a point in a magnetic field is a vector whose magnitude is equal to the force that would be experienced by a conductor of length 1 m carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field at that point.
The direction of the magnetic flux density is the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point.

The SI unit of magnetic flux density is the tesla (T).
The magnetic flux density at a point is 1 tesla ( T ) if a conductor of length 1 m carrying a current of 1 A experiences a force of 1 N when placed perpendicular to the field.

If a conductor of length $l$, carrying a current $l$, is placed in a magnetic field of flux density $B$, it experiences a force $F$, given by:

$$
F=B I l
$$

(F\&T, page 62)

## Nikola Tesla

Nikola Tesla (1856-1943) was a
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-443.jpg?height=288&width=324&top_left_y=758&top_left_x=2343)

Serbian-American engineer and inventor. He is best known for his work in the design of AC power supply systems. He invented the tesla coil, an induction coil widely used in radio technology. He was also a pioneer in the discovery of radar and X-ray technology, and even created one of the first remote-controlled devices, a boat, in 1898.

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A straight piece of wire is 3 m long and carries a current of 2 A . It experiences a force of 12 N when placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. Calculate the value of the magnetic flux density.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =B I l \\
\Rightarrow B & =\frac{F}{I l} \\
& =\frac{12}{(2)(3)} \\
& =2 \mathrm{~T}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

Calculate the force acting on a conductor of length 40 cm which is carrying a current of 3 A and is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 5.2 T .

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =B I l \\
& =(5.2)(3)(0.4) \\
& =6.24 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

Express the tesla in base units.

## Solution

$F=B I l \quad \Rightarrow B=\frac{F}{I l}$
Substituting the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~T} & =1\left[\frac{\mathrm{~N}}{(\mathrm{~A})(\mathrm{m})}\right] \quad \text { Now } 1 \mathrm{~N}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} \quad \text { (page 125) } \\
\Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~T} & =1\left[\frac{\mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}}{\mathrm{Am}}\right] \\
& =1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} A^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 26.3 Force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field

Figure 26.11 shows a coil in a magnetic field. The coil is free to rotate about the axis shown.
Suppose the coil is carrying an electric current (conventional current) in the direction shown.
Then, by Fleming's left-hand rule, the sides $x y$ and $w z$ experience forces in the direction shown.
These forces tend to cause the coil to rotate in the direction indicated. Since the coil is free to rotate, it does so. These forces are an example of the motor effect.
Figure 26.12 (which is a front view of Figure 26.11) shows

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-445.jpg?height=587&width=1183&top_left_y=2324&top_left_x=1565)
Figure 26.11

the directions of the forces on the coil as it rotates.
When it reaches the vertical position, the forces no longer tend to rotate the coil (Figure 26.12(C)).
If the coil is sufficiently free, its momentum will carry it beyond the vertical position to that shown in Figure 26.12(D).
However, the forces that act on the coil in this position tend to rotate it back again to the vertical position. Hence, the coil comes to rest in the vertical position, perhaps having oscillated for a while.
If the direction of the current in the coil is reversed as it passes through the vertical position, the forces acting on the coil will tend to keep it rotating in the same direction (Figure 26.12(E)).

If this is done each time the coil passes through the vertical position, the coil will continue to rotate, forming a simple DC motor.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-446.jpg?height=577&width=2371&top_left_y=445&top_left_x=217)
Figure 26.12 As the coil rotates, the turning effect on the coil changes.

## Simple DC motor

An easy way to make the coil rotate continuously is shown in Figure 26.13. The ends of the coil are connected rigidly to a split circular ring of conducting material that rotates with the coil. This ring is called a split-ring commutator.
Two pieces of carbon - called carbon brushes - touch the sides of the ring (usually kept in place with springs, not shown) and allow current to pass from the battery through one half of the ring, into the coil and out through the other half of the moving ring.
This arrangement always causes current to flow into the left side of the coil and out of the right side. In other words, the direction of current in the coil reverses each time it passes through the vertical.
So, this is a simple electric motor that operates on direct

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-446.jpg?height=760&width=1160&top_left_y=1321&top_left_x=1455)
Figure 26.13

current; that is, a simple DC motor.
Note that the simple DC motor is based on the principle that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. The turning effect on the coil is greatest when the coil is in the horizontal position.
The action of a simple DC motor can be demonstrated in the laboratory with simple equipment designed for this purpose.

### 26.4 Force exerted by a magnetic field on a moving charge

On page 423, it was shown that a magnetic field exists around any current-carrying conductor, due to the movement of electric charges through the conductor. You would therefore expect that a magnetic field should also exist around a stream of moving charges even in the absence of a conducting wire. This is, indeed, observed.
Figure 26.14 illustrates a beam of electrons in a cathode ray tube (see page 469). The electrons travel through a vacuum from right to left. As they pass near the fluorescent screen, they produce a visible beam of light, which makes their path visible.
The moving electrons have negative charge and so are an electric current, which means they have a magnetic field around them. This magnetic field will interact with any other magnetic field placed near it (Figure 26.15).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-446.jpg?height=746&width=966&top_left_y=2819&top_left_x=1656)
Figure 26.14 A beam of electrons in the cathode ray tube is an electric current.

Figure 26.15 shows the beam of electrons deflecting due to the presence of a bar magnet.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-447.jpg?height=796&width=2432&top_left_y=354&top_left_x=319)

Figure 26.15 The beam of electrons deflects in the magnetic field. The north pole deflects the beam in one direction, and the south pole deflects it in the opposite direction which follows from Fleming's left-hand rule.

Figure 26.16 shows a proton (a positively charged particle) moving with a speed of $v \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$.
The moving proton creates a magnetic field around itself. This field interacts with the uniform field $B$, causing a force on the moving proton, which deflects from its original path.
Fleming's left-hand rule tells you the direction in which it deflects.
Note that the direction in which the second finger points - the direction of the current - is the direction in which a positive charge is moving. If the moving charge is negative (for example, an electron), the second finger must point in the opposite direction to the motion of the charge. Figure 26.17 shows a positive charge and a negative charge entering a magnetic field. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to determine that each charge moves in the direction indicated in the diagram.
Using Fleming's left-hand rule, also confirm that the beams of electrons in Figure 26.14 are deflecting in the expected directions.

Note: A charged particle moving in a magnetic field will always experience a force unless it is moving parallel to the magnetic field.
The direction of the force is always:

- Perpendicular to its velocity, $v$
- Perpendicular to the magnetic field, $B$

It can be shown, and verified experimentally, that:
If a charge $q$ coulombs is moving with a speed of $v$ metres per second at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density $B$ teslas, then there is a force $F$ on it given by:

$$
F=B q v
$$

(F\&T, page 62)
