## Worked Example 6

## Question

A particle of charge $2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{C}$ has a velocity of $100 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 3 T . What is the force on the charge?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =B q v \\
& =(3)\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right)(100) \\
& =0.6 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Charged particle moving in a circle

When a charged particle moving at a constant speed enters a uniform magnetic field and moves at right angles to the field, it is found that the particle moves in a circular path.

- In Figure 26.18, as the charged particle moves in the magnetic field, the force on it is at right angles to its direction of motion and of constant magnitude $F=B q v$.
- The speed of the particle does not change but its direction of motion does.
- As it turns, the force always remains at right angles to the direction of motion.
- Recall from page 206 that these are exactly the conditions under which a particle moves in a circle.
So, if a charged particle moving at constant speed enters a uniform magnetic field and moves at right angles to the field, the particle moves in a circle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-448.jpg?height=870&width=737&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=1881)
Figure 26.18

The required centripetal force is equal to the force on a charged particle due to the magnetic field:

$$
\frac{m v^{2}}{r}=B q v
$$

If a particle of charge $q$, moving at constant speed $v$, enters a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$ and moves at right angles to the field, the particle moves in a circle of radius $r$, where:

$$
\frac{m v^{2}}{r}=B q v
$$

## Worked Example 7

## Question

An electron of charge $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ and mass $9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$ enters a uniform magnetic field of flux density $2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~T}$. It has a velocity of $400 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at right angles to the field. Find the radius of the path it follows in the field.

## Solution

The centripetal force is equal to the force on the electron due to $B$ field:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{m v^{2}}{r} & =B q \\
\frac{\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)(400)^{2}}{r} & =\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)(400) \\
r & =\frac{\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)(400)^{2}}{\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)(400)} \\
& =1.14 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 8

## Question

By expressing the units of both sides of the formula $\frac{m v^{2}}{r}=B q v$ in base units, show that it is dimensionally correct.

## Solution

$$
\text { Unit of } \begin{aligned}
\text { LHS } & =\frac{(\mathrm{kg})\left(\mathrm{ms}^{-1}\right)^{2}}{\mathrm{~m}} \\
& =(\mathrm{kg})\left(\mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right)\left(\mathrm{m}^{-1}\right) \\
& =\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Unit of RHS $=1(\mathrm{~T})(\mathrm{C})\left(\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\right)$

$$
1 \mathrm{~T}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} \mathrm{~A}^{-1} \text { (page 432) and } 1 \mathrm{C}=1 \mathrm{As} \text { (page 355) }
$$

Substitute these into $1(\mathrm{~T})(\mathrm{C})\left(\mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-1}\right)$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Unit of RHS } & =1\left(\mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}\right)(\mathrm{As})\left(\mathrm{ms}^{-1}\right) \\
& =1\left(\mathrm{~kg}^{2}\right)\left(\mathrm{s}^{-2}\right)\left(\mathrm{A}^{-1}\right)(\mathrm{A})(\mathrm{s})(\mathrm{m})\left(\mathrm{s}^{-1}\right) \\
& =\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, unit of LHS = unit of RHS

## Summary What I should know

- A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field will always experience a force unless the conductor is parallel to the magnetic field. This is known as the motor effect.
- The direction of the force is always perpendicular to the current and perpendicular to the magnetic field.
- Fleming's left-hand rule states that: If the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand are held at right angles, with the first finger pointing in the direction of the magnetic field, and the second finger pointing in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of the force.
- The magnetic flux density (B) at a point in a magnetic field is a vector whose direction is the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point, and whose magnitude is the value of $B$ from the equation $F=B I l$.
- If a conductor of length $l$, carrying a current $I$ is placed at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density $B$, it experiences a force $F$ given by: $F=B I l$
- The SI unit of magnetic flux density is the tesla (T).
- A charged particle moving in a magnetic field will always experience a force unless it is moving parallel to the magnetic field.
- The direction of the force is always perpendicular to its velocity, $v$, and perpendicular to the magnetic field, $B$.
- If a charge $q$ is moving with a speed of $v$ at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density $B$, then there is a force $F$ on it, given by: $F=B q v$
- If a charged particle moving at constant speed enters a uniform magnetic field and moves at right angles to the field, the particle moves in a circle.

### 27.1 Electromagnetic induction: The generator effect

In Chapter 25, you saw that an electric current causes a magnetic field in the space around it.
In this chapter, you will see how a changing magnetic field causes an electric current to flow. In other words, you will study electromagnetic induction, which is also called the generator effect.

## Keywords

- Electromagnetic induction
- The generator effect
- Induced current
- Induced potential difference
- Induced emf
- Magnetic flux

- Simple DC generator
- Rms value
- Peak value
- Mutual inductance
- Transformer

- Secondary coil
- Step-up transformer
- Step-down transformer

Whenever the magnetic field passing through a coil changes, an emf appears in the coil. This phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction or the generator effect.

## Conclusion

From the above and many similar experiments:

- Whenever the magnetic field passing through a coil is changing, a potential difference appears in that coil. Such a potential difference is called an induced potential difference or an induced emf. This induced emf causes the induced current in the circuit.
- If the magnetic field is not changing, there is no induced emf and

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-454.jpg?height=649&width=806&top_left_y=1341&top_left_x=1783)

hence no induced current, no matter how strong the magnetic field.

- Note that induced current will only flow if the circuit is complete. The emf is induced whether the circuit is complete or not.

Remember: There is no induced emf unless the magnetic field in the coil is CHANGING!

### 27.2 Magnetic flux

To calculate the size of an induced emf, a new quantity called magnetic flux is used.
Magnetic flux is a scalar quantity and is represented by the symbol $\Phi$.
Suppose a plane loop of wire of area $A$ has a magnetic field at right angles to it (Figure 27.4), and the value of the magnetic flux density at any point on the loop is $B$. Then, the magnetic flux passing through the area $A$ (that is, $\Phi$ ) is defined by:

Magnetic flux through area $A=$ magnetic flux density × area

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { i.e. } \Phi=B A \quad \text { (F\&T, page 62) }
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-454.jpg?height=727&width=756&top_left_y=2506&top_left_x=1868)
Figure 27.4

Since $\Phi=B A$, the SI unit of magnetic flux $=$ SI unit of magnetic flux density × SI unit of area

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(\text { tesla })(\text { metre squared }) \\
& =1 \mathrm{Tm} \mathrm{~m}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

This unit is called the weber (Wb).
i.e. $1 \mathrm{~Wb}=1 \mathrm{~T} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$
The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb).

If the magnetic flux density is not perpendicular to the area, the flux through $A$ is the component of $B$ perpendicular to $A$ multiplied by the area.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

What is the magnetic flux through a loop of area $0.4 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ placed at right angles to a magnetic field of 2 T ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi & =B A \\
& =(2)(0.4) \\
& =0.8 \mathrm{~Wb}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 27.3 Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction

The experiments on page 442 indicate that the size of an induced emf depends on how quickly the magnetic flux is changing. If the flux is changing quickly, the induced emf is large, and if the flux is changing slowly, the induced emf is small. The relationship between the size of the induced emf and the changing magnetic flux is given by Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.

Faraday's law states that the size of the induced emf is directly proportional to the rate of change of flux.

From Faraday's law:
induced emf $\propto$ rate of change of flux
That is:

$$
E \propto \frac{\text { change in } \Phi}{\text { time taken }} \text { or } E \propto \frac{\text { final } \Phi-\text { initial } \Phi}{\text { time taken }}
$$

So:

$$
E=k \frac{\text { final } \Phi-\text { initial } \Phi}{\text { time taken }} \quad \text { where } k \text { is a constant }
$$

The value of the constant of proportionality $k$ depends on the units in which the various quantities are measured. In SI units, its value is 1 (you do not need to know why at this stage). So:

$$
\text { Induced emf } E=\frac{\text { (final flux - initial flux) }}{\text { time taken }}
$$

This is the formula you will use in most numerical calculations involving induced emfs.
Using calculus notation, this is written as:

$$
E=-\frac{d \phi}{d t}
$$

(F\&T, page 62)

The minus sign indicates the direction of the induced emf and will be explained below under Lenz's law. You can ignore the minus sign in all numerical calculations.

Note: if a coil has several turns and if the flux through the coil is changing, then the total emf induced in the coil is the sum of the emfs induced in each turn, because the turns are in series.
Therefore, if a coil has $N$ turns, the emf induced in the coil is:
Induced emf, $E=N \frac{\text { (final flux-initial flux) }}{\text { time taken }}$
Using calculus notation, if the rate at which the flux through the coil is changing is $\frac{d \Phi}{d t}$, then the induced emf in the coil is given by:
$E=-N \frac{d \Phi}{d t}$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

The magnetic flux through a one-turn coil changes from 2 Wb to 8 Wb in 4 seconds.
a) Find the average emf induced in the coil.
b) If the coil has a resistance of $10 \Omega$ and is a complete circuit, find the induced current.

## Solution

a) induced emf, $E=\frac{\text { (final flux-initial flux) }}{\text { time taken }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{(8-2)}{4} \\
& =1.5 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) induced current, $I=\frac{\text { induced emf }}{\text { resistance }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{1.5}{10} \\
& =0.15 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

Find the emf induced in a 100 -turn coil if the flux through it changes from 0 Wb to 6 Wb in 0.2 s .

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { induced emf in one turn of the coil } & =\frac{(\text { final } \varphi-\text { initial } \varphi)}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{(6-0)}{0.2} \\
& =30 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

The coil has 100 turns connected in series with an emf of 30 volts induced in each one. Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { total emf induced } & =(100)(30) \\
& =3000 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

Or:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { induced emf in coil } & =N \frac{(\text { final } \Phi-\text { initial } \Phi)}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =(100) \frac{(6-0)}{0.2} \\
& =3000 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

To demonstrate Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction

2. Move the magnet away from or towards the coil slowly (the flux through the coil therefore changes slowly). The galvanometer gives a small deflection (indicating a small induced emf).
3. Move the magnet away from or towards the coil very rapidly (the flux through the coil thus changes rapidly). The galvanometer gives a large deflection (indicating a large

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-457.jpg?height=479&width=867&top_left_y=664&top_left_x=1422)

induced emf).

This shows approximately that the size of the induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux through the coil.

## SEC sample question (HL)

## Question

The magnetic flux density affecting a coil changes by 0.278 T in 0.017 s . The area of the coil is $225 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. The coil consists of 800 turns of wire.
Calculate the emf induced in the coil.

## Solution

First, convert area to $\mathrm{m}^{2}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \mathrm{~m} & =1000 \mathrm{~mm} \\
1 \mathrm{~m}^{2} & =(1000)(1000) \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\
& =10^{6} \mathrm{~mm}^{2} \\
1 \mathrm{~mm}^{2} & =10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, $225 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}=225 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{2}=2.25 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$
Then, calculate change in flux:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { change in flux } & =\text { change in flux density } \text { × area } \\
& =(0.278)\left(2.25 \times 10^{-4}\right) \\
& =6.255 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~Wb}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, apply Faraday's Law:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { induced emf in coil } & =N \frac{\text { change in flux }}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =(800) \frac{6.255 \times 10^{-5}}{0.017} \\
& =2.944 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

A 200-turn rectangular coil of area $0.05 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 3 T . If the flux density increases to 10 T in 0.4 s , find the average induced emf in the coil.

## Solution

Use $\Phi=B A$ to find the initial and final flux:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { initial } \Phi & =B A \\
& =(3)(0.05) \\
& =0.15 \mathrm{~Wb} \\
\text { final } \Phi & =B A \\
& =(10)(0.05) \\
& =0.5 \mathrm{~Wb}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\text { average induced emf } \begin{aligned}
& =N \frac{(\text { final } \Phi-\text { initial } \Phi)}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =(200) \frac{(0.5-0.15)}{0.4} \\
& =175 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 5

## Question

A rectangular coil of 1 turn and dimensions $2 \mathrm{~cm} \times 4 \mathrm{~cm}$ enters a magnetic field of flux density 3 T . If the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field and it moves at $6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ parallel to its 4 cm side (Figure 27.6), find the emf induced in the coil.

## Solution

Use:
induced emf $=\frac{(\text { final } \Phi-\text { initial } \Phi)}{\text { time taken }}$
From Figure 27.6:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { initial } \Phi & =0 \mathrm{~Wb} \\
\text { final } \Phi & =B A \\
& =3\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)\left(4 \times 10^{-2}\right) \\
& =2.4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~Wb}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-458.jpg?height=860&width=872&top_left_y=1872&top_left_x=1316)
Figure 27.6

Between position 1 and position 2, the coil travels 4 cm at $6 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { time taken } & =\frac{\left(4 \times 10^{-2}\right)}{6} \\
& =6.67 \times 10^{-3} \text { seconds }
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute your calculated values into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { induced emf } & =\frac{(\text { final } \Phi-\text { initial } \Phi)}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =\frac{\left(2.4 \times 10^{-3}-0\right)}{6.67 \times 10^{-3}} \\
& =0.36 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 6

## Question

A 100-turn rectangular coil of dimensions
$6 \mathrm{~cm} \times 8 \mathrm{~cm}$ rotates at constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 2 T (Figure 27.7).
a) If the coil undergoes 5 rotations per second, find the average induced emf in the coil in going from the position in Figure 27.7(A) to that in Figure 27.7(B).
b) Sketch a graph to show how the induced emf varies during this time.

## Solution

a) In Figure 27.7(A), the flux through the coil is zero.

In Figure 27.7(B):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi & =B A \\
& =(2)\left(\left(6 \times 10^{-2}\right)\left(8 \times 10^{-2}\right)\right) \\
& =0.0096 \mathrm{~Wb}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-459.jpg?height=1001&width=652&top_left_y=455&top_left_x=1595)
Figure 27.7

Time taken to go from Figure 27.7(A) to Figure 27.7(B) is the time to undergo $\frac{1}{4}$ of a rotation.
Coil does 5 rotations per second, so the time for one rotation $=1 \div 5=\frac{1}{5} \mathrm{~s}$, and the time for quarter of a rotation $=\frac{1}{5} \div 4=\frac{1}{20} \mathrm{~s}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { average induced emf } & =N \frac{(\text { final } \Phi-\text { initial } \Phi)}{\text { time taken }} \\
& =(100) \frac{(0.0096-0)}{\left(\frac{1}{20}\right)} \\
& =19.2 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) In position (A), the flux through the coil is zero, but a further small rotation causes a large change in flux. The rate of change of flux is greatest at (A), and so is the induced emf.
In position (B), a further small rotation causes only a tiny change in flux. In fact, the instantaneous rate of change of flux at (B) is zero, and the induced emf is instantaneously zero. The graph is shown in Figure 27.8.

### 27.4 Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction

On page 443 you saw that the direction of the induced current (and emf) depends on whether the magnetic flux through the coil is increasing or decreasing. Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction gives the direction of the induced current caused by a changing magnetic field.

Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change producing it.

For example, if the changing flux in a coil is produced by an approaching north pole, Lenz's law says the induced current will flow in such a direction as to oppose the approaching north pole.

- Figure 27.11 shows a woman running towards a coil with a magnet. The magnetic flux passing through the coil is increasing as the north pole approaches, and an emf is induced in the coil.
- By Lenz's law, the induced current in the coil must flow in a direction that opposes the north pole of the magnet coming towards it.
- The induced current in the coil must, therefore, flow in such a direction that the end of the coil facing the approaching magnet behaves like a north pole, thus trying to repel the approaching north pole.
- Because of this opposition, the woman must do work in bringing the magnet towards the coil (north repels north). The work she does appears as electrical energy in the coil.
If the woman runs away from the coil, the direction of the induced current must change so that her motion is still opposed. The direction of the

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-461.jpg?height=926&width=792&top_left_y=1972&top_left_x=1953)
Figure 27.11

induced current changes so that a south pole appears at the right-hand side of the coil in Figure 27.11. The work the woman does in pulling a north pole away from a south pole again appears as electrical energy in the coil. Lenz's law follows from the principle of conservation of energy.

Note: Consider what would happen in Figure 27.11 if Lenz's law was not true.

- As the north pole of the magnet approaches the coil, suppose the induced current flowed so that a south pole appeared facing the approaching north pole.
- The south pole would attract the north pole, causing the north pole to accelerate towards the coil.
- This, in turn, would cause an increased induced emf and an increased induced current.
- The magnet would be gaining kinetic energy and electrical energy would be appearing in the coil.
- Therefore, energy would be created from nowhere, which violates the principle of conservation of energy. This can't happen.


## Demonstration experiment 27.3

## To demonstrate Lenz's law

## Method

1. Suspend a light aluminium ring from a piece of thread (Figure 27.12).
2. Move one pole of a bar magnet quickly towards it. The ring moves away from the approaching magnet.
3. Move the magnet quickly away from the ring. The ring follows the magnet.

## Conclusion

As the magnet approaches the ring, current is induced in the ring, and a pole the same as the approaching pole on the magnet appears at the

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-462.jpg?height=701&width=828&top_left_y=384&top_left_x=1774)
Figure 27.12

side of the ring nearest the magnet. This repels the magnet, and the magnet repels the ring. The result is that the ring moves away from the approaching magnet.
When the magnet is taken away from the ring, the direction of the induced current changes, causing an opposite pole to appear at the side of the ring facing the magnet. This causes the ring to be attracted to the magnet and so it follows the magnet.
The direction of the movement of the ring in each case follows from Lenz's law. Therefore, the law is demonstrated.

## Alternative method

Figure 27.13 shows an alternative way of demonstrating Lenz's law. A cylindrical piece of metal is dropped through a copper pipe. How long it takes to fall through the pipe is noted. A strong cylindrical magnet (the same size and weight as the piece of metal) is then dropped through the same pipe.

- Drop a small cylindrical piece of metal through a copper pipe.
- Measure how long the piece of metal takes to fall through the pipe.
- Drop a small cylindrical magnet (the same size and weight as the piece of metal) through the same pipe.
- Measure how long the magnet takes to fall through the pipe.


## Conclusion

As the magnet falls through the copper pipe, its changing magnetic field induces currents in the pipe.
By Lenz's law, these currents flow in such a direction as to oppose the change producing them (the magnet moving downwards). So, they exert upward forces on the magnet, slowing it down. The unmagnetised metal cylinder does not experience these forces. Since the result follows from Lenz's law, the law is demonstrated.

Faraday's law and Lenz's law are sometimes known as the laws of

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-462.jpg?height=1157&width=799&top_left_y=1679&top_left_x=1783)
Figure 27.13 The magnet takes much longer to fall through the pipe than the metal.

electromagnetic induction.

## Worked Example 7

## Question

A scientist moves a magnet towards a coil at $10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. The resistance of the coil is $5 \Omega$ and the induced current is 0.2 A . Find the force on the magnet.

## Solution

Let $F=$ the force on the magnet
In 1 second:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { work done by the scientist } & =\text { force × distance } \\
& =(F \times 10) \text { joules }
\end{aligned}
$$

In 1 second:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { electrical energy dissipated in the coil } & =I^{2} R \\
& =(0.2)^{2}(5) \text { joules }
\end{aligned}
$$

By the principle of conservation of energy, these must be equal, so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
10 F & =(0.2)^{2}(5) \\
F & =\frac{(0.2)^{2}(5)}{10} \\
& =0.02 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 27.5 Changing mechanical energy to electrical energy - generators

## An electric generator is a device that converts kinetic energy to electrical energy.

Electromagnetic induction is the principle on which the electric generator operates, and so is the principle behind most modern large-scale production of electrical energy. In an electricity generating station, some form of energy - such as chemical energy from coal or natural gas - is used to produce steam, which causes a turbine to rotate. In other words, the turbine is given kinetic energy. The turbine rotates a coil in a magnetic field, causing the magnetic

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-464.jpg?height=584&width=948&top_left_y=2975&top_left_x=1673)
Figure 27.18 An alternator in a car.

flux through it to change, and an emf is induced. In this way, the turbine's kinetic energy is converted to electrical energy.
The alternator in a car (Figure 27.18) is turned by the engine and generates electricity to supply power to the car's electrical system, keeping the car battery charged.

## The simple AC generator

Figure 27.19 shows a coil in a uniform magnetic field.

- If the coil is made to rotate about the axis, the magnetic flux passing through the coil changes.
- As the coil goes from A to B, the flux passing through it increases. As it moves from $B$ to $C$, the flux passing through it decreases.
- Therefore, an emf is induced in the coil.
- The emf is in one direction when the flux is increasing and in the opposite direction when the flux is decreasing. So, if a coil is rotated in a uniform magnetic field, an alternating emf is induced in the coil.
- If the coil is connected to a complete circuit, current will flow - current is generated in the coil. The arrangement is called a generator.
In Figure 27.20 the coil is connected to the external circuit with slip rings. The slip rings are connected rigidly to the coil, and as the coil spins, so do the rings. The carbon brushes do not move. This means the same side of the coil is always connected to X and the other side always to Y . Because of this, alternating current (AC) flows in the external circuit. The magnet, coil and slip rings together are called a simple AC generator.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-465.jpg?height=1040&width=776&top_left_y=312&top_left_x=1884)
Figure 27.19 A coil being rotated in a uniform magnetic field

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-465.jpg?height=633&width=1098&top_left_y=1731&top_left_x=364)
Figure 27.20 A simple AC generator

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-465.jpg?height=372&width=1199&top_left_y=1692&top_left_x=1546)
Figure 27.21 A sinusoidal graph of the alternating current

If the field is uniform and the coil spins at a constant rate, the alternating current generated follows a sinusoidal graph (Figure 27.21). (You may have seen a graph like this in your Maths course. It is the same type of graph as $y=\sin x$ ).
Figure 27.22 also shows the position of the coil at several instants. The emf is greatest when the coil is in positions $A, C$ and $E$ because the rate of change of flux is greatest there. The emf is instantaneously zero at $B$ and $D$, as the flux is not changing at either of these instants.
The operation of a simple $A C$ generator can be shown in the laboratory. If a centre zero voltmeter is connected to the output, the pointer will move backwards and forwards, showing the AC produced.

## The simple DC generator

In Figure 27.23 (page 454), the rotating coil is connected to the external circuit with a split ring commutator. As in the AC generator, the split ring commutator is connected rigidly to the coil, and it spins as the coil spins, but the carbon brushes do not move. Every time the coil passes through the vertical, the side of the coil connected to the left-hand brush changes. So, the current always flows in the same direction in the external circuit (direct current). This arrangement is called a simple DC generator.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-465.jpg?height=1065&width=975&top_left_y=2565&top_left_x=1770)
Figure 27.22 Variation of the induced emf with time and position of the coil in an AC generator.

However, the size of the direct current varies as shown in Figure 27.24. Although it always flows in the same direction, it is not steady.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-466.jpg?height=665&width=1199&top_left_y=426&top_left_x=198)
Figure 27.23 A simple DC generator

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-466.jpg?height=283&width=1146&top_left_y=589&top_left_x=1450)
Figure 27.24 The size of the direct current varies. Although it always flows in the same direction, it is not steady.

Note: Alternating current (AC) is generated in a coil spinning in a uniform magnetic field. If the coil is connected to the external circuit with slip rings, the arrangement is a simple AC generator.
If the coil is connected to the external circuit with a split ring commutator, the arrangement is a simple DC generator.

### 27.6 Alternating current

When direct current (DC) flows in a wire, the electrons move in the same direction through the wire. When alternating current (AC) flows, the electrons change their direction of motion regularly.
For example, suppose an alternating current of frequency 50 Hz is flowing in the circuit shown in Figure 27.25.
This means that:

- For the first $\frac{1}{100}$ of a second, the electrons flow from A towards B.
- In the next $\frac{1}{100}$ of a second, they flow from B towards A.
- In the next $\frac{1}{100}$ of a second, they flow from $A$ towards $B$ again.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-466.jpg?height=564&width=763&top_left_y=1852&top_left_x=1855)
Figure 27.25

- This process repeats. Each electron undergoes a full cycle (also called an oscillation) in $\frac{1}{50}$ of a second.

Figure 27.26 is a graph of the size of the alternating current plotted against time.
Positive values signify that the current is flowing in one direction, and negative values signify that it is flowing in the opposite direction. (As on page 453, you may have seen a graph like this in your Maths course. It is the same type of graph as $y=\sin x$ ).

## AC voltage

To produce an alternating current like this, an alternating voltage is necessary. A graph of the AC voltage against time is very similar to that in

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-466.jpg?height=606&width=1228&top_left_y=2744&top_left_x=1354)
Figure 27.26

If the AC voltage is applied across a pure resistor, the current flowing at any instant is found from Ohm's law; that is:
$I=\frac{V}{R}$ So, current at any instant $=\frac{\text { voltage at that instant }}{\text { resistance }}$
Therefore, when $V$ is large so is $I$, when $V$ is small so is $I$, and when $V$ changes direction so does $I$.

If an alternating potential difference is placed across the $y$-plates of an oscilloscope, and a suitable time base voltage is placed across the $x$-plates, a display similar to Figure 27.27 will result. Note how similar this is to the graph in Figure 27.26.
If a DC voltage is placed across the $y$-plates, the display will be a horizontal line, as in Figure 27.28.

## The heating effect of an alternating current

In Figure 27.29, a current of 3 A flows through the $6 \Omega$ resistor. Heat is produced in the resistor at a rate given by:
$P=I^{2} R=(3)^{2}(6)=54 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-467.jpg?height=626&width=721&top_left_y=1966&top_left_x=325)
Figure 27.29

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-467.jpg?height=626&width=613&top_left_y=1969&top_left_x=1071)
Figure 27.30

Figure 27.30 shows an alternating current flowing through the same resistor. What is the peak value of the AC in either direction, if the AC produces heat at the same rate as the 3 A direct current?
If the AC only reaches 3 A in each direction, it will not produce heat at the rate of $54 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, because the current is less than 3 A at all other times in each cycle. So, if the AC produces heat at the same rate as the 3 A direct current, its peak value in each direction must be bigger than 3 A .
It can be proved that the peak value of the $\mathrm{AC}\left(I_{0}\right)$ needed to have the same heating effect as the 3 A DC is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{0} & =3 \times \sqrt{2} \\
& =3 \times 1.414 \\
& =4.24 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

You do not need to know the proof.

## RMS values of AC

When the size of an alternating current is given a value (for example, 5 A ), it means that this alternating current has the same heating effect as a 5 A direct current. This is called the rms value of the alternating current ( $I_{\text {rms }}$ ).
Since alternating current varies with time, to have the same heating effect as a 5 A direct current, it must have a peak value ( $I_{0}$ ) in each direction that is greater than 5 A .
The relationship between rms current and peak current is:

$$
I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}} \text { or } I_{0}=I_{\mathrm{rms}} \times \sqrt{2}
$$

(F\&T, page 62)

Mains electricity in Ireland, and the EU, is supplied at a voltage of 230 V . This means that mains voltage will produce heat in a resistor at the same rate as a steady DC voltage of 230 volts. Just like with current, 230 V is called the rms voltage, $V_{\text {rms }}$.
The peak value of the alternating voltage ( $V_{\mathrm{p}}$ ) in either direction must be greater than 230 V to have the same heating effect. The relationship between these voltages is:

$$
V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}} \text { or } V_{0}=V_{\mathrm{rms}} \times \sqrt{2}
$$

(F\&T, page 62)

When AC flows in a pure resistance, the average power $P$ (the rate at which heat is produced) is given by:

$$
P=I_{\mathrm{rms}} \times V_{\mathrm{rms}} \text { or } P=I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2} R
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{0} & =V_{\mathrm{rms}} \times \sqrt{2} \\
& =230 \times 1.414 \\
& =325.2 \mathrm{~V}

$$

The peak value of an AC current is 10 A . Find its rms value.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{0}=10 \mathrm{~A}, I_{\mathrm{rms}} & =? \\
I_{\mathrm{rms}} & =\frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}} \\
& =\frac{10}{1.414} \\
& =7.07 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 10

## Question

An alternating current flowing in a wire of resistance $10 \Omega$ produces heat at the rate of 60 W. Find:
a) The rms value of the current
b) The rms voltage
c) The peak value of the voltage across the wire

## Solution

a) $P=I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2} R$

Solve for $I_{\mathrm{rm}}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{\mathrm{rms}} & =\sqrt{\frac{P}{R}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{60}{10}} \\
& =2.45 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) $\quad V_{\mathrm{rms}}=I_{\mathrm{rms}} R$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(2.45)(10) \\
& =24.5 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

c) $\quad V_{0}=V_{\mathrm{rms}} \times \sqrt{2}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =(24.5)(1.414) \\
& =34.65 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 27.7 Mutual inductance

A changing electric current in a coil produces a changing magnetic field in the space around it. If another coil is placed in this changing magnetic field, an emf is induced in this coil. If this happens, there is mutual inductance between the two coils.

Mutual inductance exists between two coils if a changing magnetic field in one coil causes an induced emf to appear in a nearby coil.

Suppose the current in the first coil is changing at a certain rate. Then, the greater the induced emf in the second coil, the greater the mutual inductance between the two coils.
The size of the induced emf and hence the mutual inductance between the two coils may be increased by:

- Decreasing the distance between the coils
- Winding the coils on the same soft iron core
- Increasing the number of turns on either or both coils


## Demonstration Experiment 27.4

## To show mutual inductance

## Method

1. Use the equipment shown in Figure 27.31.
2. When switch $S$ is either opened or closed, the current in coil 1 changes and so the magnetic field around it changes. This changing magnetic field passes through coil 2.
3. As this happens, the galvanometer in coil 2 gives a deflection showing that an emf is induced in coil 2 . This shows there is a mutual inductance between the two coils.
If a steady current flows in coil 1, no emf is induced in coil 2. It is only when the current in coil 1 changes that an emf is induced in coil 2. If both coils are wound on the same soft iron core, the size of the induced emfs are much larger due to the increased mutual inductance.
Mutual inductance occurs in the transformer.

### 27.8 Transformers

You saw on pages 357 and 393 that mains electricity is AC, and that the voltage of mains electricity is increased to a very high value when the electricity is being transported around the country on the National Grid. This is because the $I^{2} R$ heat losses in the wires are minimised at high voltages. AC is used rather than DC because it is very easy to change the value of an alternating voltage with a device called a transformer.
Figure 27.32 shows the structure of a transformer.

- It consists of two coils of wire wound on a soft iron core.
- One coil, called the primary coil, has an alternating voltage applied to it.
- The voltage across the primary coil is the input voltage.
- The transformer causes a different voltage to appear across the other coil, called the secondary coil.
- The voltage across the secondary coil is the output voltage.

A transformer is a device used to change the value of an alternating voltage.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-471.jpg?height=864&width=2420&top_left_y=1344&top_left_x=325)
Figure 27.32 (A) A transformer. (B) A demonstration transformer for a school laboratory.

The operation of a transformer is based on the mutual inductance between the primary and secondary coils.

- The input voltage, $V_{p}$, across the primary coil causes alternating current to flow in the primary coil.
- This current causes an alternating magnetic flux in the iron core.
- This changing magnetic flux passes through the secondary coil and induces an emf in it. This is the output voltage, $V_{s}$.
- The size of the emf in the secondary coil, $V_{\mathrm{s}}$, depends on the number of turns in the secondary coil, $N_{5}$. Recall that induced emf $=N_{5} \times$ (rate of change of flux)
- Depending on the number of turns on the secondary coil, the output voltage can be less than, equal to or greater than the input voltage.
If $N_{\mathrm{p}}=$ number of turns on the primary coil, then the following is true:
If $N_{\mathrm{s}}$ is greater than $N_{\mathrm{p}}$ then $V_{\mathrm{s}}$ is greater than $V_{\mathrm{p}}$ and it is called a step-up transformer. If $N_{\mathrm{s}}$ is less than $N_{\mathrm{p}}$ then $V_{\mathrm{s}}$ is less than $V_{\mathrm{p}}$ and it is called a step-down transformer

It can be shown that:
$\frac{V_{\mathrm{s}}}{V_{\mathrm{p}}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}}$
(F\&T, page 62, where $V_{\mathrm{p}}$ is written as $V_{\mathrm{i}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{s}}$ is written as $V_{\mathrm{o}}$ )

Also, if there are no energy losses in the transformer, the power in must equal the power out:

$$
I_{\mathrm{p}} V_{\mathrm{p}}=I_{\mathrm{s}} V_{\mathrm{s}}
$$

## Worked Example 11

## Question

A transformer with 100 turns on the primary coil and 5000 turns on the secondary coil has its primary coil connected across a 230 -volt AC supply. Find the voltage across the secondary coil.

## Solution

$N_{\mathrm{p}}=100, N_{\mathrm{s}}=5000, V_{\mathrm{p}}=230 \mathrm{~V}, V_{\mathrm{s}}=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{V_{\mathrm{s}}}{V_{\mathrm{p}}} & =\frac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}} \\
V_{\mathrm{s}} & =V_{\mathrm{p}}\left(\frac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}}\right) \\
& =\frac{(230)(5000)}{100} \\
& =11500 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 12

## Question

A transformer has 500 turns of wire in its primary coil and 100 turns in the secondary coil. 230 VAC is applied to the primary coil, and a current of 2 A flows in the primary. Find:
a) The voltage across the secondary coil
b) The current flowing in the secondary coil if the transformer is 100\% efficient
c) The current flowing in the secondary coil if the transformer is 90\% efficient

## Solution

a) $N_{P}=500, N_{\mathrm{s}}=100, V_{\mathrm{p}}=230 \mathrm{~V}, V_{\mathrm{s}}=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{V_{\mathrm{s}}}{V_{\mathrm{p}}} & =\frac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}} \\
V_{\mathrm{s}} & =V_{\mathrm{p}}\left(\frac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}}\right) \\
& =\frac{(230)(100)}{500} \\
& =46 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) If it is 100\% efficient, then power out = power in, so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{\mathrm{s}} V_{\mathrm{s}} & =I_{\mathrm{p}} V_{\mathrm{p}} \\
I_{\mathrm{s}}(46) & =(2)(230) \\
I_{\mathrm{s}} & =\frac{(2)(230)}{46} \\
& =10 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

c) If it is 90\% efficient, then power out = (0.9) power in, so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{\mathrm{S}} V_{\mathrm{S}} & =(0.9) I_{p} V_{p} \\
I_{\mathrm{S}}(46) & =(0.9)(2)(230) \\
I_{\mathrm{S}} & =\frac{(0.9)(2)(230)}{46} \\
& =9 \mathrm{~A}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Factors affecting the efficiency of a transformer

If a transformer were $100 \%$ efficient, the useful energy output would equal the energy input. In practice, some of the energy is transferred to unwanted forms, which reduces the transformer's efficiency. Most of this unwanted energy is dissipated as heat. Very large transformers are oil-cooled to remove this heat. A well-designed transformer can still be 90\% efficient or better.
The main causes of unwanted energy transfer in a transformer are:

- $I^{2} R$ heat losses in the coils. This can be reduced by using thick wire, especially in the lower voltage coil.
- Induced electric currents in the core itself (called eddy currents). These can be reduced by laminating the core (Figure 27.34).
- Energy is needed to repeatedly magnetise, demagnetise, then magnetise the core in the opposite direction. These losses (called hysteresis losses) appear as heat in the core.
- Leakage of magnetic flux occurs. Not all the flux from the primary

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-474.jpg?height=694&width=877&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1744)
Figure 27.34 A laminated core, consisting of thin layers of soft iron separated from each other by thin layers of oxide

may link the secondary.
A laminated core consists of thin layers of soft iron separated from each other by thin layers of oxide which is an insulator. This reduces eddy currents.

## Uses of transformers

Generating stations usually generate electricity at between 20 kV and 30 kV . This value is stepped up to 220 kV or 400 kV for distribution on the National Grid. Its value is reduced to 230 V at substations, ready for use in houses. All changes in voltages are made with transformers.
Computers, radios, televisions and similar equipment all contain transformers to supply the necessary voltage to the appliance.

### 27.9 Powering the country: Generating electricity

Electricity is known as a secondary source of energy. This is because other forms of energy are first needed to produce the electricity. Traditionally, these have been burning fossil fuels, such as coal, oil or natural gas. The heat released boils water, producing high-pressure steam. This drives a turbine, which drives a generator producing the electricity.
The energy sources used to produce electricity can be classified as renewable or non-renewable.
A renewable source of energy is one that doesn't run out.
A non-renewable source of energy is one that does eventually run out.
Examples of renewable energy sources are wind, solar, tidal, wave and geothermal. Many renewable sources create virtually no carbon emissions when producing electricity.
Fossil fuels are the main type of non-renewable energy sources. Nuclear energy is also classified as non-renewable.
At present, in Ireland, about $40 \%$ of the electricity is generated by renewable sources. The aim is to increase this to $80 \%$ by 2030 . However, to be able to use more renewable energy on the grid, Ireland will need to increase the size of the national grid and increase the power handling capacity of many parts of it.
Every source of energy, whatever it is used for, has positive and negative impacts (advantages and disadvantages).
The most common negative impact is the unwanted effect it has on the environment. The impact of greatest concern now is $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and other greenhouse emissions, which are causing rapid global warming. Other negative impacts are dust and airborne particle pollution, toxic chemical release, destruction of waterways and environmental habitats.
When using another source of energy to produce electricity, it is important to choose carefully and wisely to minimise or reverse such damage.

## Comparing electricity generation methods

## Wind energy

The kinetic energy of moving air turns large propeller blades. This drives a wind turbine, which powers a generator to produce electricity.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| - Unlimited renewable source <br> - No CO2 emissions <br> - Almost $100 \%$ efficient | - Requires consistently windy locations <br> - Wind speed varies, so supply is unreliable without backup <br> - Some consider turbines visually intrusive <br> - Can be noisy nearby |

## Coal-fired power stations

Coal is crushed and burned to heat water. The resulting steam drives a turbine connected to a generator.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| - Coal is abundant and affordable <br> - Reliable 24/7 electricity production | - Non-renewable fossil fuel <br> - High $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions, contributing to climate change <br> - Produces other pollutants harmful to health <br> - Low efficiency (-33\%) |

## Solar energy

Photovoltaic cells generate DC electricity when exposed to sunlight.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| - No fuel costs <br> - No greenhouse gas emissions | - Energy generation depends on sunlight; no power at night <br> - Limited intensity and scalability <br> - Large surface areas needed for high output |

## Natural gas power stations

Burning natural gas heats water to produce high-pressure steam, which drives a turbine and generator.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| - Burns cleaner than other fossil fuels <br> - Abundant, affordable, and easily transported <br> - Reliable continuous electricity supply <br> - Acts as a bridging fuel during energy transition <br> - High efficiency (up to $60 \%$ ) | - Non-renewable fossil fuel <br> - Produces $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and contributes to climate change <br> - Highly flammable and explosive |

## Hydroelectric power

A dam blocks a river, creating a reservoir. Water pressure drives a turbine, which powers a generator.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| - No fuel costs <br> - No greenhouse gas emissions <br> - Very efficient (up to $90 \%$ ) | - Floods large areas, affecting ecosystems and homes |

## Nuclear power

Nuclear fission generates heat, producing steam that drives a turbine connected to a generator.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| :--- | :--- |
| - Small amounts of uranium yield large amounts of energy <br> - $\mathrm{No} \mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions in operation <br> - Releases less radiation than coal plants (in normal conditions) | - Risk of catastrophic meltdown <br> - Health risks from uranium mining <br> - Spent fuel requires long-term disposal <br> - Nuclear material can be weaponised <br> - Requires strict security <br> - Efficiency around 33-45\% |

## Issues in electrical generation Environmental impact

Electricity generation is one of the largest contributors to global $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions and climate change. Fossil fuels such as coal and gas also produce other pollutants that harm ecosystems and public health. Addressing these environmental concerns while meeting energy needs requires a shift toward cleaner, renewable energy sources.

## Rapidly increasing demand

There is an exponential growth in demand for electricity, particularly in developed and industrialising nations. How to keep up with this demand, while also reducing environmental impact, requires careful forecasting and long-term planning. Investment in grid infrastructure, generation capacity, and energy efficiency will continue to be essential.

## Reliability and stability of supply

Maintaining a steady electricity supply is a growing challenge, especially with the rise of variable renewable sources like wind and solar. In the case of wind power, for example, fluctuations in output must be managed carefully. Energy storage solutions, such as batteries or pumped hydroelectric systems, can help. In addition, sharing electricity between countries through interconnectors, especially across different time zones with differing peak demands, can improve overall grid stability.

## Security risks

The security of power generation and distribution systems is of critical importance. Natural disasters, extreme weather, terrorism, and cyberattacks all pose significant threats. Serious power outages, particularly in large cities, can have far-reaching consequences for public safety, economic activity, and communication systems.

## Issues with the grid and power distribution

Different generating stations usually generate electricity at between 20 kV and 30 kV .
This value is stepped up to 220 kV or 400 kV using transformers, for large-scale bulk transmission on the National Grid. A high voltage means a low current, so heat wasted in connecting cables is reduced to a minimum, and most of the generated power appears at the other end, ready for consumption.
If electricity was transmitted at 20 KV , most of it would be wasted as heat in the connecting cables running across the country.

## Power losses over long distances

Issue: Even at high voltages, around 5\% of electricity is typically wasted during transmission in Europe.
Solution: Move towards decentralised generation, with smaller local plants generating power closer to where it is used.

## Grid failure due to ageing infrastructure or overload

Issue: Some parts of the grid may be outdated, overloaded, or poorly maintained, increasing the risk of failure.
Solution: Expand and modernise the grid to keep up with increasing demand and changing generation patterns.

## Disruptions due to weather or accidents

Issue: Storms, fallen trees, lightning strikes, or other physical damage can interrupt supply.
Solution: Develop advanced grid management systems that can respond quickly and keep the system stable during disruptions.

## Fluctuating supply from renewable sources

Issue: Sources like wind and solar are not constant, leading to variability in electricity supply.
Solution: Upgrade grid control systems to integrate and balance these fluctuating inputs efficiently.

## Security threats to the grid

Issue: Natural disasters, cyberattacks, or extreme weather events can compromise large sections of the grid.
Solution: Ensure that grid control can be managed from multiple locations. This way, a failure or attack at one site does not affect the entire network.

## Summary What I should know

- Whenever the magnetic field passing through a coil changes, an emf appears in the coil. This phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction or the generator effect
- Magnetic flux through area $A=$ magnetic flux density × area

$$
\Phi=B A
$$

- The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb).
- Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the size of the induced emf is directly proportional to the rate of change of flux.
- Induced emf, $E=\frac{\text { (final flux - initial flux) }}{\text { time taken }}$ or $E=-\frac{d \Phi}{d t}$
- Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change producing it.
- Lenz's law follows from the principle of conservation of energy.
- An electric generator is a device that converts mechanical energy to electrical energy.
- Alternating current (AC) is generated in a coil spinning in a uniform magnetic field.
- If the coil is connected to the external circuit with slip rings, it makes a simple AC generator.
- If the coil is connected to the external circuit with a split ring commutator, it makes a simple DC generator.
- $I=\frac{V}{R}$; that is, current at any instant $=\frac{\text { voltage at that instant }}{\text { resistance }}$

$$
\begin{array}{lllr}
I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}} & & \text { or } & I_{0}=I_{\mathrm{rms}} \times \sqrt{2} \\
V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}} & & \text { or } & V_{0}=V_{\mathrm{rms}} \times \sqrt{2} \\
P_{\mathrm{avg}}=I_{\mathrm{rms}} \times V_{\mathrm{rms}} & & \text { or } & P_{\mathrm{avg}}=I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2} R
\end{array}
$$

- If a changing magnetic field in one coil causes an induced emf to appear in a nearby coil, there is said to be mutual inductance between the two coils.
- A transformer is a device used to change the value of an alternating voltage. For an ideal transformer (i.e. one that is 100\% efficient):
$\frac{V_{\mathrm{s}}}{V_{\mathrm{p}}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{s}}}{N_{\mathrm{p}}}$
$I_{\mathrm{p}} V_{\mathrm{p}}=I_{\mathrm{s}} V_{\mathrm{s}}$

### 28.1 Properties of the electron

Every atom has a dense central part called a nucleus around which electrons orbit (page 495).
Electrons have a very small mass of $9.109 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$ (F\&T, page 46 for a more accurate value) and a negative charge of $1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ coulombs, which is usually represented by $e$ (so $e=1.602 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ ).
The charge on the electron is the smallest amount of charge found in nature. In other words, it is the indivisible quantity of charge. All other amounts of electric charge are a whole number of times the charge on the electron.

Particles called quarks have a smaller charge than the charge on the electron. The charge on a quark is either $\pm \frac{1}{2} e$ or $\pm \frac{2}{3} e$. However, quarks are not found in isolation. They are always found grouped together and the overall charge of the group is $e$ or a whole number multiple of $e$ (see page 545).

## Discovery of the electron

Figure 28.1 shows a sealed glass tube with a metal electrode inside it at each end. The negative electrode is called the cathode and the positive electrode is called the anode (CNAP). If most of the air is pumped out of the tube to produce a reasonable vacuum, it is known as a vacuum tube.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-479.jpg?height=1033&width=1381&top_left_y=2737&top_left_x=1364)
Figure 28.1 A vacuum tube

In 1854 scientists started to investigate what would happen if a high voltage was put across the two electrodes in a vacuum tube. They found that current flowed in the circuit and that a greenish glow appeared on the glass wall of the tube on the opposite side of the anode to the cathode. The scientists concluded that some sort of rays in the tube produced this glow.
In 1869, Hittorff saw a shadow of an object placed in the tube between the cathode and the green glow. This shadow showed that the rays originated from the cathode, so they were called cathode rays.

Cathode rays are streams of high-speed electrons moving from the cathode.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-480.jpg?height=795&width=2423&top_left_y=885&top_left_x=198)
Figure 28.2(A) A diagram and (B) a photograph of a vacuum showing the shadow of a Maltese cross on the wall of the tube

In 1879, William Crookes repeated these experiments. He also found that the cathode rays were deflected in a magnetic field, in the same direction as a negative particle would deflect. So, he believed the cathode rays were negatively charged particles. However, at the time, experiments had failed to show that cathode rays were deflected in an electric field, and many scientists believed they were some form of radiation.
Crookes and other scientists also established that the luminance produced did not depend on what low-pressure gas was in the tube, or what metals the cathode or anode were made from. Crookes concluded

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-480.jpg?height=577&width=1199&top_left_y=1881&top_left_x=1419)
Figure 28.3 A beam of cathode rays in a modern cathode ray tube being deflected by an electric field

that cathode rays were a property of the electric current itself.
In 1897, J.J. Thomson was able to produce better vacuums in the tubes and showed that cathode rays were deflected in an electric field between two parallel metal plates. They deflected in the same direction as expected for a negatively charged particle (Figure 28.3).
Since cathode rays were deflected in both electric and magnetic fields in the same direction as a negatively charged particle, it was accepted that the rays were negatively charged particles. J.J. Thomson called the particles electrons and is, therefore, credited with the discovery of the electron. The electron was the first subatomic particle to be discovered.
Thomson also did experiments whereby the deflection produced by a known electric field cancelled the deflection produced by a known magnetic field. From these, he was able to calculate the charge to mass ratio $\left(\frac{e}{m}\right)$ of the electron.

## Joseph John (J.J.) Thomson

Joseph John (J.J.) Thomson
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-480.jpg?height=281&width=323&top_left_y=2900&top_left_x=2298)
(1856-1940) was an English physicist. He is credited with discovering the electron in 1897 and he proposed the plum pudding model (the Thomson model) of the atom. He also found evidence of the existence of different stable isotopes of atoms. He won the 1906 Nobel Prize in physics. Later, seven of his students also went on to win Nobel Prizes.

At the time, the charge to mass ratios were known for certain small atoms.
Comparing his value with the charge to mass values of the small atoms, he was able to establish that the mass of an electron was about $\frac{1}{1836}$ that of a hydrogen ion (which is a proton).

The cathode ray tube operates as follows:

- A low voltage (for example, 6 V ) is placed across the filament. Current flows through it and it becomes white hot. It heats the cathode.
- Thermionic emission occurs at the cathode, so that electrons are emitted from the cathode.
- There is a large voltage of around 2000 V (called the anode voltage) between the cathode and the anode. The electrons emitted from the cathode accelerate to a high speed as they move towards the anode due to this voltage.
- Since there is a good vacuum in the tube, the electrons do not collide with any gas molecules, so the motion of the electrons is not opposed.
- Many of the electrons that reach the anode pass through the hole in it, forming a beam of electrons that travels to the end of the tube.
- The end of the tube is coated with a layer of fluorescent material (phosphors). This is the screen. When an electron strikes the screen, most of its kinetic energy is converted into light and a bright spot of light is produced on the screen.
The streams of high-speed electrons moving from the cathode are called cathode rays. They:
- Travel from the cathode in fairly straight lines.
- Are invisible, but they cause certain substances to give out light when struck by them, such as zinc sulfide. Such substances are used as the fluorescent coating on the screen in a cathode ray tube. In Figure 28.5, the beam can be seen as it passes a fluorescent sheet, because some of the electrons in the beam strike the sheet and cause light to be emitted.
- Have kinetic energy.
- Can be deflected in electric and magnetic fields. This shows that they are charged particles.
- Can produce X-rays when they strike a metal target (page 488).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-482.jpg?height=825&width=1059&top_left_y=1204&top_left_x=1562)
Figure 28.5 A beam of electrons in a cathode ray tube

### 28.4 Deflection of a beam of electrons in an electric field

Figure 28.6 shows the path taken by an electron as it moves through the space between two parallel plates of opposite charge.

- The positive and negative charges on the plates create an electric field between them, represented by the electric field lines going from the positive plate to the negative plate.
- The field lines show the direction of the force that the electric field would exert on a positive charge, if it were to be placed in the field.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-482.jpg?height=506&width=1114&top_left_y=2467&top_left_x=1510)
Figure 28.6

- The force the field exerts on the electron, which has negative charge, acts in the opposite direction, which is to say, the force on the electron is upwards and so the electron deflects upwards.
- If the potential difference between the plates is increased, the electric field becomes stronger and the electron deflects upwards more sharply
Alternatively, the electron's path can be explained using Coulomb's law. Since the electron is negatively charged, it is attracted to the positive charge on the top plate and repelled by the negative charge on the bottom plate. The overall force on the electron is upwards and so it deflects upwards.
This can be demonstrated in the laboratory with a suitable cathode ray tube (Figure 28.3 and Figure 28.7). Here, a high voltage is placed across the parallel plates and the beam deflects. If the potential difference across the plates is reversed, the beam deflects downwards.

The larger the potential difference, the more the beam deflects. In the cathode ray tube in Figure 28.7, the position of the spot on the screen is controlled by the voltage across the $X$-plates and the voltage across the Y-plates. The Y-plates control the vertical positioning and the $X$-plates control the horizontal positioning.

## Energy of electrons in an electric field

Figure 28.8 shows an electric field. If an electron is released at $A$, the field exerts a force on it and the electron accelerates in the direction shown. As the electron moves, it loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy, the loss being equal to the gain.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-483.jpg?height=821&width=1329&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=1422)
Figure 28.7 Deflection of a beam of electrons in an electric field

If the electron is projected against the field (from $A$ to $C$ ) it loses kinetic energy and gains potential energy as it slows down. Again, the loss is equal to the gain.
From page 347, if a charge $Q$ moves through a voltage $V$, the work $W$ done (the energy lost or gained) is given by:

$$
W=Q V
$$

So, for an electron (of charge $e$ ) in an electric field:
Decrease in potential energy = increase in kinetic energy
Or
Increase in potential energy = decrease in kinetic energy
In either case,

$$
e V=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-483.jpg?height=747&width=893&top_left_y=1269&top_left_x=1852)
Figure 28.8

where, $e=$ charge on electron $=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ and $m=$ mass of electron $=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$

Use the values for $e$ and $m$ shown in the box above in the following worked examples.

## Worked Example 1

## Question

An electron is accelerated from rest through a voltage of 3000 V . Find:
a) The electrical potential energy transferred away from the electron (the 'lost' energy)
b) The kinetic energy transferred to the electron (the 'gained' energy)
c) The speed it reaches

## Solution

a) $\quad E_{\mathrm{p}}$ lost $=e \mathrm{~V}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)(3000) \\
& =4.8 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) $E_{k}$ gained $=E_{\rho}$ lost

$$
=4.8 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~J}
$$

c)

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{\mathrm{k}} & =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right) v^{2} \\
& =4.8 \times 10^{-16} \\
v^{2} & =\frac{(2)\left(4.8 \times 10^{-16}\right)}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} \\
v & =\sqrt{1.0549 \times 10^{15}} \\
& =3.2 \times 10^{7} \times \mathrm{m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 2

## Question

A high-speed electron strikes the screen of a cathode ray tube. Calculate the minimum voltage required, across the cathode ray tube, to give the electron a velocity of $2 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$.

## Solution

Let $V$ be the voltage across the tube. Then:

$$
\begin{aligned}
e V & =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \\
1.6 \times 10^{-19} V & =\frac{1}{2}\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{7}\right)^{2} \\
V & =1137.5 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}
$$

## The electronvolt

When measuring the energy of electrons or other small particles, a unit called the electronvolt is sometimes used. To convert electron volts to joules (or vice versa) you can use the following:

```
1 electronvolt (eV)=1.6 x10-19 joules(J)
```

```
If a more accurate value is needed, use:
    1 \mathrm { eV } = 1 . 6 0 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 9 } \mathrm { J }
or
    1 \mathrm { eV } = 1 . 6 0 2 1 7 6 5 3 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 9 } \mathrm { J }
```

Larger amounts of energy are expressed in these units: $\mathrm{keV}, \mathrm{MeV}$ and GeV .
1 kiloelectronvolt = $1 \mathrm{keV}=1000 \mathrm{eV}=10^{3} \mathrm{eV}$
1 megaelectronvolt $=1 \mathrm{MeV}=1000000 \mathrm{eV}=10^{6} \mathrm{eV}$
1 gigaelectronvolt $=1 \mathrm{GeV}=1000000000 \mathrm{eV}=10^{9} \mathrm{eV}$

## Worked Example 3

## Question

A particle has 4 keV of kinetic energy. Express this energy in joules.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
4 \mathrm{keV} & =4000 \mathrm{eV} \\
& =(4000)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right) \\
& =6.4 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 4

## Question

An electron has an energy of $6 \times 10^{-18} \mathrm{~J}$. What is its energy in electronvolts?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \mathrm{eV} & =1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \\
1 \mathrm{~J} & =\frac{1}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \mathrm{eV} \\
6 \times 10^{-18} \mathrm{~J} & =\frac{6 \times 10^{-18}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \mathrm{eV} \\
& =37.5 \mathrm{eV}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 28.5 Deflection of a beam of electrons in a magnetic field

A beam of electrons is a flow of charge and is, therefore, an electric current that will experience a force when placed in a magnetic field (page 419). This can be demonstrated by placing a bar magnet near the cathode ray tube, as shown in Figure 28.11. The beam of electrons deflects according to Fleming's left-hand rule. Compare the path with that shown in Figure 28.5.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-486.jpg?height=822&width=2432&top_left_y=787&top_left_x=192)
Figure 28.11(A) and (B) Deflecting a beam of electrons in a magnetic field

## Worked Example 5

## Question

Figure 28.12(A) and (B) show an electron beam moving into a uniform magnetic field. In what direction will the electron beam deflect in the field in each diagram?

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-486.jpg?height=460&width=1411&top_left_y=2142&top_left_x=240)
Figure 28.12

## Solution

In Figure 28.12(A) negative charges moving up the page correspond to a conventional current moving down the page. Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the beam of electrons deflects out of the page.
In Figure 28.12(B) negative charges moving to the left correspond to a conventional current moving to the right. Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the force is upwards and so the beam of electrons deflects upwards. This is also what is happening in the Figure 28.11(A).

## A beam of electrons in a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle

Figure 28.13 shows a beam of electrons moving at right angles to a uniform magnetic field.

- By Fleming's left-hand rule, the force on the electrons is perpendicular to their direction of motion and they deflect as shown. As they move, you can see that the force is always perpendicular to the direction of motion. This means that although their direction of motion changes, the magnitude of their velocity (their speed) does not change.
- When a particle of charge $q$ moves at speed $v$ at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density $B$, it experiences a force $F$ given by: $F=q v B$ (page 435)
- This formula gives the force on an electron in a magnetic field. Since the speed of the electrons does not change, the force on them is of constant magnitude.
- A force of constant magnitude always acting at right angles to the direction of motion is exactly the condition needed for an object to move in a circle (page 436).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-487.jpg?height=890&width=799&top_left_y=468&top_left_x=1946)
Figure 28.13

Note: A beam of electrons moving at right angles to a magnetic field moves in a circle (Figure 28.13).

In the following worked examples, use $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ and mass of electron $=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$. Recall from Chapter 26, that the SI unit of magnetic flux density, $B$, is the tesla (T).

## Worked Example 6

## Question

What is the force on an electron moving with a speed of $4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 5 T ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
F & =q v B \\
& =\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)\left(4 \times 10^{5}\right)(5) \\
& =3.2 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$

You may need to review the material in Chapter 26, Section 26.4 before studying the next worked example.

## Worked Example 7

## Question

An electron moving at a speed of $4 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field moving at right angles to the field. The electron then moves in a circular path in the field. If the flux density, $B$ of the field is $1.5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~T}$, calculate the radius of the path, $r$.

## Solution

centripetal force on electron = force on electron due to magnetic field

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{m v^{2}}{r} & =B e v \\
r & =\frac{m v}{B e} \\
r & =\frac{\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)\left(4 \times 10^{7}\right)}{\left(1.5 \times 10^{-2}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-1} 9\right)}=1.52 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 28.6 The photoelectric effect

In 1887, Heinrich Hertz discovered that an electric spark discharge between two electrodes occurred more readily when ultraviolet light fell on one of the electrodes. In 1888, Hallwachs discovered that if ultraviolet light is shone onto a negatively-charged zinc plate, the plate loses its charge rapidly. Later, it was shown that this is because ultraviolet (UV) light causes electrons to be emitted from the zinc plate. This phenomenon is known as the photoelectric effect.

The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from the surface of a metal when electromagnetic radiation of a suitable frequency falls on it.

## Demonstration Experiment 28.1

To show the photoelectric effect

## Method

1. Use the equipment in Figure 28.15.
2. Place the zinc plate on the cap of the electroscope and charge the electroscope negatively (by induction).
3. Shine UV light onto the zinc plate and notice that the gold leaf collapses quite quickly.
4. Place a sheet of glass between the UV lamp and the zinc, and notice that the leaves do not collapse. UV light from a typical UV lamp cannot get through the glass.
5. Remove the glass and replace the UV source with visible light sources of various frequencies. The leaves will not collapse.
6. Charge the electroscope positively and shine UV light on the zinc. The leaves will not collapse.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-488.jpg?height=815&width=683&top_left_y=331&top_left_x=1600)
Figure 28.14

## Conclusion

UV light causes electrons to be emitted from the zinc.
When the electroscope is charged positively, the gold leaf does not collapse because any electrons emitted by the UV light are immediately attracted back by the positive charge on the zinc.
Photoemission occurs in zinc for UV light or X-rays but not for visible light. Photoemission occurs in sodium for some wavelengths of visible light, as well as UV light and X-rays. Some other materials show photoemission even for infra-red light.

### 28.7 The photocell

Figure 28.16 shows a photocell and its circuit symbol.

- A photocell or photoelectric cell is a device that conducts electric current when light of a suitable frequency shines on it. The size of the electric current it conducts is directly proportional to the intensity of the light falling on it.
- A photocell has two electrodes (cathode and anode) in a glass tube. The anode is positive with respect to the cathode.
- The cathode is called the photocathode and is usually semicylindrical in shape. The cathode is normally coated with material that undergoes photoemission. The anode is a rod running along the centre of the tube.
- The tube contains a vacuum (it is evacuated). Some tubes contain inert gas at very low pressure.
- If light of a suitable frequency strikes the photocathode, the photoelectric effect occurs: electrons (called photoelectrons) are emitted from it. These are attracted across the tube to the positive anode and a small current of a few microamperes flows in the circuit. This current is called the photocurrent. Switch off the light and the current stops.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-489.jpg?height=1104&width=939&top_left_y=1100&top_left_x=1806)
Figure 28.16

## Demonstration Experiment 28.2

## To demonstrate the action of a photocell

## Method

1. Use the equipment shown in Figure 28.17.
2. Measure the distance $d$ from the light source to the photocathode and measure the current $I$.
3. Change the distance several times, recording both the distance and the current each time.
4. Plot a graph of photocurrent against $\frac{1}{d^{2}}$.
5. Your graph should look like the one in Figure 28.18.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-489.jpg?height=727&width=831&top_left_y=3066&top_left_x=371)
Figure 28.17

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-489.jpg?height=727&width=854&top_left_y=3066&top_left_x=1227)
Figure 28.18

## Conclusions

The graph in Figure 28.18 is a straight line passing through the origin. Therefore, the photocurrent is directly proportional to $\frac{1}{d^{2}}$.
It is a fact that the intensity of the light is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source. So, the intensity of light $\propto \frac{1}{d^{2}}$. Therefore:

$$
\text { Photocurrent } \propto \frac{1}{d^{2}}
$$

and

$$
\text { Intensity of light } \propto \frac{1}{d^{2}}
$$

So, Photocurrent $\alpha$ intensity of light
The photocurrent is directly proportional to the intensity of the light.

A white light source emits light of a continuous range of frequencies. The frequency of the light striking the cathode can be controlled by placing a coloured filter in front of the white light source. This blocks all but a very narrow band of frequencies. By changing the filter, the frequency of the light striking the cathode can be changed. Using equipment similar to that in Figure 28.17, the following can also be shown:

- For each metal, there is a definite frequency (called the threshold frequency, $f_{0}$ ) below which no photoemission occurs, no matter how intense the light. For zinc, this frequency is in the UV range. For some of the alkali metals, it is in the visible and infra-red range.
- Increasing the frequency above the threshold frequency does not change the size of the photocurrent. This means that the number of electrons being emitted per second from the photocathode does not depend on the frequency of the light. It depends only on the intensity, as mentioned above.

For a given metal, the frequency below which photoemission does not occur is called the threshold frequency. Light of frequency above the threshold frequency will cause photoemission.

Around the end of the nineteenth century scientists could not explain the above aspects of the photoelectric effect. They knew that electrons in a metal are held there by certain forces and that to remove an electron energy must be supplied to overcome these forces. The energy needed to remove the loosest electron is called the work function of the metal.

The work function, $\phi$ of a metal is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of that metal.

### 28.8 The particle model of light is needed to explain the photoelectric effect

At the time, scientists assumed light was a continuous wave, with its energy being proportional to its intensity. So, they expected that if the light were bright enough or if it shone for long enough, it should supply enough energy to an electron to overcome the work function and cause the electron to be emitted. But this does not happen. They could not explain why there was a threshold frequency.
Einstein proposed an explanation of the photoelectric effect that uses the particle model of light.

## The particle model of light

- Light must be considered as a stream of particles or 'packets of energy. Each particle of energy is called a photon or a quantum of energy.
- The energy $E$ of a photon depends only on the frequency $f$ of the light.
- The energy of a photon is directly proportional to the frequency. The energy is given by the formula:

$$
E=h f
$$

where $f$ is its frequency and $h$ is a constant called Planck's constant.
(F\&T, page 59)

- The brighter a light source, the more photons it gives out per second. Therefore, the greater the intensity of the light the more photons pass per second.

A photon is a packet of electromagnetic energy. The energy $E$ of a photon is given by $E=h f$.

## Worked Example 8

## Question

Calculate the energy of a photon of blue light of frequency $7.5 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}$.

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
E & =h f \\
& =\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right)\left(7.5 \times 10^{14}\right) \\
& =4.95 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 9

## Question

A photon of red light has a wavelength of $6 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$. Calculate:
a) The frequency of the photon.
b) The energy of the photon.

## Solution

a) $c=\lambda f$

$$
\begin{aligned}
f & =\frac{c}{\lambda} \\
& =\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{6 \times 10^{-7}} \\
& =5 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

b) $E=h f$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right)\left(5 \times 10^{14}\right) \\
& =3.3 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 10

## Question

Derive a formula for the energy of a photon in terms of its wavelength.

## Solution

$$
c=f \lambda \Rightarrow f=\frac{\lambda}{c}
$$

And

$$
E=h f
$$

Therefore by substituting $f$ :

$$
E=\frac{h c}{\lambda}
$$

a) The frequency of sodium light
b) The energy of a photon of sodium light
c) The number of photons emitted by this source per second
