a) The frequency
b) The wavelength
of a photon of energy 2.2 eV ?

## How photons interact with electrons

- Electrons in a metal are held within by certain forces. The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal is the work function of that metal.
- When light strikes the metal, an electron can only pick up the energy from one photon.
- If the energy of each photon is less than the work function, no electrons are emitted.
- If the energy of the photon is greater than the work function, electrons are emitted.
- The amount by which the energy of the photon exceeds the energy needed to remove the electron appears as the kinetic energy of the emitted electron (the principle of conservation of energy applies, as expected).
Using this model, it follows that for a given metal, light of a certain frequency or higher is needed to cause photoemission and that the greater the intensity of the light, the more electrons are emitted per second and, hence, the greater the photocurrent. The fact that Einstein could account for the known properties of the photoelectric effect with this model supports its validity.


### 28.9 Einstein's photoelectric law

It is proven by experimentation that:

- The velocities of the photoelectrons emitted by light of a frequency above the threshold frequency range from zero up to a definite maximum value.
- The maximum velocity (and, hence, the maximum kinetic energy) of the emitted electrons increases with the frequency of the light but does not depend on the intensity.
Einstein explained this as follows. By the principle of conservation of energy, the kinetic energy of the fastest electron emitted is the difference between the energy of the photon and the work function of the metal such that $\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text {max }}^{2}=h f-\phi$

Rearranging gives:

$$
h f=\phi+\frac{1}{2} m v_{\max }^{2}
$$

(F\&T, page 59)
This equation is known as Einstein's photoelectric law.

## Albert Einstein

Albert Einstein (1879-1955)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-493.jpg?height=281&width=326&top_left_y=2155&top_left_x=2425)
was a German physicist. His equation $E=m c^{2}$, relating the equivalence of mass and energy, is the most famous equation of all time. His Special theory of relativity (1905) replaces Newtonian mechanics for objects travelling at speeds near the speed of light, and his General theory of relativity (1915) is today still our best model of gravitation and is used extensively in cosmology and astronomy. In 1921, he won the Nobel Prize in physics for his huge contribution to many areas of theoretical physics, and also for his explanation of the photoelectric effect, where he introduced the idea of photons.

- Electrons that are more tightly held in the metal will be emitted with a lesser speed. Also, from the equation, as $f$ increases, so does $v_{\text {max }}$.
- If light of the threshold frequency $f_{0}$ strikes the metal, an electron is emitted, but it has no extra kinetic energy to move away from the metal. Therefore, the work function $\phi$ is given by:

$$
\phi=h f_{0}
$$

(F\&T, page 59)
Or, in words:
Work function $=($ Planck's constant $)($ threshold frequency $)$

In the following worked examples, use $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$; $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J}$ s; $c=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

## Worked Example 13

## Question

The work function of a metal is 2 eV . What is the threshold frequency of this metal?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \mathrm{eV} & =(2)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right) \mathrm{J} \\
& =3.2 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \\
& =\text { work function } \phi \\
\phi & =h f_{0} \\
f_{0} & =\frac{\phi}{h} \\
& =\frac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{6.6 \times 10^{-34}} \\
& =4.85 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 14

## Question

The threshold frequency for a certain metal is $5.2 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}$. What is the maximum kinetic energy of an electron emitted by light of frequency $9.6 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}$ ?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} m v_{\max }^{2} & =h f-h f_{0} \\
& =\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right)\left(9.6 \times 10^{14}\right)-\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right)\left(5.2 \times 10^{14}\right) \\
& =2.9 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 15

## Question

When light of wavelength 150 nm falls on a metal surface, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is 5 eV . What is the work function of the metal in joules?

## Solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda=150 \mathrm{~nm} & =150 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}=1.510^{-7} \mathrm{~m} \\
\frac{1}{2} m v_{\max }^{2} & =5 \mathrm{eV} \\
& =(5)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right) \mathrm{J} \\
& =8 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

Frequency:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f & =\frac{c}{\lambda} \\
& =\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.5 \times 10^{-7}} \\
& =2 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} m v_{\max }^{2} & =h f-\phi \\
8 \times 10^{-19} & =\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{15}\right)-\phi \\
\phi & =5.2 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Worked Example 16

## Question

When light of frequency $3.2 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~Hz}$ falls on a certain photoelectric cell, the photocurrent is 0.22 mA . If each incident photon causes photoemission and all the emitted electrons cross the cell, find:
a) The number of photons striking the cathode per second
b) The light energy falling on the cathode per second.

## Solution

a) $0.22 \mathrm{~mA}=0.22 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}=0.22 \times 10^{-3}$ coulombs per second.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { number of electrons crossing tube per second } & =\frac{\text { charge crossing per second }}{\text { charge on one photon }} \\
& =\frac{0.22 \times 10^{-3}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \\
& =1.375 \times 10^{15} \text { electrons }
\end{aligned}
$$

One photon emits one electron.
Therefore, the number of photons striking the cathode per second is $1.375 \times 10^{15}$
b) energy of one photon, $E=h f$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right)\left(3.2 \times 10^{16}\right) \\
& =2.112 \times 10^{-17} \mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { energy falling on one cathode per second } & =\text { (energy of one photon)(number of photons) } \\
& =\left(2.112 \times 10^{-17}\right)\left(1.375 \times 10^{15}\right) \\
& =0.02904 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 28.10 Real-life applications of photoelectric effect

When a beam of light falls on a photoelectric cell connected in a circuit, like Figure 28.17 (page 477), a small current flows. If the beam of light is broken, the current stops. Any change in this current (such as starting, increasing, decreasing or stopping) can be used to trigger other circuits, for example to set off an alarm, make some automatic adjustments, switch an appliance off, or simply to count or record a change. Photoelectric cells have many applications:

- Some types of burglar alarms
- Automatic doors
- Counting items on a conveyor belt
- Some types of smoke detectors
- Monitoring and controlling the flame in a central heating burner
- Testing how well light can get through an object
- Measuring intensity of light in the exposure meter in a camera
- Measuring intensity of light to trigger the turning on of streetlights when it gets sufficiently dark
However, many of these applications of the photoelectric effect have been replaced by semiconductor devices, which can detect light changes and instigate an appropriate response, just like a vacuum photocell. However, semiconductor devices are not based on the photoelectric effect.
Some film projectors use a photocell to reproduce the soundtrack in a film. Figure 28.25 shows a piece of a reel of film and the soundtrack down the left-hand side. As the film is shown, a small beam of light passes through the soundtrack and falls onto a photoelectric cell. As the brightness of the light varies due to variations in the width of the track, the current in the photoelectric cell also changes. This current varies in the same way as the current in the microphone that recorded the sound originally. It is amplified and fed to a loudspeaker,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-499.jpg?height=805&width=659&top_left_y=1165&top_left_x=2086)
Figure 28.25

producing the sound that was originally recorded.
Another interesting application is the photomultiplier tube (Figure 28.26). Very low intensity light strikes a suitable photocathode. An electron is emitted. This is accelerated sufficiently by an electric field so that it strikes another electrode and causes more electrons to be emitted. These electrons are then accelerated by another electric field such that they strike another electrode. This process is repeated, creating a measurable electric current.
Photomultiplier tubes are used in detectors of ionising radiation, in the analysis of blood samples and, sometimes, in night vision goggles.

### 28.11 X-rays

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-499.jpg?height=870&width=1463&top_left_y=2122&top_left_x=1282)
Figure 28.26

X-rays were discovered accidentally in 1895 by Wilhelm Röntgen.

- While working with a gas discharge tube (a type of cathode ray tube), Röntgen found that a fluorescent screen some distance away gave out light when the tube was operating.
- He covered the discharge tube with black cardboard. This would not allow any visible light or UV light to pass from the discharge tube to the fluorescent screen.
- Light was still produced on the fluorescent screen when the tube was operating.
- He concluded that some form of radiation was produced where the cathode rays struck the glass of the discharge tube.
- This radiation passed through the cardboard and the surrounding space and struck the fluorescent screen, causing it to give out light.

The radiation was found to be extremely penetrating and could pass through many metals but was stopped by a sheet of thick lead. The nature of the radiation was not known at the time hence it was called X -radiation or simply X -rays.
X -rays were later shown to be very high frequency (very short wavelength) electromagnetic radiation, produced when high-speed electrons collide with an anode or the glass walls of a cathode ray tube.

Note: X-rays are electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths between 0.1 nm and 10 nm or frequencies between $3 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~Hz}$ and $3 \times 10^{19} \mathrm{~Hz}$
or photon energies between 100 eV and 100 keV

## The hot cathode X-ray tube

Nowadays, X-rays are produced when high-speed electrons in a cathode ray tube strike a metal target that has a high melting point.

X-rays are high-frequency electromagnetic radiation produced when highspeed (high-energy) electrons in a cathode ray tube strike a metal target that has a high melting point.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-500.jpg?height=883&width=1749&top_left_y=1084&top_left_x=872)
Figure 28.27

Figure 28.27 is a simplified illustration of a modern hot cathode X-ray tube. It operates as follows:

- The cathode is heated by the low voltage source and thermionic emission occurs, emitting electrons.
- The very high voltage across the tube (typically 80 000 V ) accelerates the electrons to very high speeds.


## Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen

Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_557d180ac8d9f0230e1bg-500.jpg?height=285&width=323&top_left_y=1972&top_left_x=2298)
(1845-1923) was a German physicist who in 1895 discovered X-rays. In 1901, he became the winner of the first Nobel Prize in physics for this discovery.
producing a high-energy beam of electrons that moves across the tube towards the anode.

- When the electrons strike the metal target in the anode, the kinetic energy of a small percentage of the electrons $(<1 \%)$ is converted into X-rays.
- The rest of the electrons' energy appears as heat in the anode and must be removed. This is the function of the circulating coolant. The target itself must also have a high melting point - for this reason tungsten is often used.
- People operating the tube must be protected from the X-rays. The tube is, therefore, surrounded with a lead shield which does not allow X-rays to pass through. It has a small window through which the X-rays can pass.


## Worked Example 17

## Question

A potential difference of 45 kV is applied across an X-ray tube. Calculate:
a) The maximum energy of the X-rays that can be produced in this X-ray tube
b) The maximum velocity of an electron in the tube
c) The minimum wavelength of the X -rays produced by the tube

$$
\left(h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J} ; c=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} ; e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C} ; \text { mass of electron }=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}\right)
$$

## Solution

a) When an electron of charge $e$ is accelerated through a potential difference $V$, its loss in electrical potential energy is $e V$ (from $W=q V$ ).
This is also the greatest kinetic energy the electron could gain.
If all this energy is converted into an X-ray photon, it is the maximum energy of the X-rays that can be produced in this X-ray tube.
Therefore, maximum energy of the $X$-rays is:

$$
e V=\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)\left(45 \times 10^{3}\right)=7.2 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~J}
$$

b) For an electron being accelerated across the tube, the gain in kinetic energy is equal to the loss in electrical potential energy. Therefore, the kinetic energy of the fastest electron is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} & =e V \\
\frac{1}{2}\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right) v^{2} & =\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)\left(4.5 \times 10^{4}\right) \\
v & =\sqrt{\frac{(2)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)\left(4.5 \times 10^{4}\right)}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \\
\text { ron in the tube } & =1.3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

(c) If all the energy of the most energetic electron is converted into an X-ray photon, the photon's energy $E_{\text {max }}$ and frequency $f_{\text {max }}$ are related by:

$$
E_{\max }=h f_{\max }
$$

where $h$ is Planck's constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2}\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)\left(1.3 \times 10^{8}\right)^{2} & =\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right) f_{\max } \\
f_{\max } & =\frac{\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)\left(1.3 \times 10^{8}\right)^{2}}{(2)\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right)} \\
& =1.17 \times 10^{19} \mathrm{~Hz} \\
c & =\lambda f \\
\lambda_{\min } & =\frac{c}{f_{\max }} \\
& =\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.17 \times 10^{19}}
\end{aligned}
$$

minimum wavelength of the x -rays produced $=2.6 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}$

### 28.12 Comparing X-ray production and the photoelectric effect

In the photoelectric effect (page 476), electromagnetic radiation strikes a metal and its energy is given to electrons. The electrons are then emitted from the metal. (Remember: electromagnetic radiation in, electrons out.)
In X-ray production, the opposite happens: high-speed electrons strike a metal target and lose their energy. The energy is given off in the form of electromagnetic radiation (In this case: electrons in, electromagnetic radiation out).

| Photoelectric effect | X-ray production |
| :--- | :--- |
| Electromagnetic radiation in; electrons out | Electrons in; electromagnetic radiation out |
| There is a minimum frequency that the incoming electromagnetic radiation must have for the effect to occur. | There is a minimum energy that the incoming electrons must have so that X-rays are produced. |
| Increasing the frequency does not change the number of electrons emitted per second. | Increasing the energy of the incoming electrons increases the maximum frequency of the X-rays produced. |
| Increasing the frequency increases the speed of the emitted electrons. | Increasing the energy of the incoming electrons does not increase the speed of the X-rays. |
| X-rays can cause the photoelectric effect. | The photoelectric effect does not produce X-rays. |
| A quantum explanation (the particle model of light) is needed to explain the manner in which electrons are emitted. | A quantum explanation is needed to explain the fact that for a given energy there is a maximum frequency of X-rays produced. It is also needed to predict its value. |

## Summary What I should know

- The charge on the electron is the smallest amount of charge found in nature. It is the indivisible quantity of charge.
- The negative electrode is called the cathode and the positive electrode is called the anode (remember: CNAP).
- Thermionic emission is the emission of electrons from the surface of a hot metal.
- Cathode rays are streams of high-speed electrons moving from the cathode.
- The electronvolt is a unit of energy, $1 \mathrm{eV}=1.602 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}$
- A beam of electrons moving at right angles to a magnetic field moves in a circle.
- The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from the surface of a metal when electromagnetic radiation of a suitable frequency falls on it.
- The photocurrent is directly proportional to the intensity of the light.
- The threshold frequency, $f_{0}$ for a given metal is the frequency below which photoemission will not occur. Light of frequency above the threshold frequency will cause photoemission.
- The work function, $\phi$ of a metal is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of that metal.
- The fact that the particle model of light accounts for the known properties of the photoelectric effect supports the validity of this model.
- A photon is a packet of electromagnetic energy. The energy $E$ of a photon is given by $E=h f$, where $f$ is its frequency and $h$ is Planck's constant.
- X-rays are high-frequency electromagnetic radiation produced when high-speed, high-energy electrons in a cathode ray tube strike a metal target that has a high melting point.
- If an electron of mass $m_{r}$ is accelerated from rest through a voltage $V$, and reaches a velocity $v$, then:

$$
e V=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}
$$

- If an electron moves at right angles to a uniform magnetic field then:

Centripetal force on electron = force on electron due to magnetic field

$$
\frac{m v^{2}}{r}=B e v
$$

- Einstein's photoelectric law:

$$
h f=\phi+\frac{1}{2} m v_{\max }^{2}
$$

- Work function $=($ Planck's constant)(threshold frequency)

$$
\phi=h f_{0}
$$
